# What 1912 Took For Granted — Jung, *Symbols of Transformation*, Prefaces and Part One

> **The four prefaces and the five chapters of Part One of C. G. Jung, *Symbols of Transformation* (written 1911–12, revised 1950)** — a man of seventy-five looking back at the book that ended his friendship with Freud; a young American woman on a ship off Naples who cannot stop thinking about an officer singing on the night watch; a moth in a railway carriage at four in the morning between Geneva and Paris; and a French priest who had to be Judas, and so made sure first of God's mercy. Read from `RAW/books/Symbols of Transformation-Carl Jung.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
>
> ⚠ **Two worldviews are on the table at once and a third is watching.** There is what Jung says the ancient and mythological mind took for granted. There is what a Swiss psychiatrist in 1911 took for granted while saying it — recapitulation as settled biology, "primitives" as a living window on antiquity, a woman's creative problem answered by *through a child*. **And there is a fourth party who never consented to any of it**: Miss Frank Miller, whose fantasies Jung analyses at book length from a journal article, whom he never met, and who was later treated for schizophrenia. The runs report her as a person and not only as material.

## The four prefaces — What is the myth you are living?

**The shape of time**. Thirty-eight years wide, and the book is read from both ends of it.[^1] The 1950 preface opens with a man released by old age and illness from his professional duties, at last able to contemplate the sins of his youth. He has never felt happy about the book. It was written at top speed, amid the rush of a medical practice, without regard to time or method. He had to fling the material together as he found it. The whole thing came upon him like a landslide that could not be stopped.

He also dates it precisely inside a life. The book was written in 1911, in his thirty-sixth year. That time is critical, he says, because it marks the beginning of the second half of life, when a *metanoia*, a mental transformation, not infrequently occurs. He was acutely conscious then of losing his friendship with Freud and the comradeship of their work.

**What makes things happen**. Pressure that had nowhere to go, and he names the container. The urgency behind the landslide became clear to him only later. **It was the explosion of all those psychic contents which could find no room in the constricting atmosphere of Freudian psychology.** He is careful with the compliment that follows: no wish to detract from Freud's investigation of the individual psyche, only from the conceptual frame, which seemed unendurably narrow.

The objection he states is not about neurosis or dreams. It is about the reductive causalism of the whole outlook, and the almost complete disregard of the pull toward a goal that is characteristic of everything psychic. Freud's later book on religion, he says, gives the best account of the earlier views, which move inside the outmoded rationalism and scientific materialism of the late nineteenth century.

**What is real**. Something much older than the person carrying it, and the image is agricultural. The psyche is not of today; its ancestry goes back many millions of years. Individual consciousness is only the flower and the fruit of a season, sprung from the perennial rhizome beneath the earth. Consciousness would find itself in better accord with the truth if it took the existence of the rhizome into its calculations, for the root matter is the mother of all things.

**What a person is**. Someone living inside a myth, whether or not he knows which one. A Church Father's definition is borrowed for it: myth is what is believed always, everywhere, by everybody. So the man who thinks he can live without myth is an exception, and Jung's picture of him is unsparing. **He is like one uprooted, with no true link to the past, or to the ancestral life that continues within him, or to contemporary human society.** He does not live in a house like other men or eat and drink like other men, but lives sunk in a subjective mania of his own devising which he believes to be newly discovered truth. This plaything of his reason never grips his vitals.

Then the question that turns the method on the man asking it. Jung asked himself in all seriousness what myth he was living, and found no answer. He had to admit he was not living with a myth or in one, but in an uncertain cloud of theoretical possibilities. He did not know that he was living a myth, and even if he had known it, he would not have known which one was ordering his life. He then asks how he can allow for the personal factor in treating a patient if he is unconscious of his own.

**How you know**. By comparison, and never from the consulting room alone. The 1937 preface makes it the book's thankless task to show that the problems of the psyche cannot be tackled with the meagre equipment of the doctor's consulting room, nor with the layman's understanding of human nature. Psychology cannot dispense with the humane sciences, and least of all with the history of the human mind. **The psyche is not something unalterably given but a product of its own continuous development.** So a neurotic conflict can be caused by historically conditioned attitudes as readily as by altered glandular secretions.

The methodological note in the 1950 preface is the sharpest thing in the four. Amplification takes up an incredible amount of space, which is why case histories are such an arduous task. That is only to be expected: the deeper you go, the broader the base becomes. It does not narrow, and it never ends in a point — in a psychic trauma, for instance. Any such theory presupposes a knowledge of the traumatised psyche that no human being possesses.

**How people should relate**. Here the fourth party appears, and the way she appears is the run's hardest material. The 1924 preface is written to correct a misunderstanding: the book does not represent Jung's method of treatment. It is concerned with the fantasy material of an unknown young American woman, published under the pseudonym Frank Miller by his respected and fatherly friend Théodore Flournoy.

Two confirmations are then offered, both from men. Flournoy told him from his own lips that he had hit off the young woman's mentality very well. **And in 1918 an American colleague who was treating Miss Miller for the schizophrenic disturbance that broke out after her stay in Europe wrote to say that Jung's exposition was so exhaustive that personal acquaintance with the patient had not taught him one iota more.** Jung concludes from this that his reconstruction had hit the mark in all essential respects.

**What is worth having**. A wider setting for medical psychology, which is how he states the aim. One of his principal purposes was to free the field from the subjective and personalistic bias of the day, and to make it possible to understand the unconscious as objective and collective. The personalism of Freud and Adler went hand in hand with the individualism of the nineteenth century, and left no room for impersonal facts. Freud could see no objective justification for the attempt, and suspected personal motives.

The 1937 preface adds a bleaker version of the same claim, dated. History teaches us over and over that irrational factors play the decisive role in all processes of psychic transformation. And then one line, written in November 1937: it seems as if this insight were slowly making headway **with the somewhat drastic assistance of contemporary events.**

## Ch. I — A Corinthian capital in a modern street

**How you know**. By an interruption, and the picture is the best thing in the short chapter.[^2] Reading Freud on the Oedipus legend produces the uncanny feeling that would steal over us if, in the noise of a modern city street, we suddenly came on an ancient relic. A Corinthian capital of a long-immured column, or a fragment of an inscription. A moment ago we were absorbed in the hectic, ephemeral life of the present, and the next moment something remote flashes on us and directs our gaze to a different order of things.

We then remember that on this spot, two thousand years ago, a similar scene of life prevailed in slightly different forms. Similar passions moved mankind, and people were just as convinced as we are of the uniqueness of their lives.

**The shape of time**. Continuous, and the continuity is what has been forgotten rather than lost. For our psychology, Jung says, the ancient world has long been sunk in the shadows of the past. The realisation that Oedipus is still alive teaches something specific: **there is an identity of fundamental human conflicts which is independent of time and place.**

The condition attached is a moral one. What horrified the Greeks is still true, and it is true for us only if we give up the vain illusion that we are different, meaning morally better, than the ancients. We have merely succeeded in forgetting the link.

**What is real**. A layer under the culture, reachable only from inside. This is where Jung states the charter of the whole enterprise, in 1911, and it reads like the brief for a report of this kind. By penetrating the blocked subterranean passages of our own psyches we grasp the living meaning of classical civilisation. And at the same time we establish a firm foothold outside our own culture, from which alone it is possible to gain an objective understanding of its foundations.

**What makes things happen**. Traffic in both directions between the individual case and the historical record. Investigators have turned their attention mainly to individual problems, and it now seems imperative to broaden the basis by comparative study of historical material, as Freud tried in his study of Leonardo. Psychological knowledge furthers our understanding of the historical material. **And conversely, the historical material can throw new light on individual psychological problems.**

**How people should relate**. Through a school, and the chapter names it. Riklin, Abraham, Rank, Maeder, Jones, Silberer, Pfister — the leitmotiv of all these works is to find a clue to historical problems by applying insights drawn from the unconscious in modern man. Jung places himself inside that programme rather than outside it, and the 1950 revision adds Neumann's later book as carrying the same ideas forward.

**What a person is** and What is worth having are not developed separately in this run. The chapter is short and its work is to state a method and a hope. **The shape of time** and What is real carry it, and the rest of Part One does the demonstrating.

*Read: lines 677–688.*

## Ch. II — The cries of monkeys and dogs

**What a person is**. A creature with two ways of thinking, and only one of them is tiring.[^3] Follow an intensive train of thought and you notice you are thinking in words. In very intensive thinking you begin talking to yourself, or write the problem down, or draw it. Anyone who has lived a while in a foreign country begins to think in that country's language. **Directed thinking is reality-thinking: it imitates the successiveness of objectively real things**, so that images inside the mind follow one another in the same causal order as events outside it. It also causes fatigue, and is brought into play for short periods only.

The other kind arrives when the first stops. Thinking then lacks all leading ideas. We no longer compel our thoughts along a track but let them float, sink or rise according to their specific gravity. This kind does not tire us, and it leads away from reality into fantasies of past or future. Thinking in verbal form ceases. Image piles on image and feeling on feeling, with an ever-increasing tendency to arrange things not as they are but as one would like them to be. Common speech calls it dreaming.

The pair is then stated flatly. One operates with speech elements for communication and is difficult and exhausting. The other is effortless, works spontaneously with contents ready to hand, and is guided by unconscious motives. **The first produces innovation and copies reality. The second turns away from reality, sets subjective tendencies free, and as regards adaptation is unproductive.**

**What is real**. Language, and its origin is noise. It was originally a system of emotive and imitative sounds — terror, fear, anger, love, and the imitated noises of the elements. The rushing of water, the rolling of thunder, the cries of animals. Onomatopoeic vestiges remain in modern languages, and Jung lists them: *rauschen, rieseln, rinnen, rennen, rush, river, ruscello, ruisseau, Rhein.* And *Wasser, wissen, wissern, pissen, piscis, Fisch.*

Anatole France is quoted to push it further than most psychologists would. A metaphysician has nothing with which to build his world system except the perfected cries of monkeys and dogs. What he calls profound speculation is the stringing together, in an arbitrary order, of onomatopoeic cries of hunger, fear and love from the primeval forests, to which meanings have attached themselves little by little.

Jung's own version is the sentence to keep. Our directed thinking, even in the loneliest thinker in the world, **is nothing but the first stirrings of a cry to our companions that water has been found, or the bear been killed, or that wolves are prowling round the camp.** Hence the craving of a Schopenhauer or a Nietzsche for recognition, and the bitterness of their loneliness. One might expect a man of genius to renounce the approval of a rabble he despises. He succumbs to the herd instinct instead.

**The shape of time**. Directed thinking is recent, and the chapter dates its training. The clearest expression of it today is science, and science exists solely because of energetic training in directed thinking. That training was already going on before there was any science to use it for. Scholasticism took its subjects from fantasies of the past and gave the mind a gymnastics of argument.

The subjects were unbelievably fantastic. It was debated how many angels could stand on the point of a needle, and whether Christ could have performed the redemption had he come into the world in the shape of a pea. **That such problems could be posed at all proves how peculiar the medieval mind must have been.** And the achievement was real: Aquinas, Duns Scotus, Abelard and Ockham laid the foundations of a solidly built intellectual function, which is the precondition of modern science.

Go further back and science dissolves into mist. Jung refuses the flattering reading of that. It would be a ridiculous presumption to imagine we are more energetic or more intelligent than the men of the past. Our material knowledge has increased and our intelligence has not. We have become rich in knowledge, but poor in wisdom. The centre of gravity of our interest has switched to the materialistic side.

**What is worth having**. What the ancients spent their energy on, and the accounting is exact. **All the creative power that modern man pours into science and technics, the man of antiquity devoted to his myths.** That explains the bewildering confusion and continual rejuvenation of Greek myth. The activity was artistic in the highest degree: the goal was not to understand the real world accurately but to adapt it aesthetically to subjective expectations.

There was very little room among them for the coldness that Bruno's infinite worlds and Kepler's discoveries brought. The naïve man of antiquity saw the sun as the great Father and the moon as the fruitful Mother. Everything had its demon and was animated. Even the sun's disc was given wings or little feet to illustrate its motion.

**How people should relate**. Across a much shorter gap than they think, and Jung reaches for a historian to say it. A mere eighty generations separate us from the Golden Age of Greek culture, and eighty generations shrink to almost nothing beside the distance to Neanderthal man. Ferrero's paragraph is quoted at length: it is a common belief that the further man is separated from us in time, the more he differs in thought and feeling. **Man does not change so quickly. His psychology at bottom remains the same, and culture varying from one epoch to another does not change the functioning of his mind.**

**What makes things happen**. A hunger that cannot be educated away, and this is the chapter's least comfortable claim. It might be objected that children's mythological leanings are implanted by education. Jung calls the objection futile and asks whether mankind has ever really got away from myths. You can withhold the material content of primitive myths from a child. You cannot take from him the need for mythology, or his ability to manufacture it. If all the world's traditions were cut off at a single blow, the whole of mythology and the whole history of religion would start again with the next generation. Enlightenment destroys a transitory manifestation and not the creative impulse.

He then corrects his own school on the record. Freud called myths the age-long dreams of youthful humanity; Rank called myth the collective dream of a people; Abraham called it a fragment preserved from the infantile psychic life of the race. Jung puts a large question mark after all of it. **Myths are on the contrary the most mature product of that young humanity.** Just as the first fishy ancestors of man were not embryos but fully developed creatures, the myth-making man was a grown reality and not a four-year-old child.

The same correction is made about the language used for it. Non-directed thinking gets called infantile, autoerotic, autistic — expressions borrowed from pathology, and Jung says they should not be used. The instinctive, archaic basis of the mind is a matter of plain objective fact, no more dependent on personal choice than the inherited structure of the brain.

**How you know — the worked case**. By reading a fantasy for what it is doing rather than for what it is about, and the example is a priest. The Abbé Oegger was troubled by whether Judas was really damned, and took the view that God could not damn the necessary instrument of the redemption. He went to church one night and implored God for a sign that Judas was saved, and felt a heavenly touch on his shoulder. The next day he told the archbishop he would go out and preach the gospel of God's unending mercy.

Not long afterwards he left the Catholic Church. **Now we understand his Judas fantasy: he was the Judas who betrayed his Lord**, and he had first to assure himself of God's mercy in order to play the role undisturbed. The conscious sequence runs one way and the unconscious one runs the other. Because he found the damnation of Judas incompatible with God's goodness, he thought about the conflict. Because he wanted to be Judas, he first made sure of God's goodness.

Jung's generalisation from it is the method the rest of the book uses. Conscious fantasies illustrate, through mythological material, tendencies in the personality which are not yet recognised. So they are mostly about things we treat as immoral or impossible. And what would Oegger have said if told in confidence that he was preparing for the role of Judas?

*Read: lines 689–873.*

## Ch. III — The pain in her breast at the right place

**What a person is**. In this run, a woman who cannot keep a boundary, and the first evidence is physical.[^4] Miss Miller reports her own unusual suggestibility and regards it as a symptom of a nervous temperament. She identifies with the wounded Christian in *Cyrano de Bergerac* so completely that **she feels a piercing pain in her own breast, in the very place where the hero receives his death wound.**

Jung's aside about theatre is the sharpest line in the chapter. One might describe it, somewhat unaesthetically, as an institution for working out private complexes in public. The enjoyment of comedy comes from identifying one's own complexes with those the actors personify. The enjoyment of tragedy lies in the thrilling and satisfying feeling that what is happening to somebody else may very well happen to you.

**How you know**. From the timing, which she supplies without meaning to. She adds that she felt the pain when Sarah Bernhardt threw herself on Christian to stanch the bleeding. So the critical moment is the one where the love between Christian and Roxane comes to a sudden end. Her complex is awaiting a similar solution, and it whispers *today to you, tomorrow to me*.

**What is real — the figure under the figure**. Cyrano rather than Christian, and Jung says the identification is a cover. Cyrano of the long ugly nose loves Roxane, who loves Christian, because she believes Christian wrote the verses that are really Cyrano's. **He is the misunderstood one whose passionate love and noble soul nobody suspects.** He dies fighting the air with his sword against Falsehood, Compromise, Prejudice, Treachery and Folly, and departs with the one thing left unstained — his panache.

Christian in himself is not a very inspiring figure. So identification with him tells us a sudden end is destined for her love. But the tragic intermezzo is played against a background of far wider significance, which is Cyrano's unrequited love, and the report says the analysis will come back to it.

**How people should relate**. Two ways, and they contradict each other. In the bath she winds a towel round her hair, and for one breath-taking moment she is on a pedestal, a veritable Egyptian statue with all its details: **stiff-limbed, one foot forward, holding insignia in her hand.** Jung reads it as an unrecognised likeness — stiff, wooden, sublime and impassible, the qualities the Egyptian statue is proverbial for.

The next example runs the other way. She describes making an artist draw landscapes of Lake Geneva, where he had never been, and giving him the sense of an atmosphere he had never felt. She was using him, he said, as he himself used his pencil — simply as an instrument. Jung notes the abrupt contrast with the statue, and reads the need to claim an almost magical influence as belonging to someone who often fails to make a real emotional relationship.

**What is worth having**. Free-floating energy, and the run ends by naming what it is free of. The examples are not particularly striking in themselves and are valuable because they let us glimpse her personal problems. **The libido gained control of certain impressions and intensified them**, which would not have been possible but for the energy left at her disposal by her lack of relation to reality.

**What makes things happen** and The shape of time are not developed separately here. The chapter is an intake note, and the two dimensions it does carry are enough to set up the two poems.

*Read: lines 874–942.*

## Ch. IV — The officer singing on the night watch

**What makes things happen**. An impression that arrives after a long withdrawal, and the sequence is the point.[^5] In 1898, aged twenty, Miss Miller sailed from New York to Stockholm, Petersburg and Odessa. She describes the pleasure of leaving the world of cities and business — in short, of the earth — and entering the world of waves, sky and silence. She spent hours on deck, dreaming. **Histories and legends came back to her dissolved in a luminous mist, in which real things seemed to lose their being while dreams took on the aspect of the only true reality.**

Jung reads that as a state of introversion, and he names the risk. There is a mental disturbance that begins with the patient shutting out reality more and more, until the inner world's determining power increases. The process climaxes when the patient suddenly becomes conscious of the dissociation and makes pathological efforts, in a sort of panic, to get back to the environment. So he expects that after so long inside, she will succumb to some new impression from outside.

She does, and she reports it as nothing. The ship's officers outdid themselves in kindness. Off Sicily she wrote a sea-chanty, because **one of the officers, singing at night as he stood watch on deck, had made a great impression on her.** At Naples she was ill, went ashore in a carriage, came back tired and went to bed early, thinking of nothing more serious than the good looks of the officers and the ugliness of Italian beggars.

**What is real**. A poem that arrives already written, and its physical appearance matters to her. Between Naples and Leghorn she dreamt of the words *when the morning stars sang together*, mixed with choruses from New York oratorios and indistinct memories of *Paradise Lost*. Then words appeared and arranged themselves in three stanzas, in her handwriting, on ordinary blue-lined paper, in the poetry album she always carries. They appeared exactly as they did in reality a few minutes later, in her book. The poem gives glory to the God of Sound, of Light and of Love.

**How you know**. From what she read as a child and what she quotes as an adult. Her associations are a Doré-illustrated *Paradise Lost* the family owned, the Book of Job read aloud since she can remember, and Handel's *Creation*. The metre of her first line matches Milton's. **So the lost paradise is defined more precisely by the line about man's first disobedience**, which is a clear reference to the Fall.

Jung then blocks the obvious objection, and the block is a statement of method. Everyone will say she could just as well have chosen any other line, picked by accident, with accidental content. The misunderstanding arises because the law of psychic causality is never taken seriously enough: there are no accidents and no just-as-wells.

Her earlier memories are dated to puberty. At fifteen she lay awake almost all night after her mother read her an article about the Idea spontaneously creating its own object. Between nine and sixteen she sat in a Presbyterian pew struggling to stay awake, unable to understand what the pastor meant by **Chaos, Cosmos, and the Gift of Love.** Jung reads two ways of creation hinted at together: creative thought, and the mysterious gift.

**What a person is**. Someone whose creative problem has one biological answer and one other, and this is where 1911 states itself plainly. Miss Miller's problem at that age was the common human problem of how to be creative. Nature knows only one answer to that: through a child. The question of how one gets a child then runs into the father, and the incest barrier, so it cannot be tackled properly. The love that binds a child to the father turns, as she outgrows the family, to the higher forms of the father — to authority, to the Fathers of the Church, to the father-god they represent.

Mythology is not lacking in consolations there. Did not the Word become flesh, and the divine pneuma enter the Virgin's womb? Jung's gloss on why the Immaculate Mother still comforts is one of his warmest sentences: **it speaks without words to the comfortless, saying *I too have become a mother*** — through the Idea spontaneously creating its own object.

He then adds the other half, and he is careful to say it is a half. It would be less than just to trace the sleepless night solely to the sexual problem in the narrower sense. **That would be only one half of the meaning, and the lower half.** The other half is ideal creation as a substitute for real creation, and for many people spiritual fruitfulness is a vital necessity.

**How people should relate**. Through a quotation she does not identify, and this is the best piece of detection in Part One. Miss Miller closes politely: there was only this and nothing more. Then she repeats it — "Only this, and nothing more!" — without giving the source.

The source is Poe's *The Raven*. A spectral raven knocks at the poet's door and reminds him of his irrevocably lost Lenore, croaking *Nevermore* to every verse. **Her words apparently skipping lightly over the situation are taken from a poem about despair over a lost love**, and Jung says the quotation gives the show away completely. She underestimated the impression the singer made, which is precisely why the problem was not worked out consciously.

**What is worth having**. Not what the hymn says it is, and the transformation is traced step by step. First the morning stars sing together. Then *Paradise Lost*. Then the yearning puts on ecclesiastical dress and speaks darkly of world creation. Then it rises into a religious hymn and finds its way to freedom. But the hymn carries the marks of its origin: by the devious route of the father-imago, the night-watching singer becomes the Creator, the God of Sound, of Light and of Love.

**The shape of time**. A via dolorosa, and the parallel texts supply it. *Paradise Lost* and Job both describe a long way round that is a way of suffering. Job loses everything because Satan made God doubt his integrity, and suffers doubly — through loss, and through the incomprehension of his friends. **Cyrano suffers doubly too**, through unrequited love and through misunderstanding.

The Job material then produces the run's darkest passage, and Jung does not soften it. God parades his power before Job by praising two unsympathetic animals, Behemoth and Leviathan, both expressive of the crudest force in nature. What destroyed Job's earthly paradise was the unchained power of Nature. God has simply shown his other side for once, the side we call the Devil. And the God who created such monstrosities harbours qualities that give one pause. **This God dwells in the heart, in the unconscious.**

Against that, man's conscious ego is a mere bagatelle, a feather whirled by every gust of wind, sometimes the sacrificed and sometimes the sacrificer, and able to hinder neither. Jung's practical corollary is not passivity. Working in harmony with the libido does not mean drifting with it, since the psychic forces have no uniform direction and are often directly opposed. A mere letting go leads in the shortest time to the most hopeless confusion.

The chapter ends on a judgment about her solution that Jung declines to make. Opinion is divided over whether it is nobler to let an erotic tension resolve itself unnoticed into religious poetry that consoles other people. **He would rather find out the meaning and purpose of the devious path than decide the question**, and he calls what she did a more or less conscious act of repression that produced a projection: the deity takes the place of the human singer, and earthly love is replaced by heavenly.

*Read: lines 943–1279.*

## Ch. V — The moth in the carriage at four in the morning

**What is real**. Two creatures compressed into one, and the compression is the clue.[^6] Travelling from Geneva to Paris, Miss Miller slept barely an hour in a horribly hot compartment. At four in the morning she noticed a moth fluttering round the carriage light. The poem that then sprang into her mind is *The Moth to the Sun*, ending on one raptured glance of the source of beauty, warmth and life, after which the moth will die content.

Jung asks the obvious question about it. We all know the proverb about the moth that flies into the flame and burns its wings, and we know of no legend about a moth that strives towards the sun. So two things that do not belong together have been condensed: the moth at the light, and a tiny ephemeral creature, a May-fly perhaps, longing in pathetic contrast to the eternity of the stars.

**The shape of time**. An hour, and the poem says so. *And one hour more — and my poor life is gone.* Against that stands the imperishable light. The whole tension of the run sits in that mismatch, and Jung's amplifications are chosen to hold it: Faust watching the sun go down and longing to follow it on tireless wings, and knowing that the pinions won by the spirit bring no flight that mortal clay can know.

**What makes things happen**. Longing, which he treats as a force with two exits and both of them bad. **Faust's longing became his ruin.** His longing for the other world brought a loathing of life that took him to the brink of self-destruction. His equally importunate longing for the beauties of this world plunged him into doubt and wretchedness that culminated in Gretchen's death. His mistake was to make the worst of both worlds by blindly following the urge of his libido.

The historical frame Jung puts round that is the one his whole Part One has been building. Faust's conflict reflects the collective conflict at the beginning of the Christian era, running in reverse. The early Christian defended himself against the powers of seduction with an absolute hope in a world to come. Faust takes the opposite road, for whom the ascetic ideal is sheer death, and wins life by binding himself to evil.

**What a person is**. Somebody with a double office, and Jung finds it stated in the play. Faust is saviour and destroyer at once, and Wagner's admiring line about the acclamations of the crowd is answered by Faust's memory of the hellish nostrum: **these hands ministered the deadly bane to thousands who perished, and I remain to hear cool murderers extolled.**

**How people should relate**. Across an unbridgeable difference in kind, and the chapter's long amplification from Byron is where that gets a scene. In *Heaven and Earth*, two women love angels. Anah's speech is the run's most exposed material — there is a ray in her which, though forbidden yet to shine, she feels was lighted at the angel's God's and his. Though the serpent's sting should pierce her through, and though he himself were like the serpent, she would smile and curse him not. The angels descend in a vision of light that kindles all the west like a returning sunset.

Then the vision turns over in one line, and Jung stops on it. The rainbow returns to night like rippling foam **which the leviathan hath lashed from his unfathomable home.** Leviathan again — the exhibit that tipped the scales against Job. From where the deep fountains of the ocean are, the all-destroying flood ascends, and Jung reads it as the tidal wave of animal passion projected outward as a rising flood that will destroy everything so a better world can be built on the ruins.

**What is worth having**. A promise that has not arrived, and the chapter closes on a forecast rather than a finding. Japhet's prophecy of the Redeemer, coming first in pain and then in glory, is answered by the spirits: new times, new climes, new arts, new men, but still the same old tears, old crimes and oldest ill, in different forms.

**How you know**. By reading the prophecy on the subjective level, which is the technical move that makes the whole book possible. Japhet's prognostications have an almost prophetic meaning for the poetess herself. With the death of the moth in the light, the danger has been removed for the time being, **though the problem is still far from solved.** The conflict must begin again from the beginning. And this time there is a promise in the air — a premonition of the redeemer, the young dying god who mounts to the zenith with the sun and then sinks into night and the cold darkness of winter.

*Read: lines 1280–1866.*

---

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, prefaces to Part One `[SPECULATIVE]`

Paradigm-obvious in 1911, and reading any of it as insight is the modern reader's error.

Recapitulation. That ontogeny repeats phylogeny is treated as settled biology and then transferred to the mind without argument, so that infantile and dream thinking can be described as a replay of earlier evolutionary stages. Freud, Nietzsche, Abraham and Rank are all quoted inside the same assumption. **The disagreement in the chapter is about whether myth is infantile, not about whether the recapitulation holds.**

"Primitives" as a living window on antiquity. Children, savages and dreamers are placed in one class throughout, and the class does the explanatory work.

Analysing a woman from a journal article. Nothing in the four prefaces treats the absence of consent as a question. The two confirmations offered are from Flournoy and from her later doctor, both men, both about accuracy.

That a woman's creative problem has one natural answer. *Nature knows only one answer to that: through a child.* The sentence is offered as biology and passes without defence.

The classical canon as the shared property of any educated reader. Milton, Job, Faust, Byron, Poe and Cyrano are quoted at length with no expectation that a reader might need them summarised.

Paradigm-breaking, and the cost is what marks it.

Asking himself what myth he was living, and answering that he did not know. That is the method turned on the man holding it, and **the cost is that the book's authority stops being a doctor's**. He then spends years on his own unconscious to find out, which is the programme the rest of his life ran on.

Publishing the disagreement with Freud instead of managing it. The 1950 preface says the book became a landmark set up where two ways divided, and that Freud saw no objective justification for the attempt and suspected personal motives. **The cost is named in the same paragraph as the date: he was acutely conscious of the lost friendship and the lost comradeship of the work.**

Refusing to call myth infantile. He corrects Freud, Rank and Abraham in one paragraph and insists that the myth-making man was a grown reality and not a four-year-old child. It costs him the vocabulary his own school was using, and he says so: expressions borrowed from pathology ought not to be used for a normal process.

Saying the base broadens as you go down. This is a direct refusal of the trauma model, and it disqualifies the tidiest thing a case history can offer — a single originating wound.

Writing that God's other side is the one we call the Devil, and that this God dwells in the unconscious. In 1911, in a book by a physician, about the Book of Job.

## Ch. II — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: working out why an argument that satisfied you last week has stopped working, or why one that should not persuade anybody keeps doing so.

The instrument is the split, and its useful half is the cost accounting. **Directed thinking is expensive and it is the only kind that can be checked.** It runs in words, borrows its whole machinery from communication, imitates the real order of events, and tires you out — which is why it can only be sustained in short bursts. Fantasy thinking costs nothing, runs on images, and arranges things as one would like them.

The mechanism worth carrying is what happens at the boundary. Jung's claim is not that people choose between the two. **Any lessening of interest, or the slightest fatigue, is enough to end the delicate adaptation that directed thinking is**, and the other kind moves straight in. So the failure is not a failure of intelligence, and it announces itself as tiredness rather than as error.

Scope conditions. This bites where a conclusion has to be defended to somebody else, since that is the only condition under which directed thinking is worth its cost. It fails as a description of art, where the whole value is on the other side. **And it fails as a moral ranking**, which Jung says himself when he refuses the words *autistic* and *infantile* for a normal process.

The general form. **A judgment reached while tired is not a worse version of a judgment reached fresh. It is a different operation with different rules**, and its products will feel more satisfying because they were arranged to. Modern equivalent: any decision taken at the end of a long day that feels unusually clear.

The second-order finding is the one about scholasticism, and it inverts the usual story. Centuries were spent arguing about angels on a needle point and whether Christ could have redeemed the world as a pea. **That looks like the purest waste in intellectual history, and Jung's claim is that it was the training.** The gymnasium had to exist before there was anything worth doing in it. Which suggests a test worth applying to any apparently useless discipline: ask not what it produced, but what capacity its practitioners ended up with.

## Ch. IV — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

The road not taken belongs to Miss Miller and not to Jung, and it is one he names, prices, and declines to recommend.

She had an erotic impression she could not act on. She converted it, apparently without effort, into a religious hymn. Jung states the two available verdicts on that and refuses to choose between them. **It is thought much more beautiful and noble to let an erotic tension resolve itself unnoticed into sublime feelings of religious poetry**, in which other people may find joy and consolation — and a kind of unjustified fanaticism for truth to complain about the unconsciousness of the solution.

The live alternative he sketches is bleak. Had the creation not come off, she would have yielded to the erotic impression, either with the usual consequences or with a negative result that replaced the lost happiness with a correspondingly strong regret. **Those are the only two outcomes he offers**, and neither is good, which is worth noticing before treating his diagnosis as a prescription.

The counterfactual worth running is a third one his own frame allows and he never states. He has just argued that the other half of her problem was ideal creation as a substitute for real creation, and that spiritual fruitfulness is for some people a vital necessity. **A woman of twenty in 1898 who could write that poem had somewhere to put the energy, and the route was closed by circumstance rather than by psychology.** The book records her scribbling verses on deck, teaching officers English, and making a painter produce landscapes he had never seen. Nothing in it asks what she might have done with a training.

The second-order consequence is the one that makes this more than a complaint about the period. Jung's whole reading assumes the material had only two exits — the man, or the god. **A third exit changes the diagnosis rather than the outcome**, because the same fantasy system would then be evidence of a vocation being obstructed rather than of a conflict being evaded. He has the concept, he uses it in the same chapter, and he does not apply it to her.

## Ch. III and V — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take Miss Miller as she stands at the end of Part One. She is twenty. She has spent weeks on a ship deliberately cut off from company, until things lost their reality and dreams became truth. Poems now arrive complete, already laid out in her own handwriting, and she copies them down. She feels a wound in her own breast where an actor takes one. She sees herself, for one breath-taking moment in the bath, as an Egyptian statue. **Nobody around her thinks any of this is a problem**, and the man who will write four hundred pages about it never meets her. Ten years later she is treated for schizophrenia.

Jung's counsel to her is nothing, because she is not his patient. He reads the material at a distance and predicts the outcome correctly, which is the most disturbing fact in Part One.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/zen-sickness|the illness that arrives with the attainment]]** would recognise the state immediately and would not call it pathology first. This tradition has a name for what happens when the inner world opens: a sickness you catch by succeeding. **One may be filled with incomparable joy, and yet this should be handled carefully.** The counsel is not to shut the opening down, because it is the thing she came for and the thing the poems are made of. It is that an opening of this kind is a known event with a known failure mode, and that the failure mode is not recognising it as one. On this reading, the ship, the introversion and the poem arriving whole are not symptoms. **They are the beginning of a passage that has a name, and she is going through it with nobody who knows the name.**

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/chuan-fa-unmasking-and-the-monastic-container|unmasking inside a container]]** would go at the missing structure rather than at the state. The doctrine is that the unmasking is supposed to happen — and that it happens inside something built to hold it: a rule, a place, a community, and somebody who has been through it and is answerable for you. **Take the container away and the same process is simply a person coming apart in a railway carriage.** The counsel is that her problem was never the content of the fantasies, which this advisor would find unremarkable. It was that the material arrived with no holder, in a deck chair, between ports, in a life with no room for it.

They disagree about what she most needed. The first says a name for the state, so she would know what was happening. The second says a structure and a person, so it would matter less whether she knew.

**Where they converge is on the thing Jung's whole procedure takes for granted.** He treats the fantasies as a text to be read, and his measure of success is accuracy — Flournoy confirming he had caught her mentality, her later doctor confirming that acquaintance taught him nothing more. **Both advisors would say that reading is not what the situation called for.** Somebody in that state needs a container and a name, not a commentary; and the commentary was produced, published, praised for its accuracy, and delivered to everyone except her.

# What 1912 Took For Granted — Jung, *Symbols of Transformation*, Part Two I–V

> **The first five chapters of Part Two of C. G. Jung, *Symbols of Transformation*** — a Roman lawyer's definition of *libido* set beside Freud's; a woman boring a hole in her own temple with one finger; Australian men dancing all night round a pit dug in the shape of a woman and shouting that it is not a pit; a god the size of a thumb seated forever in the heart; and a series of visions that ends in a confusion of sounds, *wa-ma, wa-ma*. Read from `RAW/books/Symbols of Transformation-Carl Jung.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
>
> **This is the theoretical half.** Part One read a young woman's poems. Part Two stops to redefine the central term of the psychology of its day, and then builds the machinery — symbol against sign, libido as neutral energy, the hero as a figure the energy takes, and the mother as the thing it keeps trying to get back to.
>
