## Part Two, Ch. I — A god the size of a thumb

**What is real**. The sun, and Jung says it is the only image of God that survives translation.[^1] Following the longing in the moth poem has led into astrological territory. The Creator whose double nature was plain in Job has become the sun, and in doing so has found a natural expression that transcends his moral division into a Heavenly Father and a devil. Renan's line is borrowed for it: the sun is the only truly rational image of God, whether you take the standpoint of the primitive or of modern science.

The reason it works is that it does not have to be reconciled with itself. From the sun all living things draw life; he is the fructifier and the source of energy. **The discord the human soul has fallen into can be harmoniously resolved through the sun as a natural object which knows no inner conflict.** And the sun is not only beneficial. It is destructive too, which is why the zodiacal sign for the August heat is a devourer.

**What a person is**. A house with something enormous living in a very small room. The Upanishadic material is quoted at length and its paradox is the point. Rudra has eyes on all sides, faces on all sides, arms and feet on all sides, and created heaven and earth. The same being is then located: that Person, no bigger than a thumb, the inner Self, seated forever in the heart of man. Thousand-headed and thousand-eyed, and ruling over the ten-finger space. Smaller than small, greater than great.

Jung takes the size paradox as a formal feature rather than a curiosity. It reappears as the creative dwarf, the Cabiri, the Idaean dactyls, and the divine boy — and in the vase-painting where a bearded Dionysus labelled Kabiros stands next to a boy labelled Pais, with caricatured figures beside them. **One might call it the cult of the big and the little man.** The Upanishad's giant and dwarf becomes, in Greece, father and son.

**How you know**. By refusing to read an image as a code, and this is the distinction the rest of the book runs on. Sexual images in dreams and in everyday speech should not be taken literally, because they are not to be understood as signs. A sign has a fixed meaning: it is a conventional abbreviation for something already known. A symbol is an indefinite expression with many meanings, pointing to something not easily defined and therefore not fully known.

From which a working rule follows, and it is the opposite of the one a code-breaker would use. **A symbol has a large number of analogous variants, and the more of them it has at its disposal, the more complete the image it projects.** So amplification is not padding. Piling up the variants is the only way of getting at what the thing is a symbol of, which is why the book is the length it is.

**What makes things happen**. A force that finds its own way, and Jung reaches for Faust to describe it. Mephistopheles hands Faust a key that glows and grows in his hand, and tells him it will smell the right place from all others — follow it down, it leads you to the Mothers. The same devil had earlier introduced himself as part of that power which would ever work evil and engenders good.

What is being described, Jung says, is the libido. It is creative and procreative, and it also has an intuitive faculty, a strange power to smell the right place, almost as if it were a live creature with a life of its own. **That is why it is so easily personified.** It is a force of nature, good and bad at once, or morally neutral. The realm of the Mothers has more than a few connections with the womb, which frequently symbolises the creative aspect of the unconscious.

**How people should relate**. Through figures who are marked, and the marking is consistent enough to be a rule. The seers, artists and wonder-workers of mythology carry phallic characteristics, and they are also crippled. Hephaestus, Wieland the Smith and Mani all had damaged feet. The ancient seer who is said to have introduced the phallic cult was called Blackfoot, and it seems characteristic of seers to be blind. Ugliness and deformity belong especially to the chthonic gods, the sons of Hephaestus, to whom mighty wonder-working powers were ascribed.

**What is worth having** and **The shape of time** are not developed separately in this run. The chapter's work is to install two instruments — the sun as an image that resolves a moral split, and the symbol as something that cannot be cashed out into a sign.

*Read: lines 1867–1970.*

---

## Part Two, Ch. II — What a Roman meant by the word

**What is real**. Energy, and not one instinct among others.[^2] Freud defined libido sexually and compared it to a stream, divisible, dammable, overflowing into collaterals. So he does not explain everything by sex, as is commonly supposed, and he does posit other instinctual forces whose nature is unclear but which can take up these libidinal affluxes.

Jung's objection is a test case, and it is a hard one. If libido were really nothing but sexuality, what would happen in the case of eunuchs? Their libidinal interest has been cut off, and they do not therefore react with schizophrenia. Meanwhile in schizophrenia far more is missing from reality than could ever be laid at the door of sex. The relation to the world goes almost entirely, and no one in his senses would maintain that reality is nothing but a function of sex.

The second test is a comparison of outcomes. Introversion and regression of sexual libido lead, at worst, to neurosis, and not to schizophrenia. **Freud himself had pointed that out.** So the loss of the reality function in the graver illness needs a wider term, and Jung says he had used *psychic energy* for it years earlier in his work on dementia praecox.

**How you know**. From the word's own history, and the etymology chapter is the most patient thing in Part Two. Cicero uses *libido* for wanting in general. Will is a rational desire, and when it is divorced from reason and too violently aroused, that is libido — unbridled desire, found in all fools. Sallust makes rage a part of it, and can also use it to mean taking more pleasure in fine weapons and war-horses than in whores and drinking parties.

Augustine is quoted at length and quoted approvingly. There is a lust for revenge, which is called rage. A lust for money, which is called avarice. A lust for victory at all costs, which is called stubbornness. **A lust for self-glorification, which is called boastfulness.** And who could easily name the lust for domination, which the civil wars showed to be so powerful in the minds of tyrants? For Augustine, libido is an appetite like hunger and thirst.

The philology follows. *Libet*, it pleases; Sanskrit *lubhyati*, to experience violent longing; Gothic *liufs* and Old High German *liob*, love; and, alongside them, Gothic *lubains*, hope, and Old High German *loben*, praise. The word has always meant more than one thing, and Jung's claim is that the narrowing was recent.

**What makes things happen**. One neutral quantity moving between channels. Instinctual processes of any kind can be intensified by an influx of energy, no matter where it comes from — sexuality, hunger, thirst. One instinct can be temporarily depotentiated in favour of another. **To assume it is always and only sexuality that is subject to this would be a psychic equivalent of the phlogiston theory.**

So the concept expands into something closer to intentionality in general. We know far too little about human instincts to give priority to any one of them. Libido is better understood as an energy value able to communicate itself to any field of activity whatsoever — power, hunger, hatred, sexuality or religion — without being itself a specific instinct.

**What a person is**. Something that experiences a force it cannot see, and Jung is careful about what that licenses. The concept has the same standing in psychology that energy has had in physics since Robert Mayer. Schopenhauer's Will is the philosophical cousin: a movement perceived from outside can only be grasped as the manifestation of an inner will. **Galileo had said the concept of force originates in the subjective perception of our own muscular power**, and Jung says libido is the same kind of interpretation. We know as little about what underlies it as we know about what the psyche is in itself.

**How people should relate**. Through analogy, and this is where the chapter turns into a history of culture. Specially intense contents get reflected in countless analogies, which draw their objects into the magic circle of the psyche. Lévy-Bruhl's *participation mystique* is borrowed for the resulting relationships. **A positively overwhelming importance attaches to the little word *like* in the history of human thought.**

Jung then makes the claim that gives the process its dignity. The canalisation of libido into analogy-making was probably responsible for some of the most important discoveries primitive man ever made. And the mechanism is stated in the grammar itself: a conception gives us a handle by which to grasp things, and the resulting concept lets us take possession of them. Functionally, the concept corresponds to the magically powerful name which gets a grip on the object. That renders the object harmless and incorporates it into the psychic system.

**The shape of time**. Layered, and the layers can be fallen back through. A disturbed reality function gets replaced by an archaic substitute, on a biological principle: when a recent system deteriorates it is likely to be replaced by a more primitive one. **To use Freud's simile, one begins firing with bows and arrows instead of with guns.** Patients set up in place of reality fantasies very like archaic ideas which once had a reality function of their own.

**What is worth having** is not developed separately here; the chapter's whole value claim is that a wider term buys a wider set of facts.

*Read: lines 1971–2020.*

---

## Part Two, Ch. III — Boring a hole in her own temple

**What makes things happen**. A gesture that outlives the situation that produced it, and the case is disturbing on purpose.[^3] Jung treated a woman with catatonic depressions. Early in the treatment, while telling him of a painful experience, she fell into a dream-state showing all the signs of sexual excitement, completely unaware of his presence, ending in masturbation. The act was accompanied by one strange movement. She kept making a violent rotary motion with the forefinger of her left hand against her left temple, as though boring a hole there. Afterwards there was complete amnesia and nothing could be elicited about the gesture.

Weeks later her mother supplied the history. The boring goes back to a stage of childhood earlier than the masturbation, from a period with no individual memories. Years later, after her marriage, the death of a child with whom she had identified through overindulgent love **brought the infantile symptoms back onto the still healthy mother**, and the boring came with them.

**What is real**. A ladder of transferred rhythms, and Jung lays it out as ordinary development. In infants the libido first shows in the nutritional zone, in the rhythmic movement of sucking, and in pleasurable rhythmic movement of arms and legs. The primary model of rhythmic movement is then transferred to other zones, with sexuality as its eventual goal. Sucking still belongs to nutrition and outgrows it by becoming an analogous rhythm with no food in it.

The claim he builds on that is the chapter's engine. If earlier phases can be reactivated regressively in illness, **then in earlier stages of human development this transformation was probably not pathological at all but a frequent and normal occurrence.** So it should have left historical traces, and the rest of the chapter goes looking for them.

**How you know**. By finding the same act in a ritual, and the trail runs through fire. Abraham had connected boring with fire-making. The Indian fire-stick is the *pramantha*, and fire-making is always referred to by a verb meaning to shake, to rub, to bring forth by rubbing. **The line from *pramantha* to Prometheus does not run through the word so much as through the image**, which Jung calls an archetypal parallel rather than a case of linguistic transmission. What can be established is that thinking, precaution and foresight are somehow connected with fire-boring.

The rite itself removes any doubt about the reading. The fire-sticks are personified as man and woman. A priest takes one up saying *thou art the birthplace of fire*, lays two blades of grass on it saying *ye are the two testicles*, names the lower stick Urvasi and the upper Pururavas, anoints it with butter, and rubs. The fire that results is the child, the divine son Agni, born from the genitals of the woman. The Rig-Veda hymn says the same in verse: in the two fire-sticks lies Jatavedas, safe as the seed in pregnant women.

**How people should relate**. In ceremonies that keep the old discovery alive, and Jung's examples run from Australia to Scotland. The Wachandi dig a hole in the ground and set it about with bushes so that it looks like a woman's genitals. **They dance round it all night holding their spears in front of them, thrusting them into the hole and shouting that it is not a pit.**

The European survival is a plague measure. Ceremonial fire-making lingered as superstition into the nineteenth century, used mainly against cattle epidemics. The chronicle entry Jung reprints is from 1268: when the herds in Laodonia were ravaged by lung-sickness, certain cattle-breeders, monastery folk by habit or dress but not by disposition, taught the rustics to make fire by rubbing wood and to set up an image of Priapus. A Cistercian lay brother then dipped the testicles of a dog in holy water and sprinkled the animals.

**The shape of time**. Persistent past the point of understanding. These examples come from different periods and different peoples, and prove a widespread tendency to equate fire-making with sexuality. **The ceremonial repetition of an age-old discovery shows how persistently the human mind clings to old forms.** German colloquial speech still carries the traces: a lout is a *Bengel*, a cudgel, or in Hessian a *Stift*, a peg; and a plant called stick-root in German is called boy's-love in English.

**What a person is** and What is worth having are carried by the same argument here. A person is a creature whose energy keeps being handed on from one function to the next. What is worth having, on this account, is what that handing-on produced — which is fire, and, on the next page, everything else.

*Read: lines 2021–2252.*

---

## Part Two, Ch. IV — The world is empty only to him

**What is real**. A human figure, and Jung says it is the best symbol the material has.[^4] The finest of all symbols of the libido is the human figure conceived as a demon or hero. **Here the symbolism leaves the objective realm of astral images and takes on human form** — a figure who passes from joy to sorrow and back, who stands at the zenith like the sun and is plunged into darkest night, only to rise again.

Miss Miller's third and last creation follows that pattern. She calls it *Chiwantopel, a hypnagogic drama*, and describes how it arrived. After an evening of trouble and anxiety she went to bed at half past eleven, restless and unable to sleep though very tired. She had the impression of being in a receptive mood. There was no light in the room. She closed her eyes, felt a great relaxation, and remained as completely passive as possible.

**How you know**. From what is missing in the record, and Jung says so. Four whole years separate the first poem from this fantasy, and there is no information at all about them. **He regrets it and then finds an advantage in it**: our interest in the general validity of the fantasy is not obscured by sympathetic concern for the personal fate of the author. That sentence is worth keeping, because it is the moment the woman becomes a specimen.

The state she describes he identifies precisely. It resembles what usually precedes intentional somnambulism and has often been described by mediums. A certain willingness to give ear to these faint nocturnal voices must be there, or the experiences pass unnoticed. What can be discerned in the listening attitude is an inward-flowing current of libido, heading for an invisible goal.

**What a person is**. Someone whose world is only as full as their capacity to love it, and this is the run's hardest sentence about her. Introversion of this kind requires an exceptional condition — a lack of external objects that forces the person to seek a substitute in his own psyche. Jung refuses that explanation outright. **It is hard to believe that this teeming world is too poor to provide an object for human love.** It offers boundless opportunities to everyone, and it is rather the inability to love which robs a person of them.

Then the sentence itself: the world is empty only to him who does not know how to direct his libido towards things and people, and to render them alive and beautiful. What compels a person to create a substitute from within is not an external lack. Part of the psyche really wants the external object, and another part strives back to the subjective world, where the airy palaces of fantasy beckon.

**What makes things happen**. A third thing that unbalances a pair, and the mechanics come from muscles. Jung takes Bleuler's term *ambitendency* as a constant: the most primitive motor impulses are antithetical, since even in a simple stretch the flexor must be innervated. **Normally that never prevents the act — it is necessary for co-ordinating it.** Resistance appears only when an abnormal quantity on one side loosens the paired opposites, so they show up as a genuine *will* and *won't* that get in each other's way.

The passion he names behind that is not the one a reader expects. La Rochefoucauld is quoted at length on idleness: the most violent and mischievous of the passions, and the one we are never sensible of. It is a remora that can stop the largest ships, and a calm of worse consequence in our affairs than any rocks or storms. Jung calls this the dangerous passion hidden beneath the hazardous mask of incest, confronting us in the guise of the Terrible Mother.

**How people should relate**. Through a figure that is not a man, and the theology in the run is deliberate. The cultural point of view gives a man a meaning apart from the mass, and over centuries that produced the cult of the hero. Rationalist theology tries to preserve the personal Jesus as the last precious remnant of a divinity nobody can imagine any more. **The Catholic Church proved more adaptable, since she met the universal need for a visible hero by recognising God's vicar on earth.**

Jung then says what is actually being looked for. What we seek in visible human form is not man but the superman, the hero or god — the quasi-human being who symbolises the forces that grip and mould the soul. In loving that inheritance people love what is common to all, and turn back to the mother of humanity, the psyche, which was before consciousness existed. He calls it the problem of Antaeus, who kept his giant strength only through contact with the earth.

**The shape of time**. Regression measured in stages, and each stage has its own furniture. Repression is not directed solely against sexuality but against the instincts in general. The regression it causes leads back to the psychic past, and so to childhood, where the parents appear to be the decisive factors. **A child cannot distinguish its own instincts from the will of its parents**, which is how animals representing the instincts come to appear as attributes of the parents — the father as a bull, the mother as a cow.

Go back further than childhood and something else appears. Beyond the personal, in the preconscious and prenatal phase, archetypal images arise which are no longer connected with the individual's memories but belong to the stock of inherited possibilities of representation that are born anew in every individual. Their guise depends on the attitude of the conscious mind: hostile to the unconscious and the animals are frightening; positive and they are the helpful animals of fairytale.

**What is worth having**. A meaning that survives the individual, and the Sphinx is where the run lands. Miss Miller's first vision after the prayer is the head of a sphinx in an Egyptian setting, which appears and immediately goes. The word suggests an enigma and a creature who propounds riddles, **standing on the threshold of a man's fate as though announcing the inevitable.** Jung reads her as a half-animal figure of the Terrible Mother, and reminds the reader that in the legend the Sphinx was sent by Hera. Oedipus thought he had overcome her because he solved a childishly simple riddle, and then married his mother for the throne.

*Read: lines 2253–2593.*

---

## Part Two, Ch. V — The city is a woman, and the sea swallowed the sun

**What is real**. A crowd that means a secret, and the reading is stated as a working rule.[^5] Miss Miller's next vision is a swarm of people, which Jung says symbolises a secret, or rather the unconscious. The possession of a secret cuts a person off from other people, and since the economy of the libido depends on rapport with the environment being unimpeded, holding important secrets is disturbing. It is especially good for a neurotic to be able to unburden himself of them in treatment.

He then generalises from clinical experience. The symbol of the crowd, and particularly of a streaming mass in motion, expresses violent motions of the unconscious. **Such symbols always indicate an activation of the unconscious and an incipient dissociation between it and the ego.** Horses appear next, and a battle, which he reads for the moment as the rush of thoughts arriving.

**How people should relate**. To a city as to a woman, and the evidence is a run of texts rather than an assertion. The dream-city is a maternal symbol, a woman who harbours her inhabitants in herself like children. That is why the three mother-goddesses, Rhea, Cybele and Diana, all wear the mural crown. The Old Testament treats Jerusalem and Babylon exactly as if they were women, and Jung quotes Isaiah at length: come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon.

The grammar of the thing is then set out. Strong, unconquered cities are virgins. Colonies are sons and daughters. **Cities are also harlots** — *how is the faithful city become an harlot*. The prehistoric king Ogyges reigned in Thebes and his wife was called Thebe, which Jung reads as the city and the woman being identical rather than as a coincidence.

The political version of the same idea is the most concrete material in the run. In Hindu myth Indra is the husband of Urvara, which means fertile land. Seizing a country was regarded as marrying it. Princes on accession had to guarantee a good harvest, and the Swedish king Domaldi was killed for a failure of the crops. In the *Ramayana* the hero marries Sita, whose name is the furrow. And a Chinese emperor had to plough a furrow on taking the throne.

**What makes things happen**. A swallowing and a giving-birth, which are the same event seen at two ends of the night. Frobenius supplies the logic and Jung reproduces it. If the blood-red sunrise is the birth of the young sun, the question is how the woman became pregnant. **The primitive answer is that the sea had previously swallowed the old sun**, and so became pregnant that way.

From this comes the pattern the rest of the book keeps meeting. The sea-going gods are solar figures, shut in a chest or an ark for the night sea journey, often with a woman. During the night sea journey the sun-god is shut up in the mother's womb and threatened by all kinds of dangers. Jung reproduces Frobenius's diagram rather than list the myths separately, which is a rare economy in this book.

**What a person is**. Someone made by a prohibition, and this is the chapter's largest claim. The separation of the son from the mother signifies man's leave-taking from animal unconsciousness. **It was only the power of the incest prohibition that created the self-conscious individual, who before had been mindlessly one with the tribe.** And only then did the idea of the final death of the individual become possible.

Which reverses a familiar sentence. Through Adam's sin, which lay precisely in his becoming conscious, death came into the world. The neurotic who cannot leave his mother has good reasons for staying, and ultimately it is the fear of death that holds him there. Jung adds that no idea or word seems powerful enough to express the conflict, and that centuries of struggling for the expression cannot have been motivated by anything as narrow as incest crudely conceived.

**The shape of time**. Two mothers standing over the same death, and the medieval poem supplies the scene. The Holy Cross answers Mary: to her it owes honour, and the bright palms it bears; her fruit flourishes on it in blood colour. **The Mother of Death joins the Mother of Life in lamenting the dying god**, and as a token of union Mary kisses the cross and is reconciled. Jung notes that in Egypt the same union of opposite tendencies had been preserved without embarrassment in the figure of Isis.

**What is worth having**. A way out through the narrowest possible opening, and Faust says it. Jung takes the bay in Miss Miller's next vision through its etymology — bay, gulf, *gouffre*, abyss, and Greek *kolpos*, meaning bosom, lap, womb, and also the deep hollow between two waves. Faust's desire, like every hero's, is a yearning for the mystery of rebirth, so his way leads out to sea and down into the maw of death. He resolves not to shrink before the cavern, but to strive towards that passage at whose door, a narrow mouth, burn all the flames of hell.

**How you know**. From a sound she could not explain, and the run ends on it. The next vision is a perpendicular cliff. Then the whole series ends, she says, in a confusion of sounds resembling **"wa-ma, wa-ma."** Jung notes that she tells us nothing about where it came from, so only one conjecture is open: in the context as a whole, it might be a slight distortion of the well-known cry *Ma-ma*.

*Read: lines 2594–3664.*

---

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, Part Two I–V `[SPECULATIVE]`

Paradigm-obvious in 1912.

Ethnographic reports as transparent evidence. The Wachandi rite, the "primitives" of the fire ceremonies, and Lévy-Bruhl's *participation mystique* are all quoted as data with no question about who collected them or under what conditions.

Inherited possibilities of representation. That archetypal images are transmitted like an organ, born anew in each individual, is asserted as a biological fact of the same kind as the structure of the brain.

Race and species arranged in one series. The animal psyche, the primitive, the child and the schizophrenic are ranged along a single axis of differentiation, and the axis is not defended.

The classical languages as common property. The whole argument of chapter II is a philological one, and it assumes a reader who will follow Cicero, Sallust and Augustine in Latin without translation.

Paradigm-breaking, and the cost is what marks it.

Taking Freud's central term away and giving it back with a wider meaning. Jung does it in public, with the eunuch case and the schizophrenia comparison as evidence, and **the cost is the one the prefaces already recorded**: the man whose term it was suspected personal motives.

Insisting that a symbol is not a sign. That refusal removes the possibility of a translation table, which is what most readers wanted from the new psychology and what its rivals were offering.

Saying the world is empty only to those who cannot direct their love into it. It is aimed at a woman who is not present to answer, and **the cost is that the same sentence indicts the introversion the book depends on for its material.**

Naming idleness, on La Rochefoucauld's authority, as the passion hidden under incest. In a book written inside the psychoanalytic movement, that puts the least dramatic vice in the place reserved for the most dramatic one.

Reading Adam's sin as becoming conscious, and the incest prohibition as the thing that made the individual. It is a large theological claim from a physician, and it is the point on which the rest of the book turns.

## Part Two, Ch. II — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: deciding whether a term in an argument is doing work or hiding a gap.

The instrument is the sign-and-symbol distinction, and its value is in the direction it points. **A sign is a conventional abbreviation for something already known, and it has one fixed meaning.** A symbol is an indefinite expression pointing at something not fully known. So the two call for opposite handling. A sign is cashed out and discarded. A symbol is surrounded.

The rule that follows is counterintuitive and testable. **A symbol's variants are not noise around the real meaning — the more of them there are, the sharper the image gets.** Which means the honest response to a rich image is to collect its parallels rather than to pick the best reading. That is why amplification takes the space it does, and Jung's own defence of the practice is the one from Part One: the deeper you go, the broader the base becomes.

Scope conditions. This holds where the thing being pointed at is genuinely not yet known — a live symptom, an image that keeps recurring, a phrase in a culture that will not settle down. **It fails where a fixed convention actually exists**, and treating a sign as a symbol there is how a reader ends up finding depths in a road marking. It also fails as a defence: an unfalsifiable reading cannot be rescued by calling its object a symbol.

The general form. **Ask whether the thing has one agreed meaning or many analogous variants, and let that decide the method.** Modern equivalent: any recurring image in an organisation — a slogan that will not die, a story everybody tells about the founding. Cashing it out into one meaning destroys the information; collecting the versions is what shows the shape.

The second-order finding is the one about naming, and it is the most usable line in the chapter. A concept works like a magically powerful name: **it gets a grip on the object, renders it harmless, and incorporates it into the system.** That is offered as an account of how primitive thought worked. It reads equally well as an account of what a diagnosis does to a patient, and Jung does not make that application himself.

## Part Two, Ch. III — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: judging where a culture's technical discoveries actually came from.

The claim is that the useful ones were not aimed at. Energy that could not go where it was going gets canalised into analogy-making, and analogy-making is what produced the discoveries. **Jung says the little word *like* has a positively overwhelming importance in the history of human thought**, and that the canalisation of libido into analogy was probably responsible for some of the most important things primitive man found out.

The worked example is fire, and its structure is the transferable part. The rite is an analogy held with total seriousness: two sticks named as man and woman, grass named as testicles, butter as semen, and the fire that results named as the child. **Nobody in that ceremony is making fire in order to cook.** The ceremony is a sexual act performed on wood, and fire is what falls out of performing it.

Scope conditions. This bites where the activity is rhythmic, repeatable and charged, and where a real technique happens to sit inside the charged act. It fails as a general theory of invention — most tools were not discovered inside a rite. **And it fails as a reading of any particular rite whose history is actually known**, which is why Jung has to lean on the recurrence across unconnected peoples rather than on any single case.

The general form. **A practice charged enough to be repeated for its own sake will be repeated long enough for whatever is useful in it to be found**, and the finder will not be looking. Modern equivalent: any discipline that keeps a costly ritual nobody can justify — and whose practitioners turn out, decades later, to have the only trained hands for something else.

The uncomfortable half is the 1268 chronicle. Cattle were dying, and men in monastic dress taught the villagers to rub wood, raise a Priapus and sprinkle the herds with holy water in which a dog's testicles had been dipped. **That is the same rite, performed in a Christian country, by people who knew better, in an emergency.** It is the strongest evidence in the chapter and it is evidence for persistence rather than for discovery.

## Part Two, Ch. IV — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the person Jung describes in one line and then leaves. Not Miss Miller only — the type. Somebody who has an inward-flowing current and no object for it. Jung's diagnosis is blunt and it is not a diagnosis of circumstance. **The world is empty only to him who does not know how to direct his libido towards things and people, and to render them alive and beautiful.** The palaces of fantasy beckon, and part of the psyche really does want the external object, and cannot get to it.

His counsel is nothing, because he is describing rather than treating. He names the passion underneath — idleness, on La Rochefoucauld's account, a calm of worse consequence than any storm — and moves on to the Sphinx.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/the-hermit-love-withdrawn|love withdrawn]]** would recognise the person at once and would refuse the word *idleness*. This is a man whose feeling is entirely intact and has been severed from anything it could reach. He loves, he is moved by beauty, and he has made himself unreachable — **emotional capacity that exists internally and has been cut off from vulnerability and from mutual exchange.** The counsel is that nothing is missing and nothing is asleep. The capacity is at full strength and has no outward channel, which is exactly why the inner palaces are so well built. **So telling him the world is full is useless.** He already knows. What he does not have is a way of being seen while reaching for it.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/bhakti-fully-engages-the-senses-ambarisa|devotion routed through the senses]]** would agree about the diagnosis and give an actual procedure. This tradition's answer to a love with no object is not to find the right object and hope. It is to assign the senses their work one at a time — eyes to this, ears to that, hands to the other — **so that the feeling has somewhere to go before the person has decided how he feels.** The counsel is that direction is trained rather than chosen, and that it is trained on things rather than by resolution. On this reading Miss Miller had one of these disciplines available and used it for four days a week: writing to absent friends, teaching officers English, making a painter draw a lake. What she did not have was anybody telling her that this was the practice.

They disagree about the first move. The first says the fault is in the severing, so the repair is relational and slow. The second says the fault is in the routing, so the repair is procedural and can start on Tuesday.

**Where they converge is on the thing Jung's sentence assumes.** He treats the ability to direct libido as something a person either has or lacks, and the lacking as a fault. Both advisors treat it as a capacity with a history — cut in the first case, untrained in the second — and neither would say the world's fullness is the relevant fact. **Which matters because Jung's own case ends badly**, and the sentence he wrote about her is the one thing in Part Two that would have been no use to her at all.

# What 1912 Took For Granted — Jung, *Symbols of Transformation*, Part Two VI–IX and the Appendix

> **The last four chapters of Part Two of C. G. Jung, *Symbols of Transformation*, and the Appendix that reprints Miss Miller's own text** — a rider whose horse is called his faithful brother and dies first; a hero who thanks the snake that killed him and calls it little sister; a woman's fantasy figure buried by a volcano while he cries out to somebody who will be born ten thousand moons too late; and, at the back of the book, the woman herself, in her own words, describing what it is like to feel another person's feelings as though they were your own. Read from `RAW/books/Symbols of Transformation-Carl Jung.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
>
> ⚠ **This is where the book states what it did and did not do to its subject.** The Epilogue says outright that Jung never treated her, that the case suited his book precisely because he had nothing to do with it, and that had he treated her he would have had to tell her the things this book says. It also carries, in a footnote, the fact of what happened to her afterwards. The Appendix run reads her memoir as her document rather than as his material, and records how many translations stand between her sentences and this page.

## Part Two, Ch. VI — The horse is the other half of the man

**What is real**. A wood, which is the mother again in another form.[^1] The visions resume with trees and bushes, and Jung says the forest's meaning coincides with that of the tabooed tree. The sacred tree is generally found in a wood or a paradise-garden, and sometimes the forbidden grove takes the tree's place and carries all its attributes. The forest, like the tree, has a maternal significance, and it is the setting for the drama of Chiwantopel's end.

The scene itself is brief and staged like theatre. Chiwantopel comes up from the south on horseback, wrapped in a blanket of red, blue and white. An Indian in buckskin creeps forward to shoot an arrow at him. **Chiwantopel bares his breast in an attitude of defiance, and the Indian, fascinated by the sight, slinks away into the forest.**

**What a person is**. A rider and an animal who share one fate, and the text says so before Jung does. The horse is not a neutral prop. In the next act it dies the same death as the hero, who calls it his faithful brother. Hero and horse seem to symbolise man and the subordinate sphere of animal instinct, and Jung lines up the parallels: Agni on the ram, Wotan on Sleipnir, Christ on the ass, Mithras on the bull, Frey on the boar with golden bristles.

The old riddle he quotes puts the unity better than the theory does. Who are the two that go to the Thing? **Together they have three eyes, ten feet and one tail, and thus they travel over the land.**

**How you know**. From what legend attributes to horses, which is a list of the unconscious's own properties. There are clairvoyant and clairaudient horses. Path-finding horses who show the way when the wanderer is lost. Horses with mantic powers — in the *Iliad* one prophesies evil. They hear the words a corpse utters on its way to the grave, which no human can hear. An ass prophesied the victory of Actium to Augustus. Horses see ghosts.

So the connection with the devil follows without needing an argument. The devil has a horse's hoof and sometimes a horse's form, and shows the proverbial cloven hoof at critical moments. **The devil, like the nightmare, rides the sleeper.**

**What makes things happen**. Fertility, delivered by a foot. Pegasus struck the fountain of Hippocrene from the earth with his hoof, and Baldur's horse struck forth a spring with a kick, so the horse's foot is a dispenser of fruitful moisture. In German legend the goddess of childbirth comes on horseback, and pregnant women near their time would give oats to a white horse from their aprons and ask for a speedy delivery. Jung records the older form of the custom without comment: originally the horse nuzzled the woman's genitals.

**The shape of time**. The horse carries it, and the Upanishad makes the identification complete. Dawn is the head of the sacrificial horse, the sun his eye, the wind his breath, the universal fire his open mouth. **The year is his body.** The sky is his back, the seasons his limbs, the months and half-months his joints, days and nights his feet, the stars his bones, the clouds his flesh. Rivers are his entrails and the mountains his liver and lungs.

The Mithraic figure makes the same point in one statue. Aion, the lion-headed god, stands wrapped in the coils of a serpent, a key in each hand, a thunderbolt on his breast, the four winds on his back and the zodiac on his body. He is a time-symbol composed entirely of images of desire. The lion is the sign of the torrid summer and the symbol of frenzied craving; the snake is its antagonist. And time itself is defined by the rising and setting of the sun — by the death and renewal of libido, the dawning and extinction of consciousness.

**How people should relate** and **What is worth having** are not developed separately here. The chapter is a single sustained amplification, and its finding is that the animal a man rides is not scenery.

*Read: lines 3665–4032.*

---

## Part Two, Ch. VII — Two mothers, and a lover who is not a man

**How you know**. From a heading that is not there, and the run has to say so.[^2] This chapter's title is lost in the source file: the numeral and the words *The Dual Mother* appear only in the table of contents, and the body runs on without a break. The chapter opens at the paragraph where Chiwantopel begins his monologue, which is where the printed editions place it, and the run is bounded accordingly.

**What a person is**. In a woman's case, partly a man, and Jung names the figure here. Chiwantopel is a typical animus-figure — a personification of the masculine side of a woman's psyche, which becomes active when the conscious mind refuses to follow what the unconscious prompts. **Instead of love and surrender there is mannishness, argumentativeness, obstinate self-assertion, and the demon of opinion in every possible shape.**

His description of the figure is deliberately unflattering and it is aimed at the reader's sympathy for the hero. The animus is not a real man at all. He is a slightly hysterical, infantile hero whose longing to be loved shows through the gaps in his armour. It is in this dress that Miss Miller has put the critical decisions of her life — decisions which have not got beyond unconscious fantasy and are not recognised by her as her own.

**What makes things happen**. A search that is not for the person it names. The hero admits that his wanderings are a search for the beloved and for the meaning of life to be found in union with her. That the seeker is masculine and the sought-for feminine is not remarkable, **since the prime object of unconscious desire is the mother.** Jung reaches for the grammar of comprehension to make it concrete: *comprehend*, *begreifen*, *erfassen* all originally mean to seize something with the hands and hold it tight in the arms, which is what a mother does with a child.

The danger in that is developmental. The older the child grows, the more this kind of comprehension hinders it. The libido regresses to the sheltering ease of the mother's arms and fails to keep pace with time. The life a person ought to have lived then runs away in the form of fantasy, which in a woman's case is generally handed to a hero-figure and acted out by him.

**What is real**. Two mothers, and the doubling is everywhere. The hero is not born like an ordinary mortal because his birth is a rebirth from the mother-wife, which is why he so often has two mothers. **He is frequently exposed and then reared by foster-parents**, and Jung lists them: Heracles and Hera, Wenonah replaced by Nokomis in the Hiawatha epic, Buddha brought up by a foster-mother, the she-wolf of Romulus and Remus.

The motif can also change form without changing meaning. The dual mother may be replaced by the motif of dual birth, which has attained a lofty significance in several religions. In Christianity baptism represents a rebirth, so that a man is not merely born in the commonplace sense but born again and so partakes of divinity. Christ's own death is read the same way — *I have a baptism to be baptized with* — as birth-pangs rather than as an ending.

**How people should relate**. Through a figure who kills the man who loves her, and Wagner supplies the register. Brünhilde, the horse-woman who conducts the dead to the other side, asks Siegfried whether he fears the wild, raging woman. **Laughing let us be lost, laughing go down to death.** Jung puts these orgiastic extremes in the nature of the *mater saeva cupidinum*, the savage mother of desires, and says they determine the hero's fate.

The general shape of that fate is then stated as a rule. The hero is the ideal masculine type: leaving the mother behind him, he is driven by an unconscious desire to find her again. Every obstacle in his path wears the shadowy features of the Terrible Mother, who saps his strength with secret doubt and backward longing — and in every conquest he wins back the loving, life-giving mother. Siegfried's end is every archetypal hero's: the one-eyed Hagen's spear finds the vulnerable spot, and in Hagen's shape the one-eyed Wotan kills the son.

**What is worth having**. A vocabulary, and this is where the later Jung arrives inside the early book. Investigation of the products of the unconscious yields recognisable traces of structures that coincide with myth-motifs. **Some of them deserve the name of dominants: the anima, the animus, the wise old man, the witch, the shadow, the earth-mother** — and the organising ones, the self, the circle and the quaternity. Knowing these types makes myth interpretation easier and puts it on a psychic basis.

**The shape of time — and the danger in it**. The hero myth is an unconscious drama seen only in projection, like the happenings in Plato's cave. Since the hero is psychologically an archetype of the self, his divinity confirms that the self is numinous. Jung then runs that through a fourth-century church quarrel and means it seriously: for psychology it makes a vast difference whether the self is of the same nature as the Father or merely of a similar nature.

The practical consequence is a warning about what happens next. The hero corresponds to what Jung calls the mana personality, which fascinates the conscious mind so much **that the ego all too easily succumbs to the temptation to identify with him, bringing on a psychic inflation with all its consequences.** He adds that the repugnance felt in certain ecclesiastical circles for the inner Christ is understandable as a preventive measure against exactly that danger.

*Read: lines 4033–5113.*

---

## Part Two, Ch. VIII — Thanks, little sister, you have ended my wanderings

**What makes things happen**. A speech, and then three deaths in a row.[^3] Chiwantopel cries out that in all the world there is not a single one, that he has searched among a hundred tribes and aged a hundred moons. Then the prophecy: ten thousand moons will wax and wane before her pure soul is born, and it is from another world that her parents will come. She will know sorrow even before her mother bears her. Many suitors will court her and none will understand her. In her dreams he will come to her, and she will understand.

What follows is fast. A green viper darts out of the bushes and stings him in the arm, then attacks his horse, which dies first. He says farewell to the horse — **farewell, faithful brother, I have loved you and you have served me well.** Then to the snake: thanks, little sister, you have put an end to my wanderings. A volcano smokes in the distance, an earthquake rumbles, a landslide follows, and the earth closes over him while he calls out to the one who will understand.

**What a person is**. Somebody separated from her own hero by ten thousand moons, and Jung reads the gap as the finding. The prophecy brings the author into the closest relationship with the hero as the real object of his longing. The time-gap points to a gap in another sense: her ego is separated by a gulf from Chiwantopel, who is wholly on the other side. There will be no possibility of a meeting of conscious and unconscious, which is the one thing needed to compensate the conscious attitude and create wholeness.

The sentence he draws from it is the run's most human. She or he can at most dream of such a meeting, and only so can their souls understand one another. **But every real love-relationship consists ultimately in the girl finding her hero, and the hero his soul, not in dreams but in palpable reality.**

**How you know**. From a boast that gives away who is speaking. The next line is *I have kept my body inviolate*, and Jung notes that only a woman could utter it, since a man is not given to boasting about such matters. It confirms that all the enterprises have remained dreams. The hero's inviolateness explains the earlier failed assassination, and it is completed by the next clause — temptation will often assail her soul, but she will not yield.

He then names the attitude that follows from an animus waking up. It is as if a new instinct were aroused and the soul seized by an unknown longing. **The image of earthly love pales before that of the heavenly, which turns the heart away from its natural destination.** Jung is careful with *natural* there: the world-spurning passion of the spirit is just as natural as the marriage-flight of insects.

**What is worth having**. Nothing, if the hero survives, and this is where the unconscious does something drastic. Chiwantopel is eliminated very thoroughly indeed: bitten by the snake, deprived of his animal vitality when the horse dies, then engulfed by a volcano. Jung reads that as an attempt by the unconscious to compensate a dangerous situation. If only the fascinating Chiwantopel could be got out of the way, there would be some hope of her interest turning again to the earth and its greenness.

Then the sentence the whole book has been travelling towards, and it is a clinical judgment delivered about somebody who will never read it. An invasion from the unconscious is very dangerous when the conscious mind cannot understand or integrate what has irrupted. One does not have the feeling that Miss Miller is *the one who understands*, though it is plain that the phrase is meant for her. **Since she has not the slightest idea of what is happening, her situation is critical** — and the footnote records that the conscious mind was in fact overwhelmed a little later, with fatal results.

**The shape of time**. A wheel she is trying to stop, and Jung says the wish is legible in the text. The special emphasis on the inviolate body, and the plea that it should not fall into corruption in the grave, show a tendency to stand still. She wants to stop the turning wheel that rolls the years along with it, and to hang on to childhood and eternal youth rather than die and rot in the earth. The greying hair and the lined face are pitiless reminders that the poison of the stealthily creeping serpent of time consumes the body whether or not we expose ourselves to life.

The poetic parallel he chooses is a man who went the same way. Hölderlin's rose lies with the poet in the eternal mother-womb, where nature carries them both. **Psychologically that means he is still in the mother** — where there is endless germination and renewal, a potential life containing every possibility without his having to do the labour of giving any of them shape.

**How people should relate** is not developed separately in this run. The chapter's whole social content is one relationship that cannot happen, described from both ends.

*Read: lines 5114–5774.*

---

## Ch. IX — Epilogue: how can you treat something you do not understand?

**How you know**. By admitting the limits of the case, which the Epilogue does in three moves.[^4] The melancholy outcome is due largely to the fantasies breaking off at the critical moment, when the threat of invasion is plainly apparent. It is hardly to be supposed that Miss Miller, who had not the faintest clue as to the real meaning of her visions, could meet the next phase with the right attitude. Jung notes that even Flournoy, despite his fine feeling for values, could do nothing to explain them.

The evidence of dissociation is stated plainly and without diagnosis-language. The unconscious went ahead independently and kept churning out images she had not consciously produced and felt as strange and portentous. **To an objective observer it is clear that the fantasies were products of a psychic energy not under the control of the conscious mind.**

**What is worth having**. A stock of symbolic ideas, and Jung quotes the alchemists for it. All of this passes off smoothly provided a person's consciousness already contains certain ideas of a symbolic nature — for those who have the symbol the passage is easy. Where there is already a tendency to dissociation, every advance of the unconscious widens the gap, and as a rule outside help is needed to bridge it.

Then the sentence that indicts the book's own form. **Had I treated Miss Miller, Jung writes, I would have had to tell her some of the things of which I have written in this book**, in order to build her conscious mind up to the point where it could understand the contents of the collective unconscious. He adds that a personalistic psychology is not sufficient for that, and that anyone treating serious dissociation must know something of the anatomy and evolutionary history of the mind he is setting out to cure.

**How people should relate**. At a distance, for a stated reason, and the reason is the hardest line in the chapter. The Miller case suited my book very well because I had nothing to do with it personally and could thus refute the oft-repeated charge that I had influenced the patient. The methodological advantage is real and Jung says what it cost: had the case come up for treatment at the first sign of spontaneous fantasy, the Chiwantopel episode might have taken a very different turn, and the end, so we will hope, would have been less calamitous.

**What a person is** — to a doctor, on this account — is a situation rather than a diagnosis, and the closing paragraphs say why. Dreams, visions, fantasies and delusions are expressive of a situation. **If I do not understand the dreams, neither do I understand the situation of the patient, and of what use is my treatment then?** Doctors are not so happily placed as research workers in other fields, because they cannot choose their assignment: the sick man confronts them with unforeseeable problems and expects a therapeutic task they cannot but feel inadequate to.

**What makes things happen**. A question he says he could never ignore, and he gives it as the motive for everything in the book. The strongest incentive to unceasing research always came to him from practice, and it consisted in one simple question: how can you treat something that you do not understand? It was never his intention to justify his theories by his patients. What he wanted was to understand their situation in all its aspects.

**What is real** and **The shape of time** are not developed separately in the Epilogue. It is short, and its business is to say what the book was for and what it could not do.

*Read: lines 5775–5791.*

---

## Appendix — Miss Miller in her own words

**How you know**. Through more hands than anybody would like, and the editors put the chain on the record.[^5] Miss Miller wrote her memoir in English. Flournoy published it in French, describing the text as a translation. The original English has never come to light, so a double translation has been necessary in every edition, and Jung based his whole study on the French. Certain words he considered especially pointed are given back in French in brackets, and passages Flournoy left in English are marked as such.

A later editorial note adds a further turn. The original English article was published in New York in 1907 under her own title, *Some Instances of Subconscious Creative Imagination*, and **there is no evidence that Jung was acquainted with that version.** So the book that reads her sentences for their smallest verbal associations was reading somebody else's rendering of them throughout.

**What a person is**. In her own account, someone unusually porous, and she says it first and better than her analyst does. She calls the phenomenon curious and reports it as an observation on herself. At certain moments, and for a few seconds only, the impressions or feelings of another person are so strongly suggested to her that they seem to be her own — and as soon as the suggestion is over she is perfectly sure that this was not the case.

That last clause matters and Jung's reading passes over it. The state is brief, she notices it, and her judgment returns intact afterwards. **She is describing something she can already see from outside**, which is not what a person in the grip of a delusion can do.

**How people should relate**. Through a description that does not match the tragedy, and it is Flournoy's. In introducing the material he describes her as a young American who studied for a semester at the Geneva university, and who today pursues a distinguished career as a journalist and lecturer in the United States.

That sentence sits at the front of the primary document. The book built on the document reads her as a woman with no relation to reality and no outlet for her energy. **The source says she was working, publishing and speaking in public**, and the run records both without resolving them, because the two are not compatible and the vault does not close contradictions silently.

**What is worth having**. Her own title for the material, which is a claim of a different kind from Jung's. She called it *Some Instances of Subconscious Creative Imagination*. The subject of that title is creativity, and the instances are offered as evidence about a faculty rather than about a person. The name Jung's book carries instead is *Symbols of Transformation*, and its subject is a case.

**What is real**, **What makes things happen** and The shape of time are not separately developed in this run. The Appendix is a primary document, and what it supplies to the report is a voice, and a record of where the words came from, rather than a theory.

*Read: lines 5792–5993.*

---

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, Part Two VI to the Appendix `[SPECULATIVE]`

Paradigm-obvious in 1912.

Publishing a named case study of a living woman, from somebody else's article, without her involvement. The only ethical question the book raises about it is whether Jung might have influenced her, and he answers that by pointing out he never met her.

That a woman's fantasy hero can be read off as her animus, with the traits assigned in advance — mannishness, argumentativeness, the demon of opinion. The type is stated as a finding about women rather than as a hypothesis.

Reading Longfellow's *Hiawatha* as ethnographic access to the Native American mind. Jung is sharp about the poem's Christian sentimentality and about what the Spaniards did in Mexico and Peru, and he still uses the poem as data.

Amplification without limit. Any parallel from any culture is admissible evidence for the meaning of a symbol, and the method's own rule — that more variants sharpen the image — makes an unfalsifiable reading structurally impossible to detect.

Paradigm-breaking, and the cost is what marks it.

Predicting the outcome in print, and being right. The footnote recording what happened to her afterwards is the most convincing thing in the book and the most damaging. **The cost is that a method proved by a prediction nobody could act on is proved at somebody's expense.**

Saying the case suited the book because he had nothing to do with it. That is offered as methodological hygiene and it reads as something else, and Jung does not appear to notice the second reading.

Admitting in the same paragraph what treatment would have looked like. Had he treated her, he would have had to tell her the contents of this book — **which means the book itself was the missing intervention**, printed and sold rather than given.

Putting the *homoousios* quarrel inside a psychology of the hero. Deciding that the self is of the same nature as God, rather than merely similar, is a claim a physician had no standing to make in 1912, and he makes it anyway.

Naming psychic inflation as the risk of identifying with the hero, and conceding that the church's suspicion of the inner Christ is a sensible precaution against it. It is a rare moment of the book defending an institution against its own method.

## Part Two, Ch. VIII — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: recognising, from the outside, that somebody's inner life has stopped being a private matter.

The mechanism is a deadlock and a takeover. **The conscious mind gets stuck, and the unconscious takes over the forward-striving function** — the process of transformation in time — in order to break the deadlock. What then pours in are representations of what the conscious mind should have experienced if the deadlock was to be avoided. So the flood is not random and it is not decoration. It is the missing development, arriving in the wrong form.

The signs Jung reads are all about stopping rather than about content. The emphasis on the inviolate body. The wish to be preserved from corruption in the grave. **She wants to stop the turning wheel that rolls the years along with it.** None of that requires interpreting a symbol; it is legible from what the material insists on.

Scope conditions. This bites where the productions are unbidden — where the person feels them as strange and portentous rather than as something they made. **It fails where the material is being composed**, which is the ordinary condition of art, and Jung does not supply a clean test to tell the two apart. It also requires a deadlock that is real: a life that has genuinely stopped moving, not one that is merely quiet.

The general form. **When an inner life starts producing things the person did not intend and cannot place, the content is usually the growth that was due**, and the danger is proportional to how little the person can make of it. Modern equivalent: any sudden torrent of insight, imagery or conviction in somebody whose circumstances have not changed in years.

The second-order finding is the one that ought to frighten a reader of this book. Jung's rescue condition is a stock of symbolic ideas — *for those who have the symbol the passage is easy* — which means the protective factor is a vocabulary. **He had the vocabulary. She had the experience.** The book is four hundred pages of the first, written about the second, and the distance between them is the whole of the problem.

## Ch. IX and the Appendix — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

The road not taken is one Jung names in a single sentence, prices exactly, and does not defend.

He writes that had he treated Miss Miller he would have had to tell her some of the things this book contains, in order to build her conscious mind to the point where it could understand what had broken into it. And he adds that had the case come up for treatment at the very first sign of spontaneous fantasy, the Chiwantopel episode might have taken a different turn, **and the end would have been less calamitous.**

So the counterfactual is his, not the reader's. What makes it a road rather than a regret is that it was available. She had studied a semester at Geneva. Her material was published by a professor there who knew her, in a journal Jung read. **The distance between the case and the clinic was one letter**, and the reason it stayed uncrossed is stated in the same chapter: the case was valuable precisely because he had nothing to do with it.

The counterfactual worth running is the second-order one. Suppose he had written to Flournoy. The book as we have it could not then exist — not because the material would be gone, but because its evidential value would be. **A treated case cannot refute the charge of having influenced the patient**, which is the charge the book was built to answer. So the choice was not between a woman and a delay. It was between this book and that woman, and the book won.

Against that stands the Appendix, and it is why this section sits here rather than in the run. Flournoy describes her as pursuing a distinguished career as a journalist and lecturer. **A woman with no relation to reality is not the woman in that sentence**, and the frame the whole analysis rests on — a life with no outlet, a libido with nowhere to go — is contradicted on the first page of the document it analyses. Jung read that page. He worked from that version.

Which opens a third road nobody takes. If the material came from a woman who was working and publishing, then the fantasies are not evidence of an obstructed life. **They are the productions of a working writer**, of the kind she herself titled *Some Instances of Subconscious Creative Imagination*, and the interesting question becomes what happened to her between 1906 and the later illness rather than what her poems reveal about her incapacity. The book never asks it.

## Part Two, Ch. VII — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the danger Jung names and then leaves standing. The hero is an archetype of the self, and the self is numinous. The figure has such fascination that **the ego all too easily succumbs to the temptation to identify with him, bringing on a psychic inflation with all its consequences.** His only practical remark about it is that the church's suspicion of the inner Christ makes sense as a preventive measure.

That is a warning with no procedure attached. A person who has met such a figure is told the identification is dangerous and is given nothing to do instead.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/deity-yoga-consciousness-identity-transformation|deity yoga]]** would say the identification is not the danger, because his tradition does it on purpose. The practice is not prayer to an external deity. **It is a trained recognition that one's essential consciousness is not the limited individual it takes itself to be**, performed by deliberately taking the form of the deity. So the counsel is not *don't identify*. It is that identification is a technique with a structure — a beginning, a sequence, and, crucially, a dissolution at the end of the session, after which you are a person again. **Jung's Miss Miller has the identification with no frame around it and no way of putting it down**, which this advisor would call the actual defect. The figure is not too powerful. It is unbounded in time.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/psychic-being-as-foundation-for-siddhi-safety|the psychic being as the precondition for safe powers]]** would go behind the identification to what is holding it. The doctrine is an order of operations: something stable has to be established in the person *before* the extraordinary contents are allowed to arrive, because the powers themselves are neutral and it is the container that decides whether they build or wreck. **On this reading, inflation is not caused by the size of the archetype but by the absence of a centre for it to be referred to.** The counsel to Jung's reader is procedural and unglamorous: the question to ask about anybody meeting such a figure is not what the figure means, but what in them is doing the meeting.

They disagree about where the work goes. The first says structure the encounter — bound it, sequence it, end it. The second says build the person first and the encounter takes care of itself.

**Where they converge is on the thing Jung's chapter treats as a natural hazard.** He writes about inflation as a temptation the ego succumbs to, in the register of weather. **Both advisors treat it as an engineering failure with known causes and known preventions** — no frame, or no centre — and both would say the traditions that run this deliberately, for centuries, are not braver than European psychology. They are simply operating equipment that came with instructions.
