## Book III, Ch. 4 — Three million francs and a phrase nobody can define

**What makes things happen**. Prestige first, and everything else after.[^4] An electoral crowd is heterogeneous, but since its action is confined to one clear matter — choosing between candidates — it shows only a few of the crowd characteristics: little aptitude for reasoning, no critical spirit, irritability, credulity and simplicity. What runs it are the factors already named: affirmation, repetition, prestige, contagion.

The candidate must have prestige, meaning he can impose himself on the electorate without discussion. Personal prestige can only be substituted for by the prestige of wealth. Talent and even genius are not elements of serious importance. And this explains something Le Bon thinks needs explaining: why electors who are mostly working men or peasants so rarely choose a man from their own ranks. Such a man has no prestige among them. When they do elect an equal it's usually for a side reason — to spite an eminent man, or an employer they depend on daily, whose master they get the illusion of becoming for a moment.

**How people should relate**. By flattery and by the destruction of the other man, which he sets out as instructions. The elector wants his greed and his vanity fed. He must be overwhelmed with the most extravagant blandishments and offered the most fantastic promises. If he's a working man it's impossible to go too far in insulting employers of labour. As for the rival, the effort must be to establish by affirmation, repetition and contagion that he is an arrant scoundrel and that everybody knows he has committed several crimes. **It is, of course, useless to trouble about any semblance of proof.** If the rival doesn't know the psychology of crowds he'll try to justify himself with arguments instead of answering one set of affirmations with another, and he'll have no chance at all.

The programme gets the same treatment, split in two. The written one shouldn't be too categorical, since it can be produced against him later. In the spoken one there cannot be too much exaggeration, and the most important reforms may be fearlessly promised. The exaggerations do their work at the moment and bind nobody, because the elector never troubles to find out how far the man he returned followed the programme he applauded.

**What is real**. Whatever a phrase can be made to mean, and the case is a revolution. A new formula as devoid as possible of precise meaning, and therefore able to flatter every kind of aspiration, wins infallibly. The Spanish revolution of 1873 was brought on by one of these — a federal republic, unanimously proclaimed by the Cortes, though none of the men voting could have said what he had voted for.

The account he reprints is the best evidence in the run because it lists the incompatible readings. The formula delighted everybody, and the joy was intoxicating and delirious; a republican whose opponent denied him the title of federalist thought himself mortally insulted; men greeted each other in the street with *long live the federal republic*. Some took it to mean the emancipation of the provinces and administrative decentralisation on the American model. Others meant the abolition of all authority and the start of the great social liquidation. The socialists of Barcelona and Andalusia meant absolute sovereignty for the communes, and proposed to give Spain ten thousand independent municipalities legislating for themselves, with the police and the army suppressed. **In the southern provinces, as soon as a village had made its pronouncement, its first care was to cut the telegraph wires and the railway lines**, so as to be out of communication with its neighbours and with Madrid. Federation became cantonalism, with massacres and burning across the country.

**How you know**. By reading the report of any election meeting, which he says settles the question of whether reasoning has any influence. In such a gathering there are affirmations, invectives and sometimes blows, and never arguments. If silence falls it's because somebody with a reputation as a tough customer has announced he's about to put the candidate an embarrassing question, and the satisfaction is brief, because the questioner's voice is soon drowned by his adversaries.

He then quotes the newspapers. The organisers ask the assembly to elect a president, and the storm bursts. The anarchists leap on the platform to take the committee table and the socialists defend it. Blows are exchanged, each party accuses the other of being government spies, and a citizen leaves the hall with a black eye. At another meeting, whose watchword was *calm and tranquillity*, a comrade calls the socialists idiots and humbugs, and chairs, tables and benches are converted into weapons.

The control case is students, and it's there to stop anyone blaming the working class. A report from *Le Temps* of 13 February 1895 describes a meeting composed exclusively of students in which no orator managed two sentences without interruption, applause mixed with hissing, sticks brandished, others beating a tattoo on the floor, and shouts of *put him out* and *let him speak*.

**What a person is**. Not the author of his own opinion, on this evidence. Crowds have opinions that have been imposed on them and never reasoned ones, and here the opinions and votes are in the hands of the election committees, whose leading men are usually publicans with great influence over working men to whom they extend credit. He quotes Schérer, a champion of democracy, calling the election committee the cornerstone of French institutions and the masterpiece of the political machine, and saying France is governed by them.

His own footnote on committees is the harshest thing in the book. Under whatever name — clubs, syndicates — they are the most impersonal and therefore the most oppressive form of tyranny, because the men directing them are supposed to speak for a collectivity and are freed from all responsibility. **The most savage tyrant never dreamed of proscriptions like those the committees of the Revolution ordered.** Barras said they decimated the Convention, picking off members at their pleasure. Robespierre held absolute power for exactly as long as he could speak in their name, and was lost the moment he separated himself from them out of personal pride.

And the price of a seat is on the record. According to the admissions of the donors, three million francs were enough to secure the repeated elections of General Boulanger.

**What is worth having**. Universal suffrage, which he keeps — and the argument for keeping it is the one place he turns his method against his own preferences. He states the objection first and states it fully: civilisation has been the work of a small minority of superior intelligences at the top of a pyramid, the greatness of a civilisation can't depend on votes cast by inferior elements with nothing but numbers, and the votes of crowds have already cost France several invasions.

Then he says the objections are excellent in theory and lose all force in practice. The dogma of the sovereignty of crowds is as indefensible philosophically as the religious dogmas of the Middle Ages, and it now has the same absolute power, so it is just as unattackable. He asks the reader to imagine a modern freethinker dropped into the Middle Ages and to consider whether, in front of a judge ready to send him to the stake for a pact with the devil, he would be tempted to question the existence of the devil. **It would be as wise to oppose a cyclone with discussion as the beliefs of crowds.** Time alone acts on them.

He also thinks restricting the vote would change nothing, and gives the reason. In a crowd men always tend to the same level, so on general questions a vote by forty academicians is no better than a vote by forty water-carriers. Knowing Greek or mathematics, being an architect or a veterinary surgeon or a barrister, doesn't confer any special intelligence about social questions. The political economists are all highly educated, mostly professors and academicians — and on protection, on bimetallism, on any general question, they have never once managed to agree. Their science, he says, is only a very attenuated form of our universal ignorance.

**The shape of time**. Stable in a way that makes elections nearly decorative. Restricted or general, under a republic or a monarchy, in France or Belgium or Greece or Portugal or Spain, the suffrage of crowds is everywhere identical, and expresses the unconscious aspirations and needs of the race. **In each country the average opinions of the elected represent the genius of the race, and don't alter noticeably from one generation to the next.** So the chapter ends where every chapter ends: race and the slavery of our daily necessities are the mysterious master-causes that rule our destiny.

*Read: lines 1604–1701.*

## Book III, Ch. 5 — The room stops listening

**What is real**. The parliamentary system, which he calls the ideal of all modern civilised peoples and an expression of an idea that is psychologically false.[^5] The idea is that a large gathering of men is much more capable than a small number of reaching a wise and independent decision. Parliaments in Greece, Italy, Portugal, Spain, France and America produce great similarities in their debates and their votes, and leave their governments facing identical difficulties, so race modifies the crowd characteristics here without preventing them.

Simplicity of opinion is the leading feature. Members tend to solve the most complicated social problems with the simplest abstract principles applied to every case, and being in a crowd they exaggerate the worth of their principles and push them to extremes. Parliaments therefore represent extreme opinions especially.

The example is the Jacobins, and the sentence he borrows about them is the one to keep. Dogmatic and logical to a man, their heads full of vague generalities, they applied fixed principles without concerning themselves with events. **It has been said of them, with reason, that they went through the Revolution without witnessing it.** With very simple dogmas as a guide they thought they could rebuild society from the top down and send a highly refined civilisation back to an earlier stage — and their method came down to destroying whatever stood in the way.

**What makes things happen**. Two suggestions pulling against each other, which explains a behaviour that otherwise looks like madness. On local or regional questions every member has fixed opinions no argument can shake. The talent of a Demosthenes would not change a Deputy's vote on protection or the privilege of distilling alcohol, where influential electors have interests. The suggestion from those electors was received before the vote and outweighs every other.

On general questions — bringing down a Cabinet, imposing a tax — there's no fixity, and the leaders' suggestions work, but each party has leaders of roughly equal influence. So the Deputy stands between two contrary suggestions and is made to hesitate. That's why he can be seen voting in opposite ways within a quarter of an hour, or adding to a law an article that cancels it — taking from employers the right to choose and dismiss their workmen, and then nearly annulling the measure with an amendment. Since general questions are the more numerous, indecision predominates, produced by an ever-present fear of the elector.

The English parliamentarian's line, quoted in a footnote, is the flattest possible statement of the same thing. **During the fifty years he sat at Westminster he listened to thousands of speeches; few of them changed his opinion, and not one of them changed his vote.**

**How people should relate**. Under leaders, again, and the votes of an assembly usually represent only a small minority's opinion. The influence of those leaders comes in very small measure from their arguments and in large measure from prestige, and the proof is that when they lose the prestige the influence goes with it.

That prestige is individual and has nothing to do with celebrity, which Jules Simon demonstrates from the Assembly of 1848. Two months before he was all-powerful, Louis Napoleon was of no importance whatever. Victor Hugo mounted the tribune and failed; he was listened to as Félix Pyat was listened to and got less applause. Edgar Quinet, with an exceptional and powerful intelligence, was held in no esteem at all — popular before the Assembly opened, and unpopular in it. Le Bon keeps the facts and rejects Simon's explanation, since a crowd that credited its leaders with services rendered would immediately stop being a crowd.

He then prices one man's prestige in territory. A celebrated Deputy — the translator names Clemenceau — had only to give the signal and Cabinets fell. A writer is quoted saying it is mainly due to him that France paid three times what it should have for Tonkin, stayed precariously placed in Madagascar, was defrauded of an empire on the Lower Niger, and lost its position in Egypt. **His theories, the writer says, have cost us more territory than the disasters of Napoleon I.** Le Bon then declines to hold a grudge, on the grounds that much of the man's influence came from following public opinion, since a leader is seldom ahead of it and almost always does nothing but follow it and adopt its errors.

**How you know**. By what a phrase does to a room. The leader needs a special eloquence made of energetic affirmations unburdened with proof, impressive images, and very summary argument. Maine says debates in the House of Commons can constantly be read in which the whole discussion is an exchange of weak generalities and violent personalities, and that general formulas of that kind have a prodigious influence on the imagination of a pure democracy.

The example given is a threat wrapped in a picture. A leader of one of the French assemblies said that when the same vessel carries off to the fever-haunted lands of the penitentiary settlements both the politician of shady reputation and the anarchist guilty of murder, the pair will be able to converse, and will appear to each other as two complementary aspects of one and the same state of society. Every adversary in the room felt threatened. They saw the fever country and the ship, since it is perfectly possible they belong to the ill-defined class of politicians being menaced — the same fear, Le Bon says, that the men of the Convention felt when Robespierre's vague speeches threatened them with the guillotine, and under which they always gave way.

The corollary is that exaggeration has no ceiling. The same speaker could say without provoking protest that bankers and priests had subsidised the bomb-throwers, and that the directors of the great financial companies deserved the same punishment as anarchists. The affirmation is never too violent and the declamation never too threatening, because **those present are afraid that if they protest they'll be put down as traitors or accomplices.**

**What a person is**. In a leader's case, better off narrow, which he states as a mechanism rather than an insult. Intelligence shows how complex things are, allows explanation, promotes understanding — and so makes its owner indulgent and blunts the violence of conviction an apostle needs. The great leaders of crowds in every age, and of the Revolution in particular, have been of lamentably narrow intellect, and the most restricted have had the greatest influence.

Robespierre is the case, read through his own speeches. They frequently astound by their incoherence, and simply reading them offers no plausible explanation of the part he played. The verdict quoted is unsparing: the commonplaces and redundancies of pedagogic eloquence and Latin culture at the service of a mind childish rather than undistinguished, limited in attack and defence to the defiant attitude of schoolboys — not an idea, not a happy turn of phrase, not a telling hit, a storm of declamation that leaves the reader bored.

The counter-portrait is the Deputy without prestige, and it's the best scene in the chapter because you can watch it happen. He takes his place in the tribune, draws a document from his portfolio, spreads it out methodically, and starts with assurance. He has weighed and re-weighed his arguments, is well primed with figures and proofs, and is certain he'll convince, since in the face of his evidence resistance would be futile.

He speaks, and is at once surprised by the restlessness of the House and a little annoyed by the noise. Why is silence not kept, and what are those Deputies talking about, and what urgent motive has made that one leave his seat? An expression of uneasiness crosses his face; he frowns and stops. Encouraged by the President he begins again, louder, and is listened to less. He puts emphasis on his words and gesticulates, and the noise increases. **He can no longer hear himself, and stops again — and then, afraid his silence will bring the cry of *the closure*, he starts off once more, and the clamour becomes unbearable.**

**What is worth having**. Specialists, and the parliamentary system anyway. When assemblies reach a certain pitch of excitement they become ordinary heterogeneous crowds and their sentiments go to extremes, and the individual will vote measures against his own interests. Billaud-Varennes is the witness: the decisions we have been so reproached for, he wrote, were not desired by us two days, or a single day, before they were taken — it was the crisis and nothing else that gave rise to them.

Taine's account of the Convention is the extended version, and it turns on unanimity. The Left, supported by the Right, unanimously and amid loud applause sent Danton — its natural chief and the great promoter of the Revolution — to the scaffold. Unanimously and with the greatest applause the Right, supported by the Left, voted the worst decrees of the revolutionary government. By spontaneous and repeated re-elections the Convention kept in office the homicidal government that the Plain detested for being homicidal and the Mountain detested because it was being decimated by it. **On 22 Prairial the entire Convention offered itself to the executioner, and on 8 Thermidor, in the first quarter of an hour after Robespierre's speech, it did the same thing again.**

Against all that he sets one saving mechanism. Assemblies are only crowds at certain moments, and their members keep their individuality a great deal of the time, which is how a chamber can produce excellent technical laws. The author of such a law is a specialist who prepared it alone in his study, so the law voted is an individual's work and not an assembly's — and these are the best laws, only becoming disastrous when a series of amendments turns them into a collective effort. The specialist is a temporary leader of crowds: the Assembly has no influence on him and he has influence over it.

Then the verdict, which is not the one his reputation predicts. Parliamentary assemblies are the best form of government mankind has found so far, and the best means it has found of escaping personal tyranny. They are the ideal government for philosophers, thinkers, writers, artists and learned men.

**How people should relate — the two costs**. He names two dangers and both are arithmetic. The first is financial waste, produced by the electors' demands and their lack of foresight. Let a member propose old-age pensions for all workers, or a rise for some class of State employees, and no other Deputy will dare seem to disregard his electors by rejecting it — knowing perfectly well he is straining the budget and requiring new taxes. The consequences of the spending are remote and won't hurt him personally; the consequences of a negative vote will be perfectly visible at the next election.

The second cause is local grants, which no Deputy can oppose, since each can only get what his own constituency needs by agreeing to everyone else's demands. The footnote from the *Economiste* of 6 April 1895 puts numbers on it. Fifteen million francs for a railway to connect Langayes, a town of three thousand on a mountain, with Puy. Seven million to connect Beaumont, three thousand five hundred people, with Castel-Sarrazin. **Seven million to connect Oust, a village of 523 people, with Seix, which has 1,200.** Six million to connect Prade with the hamlet of Olette, 747 people. Ninety million francs voted in 1895 alone for railways of purely local use.

The second danger is the shrinking of liberty, and he takes the mechanism from Spencer. Dictatorial measures multiply, restricting the citizen in two ways: more regulations every year constrain him in matters where he used to be free and compel acts he used to be able to decline, and heavier public and local burdens reduce the part of his earnings he can spend as he likes. Le Bon adds the piece Spencer left out. Every restrictive law increases the number, power and influence of the officials who apply it — **and the administrative caste is the one thing untouched by every transfer of authority, alone in having irresponsibility, impersonality and perpetuity.** There is no more oppressive despotism than that triple form.

**The shape of time**. A cycle, given in the last pages as the book's summary and its prophecy. At the dawn of a civilisation there's a swarm of men of various origins brought together by migration, invasion and conquest, of different blood and language and belief, with nothing binding them but the half-recognised law of a chief. They have the transient cohesion of crowds, their heroism, weakness, impulsiveness and violence. Nothing about them is stable. They are barbarians.

Then time does its work. Shared surroundings, repeated intermingling and the necessities of common life blend the dissimilar units into a race, with heredity fixing the common characteristics harder each generation. The crowd has become a people, and it leaves the barbarous state entirely only when it has acquired an ideal — and the nature of the ideal barely matters, whether it's the cult of Rome, the might of Athens or the triumph of Allah, so long as it gives every individual the same sentiments and thoughts.

The decline is the same road walked backwards. Once a civilisation reaches a certain strength and complexity it stops growing, and having stopped it is condemned to decline. The hour is always marked by the weakening of the ideal, and as that ideal pales, every religious, political and social structure built on it begins to shake. The individual's personality and intelligence may increase — and the collective egoism of the race is replaced by the egoism of the individual, with a weakening of character and less capacity for action. What was a people and a whole becomes an aggregate of individuals with no cohesion, held together for a while by traditions and institutions. **Divided by their interests, no longer capable of governing themselves, men need directing in their smallest acts, and the State takes on an absorbing influence.**

At the end the genius of the race disappears entirely, and what's left is a swarm of isolated individuals returned to their original condition — a crowd. The civilisation still has an outward front, the work of a long past, and it is an edifice crumbling to ruin with nothing holding it up, due to fall at the first storm. That is the last sentence of the book, and it explains why the man who wrote a manual of persuasion thought he was writing a warning.

*Read: lines 1702–1903.*

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, Book III `[SPECULATIVE]`

Paradigm-obvious in 1895.

The crowd-state as barbarism, and the race-spirit as the thing that lifts a people out of it. Stated as a law in the first chapter and used as the frame of the last one.

Colonial arithmetic as the natural measure of a statesman's worth. The indictment of Clemenceau is written in lost territories — Tonkin, Madagascar, the Lower Niger, Egypt — and expects the reader to agree that losing an empire is the injury.

Crimes of passion as a lesser category. The jury's leniency towards the abandoned girl who throws vitriol is offered as instinctive good sense, and the reasoning — that it frightens seducers in advance — passes without comment.

Elections as a thing money buys. Three million francs for Boulanger's repeated elections is cited from the donors' own admissions, as a fact rather than a scandal.

Paradigm-breaking, and the cost is what marks it.

Keeping the jury while saying the jury cannot reason. Everything in his own account argues for abolishing it, and he keeps it because the alternative is a caste under no control. **The cost is that he has to concede crowds are correctable and castes are not**, which cuts against the hereditary fixity the rest of the book runs on.

Keeping universal suffrage after describing electors as unable to form opinions. He builds the whole case against it and then refuses the conclusion, on the ground that restricting the vote would change nothing and would add the tyranny of castes. Forty academicians voting no better than forty water-carriers is the line, and **it costs him the aristocracy of intelligence that the Introduction to the book leans on.**

Calling the *juge d'instruction*'s warrant the equivalent of a *lettre de cachet*. He is attacking the administrative class of his own republic in a book his republic's enemies would enjoy, and he names the case and the stupidity.

Refusing to call the September massacres criminal. The refusal is consistent with his psychology and it is also the sentence that would follow him. **The cost is a book that can be read as an excuse**, and he supplies the excuse in the same paragraphs as the benches for the ladies.

Ending a study of crowd psychology with a prophecy of civilisational death. Nothing in the method licenses it and he does it anyway, in a summary he announces as a summary.

## Book III, Ch. 2 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the cook at the Bastille. He came to see what was happening. He is kicked by accident. A stranger proposes that he should be the one to cut the governor's throat, the crowd acclaims it, and he now believes the act is patriotic and that he is owed a medal. Somebody hands him a sword. It won't cut.

The moment that matters is the one Le Bon passes over. **Between the blunt sword and the knife in his pocket there is a pause**, and in that pause a man who cuts meat for a living decides to go and get his own tool.

Le Bon's counsel to him is nothing, because Le Bon's finding is that he is not there. The act is a suggestion carried out by an automaton, criminal legally and not psychologically, and there is nobody in the pause to advise.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/ahimsa-as-dharma-bedrock-with-carved-exceptions|non-harm as bedrock with carved exceptions]]** would go straight at the pause and would not accept that it was empty. The tradition's structure is the point: harm is the floor, and the exceptions to it are *carved* — specified in advance, narrow, attached to office and to circumstance, and known before the day arrives. A cook has no such exception. He is not an executioner, he holds no office, and nothing has been carved for him. **The counsel is that the exception has to exist before the crowd names you**, because a rule invented in the moment by three hundred people is not an exception, it is the crowd's appetite wearing the shape of one. What the unanimity supplied was permission. What it could not supply was standing.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/judge-by-effects-not-intentions|judging by effects rather than intentions]]** would leave the pause alone and go after the medal. This man's defence is entirely a claim about his own intention — patriotic, dutiful, deserving. So is the slaughterers' defence a week later, when they go to the authorities to ask for a reward. The doctrine is blunt about that: intention is the thing least available to inspection and most available to invention, and the only report you can trust is what actually happened to somebody. **On that test the week produced twelve hundred corpses, fifty of them children between twelve and seventeen**, and every good intention in it is irrelevant.

They disagree about where a person can still be reached. The first says the moment of decision is real and can be prepared for years in advance, by knowing exactly which harms you are licensed to do. The second says the moment can't be trusted at all and only the effects can be counted.

**Where they converge is on the thing Le Bon builds his defence out of.** He treats the unanimous approval of fellow citizens as what makes the cook's conviction natural, and therefore as what excuses it. Both advisors read the same fact as aggravating rather than mitigating. **Unanimity is what removed the last thing that might have stopped him**, and a doctrine that has already fixed the exceptions, or that counts only the bodies, is a doctrine designed to survive exactly that.

## Book III, Ch. 3 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: persuading a body whose members are not equally worth persuading.

The finding is that they are not, and that the working number is very small. One or two energetic men are enough to carry the rest of a jury, and the counsel's real job is to find them and please them. **A man in a crowd whom you have succeeded in pleasing is on the point of being convinced**, and will then accept as excellent nearly any argument you offer him.

The mechanism separates two things that usually get run together. Persuading somebody of a proposition is slow, contestable, and often impossible. Making somebody willing to be persuaded by you is fast and has nothing to do with the proposition. Lachaud spent three-quarters of an hour on the seventh juryman with his best arguments and moved him not at all. He moved him in four seconds by noticing the sun in the man's eyes and asking the court for a curtain.

Scope conditions. This works where the body deliberates together, where a few members are visibly more energetic than the others, and where the decision-maker can be observed while the case is being made. It fails where members decide separately and never meet — nobody carries anybody. It fails where the leading spirits can't be identified, which is why the technique needs a room and faces in it. And it fails on Le Bon's own evidence where the member has a fixed prior interest: the Deputy whose electors distil alcohol cannot be reached by any orator alive.

The general form. **In a deliberating body, identify the two or three who will carry the rest, and spend your effort on being acceptable to them rather than on being right in front of everybody.** Modern equivalent: any committee, panel or board where a case is presented live. The reason the technique keeps working is that it costs the persuaded man nothing to admit — the seventh juryman did not change his mind about anything, and he was won.

The uncomfortable half is what it says about the verdicts. If two energetic men carry a jury, and juries reached identical verdicts whether they were composed of professors or of small tradesmen, then the composition never mattered because the mechanism was never about composition. **The institution is stable because the process is the same in every room**, which is an argument for its predictability and not for its accuracy.

## Book III, Ch. 4 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

The live alternative here is the one his readers were actually proposing, and he names it to kill it: restrict the suffrage to the intellectually capable.

He rejects it on a mechanism rather than on principle, which is what makes the rejection interesting. In a crowd, men level to the same point, so on general questions forty academicians vote no better than forty water-carriers. Knowing Greek, or being an architect or a veterinary surgeon, confers no special intelligence about social questions. And the economists — highly educated, mostly professors — have never agreed on protection or on bimetallism.

The counterfactual he refuses to run is the one his own examples set up. **He never asks what a restricted electorate would have done differently**, except to assert that the re-establishment of the Empire would have happened anyway. That assertion is doing a great deal of work and is offered without support, which is the failure mode Book I warned about: a claim about a vote that never happened, stated in the register of a finding.

The constructed alternative worth tracing is a third one, which nobody in 1895 was proposing and which the chapter's own material suggests. The committees are what actually decide, and their leading men are publicans with credit over their working-class electors. **So the binding constraint on French elections in this account is not who may vote but who may be a candidate**, and the price of that is three million francs. A reform aimed at candidacy and at committee finance would leave universal suffrage intact and change the outcomes — which is precisely the reform his frame cannot generate, because institutions are labels and only the genius of the race decides.

The second-order consequence is where it gets expensive. He tells the reader that opposing the dogma of popular sovereignty is like arguing with a cyclone, and that time alone acts on it. That is a counsel of passivity issued to the only people positioned to act, and it is the same counsel the Preface gave about reform generally. **Between the Preface and this chapter, the book has advised a governing class to leave the electorate alone, leave the institutions alone, and wait** — and then it ends by predicting that the civilisation falls at the first storm.

## Book III, Ch. 5 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: voting on a spending measure when the cost is deferred and the credit is immediate.

The mechanism is a ratchet, and Le Bon draws it with no economics in it at all. A member proposes pensions for all workers or a rise for some class of State employees. Every other Deputy knows this strains the budget and will require new taxes. None of them can vote against it, because the consequences of the spending are remote and will never be traced to him personally, while the consequences of a negative vote will be perfectly visible at his next election. **The asymmetry is not in the merits. It is in the timing.**

The second half is the part that makes it permanent. Local grants can't be opposed either, because each Deputy can only get the railway his constituency wants by voting for everybody else's. So the ratchet doesn't need anyone to believe in the spending. It needs only that each man's own grant depends on his assent to all the others.

The numbers make it concrete in a way an argument couldn't. Seven million francs to connect a village of 523 people to a town of 1,200. Six million to reach a hamlet of 747. Ninety million in one year for railways of purely local use. Nobody in the chamber thinks those are worth building.

Scope conditions. This holds where costs are borne collectively and benefits are local and named, where the decision-maker faces a periodic re-selection by the beneficiaries, and where the horizon of the cost is longer than the horizon of the selection. It fails where a cost lands visibly on the same people who get the benefit, and it fails where somebody who won't face re-election can refuse.

The general form. **Where the benefit is local and named and the cost is national and deferred, no member of the deciding body can vote no, and unanimity for a measure nobody wants is the equilibrium.** Modern equivalent: any legislature that appropriates by district, and any organisation whose budget is set by the people who spend it.

The finding underneath it is Le Bon's alone and he barely marks it. He has just spent five chapters explaining decisions by suggestion, contagion and prestige — and here, in the one place where he traces a mechanism with no crowd psychology in it whatever, he produces the most durable prediction in the book. **The mechanism needs no unconscious, no heredity and no hypnosis.** It works on rational men counting the dates.

# What 1951 Took For Granted — Hoffer, Preface and Part One

> **The Preface and the three chapters of Part One of Eric Hoffer, *The True Believer: Thoughts on the Nature of Mass Movements* (1951)** — a tomato and a nightshade sharing a family, a mother in the Russian pale saying she'll be fine whichever of her two sons turns out to be right, Röhm boasting he can turn the reddest Communist into a glowing nationalist in four weeks, and English lords enclosing the commons in a revolution made by rich men. Read from `RAW/books/The True Believer.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run. Hoffer numbers his chapters in roman numerals across four parts; the runs follow his numbering.
>
> **The second half of this build changes country, class and decade.** Le Bon was a French physician of independent means writing in 1895 for a governing class frightened of universal suffrage. Hoffer was an American longshoreman who worked the San Francisco docks, writing in 1951 with the camps and the purges behind him and the Cold War in front. He is not addressing rulers, and he asks the reader to notice that. **The 1951 assumptions surface anyway** — the godless age, the Communist as the live threat, and one sentence about the American South that the book passes over in a clause.

## Preface — The tomato and the nightshade

**What is real**. A family, in the botanist's sense, and the qualifier is the whole preface.[^1] The book deals with peculiarities common to all mass movements — religious, revolutionary, nationalist — and it doesn't claim they're identical. It claims they share essential characteristics that give them a family likeness.

He then defines the word so nobody can misuse it. The tomato and the nightshade both belong to the Solanaceae. One is nutritious and the other poisonous, and they have so many traits of shape, structure and function in common that even a non-botanist senses the kinship. **Saying that mass movements have much in common doesn't imply they're equally beneficial or equally poisonous.**

**What a person is**. A creature whose fanaticism can be studied apart from what he's fanatical about. There are obvious differences between the fanatical Christian, the fanatical Muslim, the fanatical nationalist, the fanatical Communist and the fanatical Nazi — and the fanaticism that drives all of them can be looked at as one thing. So can the force pushing them towards expansion and world dominion. There's a uniformity in every kind of dedication, faith, pursuit of power, unity and self-sacrifice.

The sentence that follows is the book's method in a line. There are vast differences in the contents of holy causes and doctrines, and a certain uniformity in the factors that make them effective. Anyone who, like Pascal, finds precise reasons for the effectiveness of Christian doctrine has also found the reasons for the effectiveness of Communist, Nazi and nationalist doctrine. However different the holy causes people die for, they perhaps die basically for the same thing.

**What makes things happen**. Frustration, working from inside without needing to be organised. The working hypothesis starts from a fact: the frustrated predominate among the early adherents of all mass movements, and they usually join of their own accord. From that he assumes two things. First, that frustration on its own, with no proselytising from outside, can generate most of the peculiar characteristics of the true believer. Second, that an effective conversion technique consists basically in the inculcation and fixation of proclivities and responses **already native to the frustrated mind**.

That second assumption is what makes the book different from every other one in this build. The technique isn't installing something. It's finding what's there and fixing it in place.

**How you know**. By testing the hypothesis against two things and saying so in advance. He had to inquire into the ills that afflict the frustrated, how they react against them, how far those reactions match the responses of the true believer, and how they help a movement rise. And he had to examine the practices of contemporary movements, where conversion techniques had been perfected and applied, to see whether they corroborate the view that a proselytising movement deliberately fosters a frustrated state of mind in its adherents.

**What is worth having**. Insight into the true believer, for people who will have to live near him. He gives the reason in a sentence that reverses what a 1951 reader might expect. **Though ours is a godless age, it is the very opposite of irreligious.** The true believer is everywhere on the march, and by converting and by antagonising he is shaping the world in his own image. Whether we line up with him or against him, it's well to know what we can about his nature and his potential.

**How people should relate**. Under two conditions the movements all produce. Every mass movement generates in its adherents a readiness to die and a proclivity for united action. Every one of them, whatever it preaches, breeds fanaticism, enthusiasm, fervent hope, hatred and intolerance. Every one can release a powerful flow of activity in some departments of life. And every one demands blind faith and single-hearted allegiance.

**The shape of time**. Phased, and he narrows his subject to one phase. The book concerns itself chiefly with the active, revivalist phase, which is dominated by the true believer — the man of fanatical faith ready to sacrifice his life for a holy cause. The genesis and nature of that man is what he's tracing. Everything about the later phases is deferred to the last part of the book.

He closes with a disclaimer worth keeping, because most of the book's later readers ignored it. The book passes no judgments and expresses no preferences; it merely tries to explain, and the explanations are all theories, offered as suggestions and arguments even when the tone sounds categorical. Then Montaigne, whose line he borrows to say that everything here is talk and none of it advice: **I should not speak so boldly if it were my due to be believed.**

*Read: lines 100–125.*

---

## Ch. I — Peter the Great failed for want of a holy cause

**What makes things happen**. Enthusiasm, without which large change doesn't happen at all.[^2] It's obvious that people join a rising revolutionary movement for the prospect of sudden spectacular change. Less obvious is that religious and nationalist movements are vehicles of change too. Some kind of widespread excitement seems to be needed for vast and rapid change, and it doesn't matter whether the exhilaration comes from an expectation of untold riches or from an active movement. In America the spectacular changes since the Civil War happened in an atmosphere charged with enthusiasm born of fabulous opportunities for self-advancement. Where self-advancement can't serve as the engine, other sources of enthusiasm have to be found.

He puts the point about religion in a phrase worth pausing on. **A religion's conservatism — its orthodoxy — is the inert coagulum of a once highly reactive sap.** A rising religious movement is all change and experiment, open to new views and techniques from every quarter. Islam when it emerged was an organising and modernising medium. Christianity was a civilising and modernising influence among the savage tribes of Europe. The Crusades and the Reformation both helped shake the Western world out of medieval stagnation.

**How people should relate**. Through the art he names and calls *religiofication* — the art of turning practical purposes into holy causes. The case is Peter the Great, and it's the best one in the run because the man had everything except that. He was probably the equal in dedication, power and ruthlessness of many of the most successful revolutionary and nationalist leaders. And he failed at his chief purpose, which was to turn Russia into a Western nation. **He failed because he did not infuse the Russian masses with any soul-stirring enthusiasm.** He either didn't think it necessary or didn't know how to make his purpose a holy cause.

Which is why Hoffer finds it unsurprising that the Bolsheviks who wiped out the last Romanovs feel kinship with a Czar and a Romanov. Peter's purpose is now theirs, and they hope to succeed where he failed. The Bolshevik revolution may end up figuring in history as much an attempt to modernise a sixth of the world's surface as an attempt to build a Communist economy.

The comparisons run down a list, and the list is the argument. It was a genuine nationalist movement that let Atatürk modernise Turkey almost overnight. Egypt, untouched by any mass movement, modernises slowly and haltingly, though its rulers since Mehmed Ali have welcomed Western ideas and its contacts with the West have been many and intimate. Zionism is an instrument for renovating a backward country and turning shopkeepers and brain workers into farmers, labourers and soldiers. Had Chiang Kai-shek known how to set a genuine mass movement in motion, or even sustain the nationalist feeling the Japanese invasion kindled, he might now be acting as the renovator of China — and because he didn't know how, he was easily shoved aside by masters of the art.

The British case is the control, and Hoffer states it as a live question rather than a finding. The Labour government is trying to change the economy and the way of life of forty-nine million people in an atmosphere singularly free of fervour, exaltation and wild hope, and he wonders whether its difficulties are partly that. The decent leaders of the party are shy of revolutionary enthusiasm out of revulsion at what contemporary movements have looked like.

**What a person is**. Someone who locates the shaping forces of his life outside himself, and he thinks this holds for the successful as much as the failed. Success and failure get tied in our minds to the state of things around us, so people with a sense of fulfilment think it a good world and want to conserve it while the frustrated want radical change. The tendency persists even when our condition plainly comes from personal qualities — ability, character, appearance, health. Thoreau supplies the picture: let anything ail a man so that he can't perform his functions, **even a pain in his bowels, and he forthwith sets about reforming the world.**

The surprising half is the successful. However much they pride themselves on foresight, fortitude and thrift, at bottom they're convinced their success came from a fortunate combination of circumstances. Their self-confidence is never absolute, because they're never sure they know all the ingredients that made them. **The outside world looks to them like a precariously balanced mechanism, and while it ticks in their favour they're afraid to touch it.** So resistance to change and the desire for it spring from the same conviction, and either can be violent.

**What is worth having**. A sense of power, and then faith in the future, and the second matters more. Discontent alone doesn't produce a desire for change. People awed by their surroundings don't think of change however miserable they are. When life is precarious enough to make it plain we can't control our circumstances, we stick to the proven and the familiar, and counteract insecurity by making existence a fixed routine — which gives us the illusion we've tamed the unpredictable.

The list of people who fear change is the good part, because of who's on it. Fisherfolk, nomads and farmers who contend with wilful weather. The creative worker who depends on inspiration. The savage awed by his surroundings. **And the abjectly poor, who also stand in awe of the world and are not hospitable to change**, because it's a dangerous life when hunger and cold are at your heels. There is a conservatism of the destitute as deep as the conservatism of the privileged, and it holds a social order together just as firmly.

Against that he sets the men who rush into vast undertakings, who usually feel they possess some irresistible power. The generation that made the French Revolution had an extravagant conception of the omnipotence of human reason; Tocqueville says humanity had never been prouder of itself nor had more faith in its own omnipotence, and joined to that was a universal thirst for change that came unbidden to every mind. Lenin and the Bolsheviks had blind faith in Marxist doctrine. The Nazis had nothing that potent, and had faith in an infallible leader and in a new technique — and Hoffer doubts National Socialism would have moved so fast without the electrifying conviction that blitzkrieg and propaganda had made Germany irresistible.

Then the correction that makes power secondary. You'd expect that having power would produce a cocky attitude and openness to change, and it isn't always so; the powerful can be as timid as the weak. **What counts more than instruments of power is faith in the future.** Where power isn't joined to that faith it gets used mainly to fend off the new and preserve things as they are. And extravagant hope with no real power behind it produces the most reckless daring, because the hopeful can draw strength from the most ridiculous sources — a slogan, a word, a button. No faith is potent unless it has a millennial component, and an effective doctrine must claim to be a key to the book of the future as well as a source of power.

Which yields the instruction to anyone who wants to change a nation. It can't be done by breeding and captaining discontent, by demonstrating that the changes are reasonable and desirable, or by coercing people into a new way of life. **They must know how to kindle and fan an extravagant hope**, and it doesn't matter whether it's of a heavenly kingdom, heaven on earth, plunder, fabulous achievement or world dominion. If the Communists win Europe it won't be because they know how to stir discontent or spread hatred. It'll be because they know how to preach hope.

**The shape of time**. Not a fixed direction but an attitude towards what's ahead, and it sorts people better than class does. Fear of the future makes us cling to the present; faith in it makes us receptive to change. Rich and poor, strong and weak, the accomplished and the unaccomplished can all be afraid. When the present seems so good that the most you can expect is its continuation, change can only mean deterioration — so men of outstanding achievement and people living full happy lives usually set their faces against drastic innovation. The conservatism of invalids and of people past middle age comes from the same place; they're watching for signs of decay and feel any change is likelier to be for the worse. **And the abjectly poor are without faith in the future too. It looks to them like a booby trap buried on the road ahead**, so one steps gingerly, and to change anything is to ask for trouble.

**How people should relate — the hopeful, whoever they are**. It makes no difference who is seized with a wild hope. An enthusiastic intellectual, a land-hungry farmer, a get-rich-quick speculator, a sober merchant, a plain workingman, a noble lord — they all proceed recklessly with the present, wreck it if necessary, and make a new world. So there can be revolutions by the privileged as easily as by the underprivileged.

The two English examples are the evidence, and they're chosen to make the reader uncomfortable. In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries the woollen industry prospered, grazing became more profitable than cropping, and the landowners drove off their tenants and enclosed the commons. The lords and nobles were upsetting the social order and breaking down ancient law and custom, sometimes by violence and often by pressure and intimidation. The second is the Industrial Revolution, where the potential of mechanisation set the minds of manufacturers and merchants on fire and they began a revolution as extreme and radical as ever inflamed the minds of sectarians — and these respectable, God-fearing citizens changed the face of England beyond recognition in a short time.

The warning attached is one of the best sentences in the book. When hopes and dreams are loose in the streets, it's well for the timid to lock doors, shutter windows and lie low until the wrath has passed. There is often a monstrous incongruity between the hopes, however noble and tender, and the action that follows them. **It is as if ivied maidens and garlanded youths were to herald the four horsemen of the apocalypse.**

**How you know**. By a recipe with four items, given at the end of the chapter, and by the fourth item in particular. For men to plunge headlong into vast change they must be intensely discontented and yet not destitute. They must feel that some potent doctrine, infallible leader or new technique gives them access to irresistible power. They must have an extravagant conception of what the future holds.

And finally they must be wholly ignorant of the difficulties involved. **Experience is a handicap.** The men who started the French Revolution were entirely without political experience, and so were the Bolsheviks, the Nazis and the revolutionaries in Asia. The experienced man of affairs is a latecomer who joins when the movement is already a going concern. Hoffer suspects it's the Englishman's political experience that keeps him shy of mass movements.

*Read: lines 130–203.*

---

## Ch. II — What looks like giving a hand

**What a person is**. Somebody who wants out of himself, which is the hinge of the whole book.[^3] There's a fundamental difference between the appeal of a mass movement and the appeal of a practical organisation. The practical organisation offers chances of self-advancement and appeals to self-interest. **A mass movement, in its active phase, appeals not to those intent on advancing a cherished self but to those who crave to be rid of an unwanted self.** It attracts and holds people not by satisfying the desire for self-advancement but by satisfying the passion for self-renunciation.

The state he's describing is specific. People who see their lives as irremediably spoiled can't find a worthwhile purpose in getting on. The prospect of an individual career can't move them to a mighty effort or evoke single-minded dedication. They regard self-interest as tainted, unclean and unlucky, and anything undertaken under the auspices of the self seems doomed in advance. Nothing rooted in the self can be good or noble.

What they want instead is a new life, a rebirth — or failing that, a chance to acquire new elements of pride, confidence, hope and worth by identifying with a holy cause. A movement supplies both. Full converts are reborn in its close-knit collective body; sympathisers get pride, confidence and purpose by identifying with its efforts and prospects.

**What is worth having**. Substitutes, and the chapter is a list of them. Faith in a holy cause is to a considerable extent a substitute for lost faith in ourselves. **The less justified a man is in claiming excellence for his own self, the more ready he is to claim all excellence for his nation, his religion, his race or his holy cause.** A man is likely to mind his own business when it's worth minding; when it isn't, he takes his mind off his own meaningless affairs by minding other people's — in gossip, snooping and meddling, and also in feverish interest in communal, national and racial affairs. In running away from ourselves, he writes, we either fall on our neighbour's shoulder or fly at his throat.

Then the sentence that does the most work in the book. **The burning conviction that we have a holy duty toward others is often a way of attaching our drowning selves to a passing raft. What looks like giving a hand is often a holding on for dear life.** Take away our holy duties and our lives are puny and meaningless. There's no doubt we gain enormously in self-esteem by exchanging a self-centred life for a selfless one — and the vanity of the selfless, even those who practise the utmost humility, is boundless.

**The shape of time**. The most important substitute is a future, and it hurts most where people expect one. A movement offers a substitute for individual hope, and that's especially effective in a society soaked in the idea of progress, because there tomorrow looms large and having nothing to look forward to is the more painful. Rauschning on pre-Hitler Germany is the evidence: the feeling of having come to the end of all things was one of the worst troubles we endured after that lost war.

In a modern society, he writes, people can live without hope only when kept dazed and out of breath by incessant hustling. The despair of unemployment comes not just from the threat of destitution but from the sudden view of a vast nothingness ahead. So the unemployed are likelier to follow the peddlers of hope than the handers-out of relief. And the usual charge — that movements dope their followers with future hope while cheating them of present enjoyment — misses what the frustrated are like. For them the present is spoiled beyond repair, comforts and pleasures can't make it whole, and no content or comfort can arise in their minds except from hope.

**How people should relate**. Extravagantly, because a moderate substitute doesn't work. When our own interests and prospects don't seem worth living for, we're in desperate need of something outside us to live for. All dedication, devotion, loyalty and self-surrender are at bottom a desperate clinging to something that might give worth to a spoiled life. So the embrace has to be passionate and extreme. We can have qualified confidence in ourselves; the faith we have in a nation, a religion, a race or a holy cause has to be extravagant and uncompromising, because a substitute embraced in moderation can't efface the self we want to forget.

Which gives him the line about dying that the rest of the book turns on. We can't be sure we have something worth living for unless we're ready to die for it. The readiness to die is evidence, to ourselves and to others, that what we took as a substitute for a missed or spoiled first choice is indeed the best there ever was.

**How you know**. By watching what kind of person a movement starts attracting. Among early adherents there are adventurers hoping the movement will whirl them to fame and power, and some who join corporations and orthodox parties do show selfless dedication. The rule still holds: a practical concern can't survive unless it satisfies self-interest, and a rising movement's growth depends on its capacity to evoke and satisfy the passion for self-renunciation.

**So the diagnostic is a change in the intake.** When a movement begins attracting people interested in their individual careers, it has passed its vigorous stage and is no longer moulding a new world but possessing and preserving the present. It stops being a movement and becomes an enterprise. Hitler is quoted saying the same thing from inside: the more posts and offices a movement has to hand out, the more inferior stuff it attracts, until the political hangers-on so outnumber the rest that the honest fighter of former days no longer recognises the old movement — and when that happens, the mission of such a movement is done for.

*Read: lines 204–249.*

---

## Ch. III — Whatever happens, I shall be well off

**What is real**. A readiness that exists before any particular doctrine does.[^4] When people are ripe for a mass movement they're usually ripe for any effective movement, not solely for one with a particular programme. In pre-Hitler Germany it was often a toss-up whether a restless youth would join the Communists or the Nazis. In the overcrowded pale of Czarist Russia the simmering Jewish population was ripe for both revolution and Zionism, and in the same family one son would join the revolutionaries and another the Zionists.

Weizmann's mother supplies the sentence, and it's the cleanest evidence in the chapter because it comes from a kitchen rather than a theory. **Whatever happens, I shall be well off. If Shemuel is right, we shall all be happy in Russia; and if Chaim is right, then I shall go to live in Palestine.** One son a revolutionary and one a Zionist, and a mother who can see they're answering the same question.

**What a person is**. Still convertible after conversion, which is the chapter's sharpest claim. The receptivity doesn't always stop once a potential true believer has become an ardent convert. Where movements compete violently, converts — even the most zealous — not infrequently shift allegiance from one to the other. **A Saul turning into Paul is neither a rarity nor a miracle.**

The competitors knew it about each other. Hitler looked on German Communists as potential National Socialists: the petit bourgeois Social Democrat and the trade-union boss will never make a National Socialist, and the Communist always will. Röhm boasted he could turn the reddest Communist into a glowing nationalist in four weeks. And from the other side, Radek looked on the Nazi Brown Shirts as a reserve of future Communist recruits.

**What makes things happen**. Two consequences follow, and Hoffer numbers them. All mass movements are competitive, so one movement's gain in adherents is every other movement's loss. And all mass movements are interchangeable: a religious movement may develop into a social revolution or a nationalist movement, a social revolution into militant nationalism or a religious movement, a nationalist movement into either of the others.

**How people should relate**. Under whichever mixture happens to be available, since pure cases are rare. The exodus of the Hebrews from Egypt was a slave revolt, a religious movement and a nationalist movement at once. The militant nationalism of the Japanese is essentially religious. The French Revolution was a new religion with its dogma — the sacred principles, *liberté et sainte égalité* — its form of worship adapted from Catholic ceremonial for the civic festivals, and its saints, the heroes and martyrs of liberty. **It was also a nationalist movement: in 1792 the legislative assembly decreed that altars should be raised everywhere reading *the citizen is born, lives and dies for la Patrie*.**

The Reformation had a revolutionary aspect that came out in peasant risings, and was national as well. Luther supplies the proof in his own voice: in the eyes of the Italians we Germans are merely low Teutonic swine, they exploit us like charlatans and suck the country to the marrow — wake up, Germany. And the religious character of the Bolshevik and Nazi revolutions is generally recognised. The hammer and sickle and the swastika are in a class with the cross, the ceremonial of their parades is the ceremonial of a religious procession, and they have articles of faith, saints, martyrs and holy sepulchres.

**What is worth having**. A way of stopping a movement, and his answer is that you usually have to supply another one. A social revolution can be stopped by promoting a religious or nationalist movement. Where Catholicism has recovered its mass-movement spirit it counteracts the spread of communism. In Japan nationalism canalised every movement of social protest. **In our South, he writes, the movement of racial solidarity acts as a preventive of social upheaval** — a clause offered in passing as a technical illustration, in a book published in 1951, alongside the French in Canada and the Boers in South Africa.

The method comes with a bill attached, and the warning is aimed at people who thought they were being sensible. Substituting one movement for another isn't safe and doesn't come cheap, and it's well for those who want to preserve the present not to play with mass movements — because it always fares ill with the present when a genuine one is on the march. **In pre-war Italy and Germany, practical businessmen acted in an entirely logical manner when they encouraged Fascist and Nazi movements in order to stop communism. In doing so they promoted their own liquidation.**

**How you know**. By what else does the same job, which is how he finds the safer substitutes. In general, any arrangement that discourages atomistic individualism, or makes self-forgetting easier, or offers chances for action and new beginnings, tends to counteract the rise of mass movements. The curious one he stops on is migration.

Emigration offers some of what the frustrated hope to find in a movement — change, and a chance at a new beginning — and the same types who swell the ranks of a rising movement are also likely to take a chance to emigrate. **He thinks it plausible that if the United States and the British Empire had welcomed mass migration from Europe after the First World War, there might have been neither a Fascist nor a Nazi revolution.** In America, free and easy migration over a vast continent contributed to social stability.

**The shape of time**. Movement and migration keep turning into each other, and he says it's often hard to tell which came first. Because of the quality of their human material, mass migrations are fertile ground for genuine movements. The migration of the Hebrews from Egypt developed into a religious and nationalist movement. The migrations of the barbarians in the declining days of Rome were more than shifts of population — the barbarians were relatively few, and once they invaded a country they were joined by the oppressed and dissatisfied in every walk of life, which he quotes as **a social revolution started and masked by a superficial foreign conquest.**

The closing generalisation ties the two together. Every mass movement is in a sense a migration, a movement towards a promised land, and where it's feasible an actual migration takes place — the Puritans, the Anabaptists, the Mormons, the Dukhobors, the Zionists. Migration in the mass strengthens the spirit and unity of a movement, and whether it takes the form of foreign conquest, crusade, pilgrimage or the settlement of new land, most active movements practise it.

*Read: lines 250–301.*

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, Preface to Chapter III `[SPECULATIVE]`

Paradigm-obvious in 1951.

Communism as the live case. Every general claim gets a Communist illustration alongside the Nazi one, and the reader is assumed to be watching Europe with an interest in whether it goes. The question *if the Communists win Europe* is asked as an open one.

Modernisation as the thing backward countries need and the only question being how to get it. Turkey, Egypt, China, Zionist Palestine and Russia are all scored against it. The category is not examined once.

The clause about the American South. Racial solidarity is named as a movement that prevents social upheaval, filed next to Canadian and Boer examples, in a book that has already declared it passes no judgments. **The botanist's neutrality of the Preface is doing real work here** — the tomato-and-nightshade rule licenses listing it without comment, and in 1951 nobody was going to require the comment.

Psychological frustration as a sufficient explanation for political behaviour. The whole hypothesis is that a state of mind produces the movements, and the period's confidence in that move is why it needs no defence.

Paradigm-breaking, and the cost is what marks it.

Refusing to sort movements into good and bad in a book published six years after the camps were opened. He builds the refusal into the Preface with the nightshade, and repeats it with Montaigne. **The cost is that his own century's worst case becomes a specimen**, and the sentence about businessmen promoting their own liquidation reads as diagnosis where a 1951 reader wanted judgment.

Putting the conservatism of the destitute beside the conservatism of the privileged. This costs him the left's account of who makes revolutions, in the same paragraph where it costs him the right's. **The abjectly poor are not revolutionary material in this book**, and neither is anybody comfortable.

Saying that experience is a handicap. He needs it for the recipe — the men who start these things must be ignorant of the difficulties — and it disqualifies the class of people who write books about politics, himself included by implication.

Naming the self-renouncer's vanity as boundless. That is aimed at the sincere, not the cynical, and it is the least forgivable sentence in the run for a reader who thinks of himself as devoted to something.

Locating the origin of the true believer in the man himself rather than in the demagogue. Le Bon's crowd is made by a leader; Hoffer's true believer arrives pre-made and goes looking. **The cost is that there is nobody to blame and nothing to ban**, which is a much less usable finding than the one everyone wanted in 1951.

## Ch. I — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: judging whether a proposed large change will actually happen.

The recipe is four items and the fourth is the interesting one. The people who will carry it through must be intensely discontented and yet not destitute. They must believe some doctrine, leader or technique gives them access to irresistible power. They must hold an extravagant conception of the future. **And they must be wholly ignorant of the difficulties involved.**

The mechanism behind the fourth item is that accurate estimation and reckless commitment can't sit in the same head. Experience shows a man what a thing costs, and knowing what it costs is what stops him. So the movement's early phase requires people who have never done anything like it — and the experienced man of affairs shows up later, once it's a going concern, which is also roughly when the movement stops being one.

Scope conditions. This describes what's needed to *start* a vast change, not to complete one. It fails as a test of whether the change is a good idea, and Hoffer never claims otherwise. It also depends on the change being genuinely large: a reform inside an existing arrangement needs none of this, which is why the Labour government could attempt one without fervour and why he thinks that's why it was struggling.

The general form. **A large change requires people who cannot estimate its cost, so the presence of competent, experienced leadership early on is evidence that the change will be smaller than announced.** Modern equivalent: any transformation programme staffed entirely by people who have done it before. They will deliver something, and it will not be the thing in the announcement.

The uncomfortable corollary is the one Peter the Great pays for. He had power, ruthlessness and a clear correct objective, and he could not make it holy, so it did not take. **Competence was not the missing ingredient and neither was authority.** What was missing was a story that made a practical purpose into something worth dying for — and Hoffer's word for supplying that, *religiofication*, is deliberately ugly because the thing is available to anybody.

## Ch. II — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the man this chapter is about. He is not poor and not desperate. He has decided his own life is spoiled past repair, he finds the thought of his own advancement faintly disgusting, and what he wants is to be rid of himself. A movement is available and will take him. Hoffer's account of what happens next is that he gets a rebirth in a close-knit collective body, and that his new faith has to be extravagant, because a substitute embraced in moderation cannot efface the self he wants to forget.

Hoffer offers him no alternative. The book explains and passes no judgments, so the man is described and left where he stands.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/atma-nivedana-total-self-surrender|total self-surrender]]** would say the craving is not the error and would refuse to talk him out of it. This tradition has a name for handing over everything from the body to the pure self, and it puts it last on a list of nine practices rather than first. The image it uses is a farmer who has just sold his cow: the buyer leads it away down the road, and what the man feels in his chest, almost against his will, is relief. **No more dawn feedings, no more worrying about the vet bill.** That is the same relief Hoffer's man is after, and this advisor would say he is right to want it.

The counsel is about what he hands it to, and about the order. Self-surrender comes ninth because the eight before it are what make the ninth safe — and what he hands himself to is not a body of people, a programme or a leader. **A movement can take delivery of a self and then spend it**, which is the one thing the thing you surrender to must not be able to do. The test this advisor would give him is simple and hard: after the surrender, is *my effort* still a category that applies? If he is now working harder than ever, he has not been relieved of himself. He has been recruited.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/anti-fanaticism-fanatics-cannot-work|Vivekananda's objection to fanatics]]** would not go near the man's soul and would go straight at his output. The complaint is not moral, it is practical: **fanatics cannot work, they waste three-fourths of their energy.** Something is wrong in society, and up jumps a man to denounce it, loudly and vindictively, gathering a following around the outrage. He feels like the most committed person in the room. He is burning most of his fuel on noise, and it is the level-headed, calm, practical man who actually works.

Which is a real answer to Hoffer's chapter, because it accepts the diagnosis and disputes the payoff. Yes, the man wants out of himself, and yes, the movement will take him. **What he will get is not effectiveness but the sensation of it**, and the difference shows up in what has actually changed a year later.

They disagree about whether the wanting is respectable. The first says it is the highest thing in the man and has been mishandled. The second treats it as a fuel leak.

**Where they converge is on the point Hoffer treats as settled.** He says the substitute has to be extravagant and uncompromising, because moderation cannot efface the self. Both advisors read extravagance as the symptom rather than the cure — one because a surrender that still requires effort has not happened, the other because heat and work are inversely related. **Neither would tell him to keep his self. Both would tell him that what the movement is offering is not the thing he came for.**

## Ch. III — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

The road not taken here is one Hoffer names, prices, and hands to the reader as a counterfactual: mass migration instead of mass movement.

The live alternative existed and was refused by particular governments. If the United States and the British Empire had welcomed mass migration from Europe after the First World War, he thinks there might have been neither a Fascist nor a Nazi revolution. The mechanism is that emigration supplies the same two goods a movement supplies — change, and a chance at a new beginning — to the same people. **The frustrated man who would join a movement is the frustrated man who would get on a boat.**

The counterfactual is worth running properly, because the chapter also supplies its own objection. Mass migrations are fertile ground for genuine movements, because of the quality of their human material, and it is often hard to tell where one ends and the other begins. The Hebrews leaving Egypt became a religious and national movement on the way. The barbarians entering the Empire were joined by the oppressed of every walk of life and turned into a social revolution masked as a conquest. **So the counsel is not that migration prevents movements. It is that migration disperses them across an ocean instead of concentrating them in a country that already has a state to capture.**

Which sharpens what was actually refused in the 1920s. The receiving countries had quota laws and thought they were declining a population. On Hoffer's reading they were declining a pressure valve, and the pressure stayed where it was and found the only other outlet available. He does not say this and his chapter contains every piece of it.

The second-order consequence is the ugly one, and he half-writes it in the next paragraph. If the goods a movement supplies can also be supplied by a boat, they can be supplied by other things too — by anything that discourages atomistic individualism, makes self-forgetting easier, or offers action and new beginnings. **That is a design specification for a society, and it is written in the same register as the specification for a movement.** The book that passes no judgments has just told you what to build.

# What 1951 Took For Granted — Hoffer, Part Two

> **The eight chapters of Part Two of Eric Hoffer, *The True Believer* (1951)** — a man just out of the army who cannot find the rhythm of his old life, radicals arriving in Moscow to build a new world and finding themselves absorbed by the problem of hunger and cold, society ladies financing Hitler years before their husbands had heard of him, and St Bernard breaking up so many homes that the abandoned wives founded a nunnery. Read from `RAW/books/The True Believer.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
>
> ⚠ **This is the part of the book that has aged hardest, and the runs report it rather than route around it.** Two passages in particular: a sentence about segregation in the American South offered as an illustration of minority psychology, and a page of advice to colonial powers on how to keep the ruled contented. Both are stated as findings, in a book that declares it passes no judgments. They are in the runs because the job is to record what a source took for granted.
