## Ch. XIV — It is essential to have a tangible enemy

**What makes things happen**. Hatred, which he calls the most accessible of all unifying agents.[^3] It pulls a man away from himself. It makes him oblivious of his own welfare and future. It frees him of jealousy and self-seeking. He becomes an anonymous particle craving to fuse with his like into one flaming mass. Heine's line is that what Christian love cannot do is achieved by a common hatred.

Then the sentence the chapter is built on. **Mass movements can rise without belief in a God, and never without belief in a devil.** The strength of a movement is usually proportionate to how vivid and tangible its devil is.

The evidence comes from the men who built the machinery. Hitler was asked whether the Jew must be destroyed. He answered no — we should then have to invent him, since it is essential to have a tangible enemy and not merely an abstract one. Voigt reports a Japanese mission that came to Berlin in 1932 to study National Socialism. Asked what he thought of the movement, one member said it was magnificent, and that he wished Japan could have something like it. **Only we can't, because we haven't got any Jews.** Hoffer adds that Chiang Kai-shek's worst failure was not finding a new devil once the Japanese enemy vanished.

**What is real**. A devil with the attributes of a god. He works through them one at a time. The ideal devil is one. Hitler's own line is that a great leader's genius lies in concentrating all hatred on a single foe. Adversaries far removed from each other must seem to belong to a single category. Behind England stands Israel, and behind France, and behind the United States. The ideal devil is also omnipotent and omnipresent. Every difficulty inside the movement is his work and every success a triumph over his plotting. **And the ideal devil is a foreigner.** A domestic enemy must be given a foreign ancestry first. German Jews were branded as foreigners. Russian aristocrats were given Varangian, Tartar or Western origins. French aristocrats became descendants of barbarous Germans while the commoners descended from civilised Gauls. English royalists were labelled Normans.

**What a person is**. Somebody looking for allies, and the direction of the search is the tell. We do not usually look for allies when we love. We often see those who love with us as rivals. **We always look for allies when we hate.** The puzzle is that the desire for allies is most pressing when the hatred has no visible grievance behind it.

His explanation is that unreasonable hatreds suppress an awareness of our own inadequacy and guilt. Self-contempt gets transmuted into hatred of others. There is then a determined effort to mask the switch, and the best mask is to find as many people as possible who hate the same way. **Much of our proselytising consists in infecting others with our particular brand of unreasonable hatred.** Even with a just grievance the hatred comes less from the wrong than from our own helplessness. That is why we despise and even pity tormentors we feel superior to, rather than hating them.

The released hatred often does not go to whoever caused it. Russians bullied by Stalin's police are easily inflamed against capitalist warmongers. Germans aggrieved by Versailles avenged themselves by exterminating Jews. Zulus oppressed by Boers butcher Hindus. White trash exploited by Dixiecrats lynch Blacks.

**How people should relate — guilt and its consequences**. The second engine is a guilty conscience. The causation runs the opposite way from what a reader expects. There is no surer way of infecting ourselves with hatred toward a man than by doing him a grave injustice. That others have a just grievance against us is a more potent reason for hating them than that we have one against them. Showing people their guilt does not make them humble. It stirs their arrogance and rouses a reckless aggressiveness. Self-righteousness is a loud din raised to drown the voice of guilt within.

Two rules follow, each in a line. To wrong those we hate adds fuel to the hatred. To treat an enemy with magnanimity blunts it. And the surest way to silence a guilty conscience is to convince ourselves that those we sinned against are depraved and deserve every punishment, even extermination. **We cannot pity those we have wronged, nor be indifferent to them.** We hate them, or we leave the door open to self-contempt.

He extends it to religion without softening it. A sublime religion generates a strong feeling of guilt. The contrast between loftiness of profession and imperfection of practice is unavoidable. And guilt promotes hate and brazenness. **So the more sublime the faith, the more virulent the hatred it breeds.**

**What is worth having — and what hating costs**. Here the chapter turns and takes something back. It is easier to hate an enemy with much good in him than one who is all bad, because we cannot hate those we despise. The Japanese admired Americans more than they were admired, so they could hate more fervently. Americans are poor haters in international affairs because of an innate feeling of superiority over foreigners. An American's hatred for a fellow American is far more virulent than anything he can raise against a foreigner. He notes that the backward South shows more xenophobia than the rest of the country. If Americans ever begin to hate foreigners wholeheartedly, it will mean they have lost confidence in their own way of life.

The admiration inside hatred then produces the costliest finding in the chapter. Every movement shapes itself after its specific devil. Christianity at its height realised the image of the antichrist. The Jacobins practised all the evils of the tyranny they rose against. Soviet Russia is realising the purest example of monopolistic capitalism. Hitler took the *Protocols of the Wise Men of Zion* for his guide and followed them down to the smallest detail. **The oppressed almost invariably shape themselves in the image of their hated oppressors.**

So the fanatic's influence runs far beyond his abilities. He shapes the world both by converting and by antagonising. Fanatical Christianity marked the ancient world by gaining adherents and by provoking a new ruthlessness in its pagan opponents. Hitler imposed himself by promoting Nazism and by forcing the democracies to become zealous and intolerant. **Hatred mobilises a community for defence, and it does not come cheap.** We pay for it by losing many of the values we set out to defend. Hitler sensed the admiration inside hatred and drew his own conclusion. The National Socialist should seek and deserve the violent hatred of his enemies, since the hostility he attracts is the best yardstick of his attitude.

**What makes things happen — the second unifier**. Imitation, ranked alongside obedience. A close-knit group is inconceivable without a diffusion of uniformity. The one-mindedness every movement prizes is achieved as much by copying as by command. Obedience itself is as much the imitation of an example as the following of a precept.

The frustrated are especially imitative, for a reason that follows from their burden. Wanting to shed an unwanted self, they seek either a new identity or a camouflage. Imitation supplies both. **The less satisfaction we get from being ourselves, the greater the desire to be like others.** We are readier to copy those different from us than those nearly like us. Lack of self-confidence works the same way. The more we mistrust our own judgment, the readier we are to follow an example.

His American case stings, and it is about his own country. Suppose the millions of immigrants had been superior people, the cream of the countries they left. There would have been not one United States but a mosaic of language and culture groups. **It was because most of them were the lowest and the poorest that the heterogeneous millions blended so fast.** They arrived wanting to shed an old-world identity. They were equipped with an unbounded capacity to imitate. The strangeness of the new country attracted rather than repelled them, and even the strange language helped, since having to learn to speak enhanced the illusion of being born anew.

Imitation is also a shortcut. We copy when we lack the time or the ability to work something out. So people in a hurry copy more readily, and hustling produces uniformity. Unification itself intensifies the capacity. A civilian drafted into a close-knit unit becomes more imitative than he was, because the unified man has no distinct self to resist influence.

That creates a vulnerability, and the movements know it. A thoroughly unified group is easily seduced and corrupted. So the preaching of every movement bristles with warnings against copying foreign models. Imitating outsiders is branded as treason. Whoever copies a foreigner insults the nation, like a spy who admits an enemy by a secret doorway. Some movements lead their following into the wilderness to let the new pattern settle undisturbed. And the imitativeness that creates the risk also gives great flexibility. That is why a united Japan or Turkey modernised so much faster than China or Iran.

**How you know — what propaganda can and cannot do**. Here he contradicts the discipline Le Bon founded, and he argues it from the record. We exaggerate the effectiveness of persuasion. We have come to fear the word as much as the sword. **Were propaganda one-tenth as potent as it is made out to be, the totalitarian regimes would have been mild affairs.** They would have been blatant and brazen, and without the secret police, the camps and the mass exterminations.

The truth, he says, is narrower. Propaganda cannot force its way into unwilling minds. It cannot inculcate something wholly new. It cannot keep people persuaded once they have stopped believing. It penetrates only minds already open. Rather than instilling opinion it articulates opinions already there. **The gifted propagandist brings to a boil ideas already simmering in the minds of his hearers.** Where opinion is not coerced, people can be made to believe only what they already know.

It also succeeds mainly with the frustrated. Their fears and hopes crowd at the portals of their senses. They hear the music of their own souls in the propagandist's words. And they detect their own imaginings more easily in impassioned double-talk than in precise words joined by faultless logic.

The corollary is a sword. To maintain itself, a movement must arrange that when people no longer believe they can be made to believe by force. Goebbels admits it in an unguarded moment. A sharp sword must always stand behind propaganda if it is to be really effective. And propaganda becomes more fervent when it works alongside coercion, not less. Both the converter and the coerced convert need to believe the imposed faith is the only true one. **Propaganda serves more to justify ourselves than to convince others**, and the more reason we have to feel guilty, the more fervent it becomes.

Violence and fanaticism then breed each other, and it is often impossible to say which came first. Ferrero on the terrorists of the French Revolution is the sharpest version. The more blood they shed, the more they needed to believe their principles were absolute. Only the absolute could still absolve them in their own eyes. They did not spill the blood because they believed in popular sovereignty. **They tried to believe in it because their fear made them spill so much blood.** Hoffer's American example sits in the same paragraph. Every lynching in our South intimidates the Negro and invigorates the fanatical conviction of white supremacy.

Coerced converts turn out to be as fanatical as persuaded ones, and sometimes more so. Islam imposed its faith by force. Its coerced Muslims showed a devotion more ardent than the first Arabs, obtaining, in Renan's phrase, a faith ever tending to grow stronger. **It needs fanatical faith to rationalise our cowardice.** That is why the recantations forced from Soviet scientists and writers are likely to be genuine conversions rather than lip service.

The historical claim he draws is blunt. There is hardly an example of a movement reaching vast size by persuasion alone. A Christian historian has to admit that armed force has often made it possible for the spirit of Jesus to survive. It was the temporal sword that made Christianity a world religion, and where it lacked state backing it never got a permanent hold. Conquest was primary in the spread of Islam and conversion a by-product. The Reformation advanced only where it won the local ruler. Melanchthon asked what their precepts would become without the civil authority — Platonic laws. **And it was the armies of the Revolution, not its ideas, that penetrated Europe.** Where a movement can either persuade or coerce, it usually chooses the second. Persuasion is clumsy and its results uncertain.

The reverse holds too, and he states it as a warning. A movement can be stopped by force. To do it the force must be ruthless and persistent, which can only come from fanatical conviction of its own. **Terrorism that comes from individual brutality is spasmodic and subject to moods.** As soon as force wavers and alternates with forbearance, the doctrine recovers and draws new benefit from every persecution. So ardent faith is needed not only to resist coercion but to exercise it.

**What is worth having — why they proselytise**. Not overflowing strength. The opposite. The missionary impulse is not a product of intensity of conviction, since religions of great intensity often confine themselves to despising what is not themselves. Missionary zeal expresses some deep misgiving, some feeling that something is missing at the centre. Proselytising is a passionate search for something not yet found rather than a wish to give the world something we have. What is being searched for is a final demonstration that our truth is the only truth.

So the creed whose legitimacy is easiest to challenge develops the strongest proselytising impulse. Movements with the widest gap between profession and practice are the most fervent in imposing their faith. He runs the test forward on three cases. The more unworkable communism proves in Russia, the more brazen its attack on the unbelieving world will be. The slaveholders of the South grew more aggressive in spreading their way of life as their position became more untenable. And if free enterprise ever becomes a proselytising holy cause, it will be a sign that its advantages have stopped being self-evident.

**How people should relate — the leader**. He cannot create the conditions, and he is indispensable once they exist. There has to be an eagerness to follow, and an intense dissatisfaction with things as they are, before movement and leader appear. When conditions are not ripe the potential leader stays without a following however gifted. Had the First World War been averted or postponed a decade, Lenin, Mussolini and Hitler would have ended like the brilliant plotters of the nineteenth century who never ripened a crisis into a movement.

The British case makes the point with a man everyone knows. Through the 1930s the potential leader was prominent and made himself heard, day in and day out. The will to follow was not there. **It was only when disaster made autonomous individual lives untenable that Churchill came into his own.** There is a period of waiting in the wings, often very long, for every great leader whose entrance looks to us like the crucial moment.

Once the stage is set, he is indispensable. Ripeness produces nothing by itself. It was Lenin who forced events into the channels of the Bolshevik revolution. Had he died in Switzerland, or on the way to Russia in 1917, the other prominent Bolsheviks would almost certainly have joined a coalition government. With Mussolini and Hitler the evidence is even more decisive. Without them there would have been neither a Fascist nor a Nazi movement.

The list of what a leader needs is the least flattering inventory in the book. Exceptional intelligence, noble character and originality seem neither necessary nor desirable. What is wanted is audacity and a joy in defiance. An iron will. A fanatical conviction of holding the one and only truth. Faith in his own destiny and luck. A capacity for passionate hatred. Contempt for the present. A cunning estimate of human nature. A delight in symbols. An unbounded brazenness expressed in disregard for consistency and fairness. And a recognition that the innermost craving of a following is for communion, and that there can never be too much of it.

The last requirement is the one he calls most essential and most elusive. A leader's uncanny powers show less in his hold on the masses than in his ability to bewitch a small group of able men. Those men must be fearless, proud, intelligent and capable of running large undertakings. They must also submit wholly to his will and glory in the submission. Trotsky failed as a leader because he could not build a machine of loyal lieutenants. He also had an ineradicable respect for the creative individual, so he never grasped the importance of communion.

Two further notes finish the portrait. Charlatanism of some degree is indispensable, since no movement exists without deliberate misrepresentation of facts. The leader must be a practical realist who talks the language of the visionary. And originality is not required. One of his most striking traits is a readiness to imitate friend and foe, past and present. **The clue to any heroic career is perhaps an unbounded capacity for imitation.** That indicates a man without a fully developed self, whose strength lies in his blind spots and in plugging all outlets but one.

**What a person is — under obedience and under action**. Obedient, in a way that inverts the usual picture of a rioter. Disorder and bloodshed make us think of a movement's followers as lawless by nature. Mass ferocity is not the sum of individual lawlessness. **Personal truculence works against united action.** It produces the pioneer, the adventurer and the bandit. The true believer, however violent his acts, is basically submissive. The Christian converts who lynched professors at Alexandria were submissive members of a compact church. The Communist rioter is a servile party member. The Japanese and Nazi rowdies were the most disciplined people the world has seen.

Then Hoffer turns the same sentence on his own country. In America the employer often finds in the racial fanatic of our South, so given to mass violence, a respectful and docile factory hand. The army finds him particularly amenable to discipline.

The frustrated obey readily because freedom from responsibility attracts them more than freedom from restraint. They will trade independence for relief from willing, deciding and being answerable for failure. Submission by everybody to a supreme leader is also an approach to their ideal of equality. They follow a leader less because he is taking them somewhere than because he is leading them away from their unwanted selves. Surrender is a fulfilment rather than a means. Where they are led is secondary.

Action does the same work by another route. There is less individual distinctness in the man of action than in the thinker. **One is never really stripped for action unless one is stripped of a distinct self.** So an active people tends toward uniformity. The immigrants who came to America to make money were Americanised faster than those who came to realise an ideal. The second kind measured the new country against the ideal, found it wanting, and insulated themselves.

Movements use action deliberately. The conflicts they incite down enemies and also strip followers of individuality. Clearing land, building cities and large industrial undertakings do the same. **Even mere marching serves.** Rauschning first thought the eternal marching a senseless waste and came to recognise its effect. Marching diverts men's thoughts. Marching kills thought. Marching makes an end of individuality.

The call to action meets an eager response, because frustration stems chiefly from an inability to act. **The most poignantly frustrated are those equipped for action and condemned to rust in idleness.** That is how the Lenins, Trotskys, Mussolinis and Hitlers, who spent the best part of their lives talking in cafés, could reveal themselves suddenly as the most tireless men of action of their time.

But successful action is fatal to what produced it. This is the chapter's most useful reversal. Action becomes an end in itself and drains all fervour into its own channels. Faith turns into a lubricant for the machine rather than the purpose. **The true believer who succeeds in everything becomes reconciled with himself and the present.** He stops seeking salvation in losing himself and finds it in proving his worth. So a people steeped in action is likely to be the least religious, the least revolutionary and the least chauvinist. The stability and tolerance of the Anglo-Saxon peoples owe something to the abundance of the will, skill and opportunity for action, which served them as a substitute for a mass movement.

The danger is what happens when those avenues close. Block action with a severe depression or a defeat in war and the resulting frustration is intense enough that almost any movement finds the ground ready. The explosive situation in Germany after the First World War was partly the inactivity forced on a population that knew itself equipped for action. Hitler gave them a movement. More importantly, he gave them unlimited opportunities for feverish and spectacular action.

**How people should relate — suspicion, and what unity does to a person**. Badly, and on purpose. Awareness of their own blemishes inclines the frustrated to detect ill will in others. So when they congregate the air is heavy with suspicion. There is prying and spying, tense watching and a tense awareness of being watched. **The surprising thing is that this mistrust produces conformity rather than dissension.** Knowing they are watched, the faithful escape suspicion by adhering zealously to prescribed behaviour. Strict orthodoxy is as much the result of mutual suspicion as of ardent faith.

Movements use it deliberately. The Nazi rank and file were kept in a permanent state of uneasy conscience. Now and then innocent people are accused and sacrificed to keep suspicion alive. The edge is sharpened by tying internal opposition to the external enemy. The devil plots inside the ranks as well as outside. It is his voice speaking through the dissenter. And it is the sacred duty of the true believer to be suspicious.

Loyalty runs to the whole and not to the fellow member. **True loyalty between individuals is possible only in a loose and relatively free society.** As Abraham was ready to sacrifice his son to prove his devotion, so the fanatic must be ready to sacrifice relatives and friends. Ties of blood and friendship look to a movement like a diminution of its own cohesion. So mutual suspicion is not merely compatible with corporate strength but close to a precondition of it. Men of strong convictions, leagued together, watch one another and find their strength in it. Mutual dread binds them as by an iron band and prevents desertion.

**What is worth having — and what unity costs**. Unification intensifies everything that produced it. Hatred, imitativeness, credulity and obedience all go up, even without manipulation from the leadership. Hoffer finds that surprising. The unifying factors all originated in the frustrated man's revulsion from himself, and the fully assimilated believer is no longer frustrated. He has a new identity and a new life. He is one of the chosen, protected by invincible powers. **And he displays, with increased intensity, all the reactions that are symptoms of inner tension.**

His explanation is that unification is a process of diminution rather than addition. To be assimilated, a person is stripped of distinctness. He is deprived of free choice and independent judgment. Many of his natural impulses are blunted. The faith, hope, pride and confidence that appear to be added are negative in origin. **The exaltation of the true believer flows from a sense of deliverance rather than from reserves of strength.** He has been delivered from the meaningless burdens of an autonomous existence. *We Germans are so happy. We are free from freedom.*

His invincibility depends on the line connecting him to the whole. As long as he feels himself part of it and nothing else, he is indestructible. Which is why the frustrated man still has choices — a new environment, an absorbing undertaking — and the unified man has none. **He must cling to the collective body or wither like a fallen leaf.** It is doubtful whether the excommunicated priest, the expelled Communist and the renegade chauvinist ever find peace as autonomous individuals. The true believer is eternally incomplete and eternally insecure.

The last section lists how that incompleteness is maintained, and it reads as a specification. Dogma is elevated above reason, so intelligence never becomes self-reliant. Economic dependence is kept up by centralising economic power and by a deliberately created scarcity of necessities. Social self-reliance is discouraged by crowded housing or communal quarters, and by enforced daily participation in public functions. Censorship of literature, art, music and science stops even the creative few from living self-contained lives. **And the inculcated devotions do it too, since every devotion is a socket demanding a complementary part from outside.** People raised in that atmosphere become incomplete and dependent even when they had the making of self-contained ones. They are strangers to frustration, they have no grievance, and they exhibit the peculiarities of people who crave to be rid of a spoiled existence.

**The shape of time** in this run is short and instrumental. The leader waits in the wings until the times ripen. After that everything is engineering.

*Read: lines 843–1216.*

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, Part Three `[SPECULATIVE]`

Paradigm-obvious in 1951.

That the interesting question about the camps is who survived them psychologically. The comparison of Communists, priests and individualists is made in the register of an experiment, four years after the liberations and before most of the testimony existed.

Lynching as an available illustration. It appears twice — once as evidence that violence invigorates the faith of the violent, once as evidence that the racial fanatic makes a docile factory hand — and in neither place is it the subject.

Colonial and racial hierarchy as background furniture. The Japanese admiring Americans more than they were admired, the backward South, the imitativeness of the oppressed. All offered as observations that need no defending.

Marching, uniforms and pageantry as obviously effective. A reader in 1951 had watched twenty years of it and needed no convincing.

Paradigm-breaking, and the cost is what marks it.

Saying propaganda is nearly powerless. It contradicts the discipline Le Bon founded and everything the war taught the reading public. Hoffer argues it from the regimes' own behaviour: if the word worked, the camps would have been unnecessary. **The cost is that it removes the comfortable explanation** in which ordinary people were tricked.

Explaining the Moscow confessions as a route back into communion. Bukharin confessing to break out of isolation is a claim about what the old Bolsheviks wanted, made about men whose treatment was already known.

Writing that the more sublime the faith, the more virulent the hatred it breeds. And ending a paragraph about generous enthusiasms with the line that the torture chamber is a corporate institution.

Naming the oppressed as the reliable imitators of their oppressors. He makes it general — Christianity realising the antichrist, the Jacobins practising the tyranny they rose against, Soviet Russia as the purest monopolistic capitalism. That puts every liberation movement inside the finding.

Telling America that its homogeneity was produced by the lowest and poorest of Europe having no self worth keeping. **The cost is the compliment it withdraws**, and he pays it in the same paragraph where he explains why the country worked.

## Ch. XIII — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: judging whether a body of ideas will hold people, as against whether it is any good.

The finding separates two things everyone runs together. **A doctrine's effectiveness comes from its certitude and not from its meaning.** Crude absurdities, trivial nonsense and sublime truths are equally potent if accepted as the sole eternal truth. So the test is not profundity and not validity. It is how thoroughly the doctrine insulates a person from himself and from the world as it is.

The mechanism is the part worth carrying. A doctrine that is understood is shorn of its strength. Once we understand a thing, it is as if it originated in us. And a man asked to renounce the self cannot find eternal certitude in anything that came from that self. **Comprehension and authority are in direct competition.** From which the specification follows. Unintelligible, or failing that vague, or failing that unverifiable — so that checking it requires getting to heaven or to the distant future.

Scope conditions. This holds where the doctrine's job is to produce sacrifice and united action. It fails where the job is to run something. Hoffer says so himself: when a movement begins making its doctrine intelligible, its dynamic span is over. An arrived movement needs the intellectuals, and intelligibility is what buys them. **The property that makes a doctrine effective early makes it useless later.** That is a prediction, not a paradox.

The general form. **A body of belief holds people in proportion to how little of it can be checked.** Any move to make it clear is a move toward stability and away from fervour. Modern equivalent: watch what happens to a movement's texts once it acquires institutions. The clarifications, the official readings, the authorised interpretations. Those are not signs of strength.

The diagnostic is cheap to run. Look at whether the faithful are complicating the simple parts. Hoffer's observation is that where a doctrine is plain, believers make its simple words pregnant and treat them as symbols in a secret message. **Hair-splitting is not evidence that a doctrine is deep.** It is evidence that it has to be kept uncheckable.

## Ch. XIV — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: designing, or recognising, a device for holding a heterogeneous group together.

The specification is explicit, and it is the most operational passage in either book. **A movement can rise without a God and never without a devil.** The devil should be one, so that adversaries far removed from each other seem to belong to a single category. He should be omnipotent and omnipresent, so that every internal failure is his work. And he should be a foreigner. A domestic enemy has to be given a foreign ancestry before he will serve.

The mechanism underneath is that hatred works where love does not. We always look for allies when we hate and rarely when we love. And the hatreds that unify best are the ones with no visible grievance behind them, because those are the ones that need general consent. Self-contempt is transmuted into hatred of others, and the switch is masked by finding as many people as possible who hate the same way.

Scope conditions. This requires a group heterogeneous enough that nothing else would bind it. Common hatred unites the most disparate elements, which is the whole point of using it. It requires a devil tangible enough to picture, which is the content of the Japanese visitor's remark. **And it degrades where the enemy can be despised rather than hated**, since we cannot hate those we look down on.

The general form. **A group with nothing in common can be unified by a single, omnipresent, foreign enemy, and the unity will be proportional to how vivid that enemy is.** Modern equivalent: any coalition whose only shared content is an opponent. Any organisation whose failures are always attributed outward.

The cost is stated by Hoffer himself, and it is why this transfers as a warning rather than a tool. Hatred contains an undercurrent of admiration. **So every movement shapes itself after its specific devil** — the Jacobins practising the tyranny they overthrew, Hitler working from the *Protocols* down to the smallest detail. A community mobilised by hatred loses many of the values it set out to defend. The device works, and what it delivers is a copy of the thing you built it against.

## Ch. XIV — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the man at section 77. He has done what the book describes. He renounced the self, joined the compact whole, and got the deliverance he came for. He is not a cynic and he was not tricked. And Hoffer's finding is that in losing his individual independence he has found a new freedom — **freedom to hate, bully, lie, torture, murder and betray without shame** — and that this is part of the attraction. The humbling of the self has bred pride rather than humility. The act of self-denial seems to confer the right to be merciless.

Hoffer offers him nothing. The chapter's last word is that the torture chamber is a corporate institution.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/metta-loving-kindness-universal-care|loving-kindness as systematic practice]]** would say the man has done half a practice and stopped. This tradition knows you can go a long way inward and stay defended. You can meditate on emptiness for years and remain armoured. **What cracks a defended heart is a deliberate, repeated wishing of wellbeing, extended outward by steps** until it reaches people you have no reason to like. That is a discipline with a direction, and the direction is the whole point here. The movement's version of self-loss also dissolves a boundary. It dissolves it inward only, toward the group. The counsel is that a self-loss stopping at the edge of the congregation has not gone anywhere. It has relocated the wall.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/compassion-versus-empathy-buddhist-practice-rewiring|the difference between compassion and empathy]]** would leave the heart alone and go at the mechanics. That makes it more use to a sceptic. Empathy is catching what somebody else feels. It is exactly the faculty Hoffer's unifiers exploit — contagion, imitation, the sea of upturned faces. **A group can raise empathy to a white heat and become more dangerous, not less.** Feeling with your own people is entirely compatible with feeling nothing for anyone outside. Compassion is a different operation. It is trained, it is aimed at suffering as such, and its object is not selected by membership. The counsel is to stop asking whether he feels strongly with his fellows, which he plainly does. The question is whether the feeling is available to anybody who is not one of them.

They disagree about the entry point. The first says the fault is in what he did with the boundary of the self. The second says the fault is in mistaking a shared feeling for a moral faculty.

**Where they converge is on a sentence Hoffer treats as an irony and leaves standing.** He writes that the hatred and cruelty born of selflessness are far worse than anything selfishness produces. Then he lets it sit as a paradox. Both advisors would say it is not a paradox. **It is what happens when self-loss is achieved with no specification of what it is being lost into.** The dissolution is real and the deliverance is real. Neither of them carries any information about direction. A tradition that spent two thousand years on the technique spent them on the target as well. Hoffer's movements supply the first half and take the second choice away.

# What 1951 Took For Granted — Hoffer, Part Four

> **The four chapters of Part Four of Eric Hoffer, *The True Believer* (1951)** — a Czech historian saying that if the ceiling had fallen on the room where he and a few friends were dining there would have been no Czech nation; Milton spending twenty sterile years on pamphlets with a draft of *Paradise Lost* in his pocket; a monk who covenanted with his eyes never to look out of the window at the view; and a list of the Nazi leaders' failed artistic careers. Read from `RAW/books/The True Believer.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
>
> **This is the part about phases, and it is where the book stops being a study of a type and becomes a theory of how a movement dies.** Three kinds of man take it in turn — the man of words, the fanatic, the practical man of action — and Hoffer's judgment is that a movement is good or bad depending on how long the middle stage runs. The last chapter is also the one place he says outright which movements he thinks were worth having.

## Ch. XV — The talkers go first

**What makes things happen**. Discrediting, and it does not happen by itself.[^1] Mass movements do not usually rise until the prevailing order has been discredited. That is not the automatic result of blunders and abuses by those in power. It is the deliberate work of men of words with a grievance. Where the articulate are absent, or have no grievance, an incompetent and corrupt order may hold power until it crumbles on its own. And an order of real merit may be swept away if it fails to win the allegiance of the articulate minority.

The reason the talker rather than the fanatic does this job is a matter of timing. A full-blown movement is a ruthless affair run by fanatics. They can only move in after the order has already lost the allegiance of the masses. Until then, the masses stay basically conservative. They can think of reform and not of total innovation. The fanatical extremist strikes them as dangerous, traitorous, impractical or insane, and they will not listen to him. Lenin himself admitted that where the ground is not ready the Communists find it hard to get the masses even to listen.

The man of words is heard for the opposite reason. The masses listen because they know his words cannot have immediate results. The authorities ignore him or use mild methods to muzzle him. So imperceptibly he undermines institutions, discredits those in power, and weakens prevailing loyalties. He sets the stage.

**What a person is**. Someone who wants to be recognised, and Hoffer thinks that is the whole of it. The men of words are of diverse types — priests, scribes, prophets, writers, artists, professors, students. Where reading and writing is a difficult art, as in China, mere literacy confers the status. Whatever the type, one craving is common to almost all of them. **It is a craving for a clearly marked status above the common run of humanity.** Napoleon's version is quoted: vanity made the Revolution, and liberty was only a pretext.

There is an irremediable insecurity at the core of every intellectual, creative or not. Even the most gifted seem to live in eternal self-doubt and have to prove their worth again each day. De Rémusat's line about Thiers is offered as typical. He has much more vanity than ambition, prefers consideration to obedience, and prefers the appearance of power to power itself. Consult him constantly, then do as you please. He will notice your deference more than your actions.

From which follows the most uncomfortable claim in the run. There is a moment in almost every faultfinding man of words's career when a deferential gesture from those in power would win him over. At a certain stage most of them are ready to become timeservers and courtiers. Jesus might not have preached a new Gospel had the dominant Pharisees taken him into the fold and called him Rabbi. A bishopric conferred on Luther at the right moment might have cooled his ardour. The young Marx could perhaps have been bought with a title and a government job.

The grievance behind the protest is nearly always private. However much the man of words sees himself as champion of the downtrodden, his pity is usually hatched out of his hatred for the powers that be. Thoreau states it with fierce extravagance. What saddens the reformer is not sympathy with his fellows in distress but his own private ail — let this be righted, and he will forsake his generous companions without apology.

The evidence is what happens when the status arrives. Luther, first defying the church, spoke feelingly of the poor, simple, common folk. Allied later with the German princelings, he proclaimed that God would prefer the government to exist however evil rather than allow the rabble to riot, however justified. Burke, patronised by lords, spoke of the swinish multitude and recommended patience, labour, sobriety and religion to the poor.

**How people should relate**. Rulers to intellectuals, and Hoffer treats it as the decisive relationship in politics. Wherever a dispensation endures beyond its span of competence, there is either no educated class at all or an intimate alliance between those in power and the men of words. **Where all learned men are clergymen, the church is unassailable.**

The comparison he uses is two centuries of the same institution. The Catholic Church was at its lowest in the tenth century, under Pope John XII, far more corrupt than at the Reformation. But then all learned men were priests. By the fifteenth century, printing and paper had ended the church's monopoly on learning, and it was the nonclerical humanists who formed the vanguard.

The stability of Imperial China and of ancient Egypt rested on the same alliance between bureaucracy and literati. He notes that the Taiping rebellion, the only effective Chinese movement while the Empire still worked, was started by a scholar who failed the state examination again and again. Rome's long endurance owed something to its partnership with the Greek men of words. The conquered Greeks felt they gave laws and civilisation to their conquerors. They welcomed the deformed and depraved Nero hysterically in 67 A.D. and took him to their hearts as a fellow intellectual and artist.

The British in India are the counter-case, and it is the most concrete argument in the chapter. Toynbee found a Latin poet praising Rome five hundred years after Caesar reached Egypt, and observed ruefully that no Claudian could be found in any Alexandria of Hindustan. Hoffer thinks it is not far-fetched to suppose the British could have kept India indefinitely. They cultivated the Nizams, Maharajas and Nawabs, and did not try to win the Indian intellectual. They were men of action with a faith in innate British superiority, and they scorned him twice over.

They also kept the realm of action for themselves. They did not much encourage Indians to become engineers, agronomists or technicians. The institutions they built produced impractical men of words. **It is an irony of fate, he writes, that this system hastened the end of British rule instead of safeguarding it.**

**How you know**. By watching the fate of the articulate under each regime. Both the Bolsheviks and the Nazis showed an acute awareness of the relationship. In Russia, men of letters, artists and scholars share the privileges of the ruling group as superior civil servants, made to toe the line under the same discipline as the rest of the elite. And Hitler's plan had a diabolical realism to it — make all learning the monopoly of the elite ruling his world empire, and keep the anonymous masses barely literate.

The historical pattern runs the same way in every case he checks. The men of letters of eighteenth-century France are the familiar example. The ground for the Reformation was prepared by pamphleteers who satirised the clergy. Christianity spread fast in a Roman world where the pagan cults had already been discredited by Greek philosophers who found them puerile and ridiculed them in the streets. Christianity made little headway against Judaism because the Jewish religion had the ardent allegiance of the Jewish men of words. The rabbis had an exalted status in a life where the school and the book had supplanted the temple and the fatherland.

Modern movements follow the same rule. Socialist and nationalist movements alike were pioneered by poets, writers, historians and philosophers. The generals, industrialists and businessmen who are counted as pillars of patriotism are latecomers who join once it is a going concern. Palacky said that if the ceiling of the room where he and a handful of friends were dining had collapsed, there would have been no Czech nationalist movement.

And it is humiliation that sets them off, because of the craving for status. Napoleon's humiliation of the Prussians drove Fichte and the German intellectuals to call for a Germany that would dominate Europe. Herzl and the Jewish intellectuals were driven to Zionism by the treatment of millions of Jews in Russia. The nationalist movement that forced the British out of India began, to a degree, in the humiliation of a scrawny and bespectacled Indian man of words in South Africa.

**What is worth having**. Not what the man of words thought he was buying, and this is the chapter's real finding. It is easy to see how ridicule shakes prevailing loyalties. What is not obvious is how discrediting the old beliefs makes a new fanatical faith possible. The militant man of words who sounds the established order to its source often prepares the ground for a corporate society that cherishes blind faith. **A wide diffusion of doubt leads to unexpected results.** The irreverence of the Renaissance was a prelude to the fanaticism of Reformation and Counter-Reformation. The Frenchmen of the enlightenment who preached reason and tolerance released a burst of revolutionary fanaticism that has not abated.

The mechanism he offers is a plumbing metaphor and it is worth keeping. When we debunk a fanatical faith we do not strike at the root of fanaticism. We merely prevent its leaking out at a certain point, with the likely result that it leaks out somewhere else. By denigrating prevailing loyalties, the man of words creates in the disillusioned a hunger for faith, because most people cannot endure the barrenness of their lives without some ardent dedication. So the scoffer becomes the precursor of a new faith in spite of himself.

He can get along without absolutes himself, which is the point of difference. He values the search for truth as much as truth. He delights in the clash of thought and the give-and-take of controversy. When he formulates a doctrine it is an exhibition of brilliance rather than a programme of action. The fanatics and the faith-hungry masses then invest his speculations with the certitude of holy writ. Jesus was not a Christian, nor was Marx a Marxist.

The summary he gives has four items. The militant man of words discredits prevailing creeds and detaches people's allegiance from them. He indirectly creates a hunger for faith in those who cannot live without one. He furnishes the doctrine and the slogans. And he undermines the convictions of the better people — those who can get along without faith — so that when the new fanaticism appears they cannot resist it. **They see no sense in dying for principles, and yield without a fight.** Then Yeats, quoted to close it: the best lack all conviction, while the worst are full of passionate intensity.

**What a person is — the precursor's mistake**. Wrong about what the masses want, and the error is fatal to him personally. The tragic figures in a movement's history are the intellectual precursors who live to see the old order fall. They rise against it, deride its incompetence, and call for freedom of self-expression. They take it for granted that the masses who follow them crave the same things.

They do not. The freedom the masses crave is not freedom of self-expression but freedom from the intolerable burden of an autonomous existence. They want freedom from the fearful burden of free choice, and from the responsibility of realising an ineffectual self and taking the blame for the result. They do not want freedom of conscience. They want faith — blind, authoritarian faith. They sweep away the old order to establish uniformity and anonymity and a new structure of perfect unity.

Which reverses the usual story about betrayal. It is not the wickedness of the old regime they rise against but its weakness. Not its oppression, but its failure to hammer them together into one mighty whole. So the demagogue's persuasiveness lies less in convicting people of the old order's vileness than in demonstrating its helplessness. **The immediate result of a movement usually corresponds to what the people wanted. The only people cheated are the intellectual precursors.**

**The shape of time**. A relay in three legs, announced here and run in the next two chapters. The readying of the ground is done best by men whose chief excellence is skill with words. The hatching of the actual movement requires the temperament of the fanatic. The final consolidation is the work of practical men of action. He notes the division is not categorical — Gandhi and Trotsky started as apparently ineffectual men of words and later showed exceptional talents as administrators or generals.

*Read: lines 1219–1329.*

---

## Ch. XVI — Chaos is his element

**What makes things happen**. The fanatic, at the moment the order cracks.[^2] When the moment is ripe, only he can hatch a genuine movement. Without him the disaffection the talkers engendered stays undirected. It vents itself in pointless and easily suppressed disorders. Reforms, even drastic ones, leave the old way of life unchanged. A change of government amounts to a transfer of power between sets of men of action. Without him there can perhaps be no new beginning.

The contrast with the men of words is drawn at the exact moment of collapse, and it is the sharpest scene in Part Four. When the old order begins to fall apart, many of the vociferous men of words who prayed for the day are in a funk. The first glimpse of the face of anarchy frightens them out of their wits. They forget everything they said about the poor simple folk. They run for help to strong men of action — princes, generals, administrators, bankers, landowners — who know how to deal with the rabble.

Not the fanatic. Chaos is his element. When the old order cracks he wades in with all his recklessness to blow the hated present to high heaven, and he glories in the sight of a world coming to a sudden end. **To hell with reforms. All that exists is rubbish, and there is no sense in reforming rubbish.** He justifies the will to anarchy plausibly enough: there can be no new beginning while the old clutters the landscape. He shoves the frightened men of words aside, and goes on quoting their doctrines and mouthing their slogans. He alone knows the innermost craving of the masses in action — the craving for communion, for the mustering of the host, for the dissolution of cursed individuality in a mighty whole.

**What a person is**. A man of words who cannot create, and Hoffer says the division inside that class is the significant one. The creative man of words, however bitterly he criticises the existing order, is attached to the present. His passion is to reform and not destroy. A movement left wholly in his keeping turns into a mild affair with reforms of the surface and no sudden break. That is only possible when the old order abdicates without a struggle, or when he allies himself with strong men of action the moment chaos threatens. When the struggle is bitter, the creative man is shoved aside and management falls to the noncreative — the eternal misfits and the contemners of the present.

The portrait he then gives is the same man from Part Two, at the top of a movement. Here is somebody who wants to write a great book, paint a great picture, become a great scientist, and knows he never will. He can find no peace in a stable social order, old or new. He sees his life as irrevocably spoiled and the world perpetually out of joint. He feels at home only in a state of chaos. Even when he imposes an iron discipline he is only shaping an instrument for attaining eternal flux. Only while engaged in change does he feel free and growing.

The evidence is a list, and it is the most quoted paragraph in the chapter. Marat, Robespierre, Lenin, Mussolini and Hitler are the outstanding examples. Peter Viereck points out that most of the Nazi bigwigs had artistic and literary ambitions they could not realise. Hitler tried painting and architecture. Goebbels tried drama, the novel and poetry. Rosenberg tried architecture and philosophy, von Schirach poetry, Funk music, Streicher painting. **Almost all were failures, not only by the vulgar criterion of success but by their own artistic criteria.**

**How people should relate**. Badly, once the creative man is inside a movement. He feels its whirl and passion sapping his creative energies. While he is conscious of the flow within him he will not find fulfilment in leading millions. So once it starts rolling he either retires or is pushed aside. And since he can never for long suppress his critical faculty, he is inevitably cast as the heretic. Unless he stifles the movement early or dies at the right moment, he is likely to end a shunned recluse, or in exile, or facing a firing squad.

**What is worth having — and when the fanatic stops being useful**. The danger is that he cannot settle down. Once victory is won and the new order begins to crystallise, he becomes an element of strain. The taste for strong feeling drives him to search for mysteries yet to be revealed and doors yet to be opened. He keeps groping for extremes. So on the morrow of victory most movements find themselves in the grip of dissension. The ardour that yesterday went into a life-and-death struggle now vents itself in violent factional disputes. Hatred has become a habit, and with no outside enemies left the fanatics make enemies of one another.

**How you know**. From a fanatic diagnosing other fanatics, which Hoffer treats as a self-portrait. In his order to the new chief of the SA after the Röhm purge in 1934, Hitler described those who will not settle down. Without realising it, they have found in nihilism their ultimate confession of faith. Their unrest can find satisfaction only in some conspiratorial activity of the mind, in perpetually plotting the disintegration of whatever set-up happens to exist. **As so often, Hoffer notes, Hitler's accusations against his antagonists were a self-revelation** — he too, particularly at the end, found in nihilism his ultimate philosophy and valediction.

**The shape of time** and What is real are not developed separately in this run. The chapter's whole content is one figure and one window of time in which he is indispensable. Left to themselves the fanatics split a movement into schisms, or wreck it by driving it to attempt the impossible. Only the entrance of a practical man of action can save what it achieved.

## Ch. XVII — The man who ends it

**The shape of time**. Three roles played by three men in succession, and the succession is the point.[^3] A movement is pioneered by men of words, materialised by fanatics and consolidated by men of action. It is usually an advantage, and perhaps a requirement for endurance, that different men play those roles as conditions require. When the same person leads a movement from inception to maturity it usually ends in disaster.

The Fascist and Nazi movements had no successive change of leadership, and both ended in disaster. Hoffer's reading is that Hitler's fanaticism, and his inability to settle down and play the practical man, brought ruin to his own movement. **Had Hitler died in the middle 1930s, a man of action of Goering's type would have succeeded him and the movement would have survived.**

A change of character is possible and he thinks it rarely lasts. Trotsky was essentially a man of words — vain, brilliant, an individualist to the core. The collapse of an empire and Lenin's overpowering will brought him into the camp of the fanatics, and in the civil war he showed unequalled talents as an organiser and general. The moment the strain relaxed he was a man of words again, trusting in words rather than relentless force, and he let himself be pushed aside by the crafty fanatic Stalin.

Stalin he reads as a combination of fanatic and man of action with the fanatic predominating. The disastrous blunders were the fanatic's: the senseless liquidation of the kulaks and their offspring, the terror of the purges, the pact with Hitler, the clumsy meddling with the work of writers and artists. There was small chance for the Russians to taste the joys of the present while Stalin was in power.

**What a person is**. A rare kind of leader, in the one paragraph where Hoffer names people he admires. Lincoln, Gandhi, F.D.R., Churchill and Nehru all harness men's hungers and fears to weld a following and make it zealous unto death. Unlike Hitler or Stalin, or even Luther and Calvin, they are not tempted to use the slime of frustrated souls as mortar in building a new world. Their self-confidence is blended with faith in humanity. **They know that no one can be honourable unless he honours mankind.**

**What makes things happen**. The man of action arriving, which saves the movement and ends its dynamic phase in the same act. He saves it from suicidal dissension and from the recklessness of the fanatics. The war with the present is over. The genuine man of action is intent not on renovating the world but on possessing it. Where the dynamic phase lived on protest and a desire for drastic change, the final phase administers and perpetuates the power already won.

The explosive vigour then gets embalmed and sealed in sanctified institutions. A religious movement crystallises into a hierarchy and a ritual. A revolutionary movement crystallises into organs of vigilance and administration. A nationalist movement crystallises into governmental and patriotic institutions. Establishing a church marks the end of the revivalist spirit. The organs of a triumphant revolution liquidate the revolutionary mentality. Institutions freeze a pattern of united action, and members must act as one man while representing a loose aggregation rather than a spontaneous coalescence. Spontaneity becomes suspect, and duty is prized above devotion.

**How people should relate**. Under drill rather than enthusiasm. The man of action's chief task is to fix and perpetuate unity and readiness for sacrifice. His ideal is a compact whole that functions automatically. Enthusiasm is ephemeral and persuasion unpredictable, so he leans on drill and coercion. **He finds the assertion that all men are cowards less debatable than the assertion that all men are fools.** In Sir John Maynard's phrase, he inclines to found the new order on the necks of the people rather than in their hearts. The genuine man of action is not a man of faith but a man of law.

He is still awed by what faith and spontaneity achieved in the early days, when a mighty instrument of power was conjured out of the void. The memory is vivid. So he takes great care to preserve an impressive façade of faith and keeps up an incessant flow of fervent propaganda while relying mainly on force. His orders are worded in pious vocabulary. The old slogans stay on his lips. The symbols are carried high and given reverence. The men of words and the fanatics of the early period are canonised. The pious phrases give coercion a semblance of persuasion, and habit a semblance of spontaneity.

**What is real**. A patchwork, assembled from anywhere it can be got. The man of action is eclectic and borrows from near and far, from friend and foe. He even goes back to the order that preceded the movement and takes its techniques of stability, unintentionally re-establishing continuity with the past. The institution of an absolute dictator at this stage is as much a deliberate device as a hunger for power. A rigid ceremonial style appears both at the birth of an organisation and at its decline. It gives shape to what is still amorphous, or holds together what seems to be falling apart. The infallibility of the bishop of Rome was propounded in the earliest days of the papacy, and again in 1870 when the papacy seemed close to extinction.

The examples are inventories. Stalin's Russia was a patchwork of bolshevism, czarism, nationalism, pan-Slavism, dictatorship, borrowings from Hitler, and monopolistic capitalism. Hitler's Third Reich was a conglomerate of nationalism, racialism, Prussianism, dictatorship, and borrowings from fascism, bolshevism, Shintoism, Catholicism and the ancient Hebrews. **Christianity too, once it crystallised into an authoritarian church, was a patchwork.** It patterned its hierarchy after the bureaucracy of the Roman Empire and adopted portions of the antique ritual.

**What is worth having**. Different things, now, and the change in the intake is how you spot it. In the hands of a man of action, a movement stops being a refuge from the burdens of individual existence. It becomes a means of self-realisation for the ambitious. Its new attraction for people preoccupied with their own careers is a clear indication that it has been reconciled with the present. And the influx of career men accelerates the change. Hitler, who saw the whole course of a movement while still nursing his own, warned that a movement keeps its vigour only while it can offer nothing in the present except honour and fame in the eyes of posterity.

The movement still concerns itself with the frustrated at this stage, and for the opposite purpose. It no longer harnesses their discontent for a struggle with the present. It reconciles them to it and makes them patient and meek, and what it offers them now is the distant hope, the dream and the vision. At the end of its vigorous span the movement is an instrument of power for the successful and an opiate for the frustrated.

**How you know** is answered by that same test, and **What a person is** by the inventory of the leader's qualities above.

## Ch. XVIII — How long the fever runs

**What is worth having**. A short active phase, which is the book's one real verdict.[^4] This book is chiefly about the active phase, the one moulded by the true believer, and it is in that phase that all types of movement show the common traits. However noble the original purpose and however good the end result, the active phase is bound to strike us as unpleasant if not evil. The fanatic who personifies it is an unattractive human type: ruthless, self-righteous, credulous, disputatious, petty and rude, and often ready to sacrifice relatives and friends.

The absolute unity that gives a movement its drive is bought at a sacrifice of much that is precious in the autonomous individual. So no movement can be good if its active phase is overlong, and particularly if it continues after the movement is in undisputed possession of power. The ones he counts as more or less beneficent — the Reformation, the Puritan, French and American revolutions, and many nationalist movements of the past century — had relatively short active phases. **The leader who benefits his people knows not only how to start a movement but, like Gandhi, when to end its active phase.**

Where the pattern of the active phase is preserved for generations, as in the militant church through the Middle Ages, the result is an era of stagnation. A dark age. Genuine creativeness associated with a movement almost always comes before the active phase, or more often after it. Provided the phase was not too long or too bloody, its termination often releases a burst of creativeness — whether it ended in triumph, as with the Dutch Rebellion, or in defeat, as with the Puritan Revolution. The cause is not the movement's idealism but the abrupt relaxation of collective discipline.

**What is real**. Sterility, during the fever, and the evidence is a poet's twenty years. Trotsky knew that periods of high tension in social passions leave little room for contemplation, and that all the muses have hard sledding in times of revolution. Napoleon and Hitler were both mortified by the anaemic art produced in their heroic age and clamoured for masterpieces worthy of the times. They had not an inkling that an active movement stifles the creative spirit. **Milton in 1640 was a poet of great promise with a draft of *Paradise Lost* in his pocket.** He spent twenty sterile years writing pamphlets, up to his neck in the sea of noises and hoarse disputes that was the Puritan Revolution. With the Revolution dead and himself in disgrace, he produced *Paradise Lost*, *Paradise Regained* and *Samson Agonistes*.

The interference has four routes and he lists them. The fervour drains the energies that would have gone into creative work, having the same effect as dissipation. Creative work gets subordinated to the movement, so literature, art and science must be propagandistic and practical. Where a movement opens vast fields of action there is a further drain. And the fanatical state of mind by itself can stifle all forms of creative work, because the fanatic's disdain for the present blinds him to the complexity and uniqueness of life.

The illustrations of that blindness are three men and a window. Simonov: our writers must march in serried ranks, and he who steps off the road to pick flowers is like a deserter. Rabbi Jacob in the first century: he who walks in the way and interrupts his study to say *how beautiful is this tree* has made himself guilty against his own soul. St Bernard could walk all day by the lake of Geneva and never see the lake. **And Hume tells of a monk whose cell window opened on a noble prospect, who made a covenant with his eyes never to turn that way.** The blindness is a source of strength, since the fanatic sees no obstacles. It is also the cause of intellectual sterility.

The fanatic is mentally cocky as well, and therefore barren of new beginnings. At the root of the cockiness is a conviction that life and the universe conform to a simple formula, his formula. So he is without the fruitful intervals of groping, when the mind is as it were in solution and ready for new combinations.

**How you know**. By whether a movement's originality is anything more than scale. When an active movement displays originality it is usually an originality of application. The principles and techniques it exploits were produced by creativeness outside the movement. All active movements have the unabashed imitativeness we associate with the Japanese. Even in propaganda the Nazis and Communists imitate more than they originate, selling their brand of holy cause the way an advertiser sells soap. Much of what looks new in their methods comes from running vast territorial empires the way a Ford or a DuPont runs an industrial one.

**The shape of time — what sets the length**. A concrete objective, or the lack of one. A movement with a limited objective is likely to have a shorter active phase than one with a nebulous aim. The vague objective is perhaps indispensable for chronic extremism. Cromwell's line is the epigraph: **a man never goes so far as when he does not know whether he is going.** Set a movement in motion to free a nation from tyranny, to resist an aggressor, or to renovate a backward society, and there is a natural point of termination. Make the objective an ideal society of perfect unity — the City of God, a Communist heaven, Hitler's warrior state — and the active phase has no automatic end.

Two nineteenth-century men saw it coming, and he quotes them at length because almost nobody else did. Burckhardt had a premonition that sounded to him like folly and would not leave him: the military state must become one great factory, and what must logically come is a definite and supervised stint of misery, with promotions and in uniform, begun and ended daily to the sound of drums. Renan felt socialism was the coming religion of the West, and that as a secular religion it would turn politics and economics into holy causes. Let us tremble, he wrote. At this very moment, perchance, the religion of the future is in the making, and we have no part in it.

Size and homogeneity matter too, and here Hoffer makes his one constructive proposal. In most cases where an attempt at an ideal society produced a prolonged and ugly active phase, the experiment was made on a vast scale with a heterogeneous population — Christianity, Islam, and the French, Russian and Nazi revolutions. The communal settlements in the small state of Israel and the socialisation programmes of the small Scandinavian states suggest something else. A small nation with a fairly homogeneous population can attempt the same thing in an atmosphere that is neither hectic nor coercive.

His reasons are practical. A small nation has a horror of wasting its human material. It needs internal harmony as a safeguard against aggression. And its people feel they are all of one family, which allows utmost co-operation without either religiofication or militarisation. **He proposes the principle of a pilot plant**, borrowed from mass-production industry and applied to social progress: leave the extreme social experiments wholly to small states with homogeneous, civilised populations.

There is one further variable, and it is habit. The Japanese, Russians and Germans who allowed an active phase to run on without opposition had been inured to submissiveness for generations beforehand. Lenin knew the advantage he had — how can you compare the masses of Western Europe with our people, so patient, so accustomed to privation? Madame de Staël on the Germans a century earlier is quoted as the same finding: they are vigorously submissive, and they employ philosophical reasonings to explain respect for force and the fear that turns respect into admiration.

He will not say a Hitler or a Stalin could not rise in a country with a tradition of freedom. What he asserts is narrower and more useful. In such a country a Hitler might find it easy to gain power and extremely hard to hold it indefinitely, because any marked improvement in conditions would activate the tradition of freedom, which is a tradition of revolt. In Russia the individual pitted against Stalin had nothing to identify himself with. In a traditionally free country he does not feel an isolated human atom but one of a mighty race — his rebellious ancestors.

The leader's personality is the last factor. Rare leaders like Lincoln and Gandhi curb the evil in a movement and are willing to end it when its objective is more or less realised. Stalin's medieval mind and tribal ruthlessness were a chief cause of the Communist movement's prolonged dynamism, and he moulded his successors in his own image. Cromwell's death brought the end of the Puritan Revolution, and Robespierre's death ended the active phase of the French one.

Then a counterfactual he refuses to resolve, and it is the most honest sentence in the chapter. Had Hitler died in the mid-1930s, Nazism under Goering would probably have changed course and the Second World War might have been averted. **Yet the sepulchre of Hitler, founder of a Nazi religion, might have been a greater evil than all the atrocities and destruction of Hitler's war.**

**How people should relate — the founding gesture**. With an act of defiance, if individual liberty is ever to come out the other end. The Reformation, the Puritan, American and French revolutions and many nationalist risings ended after a short active phase in orders marked by increased individual liberty. All of them started by defying and overthrowing a long-established authority. The more clear-cut that initial defiance, and the more vivid its memory, the likelier individual liberty is to emerge.

The counter-cases are the ones with no such moment. There was no clear-cut act of defiance in the rise of Christianity. It did not begin by overthrowing a king, a hierarchy or a church. There were martyrs, and not individuals shaking their fists under the nose of proud authority in view of the whole world. Hence perhaps the fact that the authoritarian order it ushered in endured almost unchallenged for fifteen hundred years. The emancipation of the Christian mind at the Renaissance drew its inspiration from the Graeco-Roman past rather than from early Christianity. Islam and the Japanese collective body lack the same founding gesture, and neither shows signs of individual emancipation. German nationalism, unlike most Western nationalisms, did not start with a spectacular act of defiance — it was taken under the wing of the Prussian army from the beginning.

**What a person is — the case for useful movements**. Somebody who might have to be welded together in a hurry, and this is where Hoffer defends the thing he has spent the book anatomising. The true believers of every colour declaim on the decadence of the Western democracies. The burden is always that people there are too soft and too selfish to die for a nation or a cause, and that this indicates moral and biological decay.

He calls it a grain of sense and more than a grain of nonsense. In normal times a democratic nation is an institutionalised association of more or less free individuals. Threatened, it must unify and generate a spirit of self-sacrifice, and to do that it has to transform itself into something like a militant church. **That transformation is difficult and slow, and it does not involve deep-reaching changes.** The true believers give the game away themselves. By their account Germany was decadent in the 1920s and wholly virile in the 1930s — and a decade is far too short to work biological or even cultural changes in a population of millions.

So the ability to produce a movement in short order matters in times like the Hitler decade. The mastery of the art of religiofication is an essential requirement in the leader of a democratic nation, even if the need to practise it never arises. And extreme intellectual fastidiousness, or a businessman's practical-mindedness, may disqualify a man for national leadership.

The measure he proposes for a nation's readiness is a good one. The measure of a nation's potential virility is the reservoir of its longing. Heraclitus said it would not be better for mankind if they were given their desires, and Hoffer applies it to nations. When a nation stops wanting things fervently, or aims its desires at something concrete and limited, its potential is impaired. Only a goal open to continued perfection keeps it ready. The goal need not be sublime: the gross ideal of an ever-rising standard of living has kept America fairly ready. England's ideal of the country gentleman and France's of the retired rentier are concrete and limited, and he thinks that has something to do with both nations' lessened drive.

**What makes things happen — the last argument**. Movements as an instrument of renewal, defended in the closing pages. They are often a factor in awakening stagnant societies. In large and heterogeneous bodies — Russia, India, China, the Arab world, even Spain — awakening seems to depend on a widespread fervent enthusiasm that perhaps only a movement can generate. **So the inability to produce a full-fledged movement can be a grave handicap.** It has probably been one of China's great misfortunes that the Taiping rebellion and the Sun Yat-sen revolution were both stifled too soon.

He goes further, and the sentence is deliberately hard. It is probably better for a country whose government shows chronic incompetence to be overthrown by a mighty upheaval, even at considerable waste of life and wealth, than to be allowed to crumble of itself. Where governments die a lingering death the result is often stagnation and irremediable decay. And since men of words are crucial to the rise of movements, an educated and articulate minority is probably indispensable to the vigour of a social body — provided it is not in intimate alliance with the government.

The mechanism of renewal, in his account, runs through outsiders and never directly. Foreign influence works not by introducing foreign fashions or manners. It works by creating an educated minority where there was none, or by alienating an existing one from the prevailing order. That minority then sets a movement in motion, and the movement shakes the body out of its stagnation. Foreign influences alienated Mohammed from the dispensation in Mecca, and Islam shook and integrated Arabia. Graeco-Roman and Arabic influences produced men of words with no connection to the church, and the Reformation shook Europe out of its torpor. European influence detached the Russian intelligentsia from the Romanovs.

Japan is the exception that makes his case, because there the influence landed on men of action rather than men of words. Emperor Meiji's group had the vision Peter the Great lacked, and they succeeded where he failed. **They knew that importing foreign customs would not stir Japan to life**, and that the art of religiofication was indispensable to the task. They set in motion one of the most effective movements of modern times. Its evils are illustrated throughout this book, and Hoffer doubts any other agency could have accomplished that feat of renovation.

Then the last sentence of the book, which is a compliment and an indictment in one breath. Haldane counts fanaticism among the only four really important inventions made between 3000 B.C. and 1400 A.D., and calls it a Judaic-Christian invention. It is strange to think that in receiving this malady of the soul, the world also received a miraculous instrument for raising societies and nations from the dead — an instrument of resurrection.
