---

## Reflecting on Hitler — Power as a thing other people make

Franz Neumann was writing in 1942, with the thing still running, and he put the problem in two sentences. Charismatic rule had long been neglected and ridiculed. It had deep roots all the same, and became a powerful stimulus once the right conditions were set — and the Leader's charismatic power was no mere phantasm, because none could doubt that millions believed in it.[^1]

That is a claim about what is real. A power that exists only because people believe in it is not fake for that reason. It behaves like a fact, and it kills like one.

**The power was a social product** — made out of the expectations and motivations that followers vested in one man.[^2] He held it in no formal sense. Not as a party leader, not from any office with duties attached. He derived it from what he took to be a historic mission to save Germany, and it depended entirely on other people's readiness to see heroic qualities in him. They did see them, possibly before he saw them himself.

So the place to look for an explanation is not the man. It is everybody else.[^3]

The clearest piece of period evidence for how that worked is one sentence spoken by a Nazi functionary in 1934, and it explains a system. It was the duty of each person in the Third Reich to work towards the Führer along the lines he would wish — without waiting for instruction from above.[^4] Nobody had to be told. Initiatives came up from below, aimed at what the man at the top would have wanted, and the things he never ordered are as much a part of the story as the things he did. Causation, in that arrangement, runs upwards. Ideas were sanctioned at the top and generated underneath it.

What is a person, in this account? Outside politics, an empty space. Napoleon, Bismarck, Churchill and Kennedy were all figures of substance outside their public lives; here there was no private life at all, no retreat, no deeper existence conditioning the public reflexes.[^5] The German people did not learn that Eva Braun existed until the Reich was ashes. He did not make his private life part of his public persona. He made the public sphere private, and the two merged until nothing was left but the role.

Two contemporaries put the opposite readings of that on record. Albert Speer, as close to him as anyone, called him soon after the war a demonic figure, one of those inexplicable phenomena that emerge at rare intervals among mankind, whose person determined the fate of a nation.[^6] Against that, the Soviet-bloc line held that personality played no part at all: he was an agent of capitalism, a cypher whose strings big business pulled.[^7] Both are claims about what kind of thing a human being is inside history, and both have the same convenience — they make everybody else a supernumerary.

There is a third view, from an observer writing in 1940, before the fall of France, and it is the sharpest thing in this section. He is the potential suicide par excellence. He owns no ties outside his own ego. He is in the privileged position of one who loves nothing and no one but himself — so he can dare all to preserve or magnify his power, which alone stands between him and speedy death.[^8]

What was worth having? Being near it. Churchmen, intellectuals, diplomats and distinguished visitors were impressed — people who would not have been captivated for a moment by the same sentiments shouted at a crowd in a Munich beerhall.[^9] Add the Chancellorship, adoring crowds and the trappings, and it was not surprising that anyone beyond the wholly naive could find him impressive. His underlings hung on every word until April 1945, then ran. And a great many women, much younger than he was, saw the man whose person seems the antithesis of sexuality as a sex-symbol; several attempted suicide on his behalf.

How would anybody know any of this? The section is blunt about the state of the evidence and about one question it refuses. One survey a decade and a half old covered more than 1,500 titles; a later attempt to draw the balance mentioned 120,000 pieces of work.[^10] Out of all of it, only a handful of full scholarly biographies. And the question of historical greatness gets thrown out — a red herring, resting on a subjective set of moral and aesthetic judgements, explaining nothing whichever way it were answered.

On time, this section says little, and what it says is about a debt not yet settled. The immediate legacy — a Germany split by a wall, a Europe split by a curtain — had ended only a decade before the writing. The deeper one, the moral trauma, had not passed.[^11]

*Read: lines 283–402.*

---

## Ch. 1 — A name worth changing, and a career worth refusing

In 1876 a customs inspector in Braunau am Inn changed his name from Alois Schicklgruber to Alois Hitler, and thirteen years before his son was born the thing was done.[^12] The point is made drily and it is not a joke: *Heil Schicklgruber* would have been an unlikely salutation for a national hero.

**What a person is, here, is substantially a name and a legitimation**. Alois was born in 1837 in the village of Strones, the illegitimate child of a forty-two-year-old woman, and the baptismal register left a blank where the father's name should go.[^13] The blank stayed there for thirty-nine years. Then a notary in Weitra recorded him as the son of Georg Hitler, three witnesses signed, and the next day the parish priest of Döllersheim struck out *Schicklgruber*, replaced *out of wedlock* with *within wedlock*, and wrote a name into the empty box. The man named had been dead nineteen years.

Illegitimacy itself carried no great stigma. The Church castigated it; country life in Austria was full of it, and Alois never concealed his own.[^14] What the paperwork was for was probably a legacy — his uncle Nepomuk, with no male heirs, seems to have made an inheritance conditional on the name.

The ladder that mattered was the state. Alois left elementary school for a cobbler's apprenticeship, went to Vienna at thirteen to train in leatherwork, and by eighteen had a modest grade in the Austrian ministry of finance.[^15] Supervisory status at twenty-four. The customs service at twenty-seven. Customs officer at thirty-three, inspector at thirty-eight, and finally Higher Collector of Customs — the highest rank open to a man with nothing behind him but elementary school. **That was the whole visible route out of a Waldviertel smallholding, and a man who had climbed it did not regard it as one option among several**.

Marriage in that world ran on the same practical logic. Alois married Anna Glassl in 1873 when she was fifty and he was thirty-six; she was relatively well off and had connections in the civil service, and it is unlikely to have been a love-match.[^16] He married three times and fathered nine children by three women, four of whom died in infancy.

The third marriage needed Rome's permission, because Alois and Klara were officially second cousins.[^17] The dispensation took four months to arrive, by which time Klara's condition was plain to everybody. They married on 7 January 1885 at six o'clock in the morning, and after a perfunctory celebration Alois went back to the customs post.

What makes things happen to children is disease, and the rate is the ordinary background of the period. Gustav born 1885, Ida 1886, Otto who died days after his birth. Then diphtheria took Gustav and Ida within weeks of each other in December 1887 and January 1888.[^18] Klara was pregnant again by that summer, and Adolf, born on an overcast Easter Saturday in April 1889, was her fourth child and the first to live. Edmund, born 1894, died of measles at five.

Inside the house, authority was one-directional and physical. Alois was pompous, status-proud, strict, humourless, frugal and pedantically punctual, respected in the community, and possessed of a temper that flared without warning.[^19] Klara could not get out of the habit of calling him *Uncle* for years after they married. After he died she kept a rack of his pipes in the kitchen and would point at them when he came up in conversation, as if to call his authority back into the room. Paula remembered her mother as the compensating element between an almost too harsh father and lively children — and said that her brother challenged their father to extreme harshness and got his sound thrashing every day, while her mother caressed him and tried to obtain with kindness what harshness could not get.[^20] Their mother sometimes waited outside the door while it happened.

**What was worth having split the household in two, and the split has a date and a room**. At thirteen the boy was taken into the Linz customs office to be shown what his life would be.[^21] It filled him with horror and a lasting disgust. He wrote later that he yawned and grew sick at the thought of sitting in an office, deprived of his liberty, ceasing to be master of his own time. Against that stood a man who had come up from nothing through industry and effort to a position of dignity and respect, watching his son dawdle over drawings.

The quarrel was not really about the civil service. It was a rejection of everything the father had stood for, and so of the father.

There was a political layer to it too, and the two sides of it were both German. Alois's nationalism was the kind that wanted German interests dominant *within* the Austrian state, and would have no truck with the pan-German variety that rejected the state altogether and looked to Wilhelmine Germany.[^22] The son, in a school that was a hotbed of it, was drawn to the shriller Schönerer version — and almost certainly riled his father by ridiculing the very state to which the man had given forty years.

What the world was made of, for the boy, came out of books and a theatre. An illustrated history of the Franco-Prussian war thrilled him. When the Boer War broke out the village games turned into Boer exploits.[^23] Then Karl May's tales of the Wild West and the Indian wars, written by a man who had never been to America. Most boys grew out of May. He did not — as Chancellor he still read the stories and recommended them to his generals, whom he accused of lacking imagination.

Wagner did the rest. *Lohengrin* was his first and stayed his favourite: the mysterious knight of the grail, sent from the castle of Monsalvat by his father Parzival to rescue a wrongly condemned pure maiden, and betrayed by her in the end.[^24] A performance could work on him like a religious experience.

Time in this chapter runs backwards from a prize that has not been won. Around 1906 the two friends bought a lottery ticket, and he was so certain of first prize that he designed their future residence in advance — an artistic life, a middle-aged lady to keep house, trips to Bayreuth.[^25] No woman their own age appeared in it. When nothing came of the flutter his fury at the state lottery knew no bounds. The same shape governs Stefanie, an elegant young woman seen promenading through Linz on her mother's arm, who did not know he existed.[^26] She was to be admired from a distance and never approached, a figure who would be waiting when the right moment came for their marriage and the villa he would design for her.

Then the examination. He went to Vienna in September 1907 with a thick pile of drawings, one of 113 candidates, and got through the first cut.[^27] Two three-hour papers followed. Twenty-eight passed. **The verdict on his file is four words: test drawing unsatisfactory, few heads**.

He asked the Rector why and was told his talents lay in architecture rather than painting. He left, he wrote, for the first time in his young life at odds with himself. He also told nobody — not his friend, not his dying mother. Klara died of breast cancer on 21 December 1907, aged forty-seven, three months after the rejection. Her Jewish doctor, Eduard Bloch, had seen many deathbed scenes and said he had never seen anyone so prostrate with grief.[^28]

How anybody knows any of this is a problem the chapter states plainly rather than solving. The record of the early years is very sparse; the account in *Mein Kampf* is inaccurate in detail and coloured in interpretation; post-war recollections of family and acquaintances are as dubious in their way as the Third Reich's own attempts to glorify the childhood.[^29] For the formative period that psychologists most want, there is little to go on which is not retrospective guesswork. The one contemporary document is a letter of December 1923 from his old class teacher, Dr Huemer, to his defence counsel after the failed putsch — a thin, pale youth commuting from Leonding, not using his talent, unable to accommodate himself to discipline, stubborn, high-handed and hot-tempered.[^30] Even that was written to help him.

## Ch. 2 — A city where hating Jews was too ordinary to notice

Vienna in 1900 held 1,674,957 people, and fewer than one in two had been born there.[^31] The population had grown two and a half times since 1860 — four times the rate of Paris or London — pulling people in from every part of an empire of fifty million with Germans, Czechs, Slovaks, Poles, Ruthenians, Slovenes, Serbs, Croats, Italians, Romanians and Hungarians in it.

The Jewish population had gone from a little over 6,000 at mid-century, about 2 per cent, to 175,318 by 1910, or 8.6 per cent.[^32] In Leopoldstadt, the old ghetto, a third of a poor population was Jewish — small traders and pedlars, many in caftan and black hat. In Brigittenau, where he would spend his last three years, about 17 per cent.

Everything in the city ran two ways at once. Imperial grandeur and opulence, with some of the direst poverty in Europe behind it. Bourgeois respectability and moral rectitude, with vice and criminality rampant underneath.[^33] The very limits of the avant-garde — Klimt, Schnitzler, Mahler, Schönberg, Freud — and a popular philistinism that fought them. **A sense that the old order was passing, and nobody knew what would replace it**. What that mood did was make impotent anger convertible into race hatred, and there were two men in the city showing how.

Georg Ritter von Schönerer welded German nationalism, social reform, anti-liberal popular democracy and racial antisemitism into one thing — antisemitism being the cement that held the anti-liberal, anti-socialist, anti-Catholic and anti-Habsburg parts together.[^34] Three particular items carried forward out of his movement into another one: the *Heil* greeting, the title of *Führer*, which he bestowed on himself, and an intolerance of anything resembling a democratic decision inside his own organisation.

Karl Lueger did the same work by a different route and with far more people. Where Schönerer neglected the masses, Lueger won over the classes whose existence was threatened — small traders, artisans, the German-speaking lower middle class squeezed between international capital, Marxist Social Democracy and Slav nationalism.[^35] His antisemitism was functional rather than doctrinal, and he said so: *I say who a Jew is*.

That did not make it mild. In 1890 he quoted, without dissent, another man's proposal that the Jewish problem would be solved and the world served if all Jews were put on a large ship and sunk on the high seas.[^36] In 1899, to thunderous applause, he spoke of Jews exercising a terrorism worse than which cannot be imagined, and of liberating the Christian people from the domination of Jewry. On another occasion he called wolves, leopards and tigers more human than Jews — these beasts of prey in human form. Taken to task for stirring hatred, he answered that antisemitism would perish when the last Jew perished. Accused of saying he did not mind whether Jews were hanged or shot, he supplied a correction: *Beheaded! is what I said*.

The Emperor had refused for years and then had to appoint him Lord Mayor in 1897.

Meanwhile the empire's parliament was demonstrating what a nation-state made of eleven nationalities looks like when it tries to legislate. In February 1909 a bill putting Czech on an equal footing with German in Bohemia had to be abandoned and the session suspended, because rattles, bells, children's trumpets, horns and banging desk-lids made debate impossible, and deputies fell to fisticuffs while rival sets sang competing anthems.[^37] After universal male suffrage arrived in 1907, Germans were no longer the largest national group in the chamber. Laws passed only by horse-trading between factions.

Social Democracy was the third force and the one that frightened him. In 1891 the party won no seats at all; in 1907 it took eighty-seven out of 516, and a third of the vote in Lueger's own Vienna.[^38] What impressed him was the organisation. Standing on a pavement watching endless columns of workers march past four abreast for two hours, he described a gigantic human dragon slowly winding by, and went home with a feeling he called oppressed anxiety. What he took from them was the value of intimidation and intolerance, and the lesson that the psyche of the great masses is not receptive to anything half-hearted or weak.

What a man is worth, in this chapter, is measured by which floor of the city he is on, and the descent is documented. By autumn 1909 he was in a night-shelter in Meidling — a bath, disinfection of clothes, soup and bread, a bed in a dormitory, and out on the street all day.[^39] Mornings meant queueing with other destitutes at a convent in Gumpendorferstraße where nuns doled out soup. He shovelled snow without an overcoat and could not stick it. He offered to carry bags at the Westbahnhof. His fellow vagrants nicknamed him *Ohm Paul Krüger*, after the Boer leader, for the long coat, the greasy trilby, the shoes like a nomad's and the fuzz on his chin.

Fifty Kronen from his aunt bought a coat from the government pawn-shop and the materials for a business. Reinhold Hanisch — a man with a police record, living under the name Fritz Walter — hawked postcard-sized paintings around pubs while he copied them out of other pictures.[^40] One a day. About 5 Kronen each, split two ways.

The Men's Home in Meldemannstraße was a long way up from the shelter: 500 residents, own cubicles at 50 Heller a night, a canteen, baths, a cobbler's and a tailor's in the basement, a small library, a reading-room with newspapers.[^41] It had been built with private donations, some of them from wealthy Jewish families. He had his own corner of the writing-room, and any newcomer who took it was told that the place was taken, Herr Hitler sits there.

Most of the dealers who took his work were Jewish, and he told Hanisch that Jews were better businessmen and more reliable customers than Christian ones.[^42] His closest business partner apart from Hanisch, Josef Neumann, was a Jew he seems to have been on friendly terms with. A one-eyed locksmith named Simon Robinson passed him small change when he needed it. Löffner, another Jewish dealer, took his side against Hanisch in the row over the parliament-building painting that put Hanisch in jail — for using a false name.

**And this is where the chapter's central question sits, unanswered on purpose**. When and why did he become the fixated antisemite of 1919 and after? In truth, we do not know for certain.[^43] His own version has a caftan and black hair locks in the Inner City, a first thought — *is this a Jew?* — and a second, after long staring, *is this a German?* Afterwards he began buying antisemitic pamphlets, and everywhere he went he began to see Jews.[^44]

Almost nothing else supports it. Hanisch was adamant that in those days he was by no means a Jew hater and became one afterwards, and had him admiring Jews for their resistance to persecution, praising Heine and Mendelssohn and Offenbach, calling them the first civilized nation for abandoning polytheism, blaming Christians more than Jews for usury, and dismissing the ritual-murder charge as nonsense.[^45] Karl Honisch, describing him in 1913, records his fury at the Jesuits and the Reds and mentions the Jews not at all. An anonymous resident in 1912 said he got along exceptionally well with Jews and once called them a clever people who stick together better than the Germans do. Against that sits one remark of Hanisch's, which points the other way. Asked why Jews remained strangers in the nation, he answered that it was because they were a different race — and added that Jews had a different smell.[^46]

The reading offered is that the hatred was there, and that it was invisible for a banal reason: in a city that vicious, anti-Jewish sentiment was so commonplace it went practically unnoticed.[^47] The argument from silence proves nothing. And as long as he needed Jewish dealers to shift his pictures, he kept quiet — which is not friendship, but is not evidence against the hatred either.

The plainest thing in the chapter is not about Jews. It is about class, and it is in his own words. The cleft between the petty-bourgeois world and the manual worker is deeper than we imagine, and the reason for the hostility is the fear of a group which has only recently raised itself above the manual worker that it will sink back into the old despised class.[^48] **He wrote that as analysis. It is a description of himself in the doss-house**. Far from producing solidarity, the descent sharpened his antagonism: not theory but survival, struggle, and every man for himself marked the philosophy of the shelter.

Time, in the end, is money. He detested the city and stayed. His share of his father's inheritance fell due on his twenty-fourth birthday, 20 April 1913; on 16 May the District Court in Linz confirmed 819 Kronen 98 Heller, to be posted to the artist Adolf Hitler in Meldemannstraße; and on 24 May he left for Munich with a light black suitcase.[^49] He had also failed to register for military service in 1909 and reckoned it safe to cross the border. He was wrong about that, and it caught him the following year.

## Ch. 3 — A country that expected a hero, and got a war instead

The chapter opens with a flat causal claim and spends itself defending it. **The First World War made Hitler possible**. Without the war, the humiliation and the revolution, the failed artist would not have found what to do with his life, and the demagogue would have had no audience for the message.[^50]

What was Germany before that? The old answer — a malformed history, a national character bent towards authoritarianism and militarism, the Second Reich as the Third waiting to happen — is set aside as too neat.[^51] Social and economic development looked much more like Britain's and France's than was once thought.

The constitution was the real difference. Party pluralism existed and had a chamber, but had not been translated into parliamentary democracy. The Chancellor was the Kaiser's appointee, made and broken regardless of the strength of parties. The government stood above the Reichstag. Whole tracts of foreign and military policy lay outside parliamentary control, guarded by big landholders, the officer corps and the upper bureaucracy — some of whom, fearing revolution, were prepared to contemplate war as a way of keeping what they had.[^52]

**What that country believed about itself came out of a mountain**. The new state took the name *Reich*, which evoked a claim to reinstate the first one — Frederick Barbarossa asleep in his holy mountain beneath the Kyffhäuser until his medieval empire was reborn.[^53] In 1896 veterans' associations funded a gigantic monument to Kaiser Wilhelm I on that same hill. Hermann the Cherusker, who destroyed three Roman legions in 9 AD, got a colossal monument in the Teutoburger Wald. Germania got the Niederwald Monument above the Rhine, which impressed the young soldier when he passed it in 1914 on his way to Flanders. Hundreds of Bismarck Towers went up the length of the country, put up by student bodies.

Then a gap opened between the myth and the man on the throne. The Reichstag, once an emblem of unity, came to look like the barometer of division — a house of squabbling politicians. Wilhelm II was promoted through a deliberate cult as the governing statesman and sleeping Hero-Kaiser in one, and disappointed everybody.[^54] Which produced a demand.

Heinrich Claß, leader of the Pan-German League, wrote it out in 1912 under a pseudonym, in a tract called *If I Were the Kaiser*.[^55] Franchise restrictions, press censorship, repressive laws against socialism, anti-Jewish legislation. And a strong able leader, whom all who had remained unseduced by the teachings of ungerman democracy yearned for, because they knew that greatness could only be brought about through the concentration of individual forces, which could only be achieved by subordination to a leader. Five editions before the war.

The racial thinking that would later be needed was already on the shelves. A widely read text of the 1890s called Jews poison for us, to be treated as such, and increasingly the language was bacteriological — a pest and a cholera.[^56] Houston Stewart Chamberlain's *Foundations of the 19th Century* was a bestseller from 1900. Theodor Fritsch's *Handbook of the Jewish Question*, a catechism for antisemites, went through twenty-five editions in seven years.

None of it was uniquely German, and the chapter insists on that. Social Darwinism was influential in Britain; the classic lands of racial antisemitism around 1900 were Austria-Hungary and France; the worst physical persecution was in Russia.[^57] What differed was how much backing these ideas got from conservatives who took them over from the populist radical Right.

The eugenics movement did the rest, and it produced a sentence worth having exactly. Sterilising certain categories of degenerates was described by one doctor in 1889 as **a sacred duty of the state**.[^58] The fear behind it was of racial degeneration through a falling birthrate among the better sort and a rising proportion of inferiors, together with resentment at the cost of supporting the handicapped, the antisocial and the mentally ill. Most Jews in Imperial Germany looked at all this and felt reasonably sanguine, taking antisemitism for a throwback to a more primitive era that was on the way out.[^59] What they underestimated was how the modern racial version differed from the old persecutions — its insistence on biological distinctiveness, its bond with assertive nationalism, and how easily a mass movement could pick it up.

Then 1914, and the emotional register changes completely. A leading social-policy journal called it a resurrection, a rebirth of the nation: Germany shocked out of everyday troubles and pleasures, united in moral duty, ready for the highest sacrifice.[^60] The Kaiser, today truly a People's Kaiser: *I know no parties any longer, I know only Germans*. Four decades of strife between parties, confessions, classes and races totally consumed by the breath of flame of national fervour. These first days of August are undying, incomparable days of glory.

He was in the crowd on the Odeonsplatz on 2 August, hoarse with singing. Years later he noticed a photograph Heinrich Hoffmann had taken of it and said he had been there; Hoffmann made enlargements, found the twenty-five-year-old face in the middle of the war hysteria, and the mass reproduction of that picture helped build the Führer myth and Hoffmann's fortune.[^61]

He got into the Bavarian army by mistake. Foreigners could be accepted only by the war ministry, not by the cabinet office he later credited, and detailed inquiries in 1924 could not establish how he had not simply been returned to Austria.[^62] In all probability, the report concluded, the question of his nationality was never even raised.

**For him the war was a godsend, and the reason is stated without decoration**. At twenty-five it gave him for the first time a cause, a commitment, comradeship, external discipline, something like regular employment, and a sense of belonging.[^63] The regiment was home. Wounded in 1916, his first words to his officer were that it was not so bad and he could stay with the regiment. He may have refused promotion because it would have moved him off the regimental staff. His years in the army were the one time, he said later, when he had no worries — food, clothing and accommodation all provided.

The reality of it was arithmetic. Within six days of arriving in Lille his battalion had its baptism of fire on the Menin Road, and in four days the regiment went from 3,600 men to 611.[^64] Initial losses ran around 70 per cent, some of it from Württemberg and Saxon regiments mistaking Bavarians for English in the gloom. Colonel List was among the dead. His initial idealism, he said, gave way to the realization that life is a constant horrible struggle.

He was a dispatch runner, carrying orders on foot or by bicycle from the regimental command post to the front three kilometres away.[^65] Two runners were sent with a message when possible, so that it would get through if one was killed. Three of the eight attached to the staff died on 15 November 1914 and another was wounded. Two days later a French shell hit the forward command post minutes after he had left it, killing or wounding almost everyone there.

His comrades thought him odd and mostly liked him. They called him Adi and referred to him as the artist, and noticed that after mid-1915 he got no mail or parcels even at Christmas, never spoke of family, neither smoked nor drank, showed no interest in brothels, and sat for hours in a corner of the dug-out reading.[^66] A telephonist suggested looking round for a *Mamsell*; he said he would die of shame looking for sex with a French girl, and somebody said, look at the monk. Brandmayer asked whether he had ever loved a girl. He said he had never had time for anything like that and would never get round to it.

What he did love was a white terrier called Foxl that had strayed over from the enemy lines. He taught it tricks and revelled in how glad it was to see him.[^67] When his unit moved on and the dog could not be found he was distraught, and years later said that the swine who took him did not know what he had done. He felt nothing comparable for any of the thousands of humans killed around him. **With the dog, as with every person he ever dealt with, the relationship rested on subordination: I liked him so much, he only obeyed me**.

At Christmas 1914 German and British troops met in no man's land, shook hands and sang carols. He objected: there should be no question of something like that during war.[^68] His comrades learned they could set him off at will by saying the war would be lost, and always got the same last words — for us the war can't be lost.

The Iron Cross First Class in August 1918 was a rare award for a corporal, and a Jewish officer, Leutnant Hugo Gutmann, put him up for it.[^69] The school books later said he had single-handedly captured fifteen Frenchmen. He had carried an important dispatch through heavy fire after the telephones failed, along with another runner. Because the action was courageous but not exceptional, Gutmann had to badger the divisional commander for weeks before permission came.

What the war did to everybody else is a set of numbers the chapter refuses to soften. Over 13 million Germans served, more than 10.5 million in the field. Around 2 million killed, almost 5 million wounded. A third of the dead had wives; nearly all had families.[^70] By 1917 rations had fallen under 1,000 calories a day, less than half a working person's minimum; three-quarters of a million died of malnutrition. Between March and July 1918, influenza took 1.75 million soldiers and 750,000 more were wounded. In four months of savage combat that year German losses came to about 800,000.

The same experience produced opposite men, and the chapter names them side by side. Where the war made him an arch-glorifier of war, it turned the playwright Ernst Toller into a pacifist and a revolutionary: the war itself had turned him into an opponent of war, and he felt the land he loved had been betrayed and sold.[^71] For one, the defeat was the betrayal. For the other, the war was. **The national community forged in the trenches was largely a myth, and there is a number that settles it**. Twice as many men joined the anti-war Reich Association of War Disabled, War Veterans and War Dependants as joined the Freikorps.[^72]

Meanwhile the search for somebody to blame found the target that was already prepared. Jews had been carried away by the spirit of 1914 like everybody else, thinking themselves at last at one with their fellow Germans; by 1916 that was destroyed for good.[^73] They were attacked as inferior immigrants flooding the country, as war profiteers, and as shirkers avoiding the front. The numbers said otherwise — the proportions of Jews and non-Jews serving at the front scarcely differed, and four or five times more non-Jews than Jews were directors of armaments companies — and it made no difference.

A statistical inquiry was carried out in late 1916 into how many Jews were at the front and how many in the rear. The results were never published. The allegation underlying it was never repudiated either, and thereafter Jews were not made officers in the Prussian army.[^74] In October 1917 Claß could report that antisemitism had already reached enormous proportions and that the struggle for survival was now beginning for the Jews. When the Pan-Germans set up a committee in September 1918 to use the Jews as lightning rods for all injustices, Claß reached for Kleist's line about the French: kill them, the world court is not asking you for your reasons.

There had been no stab in the back. Unrest at home was a consequence of military failure, not its cause.[^75] The army was exhausted, discipline had sagged, and something like a million men were ducking duty in the last months — while triumphalist propaganda was still coming out of the High Command in late October.

He heard it in a hospital in Pasewalk, partially blinded by mustard gas, on 10 November, from a pastor who told the patients the monarchy was over, Germany was a republic, the war was lost, and they must place themselves at the mercy of the victors.[^76] He wrote that he tottered back to the dormitory and dug his burning head into the blanket, and that he had not wept since the day he stood at his mother's grave. Then: in these nights hatred grew in me, hatred for those responsible for this deed. He told various people in the early 1920s that he had received a vision there, a message to liberate the German people. At his trial he dropped the vision, which would have invited ridicule, and said only that the news had made him resolve to enter politics.[^77]

The reading offered is deflationary on all counts, and it turns on what mustard gas actually does. It does not damage the eye itself; it produces a severe conjunctivitis and swelling of the lids, so sight is greatly impaired for a time. A recurrence of that secondary blindness is easily caused by rubbing the eyes — which is what would happen to a man brought to tears.[^78]

**And he was in no position at Pasewalk to decide to enter politics, or anything else**. He faced demobilisation like everyone else, had 15 Marks 30 in his Munich account when he left on 19 November, had no family and no connections that could buy him even minor patronage in a party, and made no effort to enter politics at all.[^79] What he did was stay in the army as long as he could — until 31 March 1920, longer than almost all his former comrades. Not a deliberate choice. Opportunism, and a good slice of luck.

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, Reflecting on Hitler and chapters 1–3 `[SPECULATIVE]`

A warning about this particular part, and it is unusual. **Almost nothing in these four runs is a decision by the subject at all**. Three of the four chapters cover a man with no power, no office and no followers, and the sorting below is therefore mostly about the world rather than about him. That is the correct outcome for a first part, not a shortfall — the pressures are what this section is for. Paradigm-obvious, and reading any of it as personal distinctiveness is the biographer's error rather than a finding.

Alois Hitler changing his name to secure a legacy. Legitimations of this kind were ordinary provincial business, and the chapter says so; the interest is entirely retrospective. A father pushing a son towards the civil service. It was the one ladder he knew, he had climbed it from nothing, and every other Austrian official of his standing wanted the same for his sons. Volunteering in August 1914. Tens of thousands did it in Munich alone, in the same week, in the same emotional state.

Detesting the Habsburg parliament. Anybody who watched a session collapse into children's trumpets and rival anthems came away with a similar view, and many of them were liberals.

Blaming Jews for the defeat. This was not his idea and he was not early to it. The Pan-Germans had a committee for it in September 1918, Claß was reporting enormous proportions in October 1917, and the army had run its census a year before that. Paradigm-breaking, and the cost is what marks it. Refusing the civil service outright, with nothing else in hand. Every other route out of Leonding ran through either qualifications or patronage, and he ended up in a doss-house queueing for convent soup — which is the cost, and it is legible.

Refusing promotion in the army. Amann and Wiedemann both say he declined to be considered. A corporal turning down non-commissioned rank in wartime is genuinely unusual, and the price was four years at the same grade.

Objecting to the Christmas truce. The men on both sides of no man's land in December 1914 were doing something that came naturally to them. He was the one in the dug-out saying there should be no question of it. Not telling anyone about the Academy rejection. Not a policy, but the same reflex that later ran a state: the failure was concealed from his friend and from his dying mother, and he reapplied the following year while maintaining the story.

## Ch. 1 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

A live alternative, named in the chapter by the man qualified to name it. The Rector of the Academy told him after the rejection that there was no doubt about his unsuitability for the school of painting, but that his talents plainly lay in architecture. That is a professional assessment, offered free, by somebody with no stake in flattering him — and it is the only piece of expert career advice recorded in his entire youth. He agreed with it in writing and did nothing about it, then or later. Architecture needed the educational qualifications he had walked away from at sixteen, and he never went back for them.

A constructed alternative. Suppose the *Realschule* had been finished and the entrance requirements met. The forecast is not a happy architect — it is a man with a credential and therefore with somewhere to be in August 1914 other than a Munich crowd. What the war supplied was a first structure in a life that had never had one, and a man already inside a profession has less use for that.

The scope condition, and it is what makes this transferable rather than sentimental. This only bites where the person has no alternative structure at all. A man with a trade, a family, a debt or a rank has somewhere to put himself when a crisis arrives; a man with none takes his identity from whatever institution first accepts him. The chapter's own evidence for this is his behaviour at the end: with the Armistice signed and 15 Marks in the bank, what he did was stay in the army sixteen months longer than his comrades.

## Ch. 2 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: choosing a target for a downward fear.

The mechanism is stated in his own words and it is unusually clean. The hostility between the petty-bourgeois world and the manual worker comes from the fear of a group which has only recently risen above the manual worker that it will sink back into the despised class. He wrote it as a general observation. He was in a men's hostel with a repugnant memory of the level below him and no visible route upward. What that predicts, and what happened, is that the descent produced no solidarity whatever. Sharing a dormitory with the destitute did not make him one of them in his own mind; it made distance from them the most valuable thing he had, which is why the writing-room clique of self-styled intelligentsia mattered so much and why he insisted on being the artist rather than one of the men looking for work.

Scope conditions. This holds where the fall is recent, where the person retains a marker of status the people around him lack, and where no explanation is available that makes the fall his own doing. Remove the third and the mechanism weakens sharply: a man who thinks he failed an examination looks for a better examination. A man who thinks he was cheated of one looks for who cheated him. The Academy told him his drawing was unsatisfactory. He told his friend they had laid traps for the sole purpose of ruining his career.

The general form. Downward mobility looks for a culprit at the level it fears falling to, or at a group it can define as outside the ladder altogether. Modern equivalent: any occupational group being displaced faster than it can be retrained, where the available public explanations name a population rather than a process. The mechanism does not require anybody to be unusually cruel — it requires only that the honest explanation be unbearable.

## Ch. 3 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take Pasewalk. A man is lying in a hospital bed, partially blinded, and is told that everything he committed himself to for four years has been given away. He looks for who is responsible and finds an answer he keeps for the rest of his life.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|the dichotomy of control]]** would go straight at the move he made and not at the grief. The defeat was not his to prevent and not his to reverse; the search for people to blame is an attempt to convert something outside his power into something inside it, by finding an agent where there was a process. The counsel is not consolation. It is that the question *who did this to me* is the wrong question about a lost war, because a war is lost by attrition, influenza, calorie counts and reserve depth, and none of those has a face. Every hour spent looking for the face is an hour spent making the loss into an injury.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/anicca-impermanence-constant-flux|impermanence]]** would aim at something the first advisor leaves alone: the four years themselves. The regiment was the first structure he had ever belonged to, and the pain at Pasewalk is not only about Germany. It is a man losing his home and his employment and his only community in the same week, and reaching for a political explanation of a personal bereavement. The counsel is that the regiment was always going to end — that treating a temporary arrangement as the permanent ground of a self guarantees this exact collapse when it goes, and that the collapse is not evidence of betrayal.

They do not converge, and the spread is worth keeping. The Stoic reading says the object of the grief was misidentified as an injury. The Buddhist reading says the grief was real and the object was always temporary. What both agree on is the finding that survives either way: **the search for culprits did not follow from the evidence, it followed from the need for the loss to have been done by somebody**. The chapter's own deflation of the episode supports this rather than the vision story — he heard the news, he wept, and he rubbed his eyes.

A third voice, from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/scapegoating-as-stress-displacement|scapegoating as stress displacement]], is about the country rather than the man, and it is the one with predictive value. The target was not chosen at Pasewalk. It had been assembled over four years by people with names — an army census in 1916 whose results were never published and whose premise was never withdrawn, a Reichstag investigation, a Pan-German committee constituted in September 1918 for exactly this purpose. What the man in the hospital bed did was reach for the nearest available explanation, and the reason it was nearest is that a great deal of work had gone into putting it there.

## What Transfers — the leader-shaped hole `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: a society specifying its own successor before he arrives.

This is the part of the material with the widest reach, and it comes from Claß rather than from the subject. In 1912, in a book that went through five editions before the war, the leader of the Pan-German League described the man who was wanted: strong, able, and owed subordination, because greatness could only come from the concentration of individual forces. He was not describing anyone. The Kaiser had disappointed, Bismarck was dead and had become a cult with hundreds of towers, and the description was a vacancy notice.

Scope conditions, and they matter more than the observation. A specification like this becomes dangerous only where three things hold together: an existing myth of past unity that the present visibly fails to match, a formal politics that everyone can watch failing in public, and a shock large enough to discredit the people currently in office. Imperial Germany had the first two by 1912 and did not produce anything. It took the third to make the vacancy live. Remove any one and the demand stays rhetorical. Britain had radical-Right pressure groups, social Darwinism and imperial anxiety in the same decade, and no equivalent outcome — which is the chapter's own point about how much of this was common to Europe rather than peculiar to one country.

The general form, stated about the material and not about anybody's situation: **a society that has published a description of the leader it wants has done most of the work before the candidate appears**. What remains is for someone to match the description well enough, at a moment when the incumbents cannot. Modern equivalent: any institution whose public rhetoric has already named the qualities of the saviour it lacks. The naming is not harmless commentary on a shortage. It is a specification, and specifications get filled.

---

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Ian Kershaw-Hitler Hubris.md`, lines 283–1332: Reflecting on Hitler (283–402), ch. 1 (403–676), ch. 2 (677–1050), ch. 3 (1051–1332).

The strongest documentation in this part. The Döllersheim baptismal register and the Weitra legalization protocol of June 1876. The school reports from Linz and Steyr, with the grades and the re-sits. The Academy of Fine Arts examination verdict, four words long. Dr Huemer's letter of 12 December 1923 to the defence counsel. The Austrian consular and Linz magistracy correspondence over the military-service evasion, recovered for publication in the 1950s after the Gestapo failed to seize it. The Bavarian authorities' 1924 inquiry into how an Austrian came to be in their army. The regimental records behind the Iron Cross First Class, including Godin's recommendation of 31 July 1918. Hitler's own letter to Ernst Hepp of 5 February 1915. And Claß's *Wenn ich der Kaiser wär*, in print and dated.

Where the evidence is memoir, and it is most of chapters 1 and 2. Four witnesses carry nearly everything about Vienna, and each knew him only briefly. August Kubizek's recollections began as a commission from the Nazi Party and were later lengthened, embellished, and in places plagiarised; they are treated as usable on music and theatre, where his own interests lay, and as unreliable on antisemitism, where he had an obvious post-war motive. Reinhold Hanisch had a police record and was living under an assumed name. Karl Honisch wrote for the NSDAP archive and meant to flatter. Josef Greiner's account is set aside as a fabrication, and the note that most previous historians used it is part of the finding.

The one place this report declines to follow the source. On when the antisemitism formed, the chapter reaches its conclusion by balance of probabilities and says so, against testimony from the only people who were there. That is honest reasoning and it is not a document. Both the finding and its basis are reported above at that weight, with the contrary evidence — Hanisch, Honisch, Anonymous, and the Jewish dealers, locksmith and go-between — kept in place rather than explained away.

A note on the source's own position. This is a biography written against biography. The stated method is to look at everybody but the subject, on the ground that the power was made by other people, and the register is correspondingly deflationary: the vision at Pasewalk is disposed of by an account of what mustard gas does to an eyelid, the overnight royal permission by a note on which ministry actually had the authority, the heroic capture of fifteen Frenchmen by the text of the recommendation. **The risk that carries is the mirror of hagiography** — a book committed to showing that a man was ordinary will read ordinariness into places where the evidence is thin, and the childhood chapter says outright that there is little to go on which is not retrospective guesswork before making claims about what the family circumstances must surely have produced. Bounded absence. No claim is made about material outside lines 283–1332.

# What Their World Took For Granted — Chapters 4–6

> **Chapters 4–6 of Ian Kershaw, *Hitler 1889–1936: Hubris*** — the Councils Republic and the men who put it down, an army that decided its soldiers needed lecturing, seventy-three parties in one country, the beer-table and the bouncers, a march on Rome that never happened, and a shot fired through a ceiling. Read from `RAW/books/Ian Kershaw-Hitler Hubris.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.

## Ch. 4 — A city that had to be liberated from itself

On 7 November 1918 a peace demonstration on Munich's Theresienwiese turned, with a cry of *off to the barracks*, into a march on the garrison, and the troops did not resist.[^1] There was not much revolutionary fervour in those barracks. There was also no support left for the monarchy, and war-weariness settled it. An eyewitness put it plainly long afterwards: these people wanted neither continued war nor revolutionary tribunals and burning stately homes, they wanted to get home to their farms and workshops. The House of Wittelsbach had ruled Bavaria for over seven centuries and was the first German monarchy to fall. The King and his family left that night.

What followed in six months is the material every later Nazi speech would be built out of, and the chapter is careful about the order of events. Eisner was shot on 21 February 1919 by Graf Anton von Arco-Valley, an aristocratic ex-officer then studying at Munich University.[^2] Then a Councils Republic was proclaimed at a meeting held in the one-time bedroom of the Queen of Bavaria, with Red Guards tramping the corridors where maids-in-waiting and powdered lackeys had once fawned. Then a second, Communist one under Eugen Leviné, a veteran of 1905: **today, Bavaria has finally erected the dictatorship of the proletariat**. It lasted a fortnight. A Red Army of some 20,000 workers and soldiers was gathered under a twenty-three-year-old sailor, and had no hope against the Prussian and Württemberg troops and Bavarian Freikorps massing outside the city.

The event everyone remembered came on 30 April. Eight hostages held in the Luitpold-Gymnasium — one of them a woman, several from the *völkisch* Thule Society — were badly maltreated and shot with two captured government soldiers, on an order given as retaliation for atrocities by the advancing White Guard.[^3] News of it spread like wildfire, horrified the city, and made the counter-revolutionary army speed up its assault and take savage reprisals.

**What the reprisals looked like is the part that dropped out of the memory**. Fifty-three Russian prisoners of war who had nothing whatever to do with the Councils were driven into a quarry and summarily dispatched. A group of first-aiders was mown down as supposed revolutionaries. Twelve civilian SPD supporters in Perlach were killed after being denounced by political enemies. Twenty-one members of the Catholic St Joseph's Association were shot in mistake for Spartacists.[^4] When Munich was liberated on 3 May the death toll was at least 606, of whom 335 were civilians.

Then the courts. The sentences on those involved in the socialist experiment came to about 6,000 years in total — sixty-five to hard labour, 1,737 to periods of imprisonment, 407 to lighter internment.[^5] Toller got five years, the writer Erich Mühsam fifteen. Eglhofer and Gustav Landauer were murdered by Freikorps troops. Leviné was executed for high treason.

What people knew about all this came out of the newspapers, and it was not the arithmetic. The mainstream paper of Munich's middle class wrote of the aims and methods of Russian Bolshevism, of Russian emissaries and Bolshevik agents and the practice of asiatic Bolshevism and foreign agitators.[^6] It put the criminal atrocities and the bestial slaughter of innocent hostages squarely on the communist leaders, and said any leniency towards such criminals would be a sin against the laws of humanity and justice. The troops who had liberated the city had, it reported, in strict discipline restored the spirit of order.

**The hostage shooting horrified the bourgeoisie and the far larger killing by the liberators was received with relative equanimity as restoring order**. That asymmetry is the whole finding, and it settled Bavarian politics for years. Extreme counter-revolutionary violence had become an acceptable answer to a perceived Bolshevik threat, and a regular feature of the scene. Bavaria turned into a bastion of the conservative Right and a magnet for right-wing extremists from everywhere else, several of them under order of arrest in other parts of Germany.[^7] White-blue separatists, black-white-red nationalists and *völkisch* extremists disagreed on almost everything and found common cause in hating the Left.

Now the part about the man, and it is the most awkward evidence in the chapter. His own account covers those months in a single page of an otherwise expansive book.[^8]

The record says why. A routine order of 3 April 1919 names him as his company's representative, a post he had probably held since 15 February, and the duties of representatives included cooperating with the propaganda department of the socialist government to convey educational material to the troops.[^9] **His first political work was done for the government he later called the November criminals**.

Worse, on 15 April — the day after the Communist Räterepublik was proclaimed, in fresh elections held to make sure the garrison stood behind the new regime — he was chosen as Deputy Battalion Representative.[^10] Nineteen votes were cast for *Hittler*; the winner, Johann Blümli, got thirty-nine. He wore the red armband, as almost every soldier in the Munich garrison did. He took no part in the liberation of the city, which later brought him scornful reproaches from Röhm, Epp and even Heß. Then, within a week of the end of the Councils, he was nominated — by whom is not recorded — to a three-man committee investigating whether men of his own battalion had been involved in it.[^11]

**The reading offered is opportunism rather than conviction, and the ground for it is that this was how he stayed in the army**. Every one of his close wartime comrades was discharged well before him. The demobilisation was carried out swiftly and efficiently, and what kept him on the payroll until March 1920 was political work.

What the army wanted from that work says most about how it understood a soldier's mind. In May 1919 the new Bavarian command took over an Information Department with two tasks: watching the political scene, and combating dangerous attitudes among the troops by propaganda.[^12] Educating the men in a correct anti-Bolshevik fashion became a priority, and *speaker courses* were devised to train suitable personalities from the troops — men who would stay in the army a while and function as propaganda agents, with qualities of persuasion capable of negating subversive ideas. Captain Karl Mayr ran it, with funds to build a team of informants, run the courses and finance patriotic parties and publications.[^13] Long afterwards Mayr described what he had picked up: he was like a tired stray dog looking for a master, ready to throw in his lot with anyone who would show him kindness, and totally unconcerned about the German people and their destinies.

The name *Hittler Adolf* appears on an early list of informants at the end of May or the beginning of June. Within days he was on a course at Munich University, hearing lectures on German history since the Reformation, the political history of the war, socialism in theory and practice, and the breaking of interest slavery.[^14]

The turn came at Lechfeld in August, and it comes with reviews written by the men in the room. A gunner thought he revealed himself an excellent and passionate speaker who captured the attention of all the listeners. An airship man preferred his passionate lectures, with examples from life, to the commander's. And a stretcher-bearer named Lorenz Frank wrote the sentence that got him promoted: **Herr Hitler especially is, I might say, a born popular speaker who, through his fanaticism and his populist style in a meeting, absolutely compels his audience to take note and share his views**.[^15] The camp commander asked him to tone the antisemitism down, in case the lectures were objected to as agitation.[^16] That is the first record of him speaking publicly about Jews.

It is worth being precise about what he was competing against, because the chapter supplies the surrounding noise. A remark in a Munich tram — all the Jews deserve to be hanged, they are guilty of the war — met the approval of all the other passengers.[^17] A worker on a train to Lindau thought the troops should have opened fire on the Jews on 1 May. People said major pogroms were as certain to come as the revolution had been. Reports that autumn recorded demands to hang all the Jews, and the view that only when the Reich was freed from this malicious, treacherous vermin could a revival be contemplated.

**He was not introducing an idea. He was performing one that was already in the trams**.

The Gemlich letter of 16 September 1919 is the first thing he wrote down about it, and it was written because Mayr passed him a query from a former course participant.[^18] Antisemitism, he answered, should rest not on emotion but on facts, the first being that Jewry was a race and not a religion. Emotional antisemitism produces pogroms. Antisemitism based on reason must lead instead to the systematic removal of the rights of Jews. Its final aim must unshakably be the removal of the Jews altogether.

He went to the German Workers' Party on 12 September as an informant, sent to report on one of some fifty organisations under surveillance.[^19] He thought it a boring organisation and was about to leave when a guest spoke for Bavarian separatism, and he intervened so heatedly that the man took his hat and left while he was still speaking, looking like a wet poodle. Drexler pushed a pamphlet into his hand. *Goodness, he's got a gob. We could use him*.

Two details puncture the story he later told about joining. His membership number was 555, not seven — and Drexler wrote it out in a letter to him in January 1940 that was never sent, recording that the card bearing his own and Schüssler's signatures had been falsified, the 555 erased and a 7 entered.[^20] And Mayr later claimed he had *ordered* him to join, to help the party grow, funded him at around twenty gold Marks a week, and arranged for him to stay in the army against normal practice.[^21] **So he was drawing army pay and speaker fees while every other man in the party's leadership fitted politics around a job**. Without Mayr's talent-spotting he might never have been heard of.

*Read: lines 1333–1512.*

---

## Ch. 5 — Seventy-three parties, and one of them had a shouter

When he joined, the German Workers' Party was one of about seventy-three *völkisch* groups in Germany, most founded since the war, with at least fifteen in Munich alone.[^22] The ideas were not his and were not new. They were common currency across those groups, and had already been advanced in all essentials by the pre-war Pan-Germans.

What separated the successful organisations from the rest was production. The German Nationalist Protection and Defiance Federation, set up on a Pan-German initiative, put out 7.6 million pamphlets, 4.7 million handbills and 7.8 million stickers in 1920 alone.[^23] It went from 30,000 to 100,000 members inside a year and past 200,000 in three. **It chose the swastika as its symbol**. Its members were former soldiers angry at their treatment, artisans who felt their status slipping toward the proletariat, teachers drawn to pan-German ideas, and students insulted by national humiliation.

So the question the chapter puts is not where the ideas came from. It is why one man saying them worked when others saying the same thing made no impact at all. The answer given is that it was less *what* he said than *how*, and that presentation was what mattered — then and afterwards.[^24]

**An idea, in this world, is not something you hold. It is something you use**. Ideas held no interest for him as abstractions; they mattered only as tools of mobilisation, and one that did not mobilise was useless.[^25]

What kind of person does that make? One who cannot work at any other scale. Asked to give a short speech at Hermann Esser's wedding party, he refused: *I must have a crowd when I speak. In a small intimate circle I never know what to say. I should only disappoint you all... As a speaker either at a family gathering or a funeral, I'm no use at all*.[^26]

One-to-one he could be unbearable. An acquaintance forced to sit through an involuntary lecture on the future mission of German artists eventually asked him whether they had shit in his brain and forgotten to flush it, and left him speechless.[^27]

Hans Frank, nineteen and already committed to the cause, heard him in January 1920 and wrote it down thirty years later in a Nuremberg cell.[^28] A shabby blue suit, a loosely fastened tie, clear impassioned tones rather than shrill ones, blue eyes, a hand pushing the hair back. What struck him first was sincerity — that the words came from the heart and were not a device. He took the dominant topic of the day, Versailles, and asked what now, German people. He spoke for over two and a half hours and was interrupted by frenetic applause. *In the matter itself he was certainly not original*, Frank wrote — and then said he was the one called to act as spokesman of the people.

The method was simplicity and repetition, and the mechanism ran both ways. He got his certainty from the crowd's response, which is what he otherwise lacked, and the crowd got its conviction from his certainty.[^29] What that response compensated for is stated flatly: after three decades he had no achievements of note to set against an outsized ego except a war record.

The meetings were designed to be violent. Posters were printed in vivid red to provoke the Left into attending; techniques of disruption and intimidation were learned from watching the Left's own meetings; a hall-protection squad was organised by mid-1920 and grew into the SA.[^30] **The point was not to win the room. It was to be mentioned**. *It makes no difference whatever whether they laugh at us or revile us, whether they represent us as clowns or criminals; the main thing is that they mention us*.

The first mass meeting, in the Hofbräuhaus on 24 February 1920, is worth having in its actual shape rather than in the one he later gave it. His own name was not in the publicity, because neither he nor Drexler had any public profile and an outside speaker was hired to fill the hall.[^31] Some 2,000 came, perhaps a fifth of them socialist opponents. His language was coarse and direct and his sentences short. Attacks on named targets brought applause; attacks on profiteers brought cries of *flog them, hang them*; the police reporter wrote of scenes of great tumult in which he often thought it would come to brawling.

It ended in uproar with people standing on tables yelling at each other, and about a hundred Communists and Independents pouring out on to the street cheering for the Räterepublik. The *Völkischer Beobachter*, sympathetic and not yet party-owned, gave the meeting one column on an inside page four days later and summarised his contribution in a single sentence.[^32]

The content is worth listing for what is missing from it. Not one mention of living-space in eastern Europe — in August 1920 he jotted *brotherhood towards the east* among his notes.[^33] A demand for a dictatorship in exactly one speech that year, with no implication that he was the man. His first outright public assault on Marxism not until Rosenheim on 21 July 1920. Race theory explicitly treated in one speech in the whole year.

What never stopped was the Jews. And here the chapter does something that reframes the entire question of originality. **The most extreme formulation in the section is not his**.

*You don't talk about what to do with parasites and bacilli. Parasites and bacilli are also not reared. They are as quickly and fully as possible destroyed*. That is Paul de Lagarde, a leading oriental scholar and specialist in semitic languages, writing in 1887 about how Jews should be treated.[^34] Thirty-three years later, in August 1920, Hitler told an audience not to think they could combat racial tuberculosis without freeing the people from its causative organ.

The difference, the chapter says, is not the language. It is that the atmosphere had become immeasurably more menacing in between.

His audiences loved it more than anything else. The speech of 13 August 1920, *Why Are We Antisemites?*, ran two hours and was interrupted fifty-eight times by two thousand people.[^35] The crowd was mostly white-collar workers, the lower-middle class and better-off workers, with about a quarter women.

Now the leadership, and the chapter's flat contradiction of the legend. He did not want the chairmanship. Drexler offered it repeatedly and he refused, because the chairmanship meant organisational responsibility — which he had neither aptitude nor ability for, then or later.[^36] Propaganda was what he was good at, and the only thing he would take responsibility for. Drexler wrote to Feder in spring 1921 that every revolutionary movement must have a dictatorial head and that Hitler was the most suitable, without wanting to be pushed into the background himself.

What produced the takeover was a threat, not a plan. While he was in Berlin, a rival named Otto Dickel — with a book, a following in Augsburg and Nuremberg, and a platform manner of his own — proved a major success in the Hofbräuhaus, and the party leadership was delighted to have found a second outstanding speaker with a popular touch.[^37] He came back beside himself with rage, sat through three hours of Dickel's proposals producing outbursts, and stormed out. His own delegation was embarrassed by him and impressed by Dickel. Even Eckart thought he had behaved badly. They agreed the programme needed amending and that Hitler, *as a simple man*, was not up to doing it.

He resigned on 11 July.[^38] He had resigned *for ever* from the committee once already, in December 1920, and had threatened it again in March. The pattern is described without decoration: he only knew all-or-nothing arguments, went for broke from a maximalist position, and when he could not get his way threw a tantrum and threatened to quit. Usually the tantrums were a sign of frustration rather than strength.

**What settled it was arithmetic, not argument**. Losing the only performer who could fill the Circus Krone would have split the party. Eckart was asked to intervene; Drexler asked what terms he wanted; and the terms were the post of chairman with dictatorial power, Munich fixed permanently as the headquarters, the programme inviolate, and no more mergers.[^39] The committee agreed the next day. He rejoined as member number 3680 on 26 July, and on 29 July, before 554 paid-up members, the new constitution passed with one vote against. Heß put the reason in public, and it is the argument the cult was built on: *Are you truly blind to the fact that this man is the leader personality who alone is able to carry through the struggle? Do you think that without him the masses would pile into the Circus Krone?*[^40]

One episode shows what the party actually ran on. In the small hours of 17 December 1920 he turned up agitated at Drexler's flat saying the *Völkischer Beobachter* was about to fall into separatist hands.[^41] Drexler's mother was woken to make coffee. Round the kitchen table they decided Drexler would get Eckart out of bed at dawn. By that afternoon Eckart had convinced General von Epp, stood guarantor with his own house and property for 60,000 Marks of Reichswehr funds, found 30,000 more elsewhere — and Drexler, earning 35 Marks a week, personally took over the remaining debts of 113,000 Marks to become the newspaper's legal owner.
