## Ch. 11 — Bulls must not be castrated on Tishya

Thirty years into the reign, around 243 BCE, he goes back to speaking to everybody.[^23] Six edicts on pillars, mostly across north India: Lauriya-Araraj, Lauriya-Nandangarh and Rampurva in Bihar, one at Allahabad that probably came from Kaushambi, one near Meerut, one at Topra in Haryana.

The way they were cut says something about the man who ordered them. The fourteen rock edicts had gone out over about four years and been engraved in batches, in different letter sizes, as they arrived.[^24] **The six pillar edicts were not staggered at all**. They were engraved as a single prearranged bunch, from Haryana to Bihar, at around the same time. That is a set assembled by somebody looking back over what he has already done.

Once again he did not put them in the cities. Pataliputra, Hastinapur and Mathura were all bypassed.[^25] Two of the pillars are not even where he left them — Firuz Shah Tughlaq had the Meerut and Topra columns carried to Delhi in the fourteenth century and set up on the Ridge and at Firoz Shah Kotla.

Lauriya-Nandangarh is the only one of these columns still standing entire, and what is around it is not Buddhist. There are mounds, round at the base and conical on top, and they are burial mounds older than the faith.[^26] **The pillar went to a place where people already gathered for rituals and worship, which had nothing to do with him**. Traders and travellers passing would see it.

The routes are the other half of the explanation. N.G. Majumdar traced the pillars in that part of Bihar against the communication lines — one running from Lauriya towards the frontier at Bhikhna Thori, another along the Gandak to Triveni.[^27] The goods prove the routes: lapis lazuli beads from north Afghanistan turn up on one continuous axis from the Swat valley to Burdwan in Bengal, and sea shell from the east coast turns up all through the Gangetic plains.

What he says on them starts as a summary and then breaks into parts. Dhamma is **few sins, many virtuous deeds, compassion, liberality, truthfulness and purity**.[^28] Then the demonstration, in his own person:

> On bipeds and quadrupeds, on birds and aquatic animals various benefits have been conferred by me, (even) to the boon of life.

The third edict turns the list of failings on the ordinary person. Envy, anger, cruelty, hurry, want of practice, laziness and fatigue.[^29] **That is the same list he sent to the judges of Kalinga**, and here it is aimed at everyone, with the instruction to take responsibility for evil deeds as well as virtuous ones.

The fourth is a real change in how the empire is run, and it goes the opposite way from Kalinga. The *rajukkas*, the officials of the countryside, are given functional autonomy.[^30] The *mahamatras* who judged in the cities had been told to be more sensitive and even-handed and had been put under a five-yearly scrutiny. **The country officers get independence and the city officers get inspection**, and the chapter says plainly that the reason is not clear. The result was decentralisation.

Then the animal edict of the twenty-sixth year, which is the strangest document in the corpus and the most specific. He declares a long list of creatures inviolable — parrots, mainas, ruddy geese, wild geese, bats, queen-ants, terrapins, boneless fish, skate-fish, tortoises, porcupines, squirrels, bulls set at liberty, iguanas, the rhinoceros.[^31] Then it stops listing species and starts describing situations:

> Those (she-goats), ewes, sows (which are) either with young or in milk, are inviolable, and also those (of their) young ones (which are) less than six months old. Cocks must not be caponed. Husks containing living animals must not be burnt. Forests must not be burnt uselessly or in order to destroy (living beings). Living animals must not be fed with (other) living animals.

**Then the calendar**. Fish are inviolable and may not be sold on the three Chaturmasis, and on the Tishya full-moon for three days, and on every fast-day.[^32] No castration of bulls, he-goats, rams or boars on the eighth, fourteenth and fifteenth of the fortnight, on Tishya, on Punarvasu, on the three Chaturmasis or on festivals. No branding of horses and bullocks on Tishya, on Punarvasu, on the Chaturmasis.

The list is not random and three specialists have worked on why. Norman finds parallels with Jaina texts and an organised structure — two talking birds, a run of water birds, aquatic animals, legged and legless reptiles, three of the pigeon family.[^33] The zoologist Sunder Lal Hora points out that five of the fish are inedible and not worth killing anyway — sharks, eels, porpoise, skate. **Which is a point about whose table you are picturing**. Tribal and fishing communities may well have eaten anything they caught, and it may be them he is addressing.

And the dates turn out to have biology in them. The closed days for fish fall in the rainy season, July to September, which is when several species breed.[^34] Less obviously, some freshwater fish — carp, hilsa — spawn on a lunar rhythm, with peaks at new moon and full moon. Those are the days he closes.

Two things sit inside that edict at once. A ruler asking people to spare a pregnant or lactating she-goat, and her young under six months, is doing something nobody else in the ancient world is doing.[^35] He is also **accepting that the slaughter goes on**. It is a protection of breeding, not an abolition.

His officials did take it seriously somewhere. An epigraph at Deotek near Nagpur records a lord's command prohibiting the capture and slaughter of animals, with punishments specified for anyone who disobeyed.[^36]

Whether it changed what anybody ate cannot be established, and the chapter is careful about that. At Raja Nala-ka-Tila in Uttar Pradesh nearly 1,600 fragments of animal bone came out of the early historic levels, and fish appear earlier but not in the Mauryan phase.[^37] **The period that shows the drop is longer than his reign**, so nothing about his exhortations follows from it.

The Seventh Pillar Edict is on one pillar only, at Topra, and nobody knows why.[^38] It is the last thing he wrote and it is a review of the whole attempt. Earlier kings had also wanted men to progress by the promotion of morality, and men were not made to progress. So he asks himself the question three times over — how might men be made to conform, how might they be made to progress, how could I elevate them — and answers it:

> I shall use proclamations on morality, (and) shall order instruction in morality (to be given).

**What he concludes, looking back, is that restrictions imposed from above do not work and persuasion does**. That is a man who spent thirty years running an empire on stone messages, saying at the end that the messages were the method and the orders were not.[^39]

## Ch. 12 — Half a myrobalan

Then he stops talking. No more messages on rocks and pillars, no more addresses to administrators or to the populace.[^40] The metaphors stop, the idiom stops, the whole effort to tie his own life to his subjects' lives stops. **He went on ruling for about another decade, to around 232 BCE, and never inscribed anything again**. The silence is sudden enough to be the loudest thing in the chapter.

Which puts the story back where it started. Everything about his last years comes from the same chronicles composed centuries later with an interest in deifying him.[^41]

The *Mahavamsa* gives it in six verses and a run of intervals. In the eighteenth year the great Bodhi tree was planted in Sri Lanka. Twelve years later his consort Asamdhimitta died. Four years after that he raised Tissarakkha to queen. Three years after that, in the pride of her beauty, she destroyed the Bodhi tree.[^42]

There is a possible explanation for the silence buried in that arithmetic. Asamdhimitta seems to have died in 241 BCE, **within a year of the Seventh Pillar Edict**.[^43] Grief and private preoccupation would account for a man who had nothing further to say in public.

What the chronicle actually cares about is a contrast between two women. Sanghamitra carries a sapling of the tree to Sri Lanka and protects it; Tissarakkha destroys the tree at home.[^44] The faith prospers on the island and fails in the land of its origin, and the two queens are the figures that carry it. **A wife in this literature is good or bad according to whether she helped or hindered his Buddhism**, which is most of what the tradition preserves about any of them.

His own stone says otherwise about at least one. Karuvaki appears in his epigraphs as a self-possessed, strong-willed consort who wanted an act of philanthropy recorded as hers.[^45]

The northern tradition gives the same villain more room and a stranger motive. In the *Ashokavadana*, Tishyarakshita's jealousy of the Bodhi tree starts because she did not know what Bodhi was.[^46] He gave his most precious jewels to Bodhi, so she took Bodhi for a woman and a rival.

Then Kunala, his son by Padmavati, named after a bird because his eyes were like its eyes, a boy who grew into a prince who liked being alone.[^47] She wanted him and he refused her.

Her cure for the emperor's illness is the most extraordinary passage in these chapters and it is worth having in the source's own words. She tells the doctors to bring her anyone suffering from the same disease. An Abhira man falls ill, his wife goes to a doctor, and the doctor sends the man straight to the queen.[^48]

> She, in secret, had him killed, and when he was dead, she split open his belly…

She finds the worm. Peppercorns do not kill it. Long peppers and ginger do not kill it. Onion kills it at once. Then she goes to the king with the prescription:

> 'Queen', the king objected, 'I am a ksatriya; how can I eat an onion?' 'My lord', she replied, 'this is medicine; take it for the sake of life!'

**He eats the onion and recovers**, and the grateful monarch grants her a boon.[^49] She asks to be monarch for seven days. She uses them to send a letter to the people of Taxila ordering that Kunala's eyes be put out.

The shape of that is the shape of his own youth run again. A son sent to Taxila to deal with a provincial matter, a father falling gravely ill immediately afterwards, and the succession settled by intrigue — by ministers in Bindusara's court then, by the chief queen now.[^50]

The end is quieter and it is about giving. He had been trying to match what the householder Anathapindaka gave the Buddha, a hundred *kotis* of gold, and had reached ninety-six.[^51] Falling ill, he started sending gold to the Kukkutarama monastery to close the gap.

**So his own heir shut off the treasury**. Sampadin, who was Kunala's son, and the state counsellors issued an order forbidding it.[^52] He went round them by giving away the gold dishes his food was served in, then the silver ones, then the copper ones. When they were gone, all he had left was half an *amalaka*, half a myrobalan fruit.

He sent that. He gave it to a man to carry to the monks at Kukkutarama, with the instruction that this last offering be distributed so that it was offered to and enjoyed by the whole community — and half a fruit was mashed into a soup and shared out among them all.[^53] The verse the text puts on it is the sharpest thing in the book:

> A great donor, the lord of men, the eminent Maurya Asoka, has gone from being lord of Jambudvipa to being lord of half a myrobalan.

Then the last flourish, and it is a legal one. His powers are restored to him on the strength of that gift, and he immediately donates the whole earth to the Sangha, keeping back only the treasury.[^54] He seals the document and dies. **A successor could only take the throne after the ministers of the court bought the earth back**, paying four *kotis* of gold to make up his shortfall.

And his stated reason for the gift is not merit and not rebirth. He gives it with faith, he says, in order to obtain something that cannot be stolen, is honoured by the aryas and is safe from all agitation: sovereignty of the mind.[^55]

## Epilogue — Remembered for everything except what he said

The dynasty went on and left almost no trace. Maurya kings ruled for decades after him, and the historical events of their reigns are not known even as legend.[^56] The Sri Lankan chronicles lose interest in the line entirely once his Buddhist children are established on the island. The Puranas name between four and seven successors; the Buddhist texts name between two and five.

Exactly one of them exists as a historical figure, and he exists for the same reason his grandfather does. Dasharatha cut an inscription in stone.[^57] The Vahiyaka cave, it says, has been given by Dasalatha, dear to the gods, to the venerable Ajivikas, immediately on his accession, to be a place of abode during the rainy season **as long as the moon and sun shall endure**.

That did not happen, and how it failed is legible in the rock. In the Barabar and Nagarjuni caves, one word was later removed or defaced from the Maurya inscriptions: *Ajivikehi*.[^58] Somebody took the caves and scratched out the name of the sect they were given to.

Buddhism, meanwhile, grew without needing a king. The stupas and viharas and chaityas that went up afterwards were paid for by pupils of particular teachers, lay worshippers, bankers, merchants, mothers, housewives, monks and nuns.[^59] They came from Vidisha and Ujjayini, and from as far off as Prathisthanapura and Pokhara.

**He does not appear in the earliest Buddhist art at all**, and that is not because kings are absent from it.[^60] Pasenadi of Kosala and Ajatashatru of Magadha are both at Bharhut, because both were contemporaries of the Buddha. What is at Bharhut of Ashoka is his furniture — the *vajrasana* he donated at Mahabodhi, now serving as one of the symbols that stand in for the Buddha, who was not yet shown in human form.

Two centuries later he arrives in person, and the sculptors put a defeat on the gateway. The southern *torana* at Sanchi shows his visit to the Ramagrama stupa, going to take one of the original relic deposits — in a chariot, with turban and ewer and fly whisk, elephants and armed troops.[^61] **And the Nagas, carved worshipping the stupa, resist him and successfully stop him getting the relics**.

By the second century CE, at Kanaganahalli in Karnataka, he is labelled by name — *Raya Asoko* — and he is not in a narrative at all.[^62] He and his queen fill the register, with female whisk-bearers and a female umbrella-bearer. A portrait, in the local Satavahana manner.

The Chinese pilgrims then describe an India where every site is one of his. Faxian in the fifth century explains practically every place through Ashoka legends, some from the Chinese *Ashokavadana* and some told him by local people.[^63] Xuanzang in the seventh finds his pillars at Sravasti, Varanasi, Niglihawa and Lumbini, notes that the Lumbini pillar is broken in the middle — brought down by the contrivance of a wicked dragon — and admires one near Varanasi as bright and shining as a mirror, glistening and smooth as ice.

**And here is the thing the whole Epilogue turns on**. The memory that he had put up stone pillars survived for a thousand years. What the pillars said did not survive at all.[^64] Niglihawa's was still known to be his, and was believed to record something about the nirvana of an earlier Buddha. Later even that connection was forgotten.

Legend kept filling the space. Xuanzang has a stupa outside Taxila marking the spot where Kunala was blinded on his stepmother's orders, and reports that when the blind pray before it with fervent faith, many of them recover their sight.[^65]

Some places held on to him accurately for a very long time. In the twelfth century Kumaradevi, queen of Govindachandra of Kanauj, recorded that she had restored the Lord of the Turning of the Wheel at Sarnath **in accordance with the way in which he existed in the days of Dharmasoka, ruler of men**, and even more wonderfully.[^66] That is fourteen hundred years after him, at a place his own epigraph shows he was close to.

Elsewhere he acquired a career he never had. Kalhana's twelfth-century Kashmiri chronicle has him reigning over the earth, freed from sins, having embraced the doctrine — and obtaining, through austerities, a son called Jalauka who then exterminated the Mlecchas from Kashmir.[^67] **No such son appears in any other source, and the family name Maurya is missing from the account entirely**. Four centuries later Abu'l Fazl mentions that chronicle in the *Ain-i Akbari*, so the chain of memory runs unbroken for about 1,700 years.

What ran along that chain, though, was one of the two men. The Buddhist convert survived — the royal patron, the pilgrim, the builder of stupas, the disciplinarian of the Sangha.[^68] The other one did not: the compulsively communicative and accessible emperor, reachable in the bed-chamber and on the march, who told his subjects what he had done at Kalinga and how it had felt. **There is no recollection of that man in the Buddhist chronicles at all**.

In the 1960s a sculptor put him back. Meera Mukherjee cast a massive metal Ashoka as a protest against the violence of the Naxalite movement in Bengal — big enough to carry the emperor's power, with the sword turned down.[^69]

And the chapter's last line is about what was lost rather than what was kept. If his own words had survived in their full nuance, the way the memory of his Buddhism did, **he might have been remembered as the founder of a political model of humane governance** — which is a good deal closer to the man who actually wrote them.[^70]

*Read: lines 2566–2682.*

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## Ch. 10 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and it is what nearly every other patron did**. Money spent on religious building normally goes to the patron's own religion. He was a declared Buddhist with an enormous stupa programme, and the obvious course at Barabar was four Buddhist caves. Instead the named beneficiaries are Ajivikas — the sect that has no modern adherents, whose founder was a rival of the Buddha's, and whose predictions his own legend used to legitimise him.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose Barabar had gone to the Sangha. He loses nothing immediately and gains a coherent policy; the twelfth edict's concord becomes a phrase rather than a hillside. The forecast is that the caves survive exactly as well — they are granite — and that the defacement recorded in the Epilogue never happens, because there is no sect name to scratch out. **What would be missing is the only physical proof anywhere that the tolerance was ever more than rhetoric**. A man who funds his own church has demonstrated nothing. The caves are expensive precisely because they are the wrong caves.

## Ch. 11 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the fourth pillar edict: independence for the country officers, inspection for the city judges, and no reason given.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/shih-and-strategic-depth|shih]]** would say the split is correct and that the asymmetry is the whole of it. A *rajukka* in the countryside cannot be supervised in any real way — the distances defeat it — so the choice is between formal authority he actually has and formal authority that is a fiction. A city judge sits where an inspector can reach him every five years. Grant the discretion where you cannot enforce and keep the check where you can, and you are describing the empire as it is rather than as the manual says.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|the dichotomy of control]]** reaches the same arrangement from the other end. The emperor cannot control what a man two thousand kilometres away decides in a village court. He can control what he asks of him, and what he tells him a good decision looks like. So the fifth edict's list — envy, anger, cruelty, hurry, want of practice, laziness, fatigue — is not moralising. It is the only lever available at that distance, and he had already used the same list on the judges of Kalinga, where he did have an inspector.

**They converge, which is the useful part**. Both read the autonomy as an admission rather than a gift. The chapter says the reason is not clear and wonders whether the administration had been demoralised by too much intervention; the advisors both suggest something plainer, that he had worked out where his orders stopped arriving.

## Ch. 12 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and somebody in the room chose it**. Sampadin and the counsellors could have let a dying emperor empty the treasury into a monastery. They stopped him instead, and then had to buy the earth back from the Sangha with four *kotis* of gold before anyone could succeed him.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose they had let him give. The Sangha ends the reign holding a fortune and a sealed deed to the empire, and the next king inherits a state whose legitimacy runs through a religious corporation. The forecast is not piety but a fight — and the Epilogue shows which way such fights went, with *Ajivikehi* chiselled out of his caves within a generation or two. **The counsellors' refusal is the least admirable act in the chapter and probably the one that kept there being a dynasty to record**. The half myrobalan is what an emperor has left when the people around him have correctly decided he can no longer be allowed to decide.

## Epilogue — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: choosing what will carry your meaning after you**.

The mechanism the Epilogue exposes is a split between medium and message that nobody could have predicted. The pillars lasted. The pilgrims saw them, admired them, measured them, and wrote about them for a thousand years. **What was cut into them was illegible within a few centuries, because the script died and nothing carried the language forward**. So the object survived and the content did not — and into the vacated content went legend, which is why Niglihawa's pillar ends up recording an earlier Buddha's nirvana and Kashmir acquires a son called Jalauka.

Meanwhile the message that did survive travelled by a completely different route: monks copying texts, in a religion with an institutional interest in remembering him a particular way. That route preserved the convert and dropped the administrator entirely.

**Scope conditions**. A durable medium preserves meaning only while a living community can still read it. Where the medium outlasts its readership, it does worse than fail — it becomes an authoritative-looking blank that later generations fill in. Institutional transmission is the opposite: fragile in the object, robust in the meaning, and heavily filtered by whatever the institution needs. Neither is sufficient alone. The Ashoka who is recoverable now exists because the stone survived long enough for a nineteenth-century decipherment to reach it, which is luck rather than strategy.

**Modern equivalent:** an archive on a durable format nobody can still read, versus a story an organisation keeps telling about itself. The first is trusted and empty; the second is legible and shaped. Anything meant to last needs both, and the interesting question is always which of the two is currently doing the work.

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Ashoka in Ancient India.md`, lines 2051–2682: ch. 10 (2051–2296), ch. 11 (2297–2459), ch. 12 (2460–2565), Epilogue (2566–2682).

**Where the evidence changes character, and the book says so**. Chapters 10 and 11 rest on his own inscriptions and on excavated structures, and they are the most secure material in the book. Chapter 12 rests entirely on the *Mahavamsa* and the *Ashokavadana*, composed centuries later with an interest in deifying him — the chapter opens by saying the story is back where it began, embedded in unverifiable tradition. Everything about Tishyarakshita, the worm, the onion and the half myrobalan is reported here at that weight.

**Where dating is inferred rather than known**. The chronology of the edifices cannot be fixed the way the edicts can: only some carry dates, some carry no inscription at all, and the attributions then rest on literary claims or on diagnostic features like Mauryan polish and brick size. The Vaishali stupa breach is a real archaeological fact with a contested cause.

**Where the source's own judgement is doing the work**. That no emperor in the ancient world expresses comparable concern for the underprivileged and for animals is the author's assessment. So is the closing verdict that the surviving memory preserved the Buddhist and lost the governor. Both are reported here as hers.

**Bounded absence**. No claim is made about material outside lines 2051–2682. The Appendix table of inscriptions beginning at line 2683 was not read for this pass.

# What Runs Through All of It — Ashoka in Ancient India

> **Closing pass across all fourteen chapter runs of Nayanjot Lahiri, *Ashoka in Ancient India***. Read from `RAW/books/Ashoka in Ancient India.md`, Prelude through Epilogue. Written last, out of the finished runs.
>
> **Siblings:** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/lahiri-ashoka-worldview-archaeology-part-1|Part 1 — Prelude and Chapters 1–5]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/lahiri-ashoka-worldview-archaeology-part-2|Part 2 — Chapters 6–9]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/lahiri-ashoka-worldview-archaeology-part-3|Part 3 — Chapters 10–12 and the Epilogue]]. Its sibling thread map is [[LAB/Threads/olivelle-ashoka-portrait-of-a-philosopher-king-threads|the Olivelle Ashoka thread map]].
>
> ⚠ **Supersedes the Lahiri half of** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/ashoka-worldview-archaeology|the original whole-book report]], which merged two books into one account and was built from the vault's Ashokan concept pages rather than from RAW. **The Olivelle half of that report stands**, because *Ashoka: Portrait of a Philosopher King* has no RAW file here. It is a re-ingest candidate.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/lahiri-ashoka-in-ancient-india|Nayanjot Lahiri, Ashoka in Ancient India]]*

---

## What Runs Through All of It

Everything anybody in this world wants to keep is written on something that rots. Palm leaf, birch bark, cotton cloth, wooden boards — and no specimen has ever been found. Not anywhere in India, from any reign. The single exception is a scrap of birch-bark charcoal at Sringaverapura, which lasted because it burned. **That is the fact the whole book is built on**, and it is why eleven Mauryan kings before Ashoka are names in a list and he is a person.

So the second thing running through every chapter is a man solving that problem without ever saying that is what he is doing. He dates events from his own consecration. Nobody in India had done that. He sends identical copies out so the same sentences stand in Afghanistan and in Andhra. He puts them where people live and worship rather than where a king lives. He puts his confession about Kalinga on stone, in the one century when a victorious king was expected to boast, and stone cannot be taken back.

**And then the thing he chose fails in the way nobody could have predicted**. The pillars lasted a thousand years and the writing on them did not. Xuanzang admires a column near Varanasi as smooth as ice and reports that a pillar at Niglihawa records something about an earlier Buddha. The object survived, the script died, and legend filled the hole — a wicked dragon that broke the Lumbini pillar, a son called Jalauka who cleared the Mlecchas out of Kashmir.

Third, kingship in this world is a job description he keeps declining. The *Arthashastra* runs through the book as the thing every chapter measures him against. Its king is a *vijigishu*, a would-be conqueror with an ambition to own the world — not from glory but from arithmetic, because if you do not exercise power somebody else will exercise it over you. He fought one war, recorded it as a catastrophe, and never conquered again.

The manual gets other things right about him, which is the honest part. It wants a king always accessible, hearing urgent matters and never putting them off — and he made himself reportable to in the bed-chamber and on the march. It says the happiness of the king lies in the happiness of his subjects. **He was almost certainly raised on it, and where he broke with it he broke on the one point it treats as the definition of the job**.

Fourth, and this recurs from his childhood to his funeral: **legitimacy here is manufactured retrospectively, by other people, for men who had no claim**. He was not the eldest son. Neither was Harshavardhana nine hundred years later. Both got a prophecy — Ashoka's from the Buddha in a previous life, from anonymous fortune tellers at Champa, and from an Ajivika ascetic at his father's court, all of them written down between four hundred and twelve hundred years after he died. The city got the same treatment: the Buddha is made to foresee Pataliputra, looking back at Magadha on his way to Kushinagara.

Fifth, an empire is what happens when a message leaves the room. This is the finding the by-chapter reading recovers most clearly, because it takes four separate chapters to build. The same words on the same kind of rock are four different messages. At Maski they arrive in a landscape whose gods they never mention, and no stupa was ever built there — read, heard, and ignored. At Panguraria the audience is a monastery that already agrees. At Kandahar the Greek says the king abstains from killing and the Aramaic says that for the king's feeding, little is killed. In Kalinga the dhamma edicts are removed and replaced with instructions about judges who imprison people arbitrarily.

Sixth, tolerance in his hands is expensive, active and checkable. The twelfth edict does not ask people to leave each other alone. It says that praising your own sect and running down others injures your own sect very severely. And the proof that this was more than a sentence is at Barabar. The caves there were cut out of granite, on a grid, polished to a lustre, and given to the **Ajivikas** — a sect with no modern adherents, whose founder was a rival of the Buddha's.

Within two generations somebody chiselled the word *Ajivikehi* out of those inscriptions.

Seventh, he cannot leave people's ordinary lives alone, and the book keeps both halves of that in view. The same corpus that pleads for concord among sects dismisses the ceremonies people hold at an illness, a wedding, a birth. It bans the festive gatherings where animals were sacrificed, in a world where sacrifice was how the gods were fed. It lists which creatures may not be killed, which days bulls may not be castrated, and which days horses may not be branded. **A ruler asking that pregnant and lactating she-goats be spared is doing something nobody else in the ancient world did**, and he is also telling a village what it may do on a Tuesday.

## Which dimensions the book never reached

**No account of what a Mauryan thought happened after death, outside the Buddhist frame**. There is a great deal on stupas and relics — three-quarters of the Vaishali deposit removed and the casket carefully put back — and almost nothing on what ordinary people believed they were doing when they buried animal parts with their dead in the Karnataka megaliths, beyond that they did it.

**Almost nothing on women's lives, and the book says why rather than filling it in**. The princesses were not thought worth educating and no source says anything about Ashoka's sisters. His mother's real name is lost — Subhadrangi, Dharma, Durdhara, take your pick. Devi arrives with a father, a city, and a reputation for beauty, and leaves with two children. What survives instead is a literature that sorts queens into helpers and destroyers of his religion. That, and one epigraph in which Karuvaki wanted her own philanthropy recorded as hers.

**Nothing on the economy of the empire from inside it**. Taxes, land grants and punishments were not, in his view, things to put on stone, and no other contemporary record exists. So the wealth in these pages is inferred from objects in the ground — lapis from Afghanistan at Maski, gold under the Dharwar hills, sea shell in the Gangetic plains — rather than from anyone's account of who owned what.

## Where two chapters pull against each other

**Ch. 5 and ch. 11 give two verdicts on whether it worked**. In the twelfth year he announces that slaughter and cruelty and disrespect have fallen to a degree not achievable in hundreds of years. In his last edict, on one pillar at Topra, he says earlier kings had also wanted men to progress by the promotion of morality and men were not made to progress — and that restriction from above achieves less than persuasion. The chapters do not reconcile these and neither does this report.

**Ch. 9 and ch. 11 hand the same problem opposite solutions**. In Kalinga the city judges are told to be even-handed and are put under a five-yearly inspection by a *mahamatra* neither harsh nor fierce. On the pillars, the country officers are granted functional autonomy instead. Same emperor, same worry about how officials treat people, and the two answers are surveillance and independence. The book says the reason is not clear.

**Ch. 6 and ch. 10 show two different men addressing the Sangha**. In the first minor edict he is a convert reporting that he was not zealous enough at first. At Sarnath he is ordering that any monk or nun who splits the Sangha be put in white robes and made to live outside a residence, with a copy of the order deposited in the office and another with the lay-worshippers, and every *mahamatra* to attend the fast-day reading. **A man who joined a religion is disciplining its clergy**, and nothing in that religion's own texts gives him the standing to.

## What the by-chapter reading recovered

The merged whole-book report had the confession, the dhamma policy, the edicts as a corpus, and the reputation. It could not have had these, because each appears once:

- Birch-bark charcoal surviving at exactly one site in India, and only because it burned (ch. 6).
- Capada the clerk signing three Karnataka edicts in Kharoshthi, a script from the Afghan border (ch. 6).
- The Erragudi engraver cutting part of the text boustrophedon, the lines turning back on themselves (ch. 6).
- The Greek and the Aramaic on one rock at Kandahar disagreeing about whether the king had stopped eating meat (ch. 7).
- Taxila's crooked lanes being newer than its one straight street, because householders would not sell (ch. 3).
- The Barabar caves laid out on a grid of about 85.5 cm, and finished by chiselling, pecking, then grinding with sand and water (ch. 10).
- Fish closed to the nets on the days when carp and hilsa actually spawn (ch. 11).
- Tissarakshita killing a stranger to find the worm, and testing peppercorns, long peppers, ginger and onion on it (ch. 12).
- An emperor reduced to half a myrobalan, mashed into a soup for a whole monastery (ch. 12).
- The word *Ajivikehi* scratched out of his own caves after his death (Epilogue).

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Ashoka in Ancient India.md`, lines 242–2682, in fourteen runs. The per-chapter footnotes and line ranges live in the three parts; this file cites none of its own, and every claim in it is traceable to a run.

**What kind of book this is**. An archaeologist's life of a king, which means the reconstruction leans on landscapes and objects wherever the texts run out — and they run out constantly. The author is explicit that a life of Ashoka meeting modern biographical standards cannot be written, and that context and conjecture have to serve as compensation for his early years. Where she reaches a view against her sources she marks it: that his transformation was not spiritual, that the goddesses of Taxila probably meant more to the Taxilans than their emperor's stupa, that the message at Maski was ignored.

**Her own position, stated once and not laboured**. Conquest and empire-building have been called great, and from a saner angle they are male megalomania of a revolting form. That is the author's line, in her own voice, in chapter 3.

**Bounded absence**. The gaps named above are gaps in lines 242–2682, not claims about the book as a whole or about Mauryan belief in general. The Appendix of inscriptions from line 2683 was not read.

# What 1956 Took For Granted — Meerloo, Foreword and Chapters 1–4

> **The Foreword and first four chapters of Joost A. M. Meerloo, *The Rape of the Mind: The Psychology of Thought Control, Menticide, and Brainwashing* (1956)** — a Marine colonel who signed a confession and said *the words were mine, but the thoughts were theirs*, a mentally unstable Dutchman turned into a courtroom automaton, resistance workers testing whether morphine would harden them against torture, and a psychiatrist telling a military court that anyone in the room could be broken. Read from `RAW/books/The Rape of the Mind.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
>
> ⚠ **This is Job B's first report, and the source is a different kind of object from the rest of the build**. It is neither a history nor a biography but a **theory of a society, written from inside the thing it theorises** — by a Dutch psychiatrist who fled the Nazi occupation, was imprisoned by the Gestapo, and testified as an expert at the Schwable inquiry. So there are two worldviews to excavate at once: what the totalitarian systems he describes took for granted, and what **he and his 1956 readers** took for granted while describing them. The second is the one that has aged, and it is where the run pays.
>
> **Siblings:** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/meerloo-rape-of-the-mind-worldview-archaeology-part-2|Part 2 — Chapters 5–9]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/meerloo-rape-of-the-mind-worldview-archaeology-part-3|Part 3 — Chapters 10–14]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/meerloo-rape-of-the-mind-worldview-archaeology-part-4|Part 4 — Chapters 15–18]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/meerloo-rape-of-the-mind-worldview-archaeology-synthesis|What Runs Through All of It]].
>
> **Pairs with** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/radzinsky-stalin-worldview-archaeology-synthesis|the Stalin build]] and [[LAB/Worldview Reports/kershaw-hitler-hubris-worldview-archaeology-synthesis|the Kershaw build]], which supply the events this book is theorising about.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/meerloo-rape-of-the-mind|Joost A. M. Meerloo, The Rape of the Mind]]*

---

## Ch. 0 — Foreword: naming a thing so it can be resisted

**How you know**. The book's first move is etymological and it is doing real work. *Rape* comes from *rapere*, to snatch, and is related to *rave* and *raven* — it means to overwhelm and to enrapture, to invade, to usurp, to pillage and to steal.[^1] The modern words are offered as instruments rather than labels: *brainwashing*, *thought control*, *menticide*. When a concept is given its right name, it can be more easily recognised — and it is with that recognition that the opportunity for systematic correction begins.

That is a whole theory of defence in one sentence, and it is the assumption the entire book rests on. Naming is protective. Nothing in the four chapters argues for it.

**What is real**. The method is borrowed from physics and stated openly. Under Bohr's principle of complementarity, even simple physical phenomena need different and seemingly contrasting concepts: to explain an electron you need both particle and wave.[^2] So brainwashing cannot be looked at from a Pavlovian view alone. The book uses the clinical view, the Freudian view, and the view that mental coercion belongs to every human interaction, and refuses to rank them.

The image he reaches for is a fairground. Communication is like trying to knock down a row of dolls in a throwing game — the more balls you throw, the greater the chance you hit them all. He warns in advance that this makes repetition unavoidable.

**How people should relate**. The oldest claim in the book is that this crime is not modern at all. It probably began in prehistory, when man first discovered **that he could exploit human qualities of empathy and understanding in order to exert power over his fellow men**.

**What is worth having**. He sets the stakes at the level his readers were already frightened at, and the comparison is deliberate. The danger of destruction of the spirit may be compared to the threat of total physical destruction through atomic warfare. Indeed, the two are related and intertwined.

**What a person is**. The argument moves from deliberate coercion to something broader — the influences in the modern world that tend to robotize and automatize man — and ends on what he calls inner backbone. So the book's subject is not really the interrogation cell. It is the cell as the visible extreme of something ordinary.

**The shape of time**. He is writing in January 1956, three years after the Korean armistice and twenty-three after the Reichstag fire, and he treats all of it as one continuous problem.

**What makes things happen**. A closing note on authorship that is worth keeping. Every word man speaks is a plagiarism. The task is to absorb and transform the knowledge and emotional currents of your own epoch and present them enriched by your own experience. And a complaint about his own profession: modern psychology is loaded with super-learnedness, with the secret intention of leaving the reading public awe-stricken. The man who writes simply is not always thanked for it.

*Read: lines 207–246.*

---

## Ch. 1 — You too would confess

**What makes things happen**. The chapter opens on a change in what punishment is for. A man is no longer punished only for crimes he has in fact committed — he may be compelled to confess to crimes conjured up by his judges, who then use the confession for political purposes.[^3] And the instruction that follows is the book's whole posture: it is not enough to damn the judges as evil. We must understand what impels the false admission of guilt.

**How you know**. The case is a Marine colonel taken prisoner in Korea, who after months of psychological pressure and physical degradation signed a confession that the United States was waging bacteriological warfare. **It named names, cited missions, described meetings and strategy conferences**, and was cabled round the world.

What he said afterwards is the most quoted sentence in the book, and the reason is that it describes a state nobody had a word for. The words were mine, but the thoughts were theirs. *That is the hardest thing I have to explain: how a man can sit down and write something he knows is false, and yet, to sense it, to feel it, to make it seem real*. He was clear about the boundary. He was never convinced they had used bug warfare, and knew they had not — but the rest of it was real to him: the conferences, the planes, and how they would go about their missions.

An American physician told the United Nations what distinguished the technique from older torture. It was not the rack and the thumbscrew. It was subtler, more prolonged, and intended to be more terrible in its effect — calculated to disintegrate the mind of an intelligent victim and distort his sense of values, to the point where he would not simply cry *I did it!* but become a seemingly willing accomplice to the complete disintegration of his own integrity.

**The shape of time**. The chapter dates the recognition to 1933 and a burning building.[^4] The Nazis arrested a Dutchman for the Reichstag fire whom Dutch psychiatrists already knew: a patient from a mental institution, described in their records as gay, alert, unstable, a man whose moods changed rapidly, who liked to vagabond around and had all kinds of fantasies about changing the world.

In court he was evasive, dull and apathetic. Then on the forty-second day the apathy lifted. **It became apparent that he had been aware of everything that had gone on in the previous sessions**. He criticised the slow procedure, demanded punishment by imprisonment or death, spoke about his inner voices, insisted his moods were in check — and fell back into apathy.

**In 1933 this pattern was unknown to psychiatrists**. It is now called a confession syndrome and is met constantly. He was convicted and executed, and the world worked out afterwards that the Nazis had burned the building themselves.

**What a person is**. The occupation chapters are written in the first person and they are the reason the book is not an academic exercise.[^5] The first aim of the Gestapo was to force prisoners under torture to betray their friends and report new victims for further torture — demanding names and more names, without bothering whether they were true. He remembers one meeting of a small group of resisters, all of whom could expect to be named and picked up. The question they were asking each other was whether they would be able to stand it, or would also be forced to become informers.

**How people should relate**. The answer they arrived at was structural rather than moral, and it is the coldest sentence in the run. By the second year of the occupation we realised that it was better not to be in touch with one another. More than two contacts were unsafe.

**What is real**. Then the experiments, which are the most striking thing in the chapter because they were run by the people who would be tortured. He tried to find medical and psychiatric preventives to harden them. He tested whether narcotics would harden a man against pain, and the results were paradoxical. Narcotics do create pain insensitivity — and their dulling action makes people more vulnerable to mental pressure.

The Germans had tried cocaine and amphetamine on air pilots for combat exhaustion, and neither was reliable for the same reason. **The body might not feel the torture, but the hazy mind would turn the man into an easier dupe**. They discussed suicide capsules as a last resort and rejected them: the enemy would find them and take them away. And they tried systematic mental relaxation and self-hypnosis, comparable to yoga exercises — fixing attention on breathing to reduce the alert functioning of the cortex and diminish awareness of pain.

**What is worth having**. The chapter's own conclusion is stated as a professional judgement and then tested in court. In his opinion hardly anyone can resist such treatment. Each man has his own limit of endurance, and clinical evidence supports that the limit can nearly always be reached and surpassed.

The exchange at the inquiry is the one moment where the book's argument is put to a room of people who had a stake in the answer. He testified that nearly anybody subjected to that treatment could be made to write and sign a similar confession. The colonel's attorney asked: anyone in this room, for instance? — looking in turn at each of the officers sitting in judgment.

**And in good conscience I could reply, firmly: anyone in this room**. The official American report agreed, in the flattest possible language: virtually all American prisoners of war collaborated at one time or another in one degree or another, lost their identity as Americans, and thousands lost their will to live. The British report found a third of their soldiers absorbed enough indoctrination to be classified as sympathisers.

The tortures behind those numbers are listed without comment. Standing at attention or sitting with legs outstretched in complete silence from half past four in the morning to eleven at night, and being woken constantly during the few hours allowed for sleep. Solitary confinement in boxes about five feet by three by two — one private spent more than six months in one. Liquids withheld for days *to help self-reflection*. A rope over a beam with a noose at one end and the man's ankles at the other, so that **if he slipped or bent his knees he would be committing suicide**. Kneeling on jagged rocks holding a large rock overhead. A rod pushed through a hole in the cell door for the prisoner to hold in his teeth, which a sentry would knock sideways without warning. And men marched barefoot to the frozen Yalu, water poured over their feet, kept for hours frozen to the ice to reflect on their crimes.

**How you know it ends**. The recovery is as mechanical as the breakdown, and he says so with relief. The conscious part of the personality takes no part in the automatic confessions; the brainwashee lives in a trance, repeating the record grooved into his mind by somebody else. As soon as the victim returns to normal circumstances the spell evaporates and he awakens into reality. Which is what the colonel did, the moment he was back in a familiar environment.

*Read: lines 247–425.*

---

## Ch. 2 — Pavlov's students as circus tamers

**How you know**. The chapter's method is to stop asking what the victim experienced and ask what the jailers thought they were doing. They don't speak of hypnosis or suggestion; they even deny the fact of imposed confession.[^6] They think about human behaviour and human government in a much more mechanical way, and to understand them you have to attend to their adoration of simplified Pavlovian concepts.

**What is real**. The underlying experiment is given plainly: a bell rung at each feeding until the dog's mouth waters at the bell alone. From it, the theory that learning and training are the building up of a mosaic of conditioned reflexes. And the consequence that made it politically attractive — man has the greatest capacity for learning of any animal, and is therefore the animal with the greatest capacity for such conditioning.

**How people should relate**. What the Soviet state built on top of it is described as institutional fact rather than metaphor. Moscow maintained a special *Pavlovian Front* and a scientific council on Pavlov's theory, part of the Academy of Science, dedicated to the political application of the theory and under orders to emphasise the purely mechanical aspects. Such a view reduces all human emotions to a system of conditioned reflexes.

**What makes things happen**. The political task is stated as a limitation rather than a construction: **to condition and mould man's mind so that its comprehension is confined to a narrow totalitarian concept of the world**. The belief that this is possible rests on two things — repeating a simplification often enough, and withholding every other interpretation of reality.

**And the book's objection to it is not moral but technical**. The scheme is based on the naive belief that you can permanently suppress the critical function. Yet in taming people, errors and deviations must continually be corrected — and in the correcting, a critical sense is unwittingly built up.

**What a person is**. The speech material is where this chapter earns its place, because it moves the argument out of the prison and into the newspaper.[^7] In official Pavlovian psychology, human speech is itself conditioned-reflex activity: verbal cues replace physical sound stimuli. Man learns to think in the words and speech figures given him, and these gradually condition his entire outlook on life.

So terrorising force can be replaced by a new organisation of the means of communication. Ready-made opinions distributed day by day through press and radio, again and again, till they reach the nerve cell and implant a fixed pattern of thought. Guided public opinion becomes a matter of good propaganda technique, and polls become a verification of it — though, he notes, polls may count only what people pretend to think.

The formula is given in one line. Repeat mechanically your assumptions and suggestions, diminish the opportunity of communicating dissent and opposition. And then the sentence that reaches past its subject: **this is also the actual ideal of some of our public relation machines**, who hope to manipulate the public into buying a special soap or voting for a special party.

The mechanism it produces is a loop. People are conditioned to ask themselves *what do other people think?* — and so are incited to think what other people think, until public opinion mushrooms into a mass prejudice. In psychoanalytic terms, through daily propagandistic noise backed by forceful verbal cues, people can be forced to identify with the powerful noisemaker. Big Brother's voice resounds in all the little brothers.

**What is worth having**. The occupation supplies a counter-example, and it is the most useful thing in the chapter because it is a failure. The Nazis were aware of the conditioning power of the word. The radio spread propaganda constantly and people were obliged to listen, because the simple act of turning off one's radio was in itself suspicious. He describes stopping at a café on a bicycle trip and finding it a Nazi nest with the radio on.

They printed tons of propaganda and painted slogans on the stoops of houses. And it did not work, because they did not know the correct Pavlovian strategy. By satisfying their own need to discuss and to vary their arguments — to make them seem more logical — they only increased the resistance of the Dutch people, which was further fortified by the London radio.

**The shape of time**. The distinction the chapter closes on is between two things that look alike. **Political conditioning is not training, persuasion or even indoctrination. It is taming** — taking possession of the simplest and most complicated nervous patterns of man, the battle for possession of the nerve cells.

And the state it requires is not pain but confusion. Many victims told him the most upsetting experience in the camps was the feeling of loss of logic, the state in which nothing had any validity. Freedom of discussion and free intellectual exchange hinder conditioning; terror and hopelessness accelerate it.

Which produces the chapter's one genuinely counterintuitive finding. Those with a rigid, simple belief often withstood the barrage better than the flexible, sophisticated ones full of doubt and inner conflict. The simple man with deep-rooted, freely absorbed religious faith could exert far more inner resistance than the questioning intellectual, who is handicapped by his own internal arguments.

*Read: lines 426–562.*

---

## Ch. 3 — Medication into submission

**What is real**. The chapter takes the instruments one at a time and finds the same defect in each: they are all better at implanting than at extracting.

Narco-analysis was developed in the Second World War to help soldiers who had broken down, letting the mind in half-sleep release traumatic material it could not otherwise reach.[^8] The principle is that the mind in half-sleep is unable to control its secrets. In acute anxiety cases that can relieve the pressure that caused the breakdown.

**How you know**. But the Yale experiment of 1951 is the chapter's decisive evidence and it is a designed test rather than an anecdote. Nine people were given intravenous sodium amytal. Before the injection, each had been suggested a false story about a historical period they were then questioned on — and the experimenters knew both the true and the false version. Several American courts have refused to admit truth-serum results, on the psychiatric conviction that **the treatment is misnamed and is no guarantee of getting at the truth**. And there is a further danger that belongs to this book's subject rather than to pharmacology: a criminal investigator can induce and communicate his own thoughts to his victim, so that a weak ego yields to the interrogator's synthetically injected interpretations exactly as a hypnotic subject takes over the hypnotist's suggestions.

The lie detector gets the same treatment and the same verdict.[^9] It records changes in the psychogalvanic reflex and shows that a subject reacts more emotionally to some questions than others. That overreaction may be the reaction to having told a lie. It may equally be an innocent person's reaction to an emotion-laden situation, or to fear of unjust accusation. The relationship between interrogator and subject influences the reading as much as guilt does. It is not in fact a lie detector, although it is used as one.

**What a person is**. A short passage on the people who wrote to him after he first published on menticide is the most humane thing in the chapter. Dozens were convinced somebody outside was directing their thoughts. That can be the early stage of a serious psychosis.

**And it would be a vast oversimplification to stick an easy psychiatric label on all such feelings**, because there are many real outside pressures. There are perfectly normal people continually disturbed by the barrage aimed at their minds through propaganda, advertising, radio, television, the movies and the newspapers — all the gibbering maniacs whose voices never stop. They suffer because a cold, mechanical, shouting world is knocking continually at the doors of their minds.

**How people should relate**. Then the chapter turns on his own profession, and this is where a 1956 psychiatrist says something his colleagues would not have thanked him for.[^10] Just as training can degenerate into coercive taming, therapy can degenerate into the imposition of the doctor's will on his patient — and the doctor need not be conscious that this is happening.

He is blunt about the trade. **I have seen quacks whose only knowledge was where to buy their couches**, gratifying their own need to live other people's lives by calling themselves analysts. But the honest therapist has the harder problem: his profession obliges him to make his patients temporarily dependent on him, and this may appeal to his own need for a sense of importance and power. The patient often listens in awe to the doctor who is for them the omniscient magician — and the therapist must not encourage that, because good psychotherapy aims at educating a person for freedom and maturity, not for conforming submission. The reason analytic training requires the therapist to undergo years of the technique himself is given in one clause: so that, armed with knowledge of his own unsound unconscious needs, he will not use his profession to mastermind other people's lives.

**What is worth having**. The generalisation is wider than medicine and it is the chapter's real finding. The good will that people invest in their leaders, doctors and administrators is tremendous, and can be used as a weapon against them. Family counselling, religious guidance, management counselling — each can be misused as a tool of power. And psychology itself may tend to standardise the mind.

**What makes things happen**. He names the mechanism at the end, and it is the same one running through every instrument in the chapter. The magician can increase his power by increasing the anxieties and fears of his victim, by exploiting his dependency needs, and by provoking his feelings of guilt and inferiority.

**The shape of time**. One aside dates the book precisely. Mescaline experiments, started thirty years earlier, were suddenly fashionable again, and Huxley had just described the chemical paradise of *The Doors of Perception*. **Meerloo declines to argue and simply notes that Huxley's euphoric reactions are not necessarily what other people experience** — he had run the experiment on himself twenty-five years before. The danger he names is not the trip but the habit of mind: the propaganda for chemical elation invites men to become chemical dependents, and chemical dependents are weak people.

*Read: lines 563–707.*

---

## Ch. 4 — Why do they yield?

**What a person is**. The chapter's foundation is a claim about everybody rather than about prisoners. Every individual has two opposing needs operating at once: the need to be independent, to be oneself, and the need not to be oneself, not to be anybody at all, not to resist mental pressure.[^11] The need to be inconspicuous, to disappear, to be swallowed up by society is described as common.

**What makes things happen**. What the camps did with it is the sharpest causal claim in the run, and it is about meaning rather than pain. Prisoners arrived with one unanswered question burning: why has all this happened to me? The need for a sense of direction and purpose went unsatisfied, and so they could not maintain their personalities. What Pavlovian conditioning does with artificial confusion, one shocking experience can do on its own.

The Nazis exploited it precisely. Humiliation, plus the repeated suggestion that the Allies were as good as beaten, conspired to convince inmates that there would be no end to this pointless suffering, no victorious conclusion, no future to their lives. The desire to give in becomes almost insurmountable when a man believes he has to adjust to a degrading life forever.

**The shape of time**. And then the passage the whole chapter turns on, which is about a date. **At the moment faith and hope disappear, man breaks down**. There are stories of prisoners who fixed all their expectations on liberation coming at Christmas 1944 and aimed their entire existence at that date. When it passed and they were still incarcerated, many of them simply collapsed and died.

**How people should relate**. The isolation material is the most technically interesting in the run because it was being freshly measured as he wrote.[^12] Social intercourse — colleagues, work, newspapers, voices, traffic, the people we love and the ones we do not — is daily nourishment for the senses. Remove it and the personality changes: long-forgotten anxieties surface, repressed memories knock from inside, and fantasy assumes gigantic proportions because there is nothing ordinary to check it against.

He writes about his own Nazi prison in one short paragraph. It was almost impossible for me to control my depressive thoughts of hopelessness. He had to tell himself over and over: *think, think. Keep your senses alert; don't give in*. On many days he felt it was a losing battle. The laboratory version had just been run at McGill: students in pitch-black soundproof rooms, ventilated with filtered air, hands in heavy leather mittens, who fell within a short time into a kind of hallucinatory hypnotic state.

**What is real**. The consequence for a prisoner is a relationship rather than a symptom. His guards and interrogators **become more and more his only source of contact with reality, with stimuli he needs even more than bread** — and so he develops a peculiar submissive relationship to them. Sexual starvation and latent dependency make him willing to accept a guard as a substitute.

**What is worth having**. And the guards knew to attack the future rather than the body. They constantly suggested that nobody cared and nobody knew: you are alone. Your friends on the outside don't know whether you're alive or dead. Your fellow prisoners don't even care. In both the Nazi camps and the Korean camps a kind of mass paranoia developed, prisoners cutting themselves off from each other through suspicion, hatred of the guards displaced onto the men imprisoned alongside them.

He includes himself in the finding, which is why it carries. The times that I myself wavered and entertained thoughts about joining the opposite forces always occurred after periods of extreme loneliness and deep-seated yearnings for companionship.

**How you know**. The chapter's boldest idea is the pact, and it is the one most exposed to its period.[^13] Torturer and tortured gradually form a peculiar community in which each influences the other. As a patient identifies with his psychiatrist, daily interrogation creates a transfer in which the prisoner identifies with his inquisitors and the inquisitors with him — and the prisoner, in a strange and harsh world, identifies far more with the enemy than the enemy does with him.

He reads the confession ritual as a medieval witch hunt in refined form. **Accuser and accused each afford the other assistance, and both belong together as collaborating members of a ritual of confession and self-denigration**. Through their cooperation they attack the minds of bystanders, who identify and consequently feel guilty and submissive — which is what the Moscow trials did to the Russians who listened.

Then the explanation, offered as psychoanalysis and stated as symmetry. Both torturer and tortured are victims of their own unconscious guilt. The torturer projects his onto a scapegoat and expiates it by attacking his victim. The victim's own guilt, from deeply repressed childhood hostility, is normally under control and is released by relentless interrogation. The more I accuse myself, the less reason there is for the inquisitor's existence.

And the conclusion he draws is the one a reader is likeliest to resist. There is no essential difference between victim and inquisitor. They are alike. Neither has control over his hidden hostile thoughts. It is simply easier to be the inquisitor — because it is simpler to punish others for what we feel as criminal in ourselves than to face up to it.

*Read: lines 708–911.*
