It is a re-ingest candidate.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/purandare-shivaji-indias-great-warrior-king|Vaibhav Purandare, Shivaji: India's Great Warrior King]]*

---

## Introduction — One man against an empire, and a paper trail that was burnt

Start with the mismatch. One Maratha, against the Mughal empire at the height of its power under Aurangzeb, in a Deccan already carved up between three Islamic sultanates — the Nizam Shahi of Ahmadnagar, the Adil Shahi of Bijapur and the Qutub Shahi of Golconda.[^1] Marathas had been competent soldiers for a century, and they were all serving one or another of those powers, as generals taking orders or as foot soldiers.

Aurangzeb called him a mountain rat in public. **Then he sent the full weight of the empire against him**, because he had worked out where the rat's strength lay — the hill forts and the terrain around them.[^2]

The career comes in three parts, and the book is explicit about them. Childhood to 1656, the first twenty-six years, a rebel taking forts.[^3] Then the decade from 1656 to 1666, taking on Bijapur and Aurangzeb at once, with real collapses in it. Then the last stretch, ending with a crown.

What made him hard to fight is not force. **He would not give his enemies a pitched battle**, which let him take the measure of an opponent before answering.[^4] He offered concessions. He retreated in order to re-equip. The book names the quality directly: he was as good at holding himself back as at launching himself forward.

And the thing that baffled his enemies was who stuck by him. His lieutenants were mostly from ordinary Deccan families. In 1660 one of them, Baji Prabhu Deshpande, held a narrow mountain pass against a Bijapuri assault with three hundred men so that Shivaji could reach safety, and died doing it.[^5]

In 1674 he crowned himself, and the reasoning is legal rather than ceremonial. Declaring his own state and giving his rule official status **took away from Aurangzeb, Bijapur and Golconda the charge of overstepping a line**.[^6] From that day he dealt with them as an equal.

What a soldier may take from a farmer is where his own writing is sharpest. He forbade his army to touch anything from the fields of ordinary peasants, and punished those who did.[^7] Not a blade of grass, not a grain of food taken by force — because if they did that, he wrote, **the villagers would think of them as worse than the Mughals**.

The state he was building is the question the Introduction settles, and it refuses both easy answers. Not a secular kingdom and not a Hindu theocracy: a Hindu polity, broadly inclusive and tolerant, drawing on Hindu tradition and open to everyone in it.[^8] He recruited Muslims as he recruited Marathas, and two of his navy admirals were Muhammadans. His bitterest critic, the Mughal chronicler Khafi Khan who called him a hell-dog, wrote down that Shivaji had strictly ordered his soldiers to treat the Quran with the greatest respect if they came across one.

What he noticed about his own world is what the identity is answering. Marathas had risen as soldiers of rank and **the highest military ranks were still closed to them**.[^9] So at sixteen he cut his official seal in Sanskrit, in the Persianate age, when his father's seal, his mother's seal and his agent's seal were all in Persian. Hindu Deccani kings before him had taken the title Sultan. He took Chhatrapati, from *chhatra*, the umbrella of the old Hindu rajas.

The book then names the two groups who cannot claim his state. Those who want him overstated as a protector of the faith — he did once order that cows and Brahmins not be harmed, and reading a whole politics out of that is history run backwards for modern convenience.[^10] And those who want the words Hindu and Hinduism denied altogether, and who will not discuss what centuries of conquest did to Hindu cultural identity or the religious dimension of attacks on temples.

*Hindawi* is the word from his own century that does the work. It meant the land's Hindu population, its tribal peoples, all the indigenous people — and increasingly the Deccani Muslims who had come over the western sea centuries before and made the land their own, **as against those arriving more recently from the north**.[^11]

Now the problem that shapes the whole book. **Most Maratha records of his time were burnt** — destroyed in Mughal assaults, or destroyed by the Marathas themselves after his death as the conflict intensified and Aurangzeb took Raigad and the other forts where the top documents were kept.[^12] What survived was mostly family papers and letters about land grants.

So the archive had to be built afterwards, by asking families to hand things over. V.K. Rajwade collected twenty-one volumes of private Maratha family papers and official correspondence at the turn of the twentieth century.[^13] The scholars of the Bharat Itihas Sanshodhak Mandal of Pune added to it.

The English works have a specific defect and it is worth stating. Jadunath Sarkar's *Shivaji and His Times* was the standard English book for decades and got several things wrong.[^14] **The famous one is a name**. Sarkar wrote that Shivaji renamed the fort Kondhana as Sinhagad, the lion's fort, after Tanaji Malusare died taking it — a story that has been repeated endlessly in ballads, cinema and theatre. Letters written before Tanaji's death already call it Sinhagad. It was called that first, which is *why* the lion metaphor was used.

And the English biographers almost entirely ignored the two contemporaries. Parmanand wrote the *Shivabharat* and Sabhasad the *Sabhasad Bakhar*, and both were his own officials.[^15]

The other voices are all adversaries or outsiders, which the book uses deliberately. Translated Persian records of the Mughals, of Ahmadnagar, Bijapur and Golconda, for how his enemies saw him and how that changed. Portuguese records from Goa. The diaries of the French official Francois Martin at Pondicherry.[^16] **His first foreign biographer was a Portuguese man living at Marmugao in Goa during his lifetime** — Cosme da Guarda, who published in 1695, fifteen years after the death, having talked to people across the Deccan first.

*Read: lines 22–159*.

---

## Ch. 1 — A birth date nobody can agree on

The sun had gone down behind the mountains around the craggy hill of Shivneri, at the northern end of the Sahyadri range, and the child was born that evening.[^17] **Three centuries later people were still fighting about the date**. Committees discussed whether it was 27 April 1627 or 19 February 1630.

Why the argument runs so long is a fact about the archive rather than about him. Most Maratha records of his period were destroyed after his death, so when historians began gathering documents in the late nineteenth century the first date to surface was 1627.[^18] The credible account, written by the poet Parmanand on the Chhatrapati's own orders, gives a date that works out to 1630.

The family had already buried four children. Jijabai and Shahaji had five sons before him and only one, Sambhaji, had lived.[^19] **The names of the other four were never recorded**. They probably died in infancy, and the parents were anxious this one would survive.

Even the name has two stories and the book prefers the plain one. The popular theory, from a late and unreliable chronicle, ties it to the goddess Shivai whose idol stood in a temple on the fort.[^20] Parmanand simply says he was named Shiv because he was born at Shivgiri, which is Shivneri.

What a Maratha is, in this world, is a matter of geography before anything else. For centuries the word meant a resident of the Marathi-speaking parts — a fifth-century Sinhalese document has *Maharattha*, Al Biruni in the eleventh century calls the land south of the Narmada *Marhat Des*, Ibn Batuta in the fourteenth writes about the people around Daulatabad.[^21]

The country divides into three and each part makes a different kind of person. The Konkan coastline. The Ghats — mountains that blocked the monsoon coming off the south-west and stayed rocky, dry and bad for cultivation. And the Desh, the plateau beyond them, one part of it in the mountains' rain shadow and as farm-resistant as the heights.[^22] People grew mainly wheat, cotton and pulses, and very little rice. The seventh-century Chinese pilgrim Hsuan Tsang left a description of them that the book quotes because it still fits:[^23]

> The disposition of the people is honest and simple; they are tall in stature and of a stern … character. To their benefactors, they are grateful; to their enemies, relentless. If they are insulted, they will risk their lives to avenge themselves.

The language has a longer pedigree than the politics. Maharashtra Prakrit was the vernacular child of Sanskrit, and one of the oldest surviving poetry anthologies in South Asia — the *Gathasaptasati*, seven hundred verses — was compiled in it around the second century CE by a Satavahana king.[^24] It became Marathi, and at the end of the thirteenth century a sixteen-year-old called Dnyaneshwar wrote his commentary on the Bhagavad Gita in it, at the head of a devotional movement set against ritualism, orthodoxy and caste oppression.

Then the conquests, in one paragraph that explains the century he was born into. Ala-ud-din Khilji came south in 1296, the first Muslim invasion of the Deccan.[^25] Devagiri's riches helped him take the Delhi throne. The Tughluqs took Devagiri again in 1327. The four regional Hindu kingdoms were wiped out, and by the middle of the fourteenth century two successor states had emerged — the Bahmani Sultanate and Vijayanagara. **Three things then happened almost together in the first half of the sixteenth century**: Babur founded the Mughal empire in the north, the Portuguese took Goa, and the Bahmani kingdom split into five.

So how does a Maratha rise in a world run by four Islamic kingdoms? The book gives four reasons and the first is a quarrel among the conquerors.[^26] Tension ran permanently between the Arab-Turkish Muslims coming down from the north, the "Westerners" arriving by ship from the Persian Gulf, and the Deccanis. **Ibrahim Adil Shah I, who came to power in 1535, sacked most of his Persian-origin troops and recruited Deccani Muslims — and then chose Marathas to check the power of both**.

The other reasons are administrative. A local warrior class gave the sultanates a direct connection to the population and a grip on administration down to the village. And the supply of Turkish and other Muslim recruits from the north dried up as the Mughal empire expanded southwards, because a man coming in from Central Asia would increasingly join the Mughals instead.

His grandfather Maloji rose under the Nizam Shahi, serving Malik Ambar — **the Ethiopian regent who held the northern Deccan against the Mughals from 1600 until his death in 1626**.[^27] Shahaji carried it on, distinguishing himself at Bhatvadi in 1624 when Malik Ambar's men held off the combined Mughal and Adil Shahi forces.

Jijabai's family, the Jadhavs, were *deshmukhs* — headmen of a *pargana*, a group of twenty to a hundred villages.[^28] Her father Lukhji was wanted by both the Nizam Shahi and the Mughals. Jahangir called the Bargis a hardy lot and a centre of resistance in that country, and an English factor at Burhanpur reported in 1621 that Jaddoo Raye, one of the principal generals of the Deccan, had revolted.

**Then an elephant ran amok and the two families never recovered**. Around 1623 the Nizam Shah's sardars were leaving his durbar when an elephant broke loose in the melee outside.[^29] A man from each family was killed in the fighting that followed and the sultan had to step in himself. Jijabai lost a brother; her husband lost a cousin. Believing the sultan had favoured the Bhosles, Lukhji Jadhav defected to the Mughals.

That is why she gave birth on a fort belonging to neither family. Shahaji, expecting Shah Jahan's campaign in the Deccan, left his pregnant wife at Shivneri with the in-laws of their elder son, and with the permission of his relative.[^30] **She was not celebrating**. She was sheltering in a house that was neither hers nor her parents', keeping a low profile. And the country outside was starving. A famine hit the Deccan from 1629 to 1631, and the *Badshah Nama* records it:[^31]

> Life was offered for a loaf, but none would buy; rank was to be sold for a cake, but none cared for it … The numbers of the dying caused obstructions in the roads.

What survives about the boy is physical and almost incidental. Active, agile, a sharp pointed nose, a broad forehead, an endearing smile. An English chaplain who saw him later noted a quick and piercing eye, and described him as whiter than any of his people.[^32]

Education began at seven with the Devanagari alphabet, and then horse riding, elephant riding, archery, marksmanship, the spear and the sword.[^33] At twelve his father made him responsible for the Pune *jagir* and gave him the staff to run it. At twelve he was also married, to Saibai — and he married eight times in all, twice while Saibai was alive, in an age when marriage was an instrument of politics.

**The famous story of his youth is one the book rejects**. Nineteenth-century Marathi chroniclers have Shahaji taking the twelve-year-old to Bijapur, where the self-respecting boy embarrasses his father by refusing to bow to the Adil Shah.[^34]

The anchor of his childhood was his mother, and the book is careful about what can and cannot be said of her. She lived in a deeply patriarchal society in which the lives of women like her were never described by contemporary chroniclers, **which leaves a serious hole for any modern biographer**.[^35] What is visible is a woman who had watched her own family and her husband's kill each other, and who raised him anyway.

## Ch. 2 — Wolves in Pune, and a patil sacked for a sexual offence

Pune in 1630 was a ghost town with wolves in it. It had started as a *kasba*, a village with a weekly market where the surrounding villages came to buy what they needed, and warring armies had laid it waste.[^36]

Getting people back was the first job, and the method was money. Dadoji Konddev **declared war on the wolves**, offering a cash reward to anyone who killed them, and the tigers and other animals that prowled about.[^37] Cultivators were courted with terms: land at a nominal rent for the first year, rising only slightly after; one tree in every ten planted kept free of tax; a third of the crop to the *jagirdar* and two-thirds to the man who grew it. Land was measured, ownership settled, wells and canals dug, and the people who dug them paid.

**Displaced villagers came back to be paid for killing beasts**, and stayed to farm.[^38]

The Mavals are where the teenager went and they are the most neglected country in the upper Deccan. Twelve hills and valleys west of Pune, hard to reach, rocky and poor, with cultivation thin and mostly along the streams on the hill slopes.[^39] The people there were Maratha, Kunbi, Bhil, Koli — and all of it collapsed into one word, *Mavale*, the people of the Mavals.

Administration barely existed there. Officials often did not set foot on soil they considered unusable, full of risky cliffs and ravines, and the hill people and *deshmukhs* fought endless succession battles over whatever land there was.[^40]

**So the ledges and ravines everybody else avoided became his ground**. He spent his days in them with the young men of the area, going into corners where horses could not follow, and his smile disarmed people who had kept a careful distance from a very young administrator.[^41] Tanaji Malusare, Yesaji Kank and Baji Pasalkar came out of that.

The oath in the temple is not real, and the book says so plainly. The story that he swore *Hindawi Swaraj* at Raireshwar in 1645 with a few chosen friends rests on two letters, **and the top Maratha historians who read seventeenth-century Marathi have called them forgeries**.[^42] What is real is the bond with the Mavals — and the book's own line is that this forgotten country on the outer edge of Deccani consciousness was the womb his state came out of.

What an official is, in this system, is a hereditary post-holder with land attached. The *patil* collected revenue in the village and the *kulkarni* kept its books; the *deshmukh* did the same at district level and the *deshpande* kept the district accounts.[^43] All of them were *watandars*, holders of the *watan*, and their rights passed down the family — and could be taken away the moment a ruler was displeased. A *patil* or *deshmukh* was also expected to raise and sometimes lead troops when the state asked.

**That last fact is why a boy visiting his father's district frightened a sultanate**. He was reaching the men who could mobilise the countryside.

The politics that turned it into a crisis was factional, and it happened in Bijapur rather than in Pune. Shahaji had done well under the general Ranadulla Khan, who died in 1643, and his rival Mustafa Khan rose in his place.[^44] The estates at Pune and Supe were taken from Shahaji, attacked in 1644 on suspicion that he was revolting, held for four months, and then given back by the end of the same year for reasons nobody recorded.

The other thing the young man was watching was the hardening of the court. The days of the state practising pluralism were fading and fanaticism had taken root.[^45] By the fourth decade of the century, apart from Shahaji and one other, the high barons of Bijapur were Muslims. And Muhammad Adil Shah issued three openly discriminatory regulations against Hindus, who were most of his population — **the first of them reserving provincial governorships for Muslims and confining Hindus to clerical and non-executive posts**.

Against that, a seal in Sanskrit is a sentence. His father's, his mother's and Dadoji's were all in Persian, as were those of the other Hindu chiefs.[^46] Marathi was used in correspondence and the Marathi copies never carried an official seal. His own was hexagonal and it read:

> Ever increasing in luminosity like the moon at the start of the brighter half of the lunar month and esteemed across the world, this seal of Shivaji, son of Shahaji, shines for the betterment of all.

The earliest letter carrying it is from 28 January 1646, and what it is about is the second sentence of his career. The *patil* of Ranjhe village, Babaji Bhikaji Gujar, committed a sexual offence while carrying out his duties.[^47] It was reported. Shivaji ordered him arrested and brought in, held an inquiry, established the offence, sacked him from his post — and had his hands and feet cut off. The post went to a kinsman, since Babaji had no children, and two hundred *hons* were recovered for the treasury.

**In a century when capital punishment was ordinary, that ruling made him popular**. Ordinary villagers had watched officials go unpunished for their actions and sexual offences go untaken-seriously, and here was a modicum of accountability.[^48]

Then the forts, after Dadoji died in 1647. Within a year and a half he took four, all just south of the Pune *pargana* and all useful if Bijapur attacked again.[^49] The most important was Murumbdeo, which he renamed Rajgad — over 4,574 feet, with a base running several kilometres, which makes a siege hard. He found it unoccupied, saw what it could be, and built on it.

**And the compliment on record is from an enemy**. Aurangzeb's chronicler wrote that the infernal Shiva, once he had it, terraced three sides at a lower level and built three strong forts there, making its capture impossible.[^50] Then, in an age when nothing could attack from the sky:

> Fort Rajgad is a hill second only to the fort of the towered sky … Its thorny jungles and spectre-haunted chasms can be traversed only by the wind. Nothing can descend on it except rain!

## Ch. 3 — The father in the dungeon and the fort given back

Then Bijapur reached for the thing he could not defend. On the morning of 25 July 1648, three nobles walked into Shahaji's chamber in the camp at Jinji and put him in fetters for alleged disobedience.[^51] The charge had been built by Mustafa Khan, who disliked him for having been close to Ranadulla Khan, and it tied the father to what the son was doing at Pune.

The dungeon had one small opening, and the terms were stated. If the son did not submit within a certain period, **the aperture would be closed for ever**.[^52]

Meanwhile a second force came for Shivaji, under Fatah Khan — not one of Bijapur's leading generals, because at this stage the rebel was a minor irritant.[^53] Fatah Khan set out for Sinhagad from Bijapur, over 280 kilometres away, heard on the road that Shivaji had moved to Purandar, and turned that way.

Purandar was the right hill. A string of hills running about four kilometres and rising from left to right, with both east and west visible from the summit — an advantage for a defender with a small force, unlike Sinhagad, where the vertical climb means you can be surprised.[^54] **And his intelligence was good enough that he knew Fatah Khan was coming and where from**.

The Marathas held it. Bijapur's army withdrew and left weaponry, gold, horses and elephants behind, and the first encounter went the way it was supposed to.[^55] **It was still a defeat, because his father was in a cell**.

So he paid. Bijapur would release Shahaji if Shivaji gave up Sinhagad and his brother gave up Bangalore; Purandar he could keep.[^56] Shahaji walked out on 16 May 1649, after ten months, and was sent straight off on a campaign.

**Handing back Sinhagad was the hardest thing in the chapter and the book says why**. The enterprise was new. The young Mavale soldiers had lined up behind him and defended Purandar to the hilt, and their morale depended on not seeing the disputed fort returned.[^57]

What he did next was to stop taking and start consolidating. Chakan to the north of Pune, Supe, Baramati and Indapur to the east — more ground, more local officials, more men.[^58]

And a decision about who his army would belong to. The *deshmukhs* were useful, with their local knowledge, their manpower and the levies they raised — **and he would have made an egregious mistake relying on them**.[^59] So he built cavalry and infantry, and later a navy, under his own eye, and every man in them was paid directly rather than out of a *deshmukh*'s coffers.

Some played truant. Some changed sides repeatedly. Some were openly hostile, including his own step-uncle Sambhaji Mohite, whom Shahaji had put in charge of Supe.[^60] **Shivaji arranged a family meeting with him and had him arrested there**, and confiscated his property.

Then the biggest move of his first twenty-six years, and it went into country the sultanate's own troops would not enter. Jaawali, across his southern boundary, where the only writ that ran was the More family's.[^61] They were *deshmukhs*, nominally with Bijapur, autonomous because of the terrain.

He had helped them settle a succession dispute a few years earlier. Then they turned on him — because the *deshmukhs* who had been in awe of them for decades were now submitting to him, and their standing was going.[^62]

**Their reply to his threat is the best-preserved insult in the book:**[^63]

> Come today instead of tomorrow and with whatever number of troops you wish. Why do you talk of having become an independent king? Who calls you a king? You are an upstart of yesterday.

He marched in January 1656. Yashwantrao More fled to Rairi, on the northern edge of Jaawali, with his two sons.[^64] Shivaji sat in the valleys and waited. When Yashwantrao came down in May, having been caught corresponding secretly with the Ghorpades, Shivaji had him executed — and the two sons were taken to Pune and killed there later.

**Then he took the hill and renamed it**. Rairi became Raigad, and from the early 1670s it was his capital, where he crowned himself in 1674.[^65]

The timing has the arithmetic of a patient man. Four forts as a teenager was the soft launch. Jaawali at twenty-six was the real one, and he had spent almost eight years getting to it.[^66]

## Ch. 4 — Letters to a man who called him the son of a dog

Having split the Adil Shahi in half, he moved on the ports. Kalyan and Bhiwandi, then down the coast against the Siddis of Danda-Rajpuri.[^67] And then he told Bijapur that the new gains near the coast were being held for the Adil Shah, as a check against the Mughals.

**Simultaneously he opened a correspondence with the Mughals**.

Aurangzeb was twelve years older and had been at this longer. Governor of the Deccan, then out in a huff in 1644 over his father favouring Dara Shukoh, then Gujarat, then Afghanistan against the Bukhara armies, then back to the Deccan in 1652 — an experienced general who had fought Uzbeks, Hazaras and Persians and put down Afghan and Baluch clans.[^68] And hungry.

Shivaji's first strike is a robbery, and it is well chosen. Mulla Ahmad, the Bijapuri commander of Kalyan, was summoned to the capital to deliver accumulated revenue, and Shivaji's men waylaid the convoy near Purandar and carried the lot off.[^69] Then Kalyan, Bhiwandi and the Mahuli fort. **He knew how much traffic moved through Kalyan into the Deccan**, and what controlling a trade route was worth.

The book pauses on a story about that campaign to say it is not true. Folklore has his general capturing Mulla Ahmad's beautiful daughter-in-law and sending her to Pune, where Shivaji apologises and sends her home, saying that if his own mother had possessed her beauty he too would have been handsome.[^70]

**Now the thing nobody else in his world was doing**. The land powers — Mughals and sultanates alike — had left almost the entire seafront to the *firangs*, the Portuguese, English, Dutch and French, who controlled the movement of every ship.[^71] Including the ships carrying the officials of northern Hindustan and the southern Deccan and their families to Hajj.

Part of why is a religious ruling. Hindu orthodoxy held that crossing the sea was unholy, and anyone who polluted himself that way had to be purified afterwards.[^72] **Why nobody linked a trade corridor to defence and security is, in the book's own word, bewildering**.

So in 1657 he ordered twenty small armed ships built in the creeks below Kalyan, Bhiwandi and Prabalgad — and commissioned Portuguese officers to do it, being better shipbuilders than the local men, with locals assisting.[^73] Around four hundred people worked on it. The Portuguese response is in the Goa archives, dated 19 July 1659, and it is a good picture of how a small power is handled:[^74]

> He has built some men-at-war … in Bhimdi (Bhiwandi), Kalyan and Panvel … To ensure that these men-of-war do not set sail, we have ordered the Portuguese Captain not to let them come out of these ports.

And when he asked Goa to stop its captains helping the Siddis against him, the council debated it and chose both answers at once. Keep amiable relations with him because he is powerful, holds Kalyan and Bhiwandi and the whole Konkan, and can do immense harm to Portuguese interests.[^75] **Then write to the captains telling them to offer no support ostensibly, and to do it secretly if they wish, ensuring nobody — least of all Shivaji — has any idea**.

His own letters to Aurangzeb are gone. Not one of the handful survives, most likely burnt with the rest after his death.[^76] **What exists is Aurangzeb's side of it**, which is how the chapter has to work.

In July 1656 Aurangzeb told the governor of Ahmadnagar to keep the path of correspondence with Shivaji open, and to write in a way that would encourage him to offer his loyalty.[^77] A few months later Shivaji asked to keep his Bijapuri gains on the Mughals' behalf — which would have denied Bijapur's claim and blocked Mughal aggression at once. Aurangzeb welcomed it, with a note underneath:

> If he follows our orders, fine. Else, they would be trampled underfoot by our powerful army and punished for their actions.

The pardon letter of April 1658, sent from Ujjain, is the fullest thing the chapter has, and it is worth reading for its terms rather than its tone:[^78]

> Your offences are too many and don't deserve any pardon. But you have demonstrated your intention of being loyal and in service and have expressed your contrition over your offences. Ours is not a durbar that persecutes, so I have pardoned your offences on the condition that you stay steadfast on the path of service and obedience.

Then the deal itself. Shivaji had asked for the Konkan lands and forts that had been his ancestral *watan*, once the Nizam Shahi territory then held by Bijapur came to the Mughals; in exchange he would send a force of not less than five hundred horses.[^79]

After the second coronation in June 1659 came a robe of honour, and instructions to obey the new subahdar of the Deccan.[^80] **And privately, at the same time, Aurangzeb wrote to Mir Jumla about the district Shivaji bordered: attend to it, as the son of a dog is waiting for it**.[^81] What the emperor ordered when the pretence stopped shows what a Mughal campaign in the Deccan actually meant on the ground:[^82]

> Invade the enemy's territory, don't spare any effort in ransacking the villages there, and reduce it to ashes. Destroy that territory in every way possible.

By 1659 he held forty forts, ten thousand cavalry — seven thousand on state-owned horses and three thousand on their own — and ten thousand infantry.[^83] **And the book will not let that look like parity**. Bijapur's military and civilian strength, its territory, its resources and the number of officials it could summon were all far greater. The threat he posed was, in the plain word used, manageable. Which is why the court decided to deal with him before he grew, and picked the man for it: Afzal Khan, known as a powerful crusher of enemies.[^84]

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, so far `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Paradigm-obvious — anyone in that seat would have done it, and reading genius into it is the biographer's error**. Taking unoccupied hill forts in your own father's *jagir*. Marrying eight times when marriage was the instrument of politics. Professing loyalty to Bijapur while holding forts for yourself, which is exactly what every *jagirdar* in the Deccan was doing, including his father. Cultivating the *deshmukhs*. Even the correspondence with Aurangzeb is standard practice: every Deccani sardar in the book writes to whichever bigger power is nearest, and Aurangzeb was actively recruiting them.

**Paradigm-breaking — it cost him something, and the cost is the evidence**. Three so far.

The Sanskrit seal at sixteen, in a world where his own mother and father sealed in Persian. It bought nothing and it announced everything, and the chapter reads it as a deliberate refusal to have an identity sidelined.

Paying his own soldiers directly rather than through the *deshmukhs*. That is more expensive, slower to raise, and it forfeits the ready-made levies of men whose local knowledge he needed — and it is the reason his army stayed his when the *deshmukhs* changed sides, which several of them did.

Building ships. Every land power around him had written off the sea, and there was a religious ruling saying crossing it polluted you. He had to hire Portuguese officers to do the building and then watch the Portuguese lock his own ships in his own creeks.

## Ch. 3 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and it was the standing offer**. Bijapur's terms for releasing Shahaji were Sinhagad and Bangalore. The other course — the one his soldiers wanted — was to refuse, keep the fort, and let his father take his chances behind a door that was going to be bricked up.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose he had kept Sinhagad. He keeps the morale of the Mavale who had just held Purandar for him, and he keeps a fort at the centre of the ring around Pune. He loses his father, and with him the Bijapuri protection that had kept the *jagir* nominally legitimate for a decade, and the elder brother's base at Bangalore stays exposed. The forecast — a forecast — is that Bijapur then treats the whole family as in open revolt in 1649 rather than in 1659, ten years earlier than it did, and against a rebel with four forts instead of forty. **He got the fort back later anyway, and the book notes he never explains how**. Paying a price you can recover is not the same kind of decision as paying one you cannot.

## Ch. 4 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the correspondence with Aurangzeb: professions of loyalty and contrition, sent by a man who had just robbed a revenue convoy and was building a navy.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/shih-and-strategic-depth|shih]]** would call the letters the cheapest thing he ever bought. They cost him nothing he valued, they postponed a war he could not yet win, and they kept the Mughal governor writing rather than marching. The forts and the ships were being built the whole time the letters were in transit. **Position accumulated under cover of submission is still position**.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/indirect-agency-deniable-power|deniable power]]** would notice that both sides were running the same play and both knew it. Aurangzeb grants a pardon in April and writes "the son of a dog is waiting for it" to Mir Jumla. Goa tells its captains to refuse the Siddis help ostensibly and to give it secretly. The Deccan in this decade is a system in which the written word and the intention are formally decoupled, and everybody's correspondence is written to be read by the wrong person.

**A Stoic advisor**, from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|the dichotomy of control]], is the dissenting voice and worth keeping for it. What a man writes is his own; what an emperor does with it is not. Contrition offered as a manoeuvre has spent something that cannot be replaced — the next time he means it, nobody will be able to tell.

## What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: building in the space an incumbent has declared worthless**.

Three of the four chapters run on the same move. The Mavals were country officials would not walk on, and they gave him his army. Jaawali was terrain the sultanate's troops would not enter, and it gave him his capital. The sea was ground every land power in India had conceded to foreigners, partly on a religious ruling, and it gave him the only navy in the Deccan.

**Scope conditions**. This works where the incumbent's neglect is genuine rather than tactical — where the ground is not held because holding it is judged not worth the cost, not because a trap is set. It requires that the neglected ground actually connect to something the incumbent needs: the Mavals fed men into the ring of forts around Pune, Jaawali cut Bijapur off from its own lowlands, the coast carried the trade. And it fails the moment the incumbent revalues the ground, which is exactly what the Portuguese did the year his ships were finished — they had conceded the sea to nobody, only to men without hulls.

**Modern equivalent:** the market segment the incumbent has written off as unserviceable, the platform nobody profitable is on. The advantage lasts precisely as long as the neglect, and the neglect ends when the position starts to matter.

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Shivaji-India's Great Warrior King.md`, lines 22–817: Introduction (22–159), ch. 1 (160–359), ch. 2 (360–469), ch. 3 (470–613), ch. 4 (614–817).

**Hagiography check, and this book is written against a working cult**. Shivaji is a live political symbol in Maharashtra, and the author separates himself from that repeatedly. The oath at Raireshwar is called a forgery on the authority of the Marathi historians who read the period's script. The renaming of Kondhana as Sinhagad is shown to be backwards. The Bijapur court story and the beautiful daughter-in-law are both marked apocryphal. Where the author's own view is doing the work — that the state was a Hindu polity rather than a secular or a theocratic one — he states it as his answer, and names both the groups he is arguing against.

**Where the evidence is thin and the book says so**. Most Maratha records were destroyed after his death, which is why the birth date is contested and why Shivaji's own letters to Aurangzeb are missing entirely. Those exchanges are reconstructed from the Mughal side alone. Jijabai's interior life is unavailable because contemporary chroniclers did not describe women like her, and the author flags that as a hole rather than filling it.

**Whose voices these are**. Parmanand and Sabhasad were his own officials. Khafi Khan and Aurangzeb's chronicler were enemies. The Portuguese and English records are transactional. The book uses all four kinds and marks which is which.

**Bounded absence**. No claim is made about material outside lines 22–817.

# What the Deccan Took For Granted — Chapters 5–8

> **Chapters 5–8 of Vaibhav Purandare, *Shivaji: India's Great Warrior King*** — Afzal Khan under the canopy at Pratapgad, the siege of Panhala and the English prisoners, the night raid on Shaista Khan's bedroom, and four days of Surat burning. Read from `RAW/books/Shivaji-India's Great Warrior King.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.

## Ch. 5 — The canopy at Pratapgad

His real name was Abdulla Bhatari. Everyone remembers him as Afzal Khan — tall, heavily built, one of Bijapur's leading commanders, and the man the court sent for when something had to be done by any means at all.[^1]

The court had recent proof of what that meant. Right after Muhammad Adil Shah's death, three senior generals were murdered in quick succession, allegedly at the queen's behest, **and Afzal Khan helped hatch the plot against at least one of them** — his own factional rival.[^2]

He also had a grudge against the Bhosles. He and Shahaji had once worked together under Ranadulla Khan, and he had moved to other factions since.[^3] Shivaji's associations with the name were personal too: his father's treatment, and his elder brother's death. Neither man was coming to this meeting cold. What Shahaji said when told to rein his son in is one line, and it is worth having exactly. He was in Bijapur's service and his son was taking Bijapur's forts:

> He is no longer under my control. I am a faithful dependant of the Badshah. [^4]

Afzal Khan's own boast, on the floor of the durbar, is recorded by a host of sources. Who is Shivaji? I will get him here in chains, and I won't even have to get off my horse to do that.[^5] The question people have argued over for centuries is whether he set out to kill or to capture. Here the written record settles it, because Bijapur's official historian Nurullah spells out the orders he was given:

> Ali Adil Shah, on seeing that the prevalence of the Muhammadan religion was not possible unless the bramble of infidelity was burnt up in the fire of the enemy-consuming sword, appointed Afzal Khan with 10,000 horsemen, to chastise and extirpate that wicked man Shivaji… [^6]

The *farman* itself uses the words exterminate and kill. There was no ambiguity about the mission at either end.[^7]

Before the armies met, both sides went for the *deshmukhs*, and that is where the chapter's real subject sits. Afzal Khan wrote to Kanhoji Jedhe's son and to another Maval chief, and similar letters went out to others.[^8] By the time Shivaji reached Pratapgad in July 1659, two Maratha chiefs from Utravali had gone over to Bijapur, and one of the More brothers who had fled Jaawali was riding with Afzal Khan, offering his knowledge of the terrain.

Their position was genuinely awful, and the book states it without taking sides. Bijapur could argue that these men owed their authority and their legal standing to the sultanate, and that it had every right to conscript them.[^9] Siding with Shivaji meant publicly declaring yourself a rebel. Kanhoji Jedhe wrote to Shivaji's father for guidance. What came back is a small masterpiece of hedging, from a man who had disowned his son in public a week before:

> You and he have been on friendly terms for a long time. So go you must. But if you decide to go in person, or to send any of your sons, first take his word of honour, and then go, else there may be treachery. [^10]

He read it and went straight to Shivaji instead, five sons behind him. He said Shahaji had taken an oath from him and sent him into this service, that he would stay true to it, and that he and his sons and his men would fight to the death.[^11] He was willing to give up his *watan* to do it — and asked whether he could renounce it by tipping water off his right hand, in the Hindu manner. He did, and Shivaji told him to move his family out of Kari to somewhere safer.

What a march looks like from underneath is the other thing this chapter has. On the road to Wai, Afzal Khan wrecked temple towns, Pandharpur among them.[^12] Merchants, priests and others were made to foot his army's bill, which ran to an estimated two and a half lakh rupees a month.

Then the diplomacy, which is a contest of two men lying to each other in writing. The stern letter first, demanding the surrender of Sinhagad, Lohgad, Purandar, Chakan, the country between the Nira and Bhima, and Jaawali.[^13] Then the friendly one, claiming a closeness with Shahaji that had never existed:

> Your father has long been a great friend of mine. So you are not a stranger to me. Come and see me.

Shivaji's reply is the best-written thing in the book. Every line of it is bait, and the last line names the venue he wants:

> Your prowess is beyond comparison, and your heroism is fiery. You are truly a jewel on this earth, and you don't have in you the slightest bit of deceitfulness or perfidy… It is hard for me to even look you in the eye, but once you are here… [^14]

The invitation is the whole plan. Come to Jaawali and see the glory of this forest for yourself.[^15] Afzal Khan wanted him drawn down onto the plains of Wai where numbers would tell, and instead agreed to come up into the hills, to a flattish clump of ground beneath Pratapgad.

The terms for 10 November 1659 were agreed in advance and both men broke them. Each would come to the pavilion with two or three guards; the armies would keep vigil at the distance of a bowshot; then the two of them would talk privately.[^16] Shivaji brought his companies down from the Ghats and the Konkan and put them in the jungle on either side, told to stay hidden. Afzal Khan set out with a thousand swordsmen and musketeers — **and was talked into leaving them behind by Shivaji's envoy, who pointed out that a frightened man would simply turn round and go back up the fort**.[^17]

Shivaji had also sent gifts ahead to the Khan's best generals, having learned from his spies who they were.[^18] Both men arrived expecting the other to cheat, and both were right. His order to his own men beforehand planned for the worst. It is short, and it puts the decision in their hands rather than his:

> If, in spite of himself agreeing to a pact, Afzal Khan doesn't stick to his word, I will order the horns to be blown. If you hear them, destroy his army. [^19]

The two men caught sight of each other and exchanged smiles.[^20] What happened inside the canopy comes down through several accounts that do not agree on the order of the blows. Afzal Khan's own envoy — a fellow Maharashtrian, Krishnaji Bhaskar Kulkarni — came at Shivaji with a sword and was parried. The aides charged. Sayyid Banda, an expert swordsman, was killed by Jiva Mahala. Afzal Khan's head came off.

Then the horns sounded from the fort and the Mavale came out of the jungle on every side.[^21] The booty from Jaawali and Wai together was 4,000 horses, 1,200 camels, 65 elephants, 2,000 bundles of clothing and ten lakh rupees in cash and jewellery.

What he did afterwards is the part that is easy to walk past. He ordered every captured man freed and sent home **with money, food and other gifts**.[^22] He announced pensions for the widows of the Mavale who had died. He paid the wounded 25 to 200 *hons* according to how badly they were hurt. Where a dead man had grown sons, they were provided for.

And the one who came back was not forgiven twice. Khandoji Khopde had betrayed him, and Kanhoji Jedhe spoke for the apparently remorseful man, and Shivaji took him back reluctantly — and not for long.[^23]

*Read: lines 818–1025*.

## Ch. 6 — Four months inside Panhala, and eight Englishmen in irons

After Pratapgad the two powers that had been circling each other agreed on one thing. Bijapur was reeling and Aurangzeb, now secure on the throne, was ready — **so they decided to squash him together**.[^24]

He did not wait for it. A fortnight after Afzal Khan's death he went deeper into Bijapuri territory and took Panhala near Kolhapur.[^25] Then a man who needed a success came looking for one. Siddi Jauhar was an Abyssinian chief of a province in what is now Andhra, mistrusted at the Bijapur court as self-serving, and he saw a chance to restore some standing.[^26] **He turned out to be a first-rate besieger** — no window left open, no corner unattended — and he brought in Afzal Khan's son Fazl, who wanted Shivaji dead.

The Marathas assumed the monsoon would lift the siege for them. It did not. Jauhar's tents and covers stood up to the rain, and the encirclement held through it.[^27]

**Jijabai's intervention from Rajgad is the sharpest thing in the chapter and it is delivered quietly**. Parmanand says she was filled with anger, and that when she spoke to Netaji Palkar and Siddi Hilal her tone was soft and serious.[^28] Without exploding, she told them that her life — meaning her son — was under siege, and that they had simply found their way back to Rajgad. Both apologised and went back.

Meanwhile Shaista Khan came in from the north — Aurangzeb's own maternal uncle, of Persian origin, nephew of Nur Jahan, an accomplished soldier.[^29] Reaching Pune in May 1660 he found the Marathas had destroyed the grain and fodder around the *kasba* and told the residents to leave.

Then, from inside Panhala, Shivaji saw something new below him. English East India Company men, rolling grenades in to help Jauhar.[^30] He already had a quarrel with them. Months earlier the local governors of Dabhol and Rajapur had taken refuge in the English factory while his men were chasing them, and a dispute over a seized ship followed.[^31] **What is worth keeping is how the Englishmen at Rajapur wrote about him before the quarrel — the word they used was noble**.[^32] Later, once they were his prisoners, the same men would write *being a perfidious man himself*.

Getting out of Panhala took two things and the first was a letter. He wrote to Siddi Jauhar accepting submission and offering to hand over the fort.[^33] **Writing letters of submission while keeping a sturdy resolve to be free was, the book says, never a difficulty for him**.

The second thing was rain. On the night of 13 July 1660 he went down from the fort on foot with six hundred Mavale, in the dark and the drizzle, which got heavier as they moved — horses would have given the game away.[^34] He himself was carried in a palanquin, and the reasoning is tactical: in a night skirmish men need to know where their leader is.

Jauhar's scouts saw them anyway, and the chase came on with Jauhar and Fazl at the head.[^35] Baji Prabhu Deshpande held the pass with his band while the blows came in worse than the rain, was gravely wounded, and died there.

**The chronicles disagree about the last minute of that man's life and the book keeps both**. The Jedhe Chronicle simply says he laid down his life and his men did not let Jauhar up the pass. A later chronicle says he took his last breath only after he heard the gunfire from the fort that meant Shivaji was safe.[^36]

What he did on arriving at Rajgad was spend the whole day telling his mother about it, with a flood of tears flowing from her eyes.[^37] The Mughals were meanwhile learning the same lesson at two places at once. Shaista Khan tried the small fort of Chakan and found the defenders behind a mini-mountain of earth, striking back with rockets, musket-shots, bombs and stones, thrusting ramrods into their barrels and firing afresh after every setback.[^38]

And at Umbarkhind, a narrow pass, Shivaji let a Mughal column all the way in before closing on it.[^39] **The person who talked their commander into surrender was a woman riding her own horse in his ranks** — the widow of a local ruler, called Rai Bagan. Parmanand gives her speech:

> The army was put into your care, but you behaved wrongly and thoughtlessly in entering this forest, the lair of that lion, Shivaji … A man should show his prowess only where there is a possibility of success; otherwise, what he does qualifies as rashness, and it brings on ridicule.

Then the reckoning with the English. He took Rajapur, called the Company's officials to come and see him, and had them put in fetters the moment they arrived — eight men, including the factory chief Henry Revington.[^40]

What those men then wrote to Surat is a small manual in how a trading company thinks. Get us our liberty and our goods; failing that, at least our liberty.[^41] Offer to back his campaign. **And get from him a convenient port town, with liberty to build a fort, he providing the labour and materials** — a place his own Brahmin at Rajapur had already promised them.

They were clear-eyed about the difficulty. Being a perfidious man himself, he may doubt whether the English will keep their promises once the prisoners are out.[^42] And if he should be insolent, there were threats available — they had already let it be known that if they were not released, Surat would grant Aurangzeb's wish for an army transported into the Deccan.

**Their own president would not spend money on them**. Andrews at Surat wrote that the Council had its hands full and did not want to waste time inditing and sending costly letters to a rogue that takes no notice of them, and then told the captives whose fault it was:

> How you came in prison you knowe very well. 'Twas not for defending Companies goods; 'twas for going to the Seige of Pannella and tossing balls with a flagg that was knowne to bee the Englishes. [^43]

One prisoner, Richard Napier, died a month in. The Dutch register recorded that he died of torture; the English letters, which were uncensored, make it clear it was a natural death.[^44]

And the book refuses the patriotic reading of the whole episode. Some Maratha historians treat this as proof that Shivaji saw the Company's danger to the country from the start.[^45] **That is a classic case of reading history backwards**. What was known to the Marathas, and to everyone else, was narrower and quite specific: that the English would want fortifications of their own.

*Read: lines 1026–1211*.

## Ch. 7 — A wedding party at the city gate

The subahdar of the Deccan was living in Shivaji's own house. Lal Mahal in Pune, the single-storey building with straight stone walls where he had spent his teens, was now Shaista Khan's residence — and the Khan had covered over the open door to the kitchen so the smells and the noise of the cooks did not reach the inner chambers, where he had bolsters put in to lean against.[^46]

**The comfort did not slow the work**. Villages in Shivaji's country were being taken apart — men, women, houses, belongings.[^47] A Persian document from Aurangzeb's reign records the method: intelligence that the enemy's villages lay at the foot of Lohgad about forty miles from Poona, and a general sent out to deal with them.

What a ruler does about that, when he cannot stop it, is write to his officials. He could not meet those columns in the field and he knew it. His letter to Sarjerao Jedhe of 23 October 1662 survives, and it is an evacuation order:

> Spies have brought in information that the Mughals are going to raid your subdistrict. As soon as you get this letter, you must send out warnings to all the villages… and, gathering all of the residents, along with their children… [^48]

The retaliation available to him was small and he knew it. He went in person against Naamdar Khan and it went badly.[^49] A general broke a siege at Deiri and killed four hundred men. **The book's verdict is that these were patchwork measures and they were not going to make Shaista Khan go away**.

Pitched battle was out of the question. The numbers were grossly disproportionate, and the Khan could call in more men and arms from Gujarat and Rajasthan whenever he wanted.[^50] So Shivaji gave up Panhala to free his attention, and got a modest thaw with Bijapur out of it.

**And here the book takes a swing at how this story is normally told**. In the Maharashtrian historical imagination and the Marathi literature, what happens next was near inevitable, with Shivaji the sole driver taking events to a predestined conclusion.[^51] The truth was the reverse: Shaista Khan was on top of the situation and genuinely establishing himself as the premier prince of the Mughals.

The idea he came up with was to go and kill the man in his own bedroom. Not on a field, not from a battlement — **inside Lal Mahal**, in a house ring-fenced by an army.[^52]

Getting in was the problem, and Khafi Khan — whose father served in Shaista Khan's army — records the rule that made it one. No person, and especially no Maratha, was to enter the city or the army lines without a pass, armed or unarmed, unless in imperial service.[^53] **No Maratha horseman was taken into service at all**.

There are two accounts of how about a hundred men got past the gate and the book gives both. Sabhasad has two of Shivaji's favourites walking at the head with the men and the Raje behind them, Shivaji himself carrying a shield and a sword.[^54] Khafi Khan has a stranger and better story:

> A boy dressed up as a bridegroom, and escorted by a party of Mahrattas with drums and music, entered the city.

His men applied to the local police head for a pass to admit two hundred Marathas accompanying a marriage party, and got it.[^55] Inside, he was in a house he had grown up in. They found a corner near Lal Mahal to put on arms, and at midnight he took ten men in.[^56] **The cooks were already awake, making the meal taken before dawn, and were killed soundlessly**. Then to the harem — where there was a wall between the two parts of the house with a door in it that he knew about.

Shaista Khan did not reach his weapons. Sabhasad says Shivaji took three fingers off his right hand with a single stroke; Khafi Khan says the thumb.[^57] The Khan's son Abul Fath was killed. Two of his women were attacked in the confusion — Maratha records say the darkness made it impossible to see who anybody was, and Khafi Khan, describing it in detail, does not say it was inadvertent.

Then the Marathas ran about a house they knew, killing guards and **saying to them, this is how they keep guard**.[^58] Some got into the room where the kettledrums were kept and ordered the players to beat them in the name of the Amir-ul-Umara.

The escape is where legend takes over and the book marks it. The famous story — horns blown as a signal, torches lit on cattle in the Katraj pass to pull the pursuit the wrong way — comes from the Chitnis Chronicle, a late and not very reliable document.[^59] **Its hold is measurable: in Marathi, to lead someone up the Katraj pass means to trick them**. The reliable records simply say he took the direct route out of town and across the river.

The losses by daylight: Shaista Khan's son, six concubines and forty soldiers dead, two more sons and several women wounded. Six Marathas dead, forty wounded.[^60]

**And the man punished for it was not a Mughal**. Jaswant Singh, the Jodhpur royal and governor of Gujarat, had a few thousand men in and around the town and none of them stirred in the night.[^61] Shaista Khan himself was sent to Bengal by a displeased Aurangzeb, who had been advised that the Khan's continued presence in the Deccan against Shivaji could end in nothing but the loss of his army. The official Mughal chronicle handles the whole thing in three sentences. The brevity is the finding, in a record that is otherwise generous about the emperor's affairs:

> One of the occurrences in this period was the night attack of the infernal Shiva on the camp of the Amir-ul-umara, the cutting off of his forefinger during the encounter, and the slaughter of his son Abul Fath Khan. [^62]

Everyone else in India told it at length. An English official at Rajapur got the story from Shivaji's own governor and passed on the letter Shivaji had written him.[^63] Francois Bernier, a French doctor who had come east in 1656, wrote that some idea might be formed of Seva-gi's intrepidity by his attempt on Shaista Khan's person. Niccolao Manucci, a Venetian who had run away to India at eighteen, left the detail that mattered most:

> In this confusion Shaistah Khan's sufferings from his wound were increased from not being able to call in any surgeon. [^64]

The Portuguese biographer Cosme da Guarda, writing in Goa from what he heard around the Deccan, was convinced there had been a secret pact — that Shivaji had sent Jaswant Singh gold, silver and jewels, in the name of the gods, appealing to him as one Hindu to another.[^65] **The book will not endorse it and will not throw it away either**. There is no way of knowing whether such a letter was written. What the story does show is what people in the Deccan were saying to each other at the time.

Against that, an order of 18 December 1660, after Shaista Khan had occupied Pune: the grants made to Hindus and Muslims alike in those parts were to continue.[^66] He was fighting in the name of the gods and paying the stipends of both. The chapter ends with his taunt to the Mughal court. It is mostly a lesson in terrain, delivered to men who had spent three years learning it the hard way:

> It has lofty hill-ranges, 200 leagues in length and 40 leagues in breadth; everywhere there are nalas hard to cross; sixty forts of extreme strength have been built in this region… To maintain your prestige and save your reputation, you send false reports to the emperor. But I am blessed with Divine favour. An invader of the beloved country of this man, whoever he may be, has never succeeded. [^67]

*Read: lines 1212–1425*.

## Ch. 8 — Four days of a city burning

The afternoon of 5 January 1664 was ordinary at Surat until a hot alarme arrived that Shivaji was within ten or twelve miles.[^68] **Nobody had seen him coming**. There had been no sign of movement from the Deccan towards Gujarat, and he had left days earlier and rested in the meantime. The route was found by his spy-in-chief, Bahirji Naik, who had shown him the quietest way to the gates.[^69] Surat was worth taking and impossible to defend, which the English record plainly:

> The whole town is unforteified either by art or nature and its situation is upon a large plaine of many miles' extent … They have only made against the cheefe avenues of the town some weake and ill-built gates. [^70]

Two lakh people lived in it, in narrow ill-contrived lanes. He camped at Gandevi with eight thousand men and sent two envoys ahead with a letter, summoning the governor and the three richest men in the town to come to him in person and settle terms.[^71] And he told the English what this was about, in writing. He wanted them to know that the fires were aimed past them:

> he was not come to doe any personall hurt to the English or other merchants, but only to revenge himself on Orom Zeb (the Great Mogol) because he had invaded his country [and] had killd some of his relations. [^72]

The English president's own reading, in a letter home, was that Shivaji's designe was not altogether riches but revenge upon this King.[^73] The debt was three years of Shaista Khan.

He reached the city at about eleven the next morning and pitched his tent a quarter of a mile beyond the eastern gate while his soldiers went in.[^74] **The city burnt for four straight days**. The only resistance came from the English and the Dutch firing out of their factories, and he did not press it — he had no wish to spend ammunition or Maratha lives on a fight he was not there for.

The richest merchant in the world at the time, by contemporary reckoning, was a Gujarati Hindu called Virji Vora, with assets of eighty lakh rupees, and his property burnt.[^75] The Muslim merchant Haji Said Baig's house was plundered too. **Wealth was the criterion and not religion**, which the chapter shows by listing who lost what.

On the second day somebody tried to kill him. An emissary from the governor had come with terms that pleased Sevagee not at all, and in the confusion after the attempt his men began killing the prisoners.[^76] Shivaji got up off the ground and stopped it, and had the prisoners — more than a hundred — brought before him instead.

Then he ordered mutilation, and the number is recorded: **four heads and twenty-four hands**.[^77] One Englishman, Anthony Smith, was in that line and told in Hindustani that Shivaji had said to cut off his head. His hat was taken off and the execution was stopped.[^78] Sarkar concluded that Shivaji spared him on realising he was English. **The truth is he had known that all along** — Smith had agreed, more than once, to carry a message to the British camp.

The fires were worst on the Thursday and the Friday night, when the chaplain L'Escaliot recorded a blaze so great that it lit the whole place.[^79] And three European travellers all wrote down the same exception. Father Ambrose, a Capuchin priest, went to Shivaji on the day he arrived and his church and his people were spared.[^80] So was the house of a Hindu money-changer of the Dutch Company, Mohandas Parekh, **because Shivaji was told the man had been very charitable while alive**.

He left on the Sunday morning, 10 January, hearing that a Mughal army was coming down from the north.[^81] The traders stayed away from their own houses for a week afterwards, in case he came back. Nobody knew whether he had finished.

The take is put at between one and one and a half crore rupees.[^82] That is a treasury, taken in four days, out of a town nobody had thought to wall.

**What that operation was, stated plainly, is stripping an adversary of his economic power to make up losses on your own land** — and showing yourself able to hurt him where he had assumed he was safe.[^83]

The consequences arrived fast and they were administrative. Merchants and both companies petitioned Aurangzeb for exemptions given what the Mughal defence administration had failed to prevent.[^84] The governor Inayat Khan was sacked. **And Aurangzeb ordered a stone wall built round Surat**.

The English merchants had held their factory and were offered a soldier's reward for it, and refused it in a sentence that says what they were. A general offered Oxenden a horse, a sword and a vest; Oxenden replied that those were things becoming a soldier, but they were merchants and expected the Emperor's favour in their trade.[^85]

**What the raid did to his name is the last and largest thing in the chapter**, and the English put it best:

> Sevagy is so famously infamous for his notorious thefts that report hath made him an airy body, and added wings or else it were impossible he could bee at so many places as he is said to bee at, all at one time. [^86]

His father died that same month. Shahaji fell off his horse hunting in what is now Karnataka and died of his injuries on 23 January 1664.[^87] The Dutch factory at Vengurle recorded it as the passing of **the old preying bird Shahaji, father of the great rebel Shivaji**.

And a document found by Rajwade in the early twentieth century added a side of the father nobody had recorded. A poet called Jayram Pindye travelled from near Nasik to Bangalore **having heard of the fame of Shahaji and of the patronage he extended to learning** — which establishes his fluency in Sanskrit and the scholars he kept at his court.[^88]

Through 1664 and into 1665 the fleet became real. Sixty-five frigates, which the English dismissed as pitiful things and the Portuguese did not.[^89] Everyone expected Goa next; the British told their Karwar factory not to sleepe too secure, and the Portuguese made lists of how many armed men each town could raise.

**He bypassed Goa entirely**. In February 1665 he sailed past Karwar and Bhatkal with eighty-five frigates and three great ships, curved in, and hit Basrur, deep into the Kannada-speaking country where nobody had thought he would go.[^90] Then Gokarna, where he washed his body according to the ceremony of the place at the Mahabaleshwar temple.

His admirals are worth naming because of what they were. Darya Sarang, Daulat Khan and Mainak Bhandari — **two of the three Muslim, by Sabhasad's account**, and the third from the coast-dwelling Bhandari community.[^91] All three were his own appointments, in a service nobody around him had thought worth building.

*Read: lines 1426–1855*.

---

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, chapters 5–8 `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Paradigm-obvious**. Meeting an enemy general under a flag of truce with hidden troops in the woods is not an invention; both sides in these chapters plan for treachery and Shahaji's letter advises taking an oath first because there may be treachery. Sacking a rich enemy city for its cash is what every army in the century did. Writing a submission you do not mean, which he does to Jauhar exactly as he had to Aurangzeb, was standard Deccani correspondence.

**Paradigm-breaking, and each one cost him something**.

Paying the widows and the wounded after Pratapgad, on a published scale, and sending captured enemy soldiers home with money and food. That is expensive, and the going rate for prisoners in this book is ransom or execution.

Going into Lal Mahal himself. Every advisor around him would have said the same thing, and the chapter says his mother and his council were frightened. A ruler with sixty forts does not need to be the man in the room at midnight, and if he had died there the state died with him.

Stopping the killing at Surat after an attempt on his own life, then ordering mutilations instead. That is neither mercy nor policy in the ordinary sense — it is a man choosing, in the middle of his own rage, to convert a massacre into a punishment with a countable number attached.

## Ch. 5 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, argued at the time and by the enemy**. Afzal Khan wanted the meeting on the plains of Wai, where ten thousand horse would decide it. Shivaji wanted it under Pratapgad. That is the entire negotiation, conducted through two envoys over several letters, and the flattery was the instrument.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose he had gone down to Wai. The forecast is not that he loses a battle — it is that there is no battle, because on open ground with those numbers the meeting itself becomes the arrest Afzal Khan had promised the durbar. What the hills gave him was not cover for an ambush so much as **a place where the enemy's main advantage could not be brought to bear at all**, which is the same asset the Mavals and Jaawali gave him earlier and Umbarkhind gave him later. The letters were the cost of moving the venue, and flattery is cheap.

## Ch. 7 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the decision to lead the raid on Lal Mahal in person.

**A Stoic advisor**, working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|the dichotomy of control]], would object on the grounds the chapter itself supplies. A man in a bedroom at midnight has handed the outcome to a hundred things outside his power — a sleepless cook, a guard who is awake, a door that has been bricked up since he lived there. The plan required the interior layout of a house to be unchanged after three years of another man's occupation, and that was not his to know.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/shih-and-strategic-depth|shih]]** would answer that the raid is not an attack on a man but on a position. Shaista Khan's whole standing rested on being untouchable in the middle of an army; take three fingers off him and the position is gone whether he lives or dies. And it worked exactly that way — Aurangzeb moved him to Bengal, and the Mughal chronicle could only manage three sentences about it.

**They do not converge, and the split is the honest outcome**. One reads it as an unrepeatable gamble that happened to come off; the other reads it as a precise strike on the one thing an occupying general cannot afford to lose. **Both are right, which is why it is in the paradigm-breaking pile**: it cost him a risk nobody in his position would have been advised to take.

## Ch. 8 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: attacking an opponent's revenue instead of his army**.

Surat is the clean case. He could not beat Shaista Khan's numbers in the field and had spent three years watching his own villages burned. So he went four hundred kilometres to a city with no walls, took a crore and a half in four days, and left before the relief column arrived. The English president, an unfriendly witness, read the intent correctly: not altogether riches but revenge.

**Scope conditions**. This works where the target is undefended *because* it is commercial — a place whose wealth is the reason nobody thought to fortify it — and where the raider can leave before a field army arrives. It requires accurate intelligence about the route, which is why the chapter names the spy who found it. And it fails permanently the moment the opponent responds structurally rather than punitively: Aurangzeb sacked the governor, which changed nothing, **and ordered a stone wall, which did**.

**The second-order effect is the one worth keeping**. The raid's largest yield was not the money. It was that report hath made him an airy body, and added wings — a reputation for being in six places at once, which then did work for him in every subsequent negotiation. A commercial target produces witnesses who write letters, and the letters travel further than the army ever could.

**Modern equivalent:** hitting a competitor's revenue channel rather than its product. Same conditions, same limit — it works until they build the wall, and by then the reputational effect has already been banked.

---

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Shivaji-India's Great Warrior King.md`, lines 818–1855: ch. 5 (818–1025), ch. 6 (1026–1211), ch. 7 (1212–1425), ch. 8 (1426–1855).

**Where the accounts disagree, and the book keeps them apart**. The killing of Afzal Khan comes down through several versions that differ on who struck first and in what order; the report here reflects that. Shaista Khan lost three fingers by Sabhasad's account and a thumb by Khafi Khan's. Baji Prabhu's death has two endings, one plain and one heroic, and the plainer one is in the more reliable chronicle. How a hundred Marathas got through the gates of Pune has two explanations and neither is confirmed.

**What the book rejects outright, and on what grounds**. The Katraj pass torches are from a late and unreliable chronicle. The reading of the Rajapur arrests as early anti-colonial insight is called reading history backwards, and the narrower thing that *was* known — that the English wanted forts — is stated instead. Sarkar's explanation for sparing Anthony Smith is corrected from the English records themselves. Cosme da Guarda's secret pact between Shivaji and Jaswant Singh is neither endorsed nor discarded: it is treated as evidence of what people in the Deccan were saying, which is a different and smaller claim.

**Whose voices these are**. Parmanand and Sabhasad were his officials. Khafi Khan's father served in Shaista Khan's army. The English letters are commercial correspondence never meant to be read outside the Company, which is why they swing from "noble" to "perfidious" inside a year and why they are useful. Bernier, Manucci, Tavernier, Thevenot and da Guarda were foreigners collecting talk.

**Bounded absence**. No claim is made about material outside lines 818–1855.

# What the Deccan Took For Granted — Chapters 9–13

> **Chapters 9–13 of Vaibhav Purandare, *Shivaji: India's Great Warrior King*** — Jai Singh's methodical destruction of the Maratha country, the humiliation at Agra and the escape in a basket, three years of land reform, the coronation, and the last letter. ## Ch. 9 — The man who asked for full powers before he started

The third general Aurangzeb sent was a Hindu, and he was the one who nearly finished it. Mirza Raja Jai Singh of the Jaipur royal house had entered Mughal service as an orphan at eight and distinguished himself from Balkh and Kandahar to Bijapur.[^1] He brought 14,000 troops with him, and the men left over from Shaista Khan were still in Maratha country.

The first thing he did was ask the emperor for something the other two never asked for. He wanted full freedom of decision at every level — local appointments, payments, civil and military matters — without the Mughal bureaucracy in the way.[^2] He got it, and then he moved.

He was not satisfied with being ahead on numbers. He wanted crushing superiority, and to get it he used persuasion, force, bribery and threats as each occasion required.[^3] That meant working on everybody else first. He sent two Portuguese men in his employ to Goa asking for cooperation, and complained that some Portuguese had been actively involved with Shivaji.[^4] He set about sowing dissension in Bijapur — bribing Adil Shahi fort commanders, offering office and cavalry to Bijapur generals — so that the two could not combine against him.[^5]

Then he picked his camp with the same care. Not Pune, the obvious choice, but Saswad to the east, which put him between Shivaji's state and Bijapur at once.[^6] And in Saswad stood Purandar. What he told Aurangzeb about method is the technical heart of the chapter. All the Deccan territory was needed, but *we have primarily to attack the hill forts* — so send the big guns already in Mughal hands and the cannons recently cast.[^7] Then he wrote back with what the guns had proved:

> But our campaign has established one thing. It is indeed possible to carry the big guns half-way up the hill forts, to the very place the people of these regions called the machi. From that spot, a highly effective assault can be launched on the fort. [^8]

That single paragraph is the end of Shivaji's basic advantage. Until then the belief had been that cannon worked only against forts standing near the ground.

The rest of the campaign was designed to break a mind rather than a wall. Jai Singh explained his reasoning to the emperor: he wanted to show Shivaji that a siege at Purandar would not stop the Mughals doing everything else at the same time.[^9] So more than six thousand troops went out under Daud Khan and others with orders to **depopulate and reduce to ashes** the whole region around Rajgad and Sinhagad. Every village along the route to Rajgad was torched and the cultivation destroyed.

And the seduction ran alongside the burning. Jai Singh gloated that Shivaji's troops, collected over so long, were seduced by us — **passports and promises of safety, and then imperial service with proper ranks and stipends**.[^10]

The defence of Purandar produced the chapter's one clean refusal. Murar Baji Deshpande, the Maratha commander, was offered a *kaul*, an assurance of safety, by Diler Khan, with promotion attached: *you are an extremely intrepid soldier, I will promote you*.[^11] The reply:

> What is your kaul? Do I, a soldier of Shivaji Raje, take your kaul?

He raised his sword and stepped forward, and Diler Khan had his bow ready and shot him first. About three hundred Marathas died there.[^12] So Shivaji concluded that the best available option was to stop fighting.[^13] Afzal Khan had been hard, Shaista Khan twice as hard, and this was several times harder — and almost everything he had taken, except southern Konkan, was overrun.

What he negotiated matters more than what he gave up. One condition he insisted on, and got, was that **he would neither hold military rank in Mughal service nor be obliged to attend the emperor's court**.[^14] The whole subsequent chapter turns on that clause being broken.

He did not want to go to Agra and the book is clear about why. He had no trust in a man who had neutralised and murdered three of his own brothers to get the crown.[^15] Jai Singh promised everything — including religious promises, as one Hindu to another, that no one would so much as touch him.[^16]

Before leaving he arranged the government. His mother Jijabai would be regent, assisted by the prime minister.[^17] He left Rajgad on 5 March 1666 with his nine-year-old son, and with a promise in his pocket that had already been broken once on paper.

*Read: lines 1856–2239*.
