---

## Ch. 19 — The other life, which had its own hours

There was a second life running under the first one and everybody knew not to mention it. The black cars came out onto the streets of Moscow after midnight, and everything belonging to that life happened in the dark and was secret.[^1] If somebody was taken from a communal apartment, the neighbours knew what not to say in the morning.

The paperwork had been streamlined. Prosecutors signed blank forms on which NKVD investigators could enter any name they liked.[^2] When the prisons overfilled, troikas began operating in all major NKVD directorates from July 1937 — three men, and a case. What happened to the troikas is on record in an exchange between two men who had been there. At the 1957 Central Committee plenum, Khrushchev said every single member of those boards was shot; Kaganovich said not every one; Khrushchev said the great majority.[^3]


The chapter names the design: a self-service system of elimination, in which each victim killed his predecessor and was killed by his successor.[^4] Thousands of senior Party officials sat on the boards that condemned people, and were condemned in turn. And the anniversary was celebrated in the middle of it. In 1937 the Cheka turned twenty and the Boss made a national occasion of it. Poets sang of the people's love for the secret police. Meanwhile the secret police were dying like flies, many of them echoing Yagoda's line: *God does exist after all*.[^5]


There is a small operational detail that says how the work was organised. The Boss forbade Yezhov to touch Yagoda's prize executioners, for the time being, and had them sent to work elsewhere pending their own disappearance.[^6] One of the men who had shown particular zeal in destroying rightists was shot as a member of a conspiratorial organisation of rightists inside the NKVD, which the chapter notes as evidence that his sense of humour was intact. The founders went too. Peters, Latsis, the Latvian riflemen who had been Lenin's own bodyguard. And Krylenko, the first Bolshevik commander-in-chief and then the state prosecutor who had sent gentlefolk, SRs and Bolsheviks alike to their deaths.[^7]


**His replacement is the chapter's sharpest irony and it is factual**. Vyshinsky had called for Lenin's arrest in 1917 as a traitor and a German spy, and now stood accusing the victorious Bolshevik leaders of betraying Lenin and of spying — and this time the charges stuck.[^8]

He lived permanently frightened. Through the twenties the former Menshevik had lived under constant threat of expulsion from the Party and had wept in his office when his card was in danger.[^9] He knew that if he ever lost the Boss's favour his past would be produced, so he served like a devoted dog.

*Read: lines 5357–5604.*

---

## Ch. 20 — Slaves, and the men who were told to eat cake

The Terror had been aimed at the Party and then turned on everybody. Families of enemies of the people, their acquaintances, and the acquaintances of those acquaintances — endless chains of people.[^10] What that produced was an economy. A considerable proportion of the country's copper, gold, coal and timber in the thirties was produced by this secret unpaid workforce. Before any major project began, the NKVD received direct instructions about the labour it would supply.[^11] The chapter does not spare the detail of what it was like. In Kolyma, a region of marshland and permafrost in the north-east, a commandant called Garanin was let loose.[^12]


And the value placed on that labour is measurable, because it was defended in a meeting. On 25 August 1938, as the Terror ebbed, the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet discussed early release for prisoners — and the objection raised was about output.[^13]

The scientists were a deliberate case rather than an accident, and Molotov confirms it in old age. Asked why brilliant designers were arrested, he explains the arrangement: the Tupolevs were put behind bars and the Chekists were told to make sure they had the best possible conditions.[^14] Let them eat cake, but don't let them out. Let them work. The author says he had always taken that plan for a myth, and that the fundamentals of it emerge clearly from Molotov's own account.[^15]


The writers were handled in two movements, and the second one is the surprising half. The 1936 campaign opened with an abrupt attack on culture, and Party critics spent the year bombarding non-Party writers, so that people denounced an opera they had not heard.[^16] **Then in 1937 he called a halt and destroyed the accusers**. The Party administrators of the arts had done their job and left the artistic intelligentsia frightened. Now the former leaders of the proletarian writers' association went into the night one by one, the men who had persecuted everybody.[^17] Bulgakov's wife recorded each day's disappearances in her diary in raptures, listing who had got it in the neck.[^18]


And in the same rooms, in the same months, her husband was reading a novel aloud to friends. *The Master and Margarita*, published only after his death, in which the Devil visits Moscow and turns his diabolical power on people in authority who act illegally, and deals with the persecutors of a writer.[^19] The chapter's observation about that is the one to keep. Bulgakov, like every writer of note, was under continuous NKVD surveillance and surrounded by informers. So the omniscient Boss must have known about the strange novel, parts of which were being read aloud.[^20] The diary entry for 6 June 1937 is what a good day looked like from inside that flat. She rushes to wake Misha because of what is in *Pravda*. The manager of the Arts Theatre has been arrested. Misha afterwards imitates an actress wringing her hands.[^21]


*Read: lines 5605–5737.*

---

## Ch. 21 — Disposing of the man who did it

The stocktaking at the end of 1937 goes back twenty years. The Promised Land had seemed near in 1917, then unattainable, and now he had set foot in it.[^22]

His own account of what he had been doing is in a remark to a film director. Talking to Eisenstein about *Ivan the Terrible*, he said that one of Ivan's mistakes was that he did not finish off the five great feudal families.[^23] He would not repeat it. Meanwhile the NKVD had spent the whole period cultivating a myth: that Stalin knew nothing about Night Life, and that spies who had wormed into the NKVD were concealing the Terror from him.[^24] The intelligentsia believed it. The Party Archive holds remarks by people who did not — a People's Commissar on record saying it looks as if they are deliberately destroying the Party cadres, and betting his life that Joseph Vissarionovich does not know.


So the myth needed proof, and the proof was Yezhov.[^25] An NKVD department head put it on record that he had frequently reported and been ignored, and Yezhov was slow-marched to the grave — kept in his Party posts while his assistants were arrested one after another. At the Eighteenth Congress in March 1939 the kind Boss spoke candidly about serious mistakes by the NKVD, more than should have been expected, and the country rejoiced.[^26]


The Congress is also where he displayed what the Terror had produced. **Half a million new appointments to responsible posts in the state and the Party** — the educated generation that had grown up under him, now installed.[^27] The new Party broke records in homage: the genius of the modern era, the wisest man of the epoch, and an audience that stood.

Then the trappings started coming back. Cossack headmen appeared in a box at a GPU anniversary in the Bolshoi.[^28] New history textbooks explained that all the conquests of the Russian tsars had been progressive. An empire was rising on the grave of the old Party — an atheist empire, without a god, but with a Boss.

Lenin's widow died shortly before that Congress, which meant he needed to see none but pleasant faces at it.[^29] The declassified history of her illness is in the Party Archive, laid out without asserting more than it shows. An examination in January 1939. A reason to be afraid of the medicine. An admission to the Kremlin Clinic with a sudden attack of appendicitis, and a death. As with her brother-in-law's case, the doctors reported directly to the Boss, and he kept their final report in his personal archive.

*Read: lines 5738–5921.*

---

## Ch. 22 — The pact, and the version the chapter refuses

Foreign policy had been subordinate to domestic policy until 1938. Once the new country existed he could pursue the external aim — the Great Dream, which the chapter says was Lenin's Dream by a different name, world revolution, now pursued in secret rather than announced by defunct big mouths.[^30]

The archive shows preparation rather than reaction. The Red Army was rearming rapidly through the thirties, before Hitler came to power, and Tukhachevsky wrote to Stalin anxiously about it.[^31] While the Moscow Metro was being designed, aircraft dropped high-explosive bombs to test the depths. Hitler took Austria in March 1938 and it was as expected: Hitler really was drawing Europe into war, and Germany would bring the capitalist system down in ruins.[^32]


Then the manoeuvre, and the chapter calls it typical. He opened contact with Hitler while pressing negotiations with France and England — knowing in advance that the Western democracies would never trust him, and using the talks as leverage.[^33] The gambit worked. Fearing an alliance between Stalin and the West, Hitler responded, and the fulminations against the USSR disappeared from German front pages. The offer to Czechoslovakia is the same technique, and the chapter is explicit that it was safe. He offered to help the Czechs on condition that England and France did the same, which was courageous and cost nothing.[^34]


After Munich the reasoning is stated plainly. Hitler was insatiable and Czechoslovakia was only the beginning, and to go further he needed an alliance with the USSR — **so he would give Hitler that alliance, to make sure that further meant further away from the Soviet Union**.[^35]

And the ideological cost was nil, because there was no ideology in it. Hitler and the Western democracies were both enemies; alliance with either was a turn on the road to the Great Dream.[^36] What it did cost was the claim to be a champion of democracy, and the Comintern. The occupied territories then got the treatment the Soviet Union had already had. The NKVD purged the annexed areas of alien elements, and train after train carried fresh convicts.[^37]


The last movement of the chapter is the author refusing the standard story. The accepted version runs like this. Hitler decided to attack an unsuspecting ally. Churchill and Sorge and the Comintern agents who stayed in Germany all warned him, he believed none of them, and the invasion took him completely by surprise.[^38] The chapter says this beggars belief, and gives its reason as character rather than evidence. A man whose first rule was trust no one, whose whole strategy consisted in misleading the enemy, suddenly gullible with the archenemy. Believable of a different man. Not of this one, who had proved otherwise over sixty years.[^39]


*Read: lines 5922–6198.*

---

## Ch. 23 — A visitors' book against a legend

The Germans attacked on a Sunday, in a country that took its day of rest seriously, and the street lamps were still burning when his car reached the Kremlin.[^40] He was the first to arrive. The rest of the Politburo, woken by his secretary, filed in shortly afterwards. The persistent legend is that he was stunned and at his wits' end, incapable of action, and that he then left for the dacha and stayed there bewildered.[^41]


Two documents dismantle it and both are administrative. The visitors' book, in which the duty officer recorded every arrival and departure — Molotov, Beria, Timoshenko, Mekhlis, Zhukov, Malenkov, Mikoyan, Kaganovich, on 22 June.[^42] And the unpublished memoirs of Chadayev, who took brief notes at every Politburo and government meeting held in that office and whose name is not in the book because he was not a visitor.

What Chadayev records is a man functioning. Timoshenko reported that the attack must be considered an accomplished fact.[^43] Molotov went to his own office, saw the German ambassador, came back and said the German government had declared war. The Politburo were thrown into confusion. They had gone on hoping it was a provocation. **Stalin said calmly that the enemy would be beaten all along the line**, and then asked the military what they recommended.[^44] Zhukov proposed attacking along the whole front, and the order went out that the armies would fall on the enemy with all forces and destroy them where the frontier had been breached.


The author's own correction of Chadayev is worth having, because it is about how such rooms work. Chadayev thought the generals meant it. Set against that: Timoshenko and the Politburo were playing up to the Boss, because they dared not say anything different. He would never forgive them, and would harbour a grudge.[^45] The public broadcast was Molotov's, and he made it with difficulty, stammering slightly, ending on the sentence that would be drummed into the country for four years: the enemy will be smashed, victory will be ours.[^46] Afterwards Stalin told him the speech went well although he had sounded a bit flustered, and Molotov was happy — because he knew the Boss, and knew what looking for someone to blame would have meant.


Then his own son. Yakov was captured, and the propagandists invented a story about him which turned out to be true.[^47] Zhukov remembered asking whether there was any news of his fate, and the answer taking a hundred paces to arrive.

The interrogation record came into his hands only after Germany was defeated, and the chapter prints from it.[^48] Asked whether he came over voluntarily or was captured, Yakov describes a rout — everybody running, the panic, being picked up. Asked whether the Soviet government consists mainly of Jews, he calls it rubbish and stupid talk. Asked about his father's second wife being Jewish, he corrects it flatly: the first wife was Georgian, the second Russian, her name was Alliluyeva, and she died.

Then the questions that were meant to break him and did not. Asked about burning the food stocks when a place is abandoned, and whether that is right, he says frankly that he thinks so.[^49] Shown a captured Russian officer's letter hoping to get home in the autumn if there is no war, he reads it and says I'll be damned. And the last line of the interrogation is his own verdict on himself: I don't know how I could face my father. I'm ashamed to be alive.[^50] His father did not make the report public. His son was right. It was a disgrace that he was still alive, and Yakov had understood that when the decree on prisoners of war signed by his father reached him.[^51]


*Read: lines 6199–6614.*

---

## Interlude — A family in wartime

The daughter announces her own growing up in a letter, before the war. She is not going to write any more *orders*, because she is no longer a child to amuse herself that way.[^52] **She was fifteen when it began, and her father policed her clothes**. He was furious at bare knees and arms, and gave orders that her skirts be made longer.[^53] Evacuated to Kuibyshev, she pined for Moscow and wrote about what she saw there: so many lame people, blind people, cripples of all sorts — every fifth person in the streets a cripple.[^54]


He would not let her come home for good until the summer of 1942, when the Germans had been pushed back from Moscow.[^55] And she came back a different Svetlana, having made a discovery during the preceding winter which the chapter calls terrible and which she later wrote about herself. The dacha at Zubalovo was damaged in the war and rebuilt, and she moved in with her brother's wife and child and her half-brother's daughter and the daughter's nurse.[^56]


Her brother is the chapter's other subject and the treatment of him is unsentimental about both men. At twenty, having scraped through school, Vasily was sent where every Soviet youngster dreamed of going, the Air Force Training School.[^57] Stalin kept the letters about his progress, and kept his graduation certificate. An excellent pilot, enjoys flying, promoted to lieutenant. And he knew perfectly well what such scraps of paper were worth. The author asks the reader to try to imagine what it was like to be a dictator's son, fatherless and motherless in adolescence for all practical purposes, after his mother's suicide, the imprisonment of his relatives and the execution of family friends.[^58]


*Read: lines 6615–6684.*

---

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, chapters 19–23 `[SPECULATIVE]`

Paradigm-obvious. Purging the intelligence service after purging the people who built it — the connection is mechanical and anyone doing the first would do the second. Signing a pact with Hitler while negotiating with the West, which is ordinary great-power practice and which Britain and France were also doing in their own way. Blaming the excesses on the man who executed them, which every regime that has run a terror has done. Rearming through the 1930s, which everybody was doing. Paradigm-breaking, and the cost is legible.


Destroying his own foreign intelligence service in the years before a European war. He recalled competent agents from Spain, Turkey and elsewhere with offers of promotion and shot them, and the chapter notes that only a handful refused to come home. That is a capability deliberately destroyed at the moment of maximum need.

Publishing his own son's shame — or rather, refusing to. Yakov's interrogation record was suppressed, and the decree on prisoners of war which condemned him had his father's signature on it. The cost is borne entirely by the son, and it is the one decision in this part where the personal and the political are the same act.

Running the whole terror through boards whose members he then killed. The self-service system removes every witness, and it also removes every experienced administrator. The chapter documents both halves.

## Ch. 20 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: converting punishment into a factor of production.

The mechanism is documented at both ends of the scale. At the bottom, a considerable share of the country's copper, gold, coal and timber came from unpaid labour, and the NKVD received direct instructions about supply before any major project began. At the top, the aircraft designers were imprisoned and then given the best possible conditions, on Molotov's own account — **let them eat cake, but don't let them out**.

Scope conditions. This works where the accused are genuinely productive, where the accusation is elastic enough to reach whoever is needed, and where the accounting never has to compare the output against what free labour would have produced. It fails at the third condition every time somebody tries the comparison — and the chapter catches the system defending itself on exactly that ground in August 1938, when early release was discussed and the objection raised was about output rather than about guilt.

The uncomfortable general form. Once a punishment system produces something the state depends on, the state acquires an interest in the supply of the guilty. That interest is not a corruption of the system; it is a function of it, and it is why the discussion of releases turns into a discussion of production targets. Modern equivalent: any enforcement regime whose budget or output depends on the volume it processes. The incentive does not require anybody to be cynical; it operates through people making entirely reasonable arguments about capacity.


## Ch. 21 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

A live alternative, and the regime chose against it in public. At the Eighteenth Congress he could have said nothing about the NKVD. Instead he spoke candidly about serious mistakes — more than should have been expected — and the country rejoiced.

A constructed alternative. Suppose the Terror had simply stopped, with no admission and no scapegoat. The forecast is that the myth cultivated for two years — that Stalin did not know — collapses, because a terror that ends silently ends by somebody's decision, and there is only one somebody. The confession is what preserves the innocence. By naming errors and producing the man responsible for them, he converted two years of documented mass killing into an administrative failure that had now been corrected, and the archive shows people who did not believe it saying so privately and betting their lives on it.

Scope condition, and it is what makes this transferable rather than merely grim. A limited confession absorbs a much larger unspoken charge, but only where the confessor controls both the timing and the size of what is confessed, and where somebody else can be made to carry the remainder. Where either fails, the admission opens the question instead of closing it.

## Ch. 22 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the author's refusal to accept that the invasion surprised him, which is the largest interpretive claim in this part and rests on character rather than documents.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/shih-and-strategic-depth|shih]]** would find the standard version incoherent for the reason the chapter gives. A man whose entire method was misleading opponents, and who assumed everybody was lying to him, does not make an exception for the one opponent whose word was worth least. Something else was being prepared, and the warnings were not being disbelieved so much as absorbed into a plan the warnings did not fit.

A Stoic advisor, from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|the dichotomy of control]], would push back hard, and the pushback is the more useful half. Character is not evidence. The claim that a man was too clever to be deceived is unfalsifiable, and it is exactly the reasoning that produced the confessions in chapter 16 — where the conclusion came first and the memory was searched afterwards for meetings that would fit. A biographer who has spent three hundred pages showing how the regime manufactured coherence out of coincidence should be slowest to do the same. They do not converge, and the report keeps both. The chapter's own evidence for its position is the visitors' book and Chadayev, and both of those establish only that he functioned on the day, not what he had expected the day before.


---

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Stalin.md`, lines 5357–6684: ch. 19 (5357–5604), ch. 20 (5605–5737), ch. 21 (5738–5921), ch. 22 (5922–6198), ch. 23 (6199–6614), Interlude (6615–6684).

The strongest documentation in this part. The 1957 Central Committee plenum minutes, in which Khrushchev and Kaganovich disagree about how many of the troika members were shot. Stalin's visitors' book for 22 June 1941. Chadayev's unpublished memoirs, which the author read during perestroika. The Luftwaffe interrogation record of Yakov Dzhugashvili. The declassified history of Krupskaya's illness in the Party Archive. Molotov's own explanation, in the Chuyev conversations, of why designers were imprisoned.

The two claims that rest on inference rather than documents. That Krupskaya was helped to die — the author sets out what the medical file shows and stops short of asserting it, and this report does the same. And that Stalin was not surprised on 22 June, which the chapter argues from character, and which is marked above as the author's position and questioned below the line.

A note on the source's own position. This part contains the author's clearest statement of method: he says the standard account of June 1941 beggars belief, and gives as his ground what the man had proved over sixty years. That is reasoning of the same kind the book elsewhere warns about, and it is reported here at that weight. Bounded absence. No claim is made about material outside lines 5357–6684.

# What the Bolsheviks Took For Granted — Chapters 24–28 and the Afterword

> **Chapters 24–28 and the Afterword of Edvard Radzinsky, *Stalin*** — the second front and the partition of Europe, the deportations, the Druzhkov telegrams and the bomb, the return of fear, the cult and the doctors' plot, the night at the nearer dacha, and the portraits coming back out in 1995. ## Ch. 24 — Winning, and what winning was for

Churchill wrote the numbers on a scrap of paper during a night meeting in the Kremlin in October 1944. Romania 90 to Russia. Greece 90 to Britain. Yugoslavia 50/50. Then the foreign ministers haggled over the rest — Hungary, Bulgaria — and settled at 80/20. The American ambassador was told after the bargain was struck, and the whole thing was sealed with a handshake.[^1]

What kind of thing is a country, in a world where that conversation is possible? A quantity of influence, divisible into tenths. Nobody in the room thought the arithmetic was strange. And the percentages were fiction anyway, because he had no intention of accepting anything less than the whole of what his armies stood on.[^2]

Nations were real when they were useful and unreal when they were not. Late in 1943, with the war at its worst, the Politburo was convened for over an hour to discuss a film script.[^3] The Ukrainian director Dozchenko had written that whichever front they fought on, it was the Ukraine they were fighting for — a people forty million strong which had never found itself. Stalin read the line aloud to the room. Then he said there is no separate Ukraine. It does not exist.

Dozchenko sat there pale while the meeting ran on. He was driven out of the Kiev Film Studio afterwards. In his diary he wrote that he had been hacked to pieces and the remains distributed for desecration wherever an ugly mob could be gathered.[^4]

Nationalism leads to treason. That is the causal claim the whole spring of 1944 runs on, and Beria wrote it out in a note for the file. The Balkars had given a friendly welcome to the German occupation. As the Germans retreated, they organised Balkar detachments.[^5] **If a people had betrayed, they could not go on living in the Caucasus.**

The numbers were reported like freight. 37,103 Balkars loaded onto special trains for Kazakhstan and Kirghizia, no incidents requiring attention. 342,647 Chechens and Ingush by 25 February, risen to 478,479 four days later — 91,250 Ingush and 387,229 Chechens. 93,139 Kalmyks, without excesses. From the Crimea, 225,009 persons, and the NKVD applied for medals for the 23,000 officers and men who took part.[^6]

A bank manager called Ruslan G. described what the reports called an organised fashion. It was cold and the floor of the hut was coated with hoarfrost. The soldier who came in did not want to bend down, so he raked the hut with his tommy gun. Blood came out from under the bench where a child was hiding. The mother screamed and threw herself at him and he shot her too. There was not enough rolling stock, so those left behind were shot and covered over with sand, carelessly. The shooting had been careless too, and people started coming up out of the sand. The NKVD men spent the whole night shooting them again.[^7]

Time in this chapter is long and the moves are set years before they are used. In 1944 the Jewish Antifascist Committee wrote to Stalin proposing a Jewish republic in the Crimea, on the land the Tartars had just been cleared off. The letter was written by Lozovsky, who would never have risked it without agreement from above, and one of the people behind it was Molotov's wife.[^8] It would have won American money and diverted attention from the deportations. It was also the charge that killed the committee eight years later.

The men who wrote it did not know what they had walked into. **The long game was always his preference.**[^9]

Knowledge here is something a commission produces. More than twenty thousand Polish officers had been shot in 1940; when the Germans found the graves at Katyn, a special Soviet commission was set up with his own writers, academics and clergy on it, and it confirmed his version.[^10] Roosevelt and Churchill had to take their ally's word for it. The real figure came out at a press conference in Smolensk in April 1995: 21,857 Polish prisoners killed across the camps.[^11]

There is a second document, and it is about the record rather than the killing. Shelepin, then head of the KGB, wrote to Khrushchev in 1959 asking permission to destroy the files on the men who had been shot, on the ground that they had neither operational nor historical importance. Permission was given.[^12] A dacha belonging to a rich businessman now stands on the site of the grave.

What is a person? Somebody who can be infected. Anyone who had been in contact with foreigners was carrying an incurable disease and had to be kept away from healthy people.[^13] That covered prisoners of war, who had disobeyed the order to die on the battlefield and dared to survive; Zhukov told a Central Committee meeting in 1957 that 126,000 officers came back from captivity, were stripped of rank, and went to the camps.[^14] It also covered civilians the Germans had deported for labour, who had done nothing at all.

At Yalta he had signed an agreement with Roosevelt and Churchill that every Soviet citizen taken prisoner or interned must be returned. The Allies carried it out. A British sergeant escorting one convoy described a woman at Graz throwing her child off a viaduct into the river and then jumping after it.[^15] Old White officers who had fled the Civil War twenty-five years earlier were hunted out of Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, Romania and Hungary. Generals Krasnov, seventy-eight, and Shkuro, sixty, were tried, condemned and hanged.[^16]

What is worth having? Good next-door neighbours. That is the whole of the Polish policy, stated plainly: he had won the war in order to have them, and he would let the Allies surrender Poland by easy stages because Roosevelt had a Polish vote to think about.[^17] In August 1944 his armies stopped in sight of Warsaw and stood watching while the Germans destroyed the city and the rising organised by the exile government.[^18] The church got the same treatment as everything else: a body to supervise it, and an NKVD colonel named Karpov running that body while also running the department whose job was to fight the clergy. In the council he assisted the church, in the NKVD he fought it.[^19]

At the Kremlin banquet for de Gaulle he raised a toast to Kaganovich, a brave man, who knows that if the trains do not arrive on time — a pause — we shall shoot him. Then one to Air Marshal Novikov, and if he doesn't do his job properly, with a kindly smile, we shall hang him. People call me a monster, he said, laughing, but as you see I make a joke of it.[^20] The French stopped finding him funny on the spot. On the train de Gaulle said that these were the people they would be dealing with for the next hundred years.

One of the French party wrote down something else from that evening. There was a look about him like the despair of a man who has reached such heights of power that he has nowhere else to go. And he had remarked, to de Gaulle, that in the long run death is the only victor.[^21] It was December 1944. He was about to turn sixty-five.

## Ch. 25 — A man signing himself Friendly

Western diplomats spent 1945 being impressed by Molotov. They found him unreadable — slow, immovable, refusing to say yes or no to the simplest question. They took it for a kind of genius.[^22]

The archive explains it. All that year Molotov was receiving detailed telegrams from Moscow signed "Druzhkov," a name suggesting friendliness. Every diplomatic move was dictated in advance. There was no Soviet Metternich. There was a man who dared not decide anything on his own, and whose famous leisureliness was the time it took to get an answer back.[^23]

The fine-tuning went all the way down. After a relaxed dinner at Attlee's residence, Bevin suggested exchanging football teams and sending an opera and ballet company to London. Molotov cabled home: it would be good if I could give them more definite answers on both of these matters.[^24] The Foreign Minister of the Soviet Union could not say yes to a ballet tour.

What makes something happen, in this world? Occupation, and dead men. When Truman began asking for concessions he was met with a flat nyet — nyet because the armies were already standing in Eastern Europe, and nyet because that word had been bought with the lives of millions of Soviet soldiers.[^25] The price paid is the title deed. Molotov went on repeating it until Bierut was installed in Poland.

Molotov took a while to grasp what was wanted. He kept reporting Western proposals and mentioning possible compromises, and the answers got louder. On 27 September: they are putting pressure on you to break your will, so be absolutely inflexible; the conference may end in complete failure, and even if it does we need shed no tears.[^26] Better to let it collapse than concede, and now we can tear off the veil of amity. Then Molotov understood, and became icily arrogant overnight. His life depended on guessing what was wanted before it was said.[^27]

The bomb is where the chapter's picture of reality is clearest. At Potsdam, Truman was told the baby had been born and went over to stun Stalin with the news. Stalin barely reacted, and Truman concluded the old man had not understood.[^28] He had been reading reports on the baby's progress for two years.

The route in was a physicist in Britain named Klaus Fuchs, a German Communist émigré, who learned the work was being kept from the USSR and walked into the Soviet embassy in London.[^29] Until then nobody in the leadership had cared. Zeldovich and Khariton had worked out the conditions for a nuclear explosion and estimated its force before the war, and Stalin was not even told.[^30] Tanks and aircraft were what a war was made of. Laboratory needles were not.

The job went to Beria, and the reasons are a small map of how the state thought. His department had spies who could get the information. It had unlimited resources. It had brilliant scientists already locked up in the *sharashki*, the prisons that were also research institutes. And its secrecy was total.[^31] Recruiting foreigners ran on a formula he authorised himself, and it was aimed at people whose friends he had shot: **Stalins come and go, but the first socialist state in the world remains.**[^32]

A retired intelligence general named Sitnikov gave the other half of the doctrine, quoting Beria quoting Stalin. No public figure in the bourgeois world is incorruptible. You only have to know what kind of bribe. For most of them it is money, and if one resists you have been too miserly. Where money will not do it, a woman may. And where a woman will not, Marx will.[^33] Then Sitnikov added the part that matters: the best people worked for us for idealistic reasons.

Time here is a race with a fixed finish. Beria passed the message on: the bomb must be made in a very short time whatever the cost, with the camps promised in the event of failure.[^34] Kurchatov had ideas of his own and dropped them. He copied the American design instead, because that one was known to work and there was no time to be original.[^35] It was tested on 29 August 1949. Afterwards Stalin told his scientists that if they had been a year and a half late it would probably have been tried out on them.

What was all this for? Molotov saw the answer pinned to a wall. After the war a map of the new borders was brought out to the dacha, and Stalin fixed it up with drawing pins and read it aloud. Finland's frontier moved back from Leningrad. The Baltic states back. Belorussians, Ukrainians, Moldavians, all ours. The Kuriles, Sakhalin, and look, isn't it great, Port Arthur is also ours. He ran the stem of his pipe over China.[^36]

Then he pointed south of the Caucasus and said he did not like that frontier at all. The Dardanelles. Claims on Turkish territory, and on Libya.[^37]

Molotov went cold. He was hearing a proposal to partition the world again, and he had lived through what came before the last one. In 1937 the Terror had been the preparation for the war they had just finished fighting. His fear was not for mankind. It was that another bloodletting was scheduled, and he would be in it.[^38]

## Ch. 26 — Fear as an input, and where it gets manufactured

He needed an open quarrel with the West, and Churchill supplied it at Fulton. Both Truman and Attlee thought the speech had gone too far. It was too late — the threat could now be announced, the democratic pretence in Eastern Europe dropped, and the screws turned at home.[^39]

Enemies are not a problem to be solved here. **They are a supply.** Tito is the clearest case. He had annexed Albania without asking, signed a pact with Dimitrov without reporting it, and floated a confederation reaching toward Poland, Czechoslovakia and Greece.[^40] At the Kremlin in February 1948 Stalin shouted at Dimitrov that he was kicking up his heels like some young Komsomol. When a Yugoslav said there were no disagreements, the answer was that there were disagreements and very profound ones, and that they did not just make mistakes, they did it on principle.

They all agreed to consult in future. The decision had already been made. Tito would be more useful as an enemy — the way Trotsky had been — because a named heretic lets you punish everybody who ever stood near him.[^41] One bad sheep can spoil the flock. Yugoslavia was expelled and the rest of the camp closed ranks.

How do you know what people think? You listen. From 1943 Abakumov was ordered to monitor the telephones of marshals and generals, and the transcripts are in the KGB archive.[^42] On 28 December 1946, Colonel General Gordov and his chief of staff Rybalchenko discussed how everything now depended on bribery and bootlicking, and how people said so openly on the trains and in the Metro. Three days later Gordov told his wife he could not bear to look at Stalin, could not breathe the same air, and that it was like the Inquisition. She said she felt sure he would not last more than a year.

Gordov, his wife and Rybalchenko were arrested in January 1947 and shot.[^43] But one line stayed with the listener: you think I'm the only one, but I'm not, not by a long shot.

The bugging went both ways and everybody knew it. At a Central Committee meeting in 1957, Malenkov tried to excuse himself by saying his own conversations had been listened to as well, it was the general practice. Khrushchev objected that Malenkov had not been bugged — they had lived in the same building, Malenkov on the fourth floor, himself on the fifth, and the device was under his own flat. Malenkov replied that he and Budenny were overheard through his apartment, and reminded Khrushchev that when they were planning to arrest Beria they had been afraid to talk in there.[^44] Fifty-eight volumes of eavesdropping on Budenny, Timoshenko, Zhukov and Voroshilov came out of Malenkov's private safe.

Getting Zhukov required bait. In April 1946 Air Marshal Novikov was taken from outside his house, driven somewhere, stripped of his uniform and given a ragged shirt and trousers.[^45] The aircraft industry chiefs went the same night. Soon they were confessing to approving defective aircraft in which fliers had died, and, more to the point, testifying against Zhukov.

Then the charge shifted from words to property. General Kryukov and his wife, the singer Lidia Ruslanova, were arrested in September 1948. He had brought back from Germany antique carpets, tapestries, dinner services, furniture, furs and pictures, on four looted lorries. He had sent Zhukov cloth, carpets and crockery, as he had to several other generals.[^46]

In the first flush of victory that sort of thing had been encouraged, with an eye to the future. The future had arrived. The interrogator's line of attack is worth having in front of you: in the end you sank so low that you turned into a looter and a robber — can we say that Zhukov, who accepted presents knowing their origin, was just as much of a looter?

Ruslanova had given Zhukov's wife a diamond brooch at his dacha the day after the victory parade, with a toast to faithful wives and the remark that it never occurred to the government to give medals to valiant wives.[^47] The investigator's real complaint was different. They had toadied to him. Kryukov had started calling him Georgi, Bringer of Victory, which is what the Orthodox Church calls St George.

The intelligentsia came next, because they had come back from the war with private thoughts.[^48] Eisenstein's *Ivan the Terrible, Part II* was watched at the dacha; the Minister of Cinematography came back with one eye half closed and red spots on his face and could not speak for the rest of the day. The film was a nightmare, and the parting words were that they had never quite got around to him during the war, but now he would get the full treatment.[^49]

Zhdanov was sent to Leningrad to call Akhmatova a whore and vilify Zoshchenko. He asked the hall why they were still free to stroll through the parks and gardens of a city sacred to Lenin.[^50] Then nothing happened to either of them. Showing mercy while preparing a bloodletting was ordinary practice, and the story put about afterwards — that Stalin had personally ordered Akhmatova be left alone, because the poet Soso had once liked her verses — came from his own secret police.

Prokofiev and Shostakovich were condemned by edict in February 1947. Prokofiev wrote a penitential letter and it was read out to a meeting of Moscow composers, who warmly welcomed the decision.[^51] He locked himself in his study at the dacha and burned his set of Nabokov and his run of the magazine *America*.

Then the warning arrived in person. His two sons came out to the dacha at the end of February to tell him their mother had been arrested — Lina, his Italian first wife, a singer.[^52] His son Svyatoslav said that afterwards his father had exhausting headaches and always looked sad and hopeless. Lina hauled slop buckets on a handcart in the camp. A writer who was there remembered her sometimes stopping, standing beside the buckets, and telling them about Paris.

Shostakovich took a different route and wrote scores for *The Fall of Berlin* and *Unforgettable 1919*. After Stalin was dead he was still writing that in his creative work he had always been guided by the Party's inspiring instructions.[^53] Both men had been frightened once and for all.

What is a person here? Somebody who can be taken away from the middle of an ordinary life, for no stated reason, and never explained. Peter Shirshov was a Commissar, an academician, a polar explorer, married to a thirty-year-old actress called Zhenya Garkusha. She was arrested in 1946 and he was not told why.[^54]

His diary is in the chapter at length. He describes the last ordinary Sunday — the balcony, the plan for another child, the talk of the South, her saying as they went in that she was happy with him. Then the morning of telephones and telegrams, and at seven in the evening being sent for and told. They had been waiting for her on the riverbank. She was laughing when she got into the car, with nothing over her light summer frock.

Then three months of coming home quietly in case the miracle had happened. The telephone ringing and his heart missing a beat. And the sentence he writes for his daughter to read one day: I hope you'll never know how hard it can be to wrench your hand away from a pistol that has gotten hot in your coat pocket.

Zhenya Garkusha was sent to pan for gold, work so dangerous that women were not normally made to do it. She died in the camp at thirty-three.[^55] Shirshov stayed at his desk and held his tongue, as any good Communist should, and died of cancer in 1953. He never found out why she had been arrested.

The Alliluyevs were pulled in for the same purpose — so that everyone would learn what was happening and be afraid.[^56] Kira Alliluyeva remembered the ring at the door in December 1947, two men asking for her mother, and her mother walking down the corridor saying loudly that prison and poverty can't be kept waiting. She kissed her daughter on the cheek and left. She had meant to throw herself down the stairwell from the eighth floor so they could not torture her, and they grabbed her before she got there. A month later they came for the daughter, with instructions to bring warm clothes and twenty-five roubles just in case. When Svetlana asked why, the answer was short and honest: they knew too much and chattered too much, and that helps our enemies.[^57]

Then the henchmen. The chapter is blunt about what they were — handpicked nonentities, chosen because they could not be dangerous, organised into rival groups and set on each other.[^58] Beria's cunning consisted of guessing what was wanted and manufacturing the conspiracies to match. Every report from the capital went up: the discussion of a play at the Maly Theatre, a foreign delegation's visit to a building. When Khrushchev proposed amalgamating collective farms on his own initiative in 1951, he had to write a schoolboy apology asking for help in correcting his gross mistake.

**Two of them were not nonentities, and that is why they died first**. Voznesensky was an able economist and Stalin's deputy in the Council of Ministers. Kuznetsov had charm, honesty and a Leningrad record, like Kirov before him, and had been given supervision of Beria's two ministries.[^59] They were capable of independent decisions, which the war had needed and the peace did not.

The pretext was a trade fair. Leningrad hosted an all-Russian fair in January 1949 without telling the Central Committee, and Kuznetsov was charged with a demagogic bid for popularity and an attempt to alienate the city from the centre.[^60] Party officials across the country read the nonsense and understood the message underneath it. Get ready.

Voznesensky was dismissed in March and sat at his dacha writing a book about the political economy of communism and waiting. Then he was summoned to the nearer dacha, embraced, sat down among his old Politburo friends, and toasted by Stalin himself. He went home happy and was arrested at once.[^61]

Two thousand Party officials were arrested in Leningrad. After sentence was passed, secret policemen wrapped the condemned men in white shrouds and carried them like sacks across the courtroom to the exit. They were shot in one batch an hour later.[^62]

The Jewish thread runs alongside all of this and eventually joins it. Mikhoels, the great Yiddish actor and head of the Antifascist Committee, had become too famous.[^63] What happened is in a letter Beria wrote to the Presidium in 1953, quoting Abakumov's interrogation: instructions to liquidate him urgently, an invitation to a night gathering, a car to his hotel, a dacha outside Minsk belonging to the local security minister, then the body laid on a back street on the road to the hotel and run over with a truck. Medals were awarded afterwards. The agent who delivered him to the party, Golubov, was liquidated as well, for secrecy. Mikhoels himself was buried with full honours.

Then the committee was left alone for a while, because Israel was being founded and might be useful — a Soviet outpost in the Near East, against Britain and ahead of the Americans.[^64] Gromyko had announced Soviet support at the UN in May 1947.

Golda Meir arrived as ambassador on 3 September 1948, the day Zhdanov was buried, and was struck by the millions who turned out to mourn him. She did not yet know that grief in that country was organised.[^65] Ehrenburg was commissioned to explain in print that antisemitism did not exist in the USSR, that there was no Jewish people there, only a Soviet people, and that Israel was for the Jews of capitalist countries.

Soviet Jews read it as good news rather than as a warning. Fifty thousand people gathered outside the synagogue Meir attended at the New Year, soldiers and officers and old people and children held up to see her. She wrote that an ocean of love overwhelmed her and she nearly fainted. What she said to them was: thank you for still being Jews.[^66] It was a dangerous thing to say there.

At a Foreign Ministry reception, Molotov's wife came up to Meir and spoke to her in Yiddish. Meir asked in surprise whether she was Jewish. Polina answered, in Yiddish, that she was a daughter of the Jewish people.[^67] That sentence was in the file within months.

The campaign against "homeless cosmopolitans" opened in early 1949 and went strange fast. Historians revealed that the steam engine was Polzunov's, not Watt's; the lightbulb Yablochkov's; the radio Popov's, not Marconi's; the first flight Mozhaisky's, not the Wright brothers'.[^68] Whatever later Russians had not invented, Lomonosov had already discovered in the eighteenth century. The great majority of those unmasked as cosmopolitans were Jews.

Lozovsky was summoned and abused. The charges were that Meir's reception had shown thousands of Jews to be potential spies with their hearts in a hostile state, and that the committee had planned an American-backed outpost in the Crimea.[^69] He was old enough to know that mentioning who had actually authorised that scheme would mean a slow death. He confessed and hoped. The committee members were arrested, and shot in the summer of 1952 — all but the academician Lina Stern.

Polina Zhemchuzina was the point of the whole thing. When the Politburo heard the material on her, Molotov's knees were knocking. Stalin told him he would have to divorce his wife; she said that if that was what the Party needed she would get a divorce.[^70] They parted at the end of 1948 and she was arrested in 1949.

Then comes the note, and it is the whole of what this chapter thinks worth having, in one page. When the Central Committee voted to expel his innocent wife from the Party, Molotov abstained. Shortly afterwards he wrote to Stalin acknowledging that abstaining had been politically incorrect, voting in favour after thinking it over, and adding that he had been gravely at fault in not restraining a person near to him from dealings with anti-Soviet nationalists.[^71] **Betraying his wife was the price of liberty, and he paid it in the proper form.**

Under interrogation she denied everything, including ever having been to the synagogue. A witness named Slutsky, who sat on the board of twenty running the Moscow synagogue, testified that she had been there on 14 March 1945 — that the rule was men below and women in the gallery, and that they had made an exception and given her an honourable place in the hall.[^72] She said it was untrue. She may have been telling the interrogator the only thing she was permitted to say: going to the synagogue had been a Party assignment, her husband knew, and so the Boss knew, and none of that could be spoken.

She was exiled to Kustanai and filed under a name: Object Number 12.[^73] Informers reported her conversations. She said nothing treasonable, and after his death both Molotovs went on praising him for the rest of their lives.

A prison was going up on Matrosskaya Tishina Street for forty or fifty people, the elite of the ruling group, with interrogators on a direct line to Stalin.[^74] Documents later found in Malenkov's papers included the questions to be put to certain future prisoners, together with the answers they would give. The prisoners were still at liberty. Their statements were already on file.

## Ch. 27 — A god with a pruning shears

Two films tell you what the state thought a person could be. *The Vow* was built on an instruction Beria passed to the director: Lenin is John the Baptist and Stalin is the Messiah.[^75] *The Fall of Berlin* finished the job. He arrives in conquered Berlin not by train but by plane, in a dazzling white uniform, and reveals himself to the waiting peoples, who glorify him each in their own tongue.

The titles kept escalating — Leader and Teacher, Coryphaeus of Science and Technology, Greatest Genius of All Times and All Nations. One of them was the Sun of Our Planet. Dozchenko coined it. He had learned his lesson.[^76]

None of this was vanity, and the chapter is firm about that. The Great Dream was close, the last war was coming, and the image of a god was what would lead the peoples into it.[^77] That is what the cult was for. A woman's diary from the period gives what it felt like from underneath: Stalin here, Stalin there, you can't go out to the kitchen or sit on the toilet or eat without Stalin following you, he creeps into your guts and your soul, gets into bed with you under the blanket, haunts your memories and your dreams.

How does anybody know anything, when one man is the arbiter? Konstantin Simonov watched the method at a Stalin Prize committee meeting. Stalin walked about behind their backs so they could not see his face. The novel *Stepan Razin* by S. Zlobin came up, and Malenkov said Zlobin had been in a German camp and behaved badly.[^78]

Silence. Then a quiet question: should we forgive him, or shouldn't we? Nobody answered. He circled the table sucking his pipe and asked again. Silence again — the accusation was a capital one. A third circuit, a third asking, and then he answered himself. He is forgiven.

Zlobin became a laureate instead of a prisoner. That was the teaching: he alone could pardon any crime, and the lesson was in the two minutes of terror before the verdict, not in the verdict.

The seniority system had a physical form. When he destroyed a man he gave the dacha to the next in line — Beria had Chubar's, Molotov had Yagoda's, Vyshinsky had Serebryakov's.[^79] They would all be handing theirs on soon enough.

And there was a list. After his death an archivist sorting the library found the stenographic record of the 1939 Congress, in which he had gone down the names elected to the Central Committee and put a cross against everyone who had since ceased to live at his wish.[^80] Among the survivors he had distributed question marks.

What was he, at the end of it? The chapter shows the answer at night. The banquets ran till four, self-service so no servant could overhear, every dish certified free of poison and the air tested periodically by a doctor.[^81] Portraits of the Politburo hung on the wall and he liked each man to sit under his own. Voznesensky's and Kuznetsov's had been taken down. Molotov was no longer invited and turned up anyway, dejected, like a faithful dog, and was openly called an American spy to his face.

They told dirty jokes and played practical jokes. A tomato on a chair as a man stood to propose a toast, salt in a neighbour's wine, somebody pushed into the shallow pond.[^82] Being laughed at meant he was not angry, so they were happy. He sucked his pipe and watched the humiliation of the living dead.

Then they went home and his own night went on. He liked cutting flowers in the dark with pruning shears, by lamplight, and the guards picked up the severed heads.[^83] His hands trembled and he often cut himself. When a paramedic came to dress the cut, the paramedic's hands trembled too, and he would laugh and bandage the finger himself.

He slept a little towards morning, sometimes on a trestle bed under the stairs with his cap over his face to keep the sun off. He lived in one room of a house with many rooms, ate at his desk in a cleared space among the papers, and kept a lamp burning under a portrait of Lenin day and night.[^84] The guards were his best friends now, and he told them stories about his years in exile, exaggerating as old men do. One of them told the writer, forty years later, that he was lonely and showed his age and that he had felt sorry for him.

Svetlana's letters are the family record and they are short. She wrote in October 1952 asking to spend two days of the November holiday with him, saying she had no business and no problems to discuss, she just wanted to see him.[^85] In February 1953 she wrote that she and Zhdanov's son had decided to part for good.

On her rare visits she found pictures cut out of magazines pinned to the walls. A little girl giving milk to an elk calf. A boy on skis. Children under a cherry tree. They were substitutes for grandchildren.[^86]

Vasily was the other half of it, and his file is a study in what a hereditary prince becomes in a state with no hereditary principle. He commanded the air arm of the Moscow Military District at twenty-seven. A marshal said afterwards that the story of him leading the Tushino displays was a myth — he sat in the right-hand seat while the flight commander flew the plane.[^87]

His adjutant testified that he drank almost every day, missed work for weeks, and had so many affairs that if asked the number he would not know what to say. He built a 135-acre hunting reserve with air force funds, three villas linked by a narrow-gauge railway, and stocked it with fifty spotted deer.[^88] His chauffeur said traffic regulations did not exist for him and that he would push the accelerator down from the passenger seat, often into oncoming traffic.

He wanted to be like his father, and the worst page in the chapter is where he tries. He summoned an officer one night before the November holiday to help interrogate a terrorist. He had a subordinate take off his shoes and kneel on a chair so he could try out a thin rod on the soles of his feet first. Then the prisoner was brought in and felled with a blow. The rod broke after the first stroke. They kicked him whenever he fell down. Then they all started drinking.[^89]

Eleven men died because of one telephone call. The air force hockey team's plane could not land at Chelyabinsk in a blizzard and put down at Kazan; the players got restless and rang Moscow; Vasily ordered the pilot to continue.[^90] The plane crashed on approach and the entire team was killed. His father ordered that the disaster be given no publicity. Disasters did not happen in that country, and the public knew only that the best hockey players had disappeared.

The football story is lighter and shows the same machinery. Spartak's trainer Nikolai Starostin was serving a sentence somewhere in the Far East when a voice came over the camp commandant's government line saying hello Nikolai, this is Vasily Stalin.[^91] A plane collected him. He was home with his wife and daughter, weeping for joy, in the eight square yards left of their flat — and then two uniformed men arrived to say he had come illegally and must go back within twenty-four hours, because Beria was a Dynamo man.

So Vasily kept him in the house. They went everywhere together and slept in the same extra-wide bed, and Vasily went to bed with a revolver under his pillow.[^92] Starostin climbed out of a window one night to see his family and was on a train out of Moscow by morning, until Vasily's counter-espionage chief caught up with him by plane. In the end the father had to intervene. Order had to prevail. Starostin went back.

Meanwhile the machinery was warming up. A group of doctors at the Stalin Automobile Works was arrested with some executives and a woman journalist. The names were Finkelstein, Smorodinsky, Eisenstadt, Lifshits.[^93] They were all shot in November 1950 and the case attracted no publicity at all. It was practice for the interrogators.

The reasoning behind what came next is stated coldly. With his mind on the Great Dream, he knew there were two emotions that could unite a society: fear, and hatred of the Jews.[^94] The anti-cosmopolitan campaign had been the pilot study and the results had exceeded expectations. As a Russian writer put it, antisemitism makes your vodka stronger and your bread more appetising. The most downtrodden Russian would be given one thing to be proud of — that he was not a Jew.

The story he composed ran like this. A Jewish organisation called Joint was out to destroy the Russian people, probably since Trotsky's day. Its agents had infiltrated everywhere and were poisoning the country's ideology. Doctors were killing statesmen. Zionists had reached the top of the political elite, and that was where Zhemchuzina came in — the channel through which Molotov had been recruited.[^95] From there he could write in group after group.

He extended it abroad. In Czechoslovakia, Slánský and several senior officials were tried together, with one thing in common, and Slánský was shot as an agent of international Zionism.[^96]

The interrogator who was insufficiently ruthless got removed for it. Abakumov had been slow collecting evidence against Beria — he was frightened — and was arrested, and the decree said that Chekists had lost their vigilance and were working in white gloves.[^97] His staff wandered the corridors stunned, poring over the edict. Then everyone understood that this was 1937 again. By then a group of eminent Jewish doctors had been arrested — Kogan, Feldman, Ettinger, Vovsi, Grinstein, Ginzburg. The story required the plot to be against himself, so he added his own doctor, Professor Vinogradov, to the list.[^98]

Vlasik went too, and his 1955 trial is the clearest picture in the book of what these men actually were. He had run the bodyguard for years and then the body that appointed the bodyguards of everyone else, which in practice meant planting informers on them.[^99] His mistake was human: an agent planted on Beria reported Beria's debauchery, and Vlasik not only failed to pass it up, he rebuked the man for submitting it.

The trial transcript is short questions and short answers. How did you and Stenberg become friends — we obviously became friends because of drinking together and because of the women we knew. You revealed the names of Ministry agents to him — admitted. Where my duties were concerned I was always in order; meetings with women were on account of my health and in my spare time; I admit that I had a lot of women.[^100]

Then the money. How could you permit the enormous overexpenditure of state funds by your department? **My literacy is very poor, my whole education consists of three classes in a parish school.** And the captured property: an upright piano, a grand piano, three or four carpets. What about the fourteen cameras, and the cut glass and the porcelain in such quantities.

They had promised in their anthem to build a world of their own, to build the world anew. They had built it, and the Vlasiks and Yezhovs and Vasya Stalins were what it produced.[^101]

Arresting Vlasik cost him. For the first time in his life he had been in too much of a hurry, and he had thrown away an experienced watchdog with nobody to replace it.[^102] Beria, whose interrogation of Vlasik revealed a knowledge of private conversations he could only have got by listening, had by then recruited inside a guard that was no longer properly supervised.

The weapons were nearly ready. A new bomb tested in 1951 under Beria. A transportable hydrogen bomb expected to yield twenty times Hiroshima, with nothing else like it in the world.[^103] And two concrete rings around Moscow with rocket emplacements at intervals, six hundred rockets each, twenty launchable at once. Coordination was poor; Beria told the chief designer it had to work, or else. It began to work.

His words to Molotov after the war set the sum out: the First World War delivered one country from capitalist slavery, the Second created the socialist system, and the Third will finish imperialism for ever.[^104]

Ordinary people could feel the weather changing. On 13 January 1953 the country read the communiqué on a terrorist group of poisoning doctors, and *Pravda* recalled the 1937 formula that successes lead not to the damping down but to the exacerbation of the class struggle.[^105] Loudspeakers ran all day. The promise that struck people cold was that retribution would soon find its way to the inspirers behind the hirelings. The Kremlin doctors had dachas near Mamontovka Station. That winter the dachas were empty and none of them came out to ski.[^106]

Then the moment where the plan shows itself. A collective letter had been prepared from eminent Soviet Jews condemning the murderers in white gowns and declaring that antisemitism did not exist in the USSR.[^107] It was to run at the start of February. On the 2nd, *Pravda* was forbidden to print it, and only one person could have stopped a letter drafted on Central Committee instructions.

One signatory told the author afterwards that they had signed out of animal fear, telling themselves the doctors could not be saved and the others had to be. The veto meant he would not divide the Jews into good and bad, and would not let them buy immunity by handing over a handful. People who understood that understood what it implied. On 8 February the paper ran an article called "Simpletons and Scoundrels" instead, listing Jewish names of swindlers and saboteurs whom insufficiently vigilant Russians had employed.

By the end of February the rumour was that the Jews would be deported to Siberia. Rumours he disliked were normally silenced within days and their carriers jailed; this one grew.[^108] The neighbour asked how many freight cars it would take and said, no, he simply can't do it. They knew he could. He had moved hundreds of thousands out of the Caucasus at the height of the war.

The author's mother came home from work and told his father in a whisper, so the boy would not hear, that the house management committees were drawing up lists of Jews and knew the date already. His father said feebly that it was just rumours.[^109]

What was it all for? Not paranoia and not simple hatred. Some of his most trusted people were Jews — Kaganovich was third man in the state.[^110] He was a cold pragmatist who always had precise reasons. So the question is why a man that careful would want a rupture with the West that was certain to enrage America.

The answer offered is that he wanted the rupture. Terror in the thirties had prepared the country for a war, on Molotov's own explanation; terror in the fifties was preparing it for another one.[^111] A final war against the West, fought under two slogans his people would follow: crush capitalism, crush its agent, international Jewry.

And the window was closing. His troops were in Germany and Eastern Europe, his army was the strongest in the world, Moscow had its ring of rockets, the new weapon was days from testing, a third of mankind was under his banners.[^112] All of it temporary. Tomorrow a half-ruined, half-starved country starts falling behind. An old predator who can feel his strength going does not let the last chance pass.

There would be no document proving any of this, because the screening of his archives began on 5 March 1953, the day he died — a secret clause instructing Malenkov, Khrushchev and Beria to put his papers in proper order, published forty-one years later.[^113] So the chapter turns to the other kind of source, and Mme de Staël supplies the licence: in Russia everything is a secret, and nothing is a mystery.

Two secondhand stories describe a February outburst. In both, Vyshinsky raised the Western reaction to the doctors' trial and got savaged for it, his statement called Menshevik, his past mentioned.[^114] In one version Stalin told the room that they were afraid of no one and there was no more favourable moment than the present if the imperialist gentlemen felt like going to war. In the other he said it would have to be either-or: either we liquidate them, or after my death they will liquidate you like blind kittens.

The check on the stories is the visitors' book, and it is a nice piece of work. On 7 February 1953 the Argentinian ambassador was received from six to six forty-five with Vyshinsky present; when Vyshinsky left, the four closest aides came in; and "Simpletons and Scoundrels" ran the next morning.[^115] On 17 February the Indian ambassador came, Vyshinsky was not there, and afterwards Beria, Malenkov and Bulganin arrived. That was the last day he spent in his office.

After 17 February the register records no visitors. Somebody has drawn a red line down the margin, as though closing the account.[^116] Visitors would enter the office again on 2 March, in his absence.
