## Ch. 28 — Thirteen hours on a dining-room floor

A boy in Moscow heard Levitan's voice on the radio reading the bulletins on the illness — the announcer whose menacing tone people associated with the Boss himself — and the country listened, numb, to news of his white blood-cell count.[^117] So he had white blood cells just like the rest of us. People wrote to the newspapers offering their own lives instead. **A god's biology is news, because until that week nobody had been told he had any.**

The order that starts everything was given at four in the morning on 1 March. Malenkov, Beria, Khrushchev and Bulganin had watched a film at the Kremlin and come out to the nearer dacha, and left around four.[^118] As the doors were closing, the guard Khrustalev heard him say: go to bed, all of you, I don't need anything, I shan't need you today.

Khrustalev came back and told the others, happily, that here was an order they had never been given before. Lozgachev, who was on duty, said in all the time he worked there it was the only occasion Stalin said go to bed. The usual line was want to go to bed, delivered with a look. As if we'd dare.[^119] They were glad, and went off without thinking twice.

Khrustalev left the dacha at ten that morning and was replaced by Starostin, which is why Starostin, telling the story at a small gathering in 1977, did not mention the order. He had not been there to hear it.[^120] The order authorised the guards not to guard his rooms. It also authorised them not to keep an eye on each other.[^121]

Then the day. At ten there was no movement — their phrase for when he was sleeping. Eleven, twelve, still nothing; he usually got up between eleven and twelve and sometimes by ten. One o'clock, three, four, no movement.[^122] The standing order was that if there was no movement nobody entered, and anyone who did would be severely punished. So two grown men sat in the staff quarters, twenty-five yards down a corridor, for six hours, wondering what to do.

At some point the sentry outside rang to say the light had gone on in the little dining room. Thank God, they thought. Eight, nine, ten o'clock. Lozgachev told Starostin he was in charge of the guard and ought to be getting worried, and Starostin said I'm afraid, and Lozgachev said you're afraid — what do you think I am, a hero?[^123] The mail from the Central Committee arrived and it was his job to take it in. That is the only reason anybody went.

He walked noisily on purpose, because you were not supposed to creep up and he reacted badly to a quiet entrance. Through the open door of the little dining room the Boss was on the floor with his right arm crooked and raised slightly.[^124] Lozgachev's hands and legs would not obey him. He had good hearing, Lozgachev said, he'd obviously heard me coming, and probably raised his hand to call me in to help.

He had wet himself. He could not speak, only make a noise like dz, dz. His pocket watch and a copy of *Pravda* were on the floor, and the watch had stopped at half past six, so half past six was when it happened. There was a bottle of Narzan on the table he had probably been going for.[^125]

They lifted him onto a sofa and then onto a bigger one in the big dining room, where there was more air, and covered him with a rug because he had got very cold. Butusova rolled his shirtsleeves down.[^126] Starostin rang Ignatiev at State Security, who was frightened and referred him to Beria and Malenkov. Half an hour later Malenkov rang back to say he had not found Beria. Half an hour after that Beria rang to say: don't tell anybody about Comrade Stalin's illness.

Beria and Malenkov arrived at three in the morning, four hours after the first call. Malenkov's shoes creaked so he took them off and carried them under his arm.[^127] Beria looked at the man on the sofa and swore at Lozgachev for starting a panic. The Boss is obviously sleeping peacefully. Let's go, Malenkov. Don't bother us, and don't disturb Comrade Stalin.

Khrushchev's memoir tells it differently — that all four went out at once, were told he was asleep, decided it would be embarrassing to appear while he was in such an unseemly state, and went home.[^128] Lozgachev says Khrushchev was not there at three in the morning at all, and first appeared around eight. The doctors arrived between half past eight and nine. He had been on the floor and then on a sofa, without help, for thirteen hours.[^129]

There are two possible readings and the chapter states both. Either he lost his mind, ordered everybody to bed, and had a stroke. Or somebody instructed Khrustalev to send the others to bed so that a person could be alone with him.[^130] After Vlasik's arrest the guard was no longer properly supervised and Beria had recruited inside it. The suggestion made is an injection into a man asleep after his wine, which would explain why nobody was in any hurry the next night: they knew he was no longer dangerous.

The verdict offered covers both readings. Even on the first, four men calmly and deliberately withheld help and left him to die.[^131] Beria later told Molotov: I took him out.

The doctors were terrified. They had to examine him and their hands were shaking. The dentist dropped the false teeth. Professor Lukomsky said they would have to take his shirt off to measure the blood pressure and Lozgachev ripped it open. Then they all took a good look and asked who had been present when he fell, and the guards thought this is it, they'll put us in a car and we're done for.[^132]

Vasily was brought in drunk and went looking for the guards, shouting in the staff quarters that they had killed his father, then went home.[^133] Leeches were applied. His lungs were x-rayed. The whole Academy of Medical Sciences met to decide what else could be tried, and an artificial respirator was wheeled in and stood there unused while young technicians looked goggle-eyed at what was going on around them.

Meanwhile the office was working. On 2 March at twenty to eleven in the morning the three who had come back from the dacha assembled in his room, joined by the four who had fallen out of favour and the rest of the Presidium, and began dividing his power among themselves — in his office, while he was alive.[^134] Then some of them drove back out to keep an eye on the dying man. At half past eight in the evening they reassembled and carried on. That was now the daily routine.

The physician Myasnikov recorded the medical answer and the political question. The diagnosis was clear and the prognosis could only be that death was inevitable. Malenkov gave them to understand that he hoped medical measures could prolong the patient's life for a sufficient period — meaning long enough to organise a new government and prepare public opinion.[^135]

They kept the order of precedence at the bedside. Malenkov and Beria in front. Then Voroshilov, Kaganovich, Bulganin, Mikoyan. Those of lower rank looked in through the door, and Khrushchev kept to the doorway.[^136] Voroshilov leaned in and said Comrade Stalin, we are here, your loyal friends and comrades, how do you feel, dear friend. There was no expression on his face by then. Molotov remembered that whenever the eyes opened, Beria rushed over and kissed his hand — and that after the funeral Beria said "the Coryphaeus of Sciences, eh?" and roared with laughter.

Svetlana described the end. The face discoloured and the features becoming unrecognisable. The death agony choking him slowly while they watched. At the last minute he opened his eyes, and the look was either mad or angry and full of the fear of death.[^137] Then he raised his left hand and seemed either to point upward or to threaten all of them, and his spirit tore itself from his body.

Everyone present read the gesture differently. A resuscitator said the breathing changed abruptly, agitation appeared, the left hand rose as if in greeting, and that was the death agony.[^138] Lozgachev said: they say when he died he raised his hand, as he had that other time by the table, begging for help. But who could help him. Death at 21:50.

Beria was first out of the room, and Svetlana caught what he said in the corridor in a loud, undisguisedly triumphant voice: Khrustalev — the car.[^139] Of all the guards, that was the name he called. Behind him, Valechka Istomina put her head on the dead man's chest and wept out loud.

The others stayed a little while and then went after him to the Kremlin, to legalise what they had already agreed. Simonov sat in a hall with three hundred people for forty minutes in a silence he never forgot, believing Stalin was lying somewhere nearby unable to recover consciousness.[^140] Malenkov explained that Comrade Stalin continued to struggle against death, but that even if he won the fight his condition would be such that the country could not be left without leadership. They did as they were told. Afterwards Simonov went to the *Pravda* offices, and the editor put down the telephone and told him Stalin was dead.

Nobody called the guards in to say goodbye. They went in without being asked and stood watching while a car came with a stretcher and took him away.[^141] Then they were dispersed one by one — leave the city immediately and take your family with you. Starostin, Orlov and Tukov went to Beria to ask not to be sent away, and he pointed at the ground and said if you don't want to be there, you'll be there. So off they went. Khrustalev fell ill and died soon after.

The funeral killed more people. Trainloads arrived from every town. The crowd crushed the author against a girl whose eyes he still remembers, the militia hemmed them in, something gave, and people began falling.[^142] He came out of it flung onto the roadway with the skirt of his overcoat torn. Thousands were carried to mortuaries that day. He had refused to depart without a blood sacrifice.

Sergei Prokofiev died the same day and nobody noticed. His widow could not get flowers of any kind because everything was shut, and a neighbour took cuttings from her indoor plants so there would be something on the coffin.[^143] Prokofiev's favourite pianist, Richter, was being flown in from Tiflis to play beside the other coffin. The plane was crammed with flowers and he was nearly suffocated by the scent.

The Burial Commission specified gold. Long-term embalmment in the Mausoleum laboratory, the body in military uniform with the Hero stars, and the shoulder boards and buttons and stars to be made of gold.[^144] A decree on building a Pantheon was to be drafted.

Eight years later they took him out at night. On 31 October 1961 the militia cleared Red Square and closed the entrances, and when it was fully dark they dug a grave by the Kremlin wall.[^145] The staff wept as they switched off the installation. They replaced the golden buttons with brass ones and took off the golden shoulder boards, covered the body with a dark veil and left the face showing, and lowered him in after a minute's silence. No relatives were present. The order was to cover him with two concrete slabs. They just shovelled earth on him.

Then a letter arrives, decades later, from a man asking for information about his relatives. Pepelyaev, major general in the tsar's army, killed 1916. Pepelyaev, president of Kolchak's Council of Ministers, shot 1920. Pepelyaev, lieutenant general, sentenced to death and shot 1938. Pepelyaev, white officer, killed in the Civil War. Pepelyaev, staff captain, convicted 1933, died in a camp. Pepelyaev, surgeon in Kolchak's army, convicted 1942, died in Siblag 1946. Pepelyaev, Socialist Revolutionary, shot by the Cheka at Perm in 1918. Pepelyaev, the writer's grandfather, convicted in the thirties. Pepelyaev, killed in the Second World War.[^146]

Nine men from one family. A concise history of Russia in the twentieth century.

Two of the comrades-in-arms outlived everything. Molotov began to forget things, and at times believed he was Chairman of the Council of Ministers again — calling for his suit and a tie and sitting waiting for Gorbachev's ministers to come and report to him.[^147] He died in 1986, in a red-lined coffin, having been born under Alexander III.

Kaganovich lasted into the nineties. His maid heard him say "it's a catastrophe" in front of the television, which was showing Gorbachev and Yeltsin, and when she looked round he was dead in his chair.[^148] Three weeks later the crowd smashed the statues.

## Afterword — The portraits come back out

Fifty years after the victory there was a parade again, and Yeltsin stood where the Boss had stood. A little green curtain had been hung over the word "Lenin" on the Mausoleum.[^149] Clinton and Major stood at the base of it, beside the Sacred Body, watching what was left of the army that had been meant to conquer the world go past. Another procession moved through Moscow the same day, fifty thousand strong, singing songs from the Stalin era, from the Belorussian Station to Mayakovsky Square.[^150] For the first time since his death, dozens of portraits of him floated over the heads of the marchers.

Communists, monarchists and Russian fascists walked side by side, at one in their devotion to him.[^151] The observation offered is that they were all correct to be there: he was a greater national socialist than Hitler, he built the greatest of monarchist cults, he enlarged the empire of the Romanovs, and he served the Great Dream. Some of the placards read: Jews Beware! Stalin Will Soon Return![^152] Priests in cassocks walked under the portraits.[^153]

The temporal claim is the one the Afterword rests on, and it is about how long a thing has to stay buried before it can come back. He had waited underground for over forty years while the surviving victims died off one by one and their children grew old. Then the Great Amnesia came, and he rose.[^154] The Russian religious philosopher Georgi Fedotov had written at the end of the 1920s that the malice then aimed at building a godless International would one day be turned to building a nationalist and Orthodox Russia — and that the hand which today kills kulaks and the bourgeois will kill Jews and non-Russians, and man's black soul will remain as it was, or rather it will become blacker.[^155] Fedotov's article carried an epigraph: and Satan exults and mocks you, because you were called Christ's.

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, chapters 24–28 `[SPECULATIVE]`

Paradigm-obvious, and reading any of these as personal genius is the biographer's error rather than a finding about the man. Bargaining over spheres of influence with Churchill, which is ordinary great-power behaviour and which Churchill proposed. Taking reparations in territory and satellites, which every victor in that war did in its own currency. Building a bomb once an enemy had one. Cultivating a cult, which Mussolini, Hitler, Mao and Kim all did without needing to learn it from each other. Screening the archives after a leader's death, which the successors of every secretive regime have done.

Paradigm-breaking, and the cost is what marks them.

Deporting whole peoples in the middle of a war he was still fighting. Half a million people and 23,000 NKVD men were moved out of the line at the moment of maximum need for both. Nobody forced this and nothing compelled the timing; the cost is measured in divisions not at the front. Destroying the two competent administrators he had. Voznesensky and Kuznetsov were the only men near the top capable of deciding anything alone, which is exactly why they were killed, and the state that survived him was run by the nonentities who were left.

Refusing the collective letter in February 1953. He was offered a way to end the crisis at the price of a handful of doctors and turned it down, because taking it would have divided the Jews into good and bad and he wanted them undivided. That refusal converted a manageable show trial into a deportation, and it is the clearest single instance in the book of an aim overriding an advantage. Arresting Vlasik four months before he died. This is the one decision the chapter itself names as a mistake, and the cost landed on him personally within the year.

## Ch. 26 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: manufacturing an enemy to discipline an alliance.

The mechanism is set out in one move. Tito had done real damage — annexations and pacts without permission, a confederation forming inside the camp. The obvious response is to remove him. Instead he is anathematised and kept, because a named heretic still standing is a test everybody else has to pass, and the passing is what tightens the camp. Trotsky had already served this purpose once, which is what makes the choice recognisable rather than improvised.

Scope conditions. This works where the heretic is out of reach, where the accusation is broad enough to touch anyone who ever dealt with him, and where nobody can see the arithmetic — that is, where the cost of losing the heretic's actual cooperation stays hidden. It fails on the third condition first. Yugoslavia was genuinely lost, and the loss was carried because the disciplinary yield across six other countries was worth more.

The general form. An enemy inside the walls disciplines allies. An enemy outside them disciplines a population. Both are cheaper than the enemy's defeat, which is why a regime that has fully won a quarrel often has to start another one. Modern equivalent: any coalition held together by a rival rather than by a shared aim, where the leadership's incentive runs against the rival ever actually collapsing.

## Ch. 27 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

A live alternative, named in the chapter and argued by people who were there. Vyshinsky told him, twice, that the doctors' affair was creating serious difficulties for Soviet diplomacy — that the Western reaction was enormous and the cost real. That is a rejected proposal with a named author, and the author was the man who had run the show trials of the thirties, so it cannot be dismissed as squeamishness. He was called a Menshevik for it and his past was mentioned, which in that room was a threat.

A constructed alternative. Suppose the collective letter had run on 2 February as drafted. The forecast is that the trial proceeds on a narrow front — a handful of doctors, condemned by their own community, executed, and the campaign closed. The Jews of the USSR remain frightened and available for the next round rather than deported. Western reaction is severe but survivable, because the regime has produced Jewish signatories to say there is no antisemitism.

What that forecast implies about the veto is the interesting part. If a narrow trial was available and was refused, the deportation was not a consequence of the trial getting out of hand. It was the point. And the war footing behind it is then not an inference from character but a reading of a decision with a date on it.

The counter-reading, which the report keeps rather than resolving. The veto may have been vanity — a refusal to let anybody purchase anything from him, of a piece with the three circuits of the Stalin Prize table before pardoning Zlobin. On that reading the deportation rumour is a rumour, the war plan is a construction, and February 1953 is an old man refusing an off-ramp because being offered one was intolerable. Nothing in the visitors' book distinguishes the two.

## Ch. 28 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the thirteen hours. Two men sat twenty-five yards from a dying man for most of a day, and neither would walk down the corridor.

An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/indirect-agency-deniable-power|deniable power]] would say the night was designed and would point at the shape rather than at any evidence. Nobody gave an order to let him die. An order was given to go to bed — by him, or reported as by him, through one guard who left at ten the next morning and died soon after. Everything that followed was people obeying standing rules. The rule that no one enters when there is no movement did the killing, and it had been written by the victim. That is the signature of the form: the outcome is produced entirely by other people's compliance, so no instruction exists to be found afterwards.

An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/equanimity-as-operational-advantage|equanimity as an operational advantage]] would look at the same corridor and see something duller and more likely. Fear had degraded the decision-making of every person in the building to the point where nobody could act on plain evidence. Lozgachev found a man on the floor unable to speak and his first move was to ask whether he should perhaps call a doctor. Beria stood over him and called it peaceful sleep. Starostin said I'm afraid. On this reading no design is required: a system that has spent twenty-five years teaching people that initiative is fatal will eventually meet a situation where initiative is the only thing that helps, and will fail it.

They do not converge, and the spread is the useful part. The first reading needs a conspiracy and explains Beria's "I took him out" and his choice of Khrustalev's name in the corridor. The second needs nothing and explains why four separate men, with four separate interests, all behaved identically. What both agree on is the finding that survives either way: **the standing orders were sufficient**. Whether or not anybody arranged the night, nobody had to.

A third voice, from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/archive-as-resistance|the archive as resistance]], is about how any of this is known at all. The documents were screened starting the day of the death, by three of the four men in the corridor. What defeated that is not a surviving file but an old man in a kitchen with thick-lensed glasses, reading a typescript slowly and signing it with a shaking hand — and a visitors' book that nobody thought to destroy because it recorded nothing but arrivals and departures. The lesson generalises past this book: a regime destroys the records that make claims, and leaves the ones that only make timestamps. Timestamps are what later reconstructs the claims.

## What Transfers — the last February `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: timing a bold move against a closing window.

The reasoning attributed to him in chapter 27 is a clean instance of a general pattern, and it is worth separating from its horrors. Every advantage he held in early 1953 was temporary and he knew it: the army's edge would erode, the nuclear lead would close, the economy was already the weakest thing he had. An actor who believes his position peaks now and declines afterwards will accept a worse expected outcome for a nearer one.

Scope conditions. This holds where the decline is real, where the actor can still choose the moment, and where no successor is trusted to hold the position later. Remove the third and the urgency drops — a man with an heir he believes in does not have to move now. He had spent thirty years making sure no such person existed. The window closed on him partly because he had shot everybody who could have kept it open.

The general form. Manufactured indispensability creates a deadline. Modern equivalent: any leader whose organisation has no credible succession, where the strategic clock and the personal one are the same clock, and where waiting therefore reads as loss rather than as patience.

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Stalin.md`, lines 6685–7878: ch. 24 (6685–6858), ch. 25 (6859–6946), ch. 26 (6947–7218), ch. 27 (7219–7610), ch. 28 (7611–7846), Afterword (7847–7878).

The strongest documentation in this part. Beria's operational reports on the deportations, with headcounts and dates. The Druzhkov telegrams in the President's Archive, unpublished at the time of writing. Shelepin's 1959 letter to Khrushchev asking permission to destroy the Katyn files. The Smersh transcripts of Gordov and Rybalchenko, December 1946. The Kryukov and Ruslanova interrogation records. Molotov's note of 20 January 1949 reversing his abstention. Beria's 1953 letter to the Presidium quoting Abakumov on the killing of Mikhoels. Vlasik's 1955 trial transcript. Shirshov's diary, preserved by his daughter. Myasnikov's medical account of the death. Stalin's office visitors' book for February and March 1953. And Lozgachev's signed statement, taken in his kitchen and read back to him before he signed.

The claims that rest on inference rather than documents, and they are the two largest in this part. That a world war was planned for 1953 — the argument runs from the coincidence of the rocket ring, the hydrogen bomb, the planned deportation and the February outbursts, and no document survives or could be expected to. And that Stalin was helped to die, which is offered as one of two readings and not asserted; the chapter's own summary is that even on the innocent reading, four men withheld help for thirteen hours.

A note on the source's own position. Two of the February stories are third-hand — told to the author by Borshchagovsky, who heard them from two men both since dead. The author says so, prefers the second story to the first on grounds of plausibility, and then does something better than either: he checks both against the visitors' book and dates the episode to 7 February. The reporting of the Zhemchuzina interrogation goes the other way. Her flat denials are explained by a reconstruction of what she was not permitted to say, and that reconstruction is the author's, not the file's.

Hagiography runs in reverse here, and it is worth naming once. This is a hostile biography, and the risk it carries is the mirror of the usual one: where a hero-narrative reads paradigm-obvious acts as genius, this book is inclined to read them as design. Bounded absence. No claim is made about material outside lines 6685–7878.

# What Runs Through All of It — Radzinsky's *Stalin*

> **The closing cross-chapter pass over Edvard Radzinsky, *Stalin***, written last, out of the finished chapter runs. It does not replace them. Every finding here was first made inside a run and is cited back to the part that made it. Read from `RAW/books/Stalin.md`, lines 302–7878, in twenty-eight chapter runs plus preface, prologue, introduction, interlude and afterword.
>
> **The runs:** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/radzinsky-stalin-worldview-archaeology-part-1|Part 1 — Preface to Chapter 5]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/radzinsky-stalin-worldview-archaeology-part-2|Part 2 — Chapters 6–11]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/radzinsky-stalin-worldview-archaeology-part-3|Part 3 — Chapters 12–18]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/radzinsky-stalin-worldview-archaeology-part-4|Part 4 — Chapters 19–23 and the Interlude]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/radzinsky-stalin-worldview-archaeology-part-5|Part 5 — Chapters 24–28 and the Afterword]].
>
> ⚠ **Supersedes** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/radzinsky-stalin-worldview-archaeology|the original whole-book report]], which was written from vault concept pages rather than from the chapters, and merged the book into a single account.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/Radzinsky-Stalin|Edvard Radzinsky, Stalin]]*

---

## What surfaced in more than one place

Making a god turns out to be an industrial process, and it runs the length of the book. It starts with a corpse in chapter 11, with the decision to embalm Lenin and the machinery that had to be built around a body. It reaches its finished form in chapter 27, in two films — Lenin as John the Baptist, Stalin as the Messiah, arriving in conquered Berlin by plane in a white uniform while the peoples of the earth glorify him each in their own tongue. Chapter 28 then shows what the thing costs to maintain, when a country listens to a white blood-cell count on the radio and finds out that a god has blood. And the Afterword shows it outliving the man by forty years, as the portraits come back out over Mayakovsky Square in 1995.

Four separate runs, four phases of one operation. `[n≥3 PATTERN]` The merged whole-book reading had this as a single observation about a personality cult. Read chapter by chapter it is a sequence with a purpose, and chapter 27 states the purpose outright: a god was needed to lead the peoples into a last war.

Terror as preparation for a war is said twice, and the same witness says it both times. Molotov explained to Chuyev that the point of the Great Terror in the thirties was to get the country ready for the war it then fought. Molotov is also the man who goes cold in chapter 25, standing in front of a map with drawing pins in it, hearing the Dardanelles and Turkey and Libya named aloud, and working out what that implies about the next few years for people like him. **The second time he makes the connection, he is making it about himself.**

Everyone who runs an operation gets consumed by it, and the consumption is designed rather than incidental. Chapter 19 has the self-service system, where each victim killed his predecessor and was killed by his successor, and where the great majority of the troika members were shot. Chapter 21 disposes of Yezhov. Chapter 27 removes Abakumov for insufficient ruthlessness, in a decree complaining that Chekists were working in white gloves, and arrests Vlasik, who had guarded him for decades. Chapter 28 clears the guards out of the dacha within weeks, with Beria pointing at the ground.

A limited confession absorbs a much larger unspoken charge, and the form turns up three times. Part 4 found it at the Eighteenth Congress, where admitting serious mistakes in the NKVD closed off two years of documented mass killing. Part 5 found it twice inside one chapter — Prokofiev's penitential letter, read out to a meeting of composers who warmly welcomed the decision, and Molotov's note of 20 January 1949 reversing his abstention on his own wife's expulsion. `[n≥3 PATTERN]` In every case the confessor controls what is confessed, and somebody else carries the remainder.

A person, in this world, is somebody who can be contaminated by contact. Chapter 24 sends prisoners of war from German camps straight into Soviet ones, on the stated ground that anyone who had touched foreigners carried an incurable disease and had to be kept away from healthy people — and sends the civilians the Germans had deported for labour after them. Chapter 26 runs the same logic on people who never left the country: unmasked cosmopolitans, kowtowing to things foreign, hearts in a hostile state. **Nothing in the accusation requires an act, because proximity is the offence.**

---

## Where the runs pull against each other

The visitors' book gets better across the book, and the method gets better with it. In chapter 13 it establishes when Kirov last walked into the office, to the minute. In chapter 23 it establishes that the man functioned on 22 June 1941 — and Part 4 flagged the trouble, because chapter 22's claim that he was not surprised by the invasion rests on character rather than on that register. By chapter 27 the same tool is doing something much stronger. Two third-hand stories about a February outburst get checked against the register, dated to 7 February by the presence of the Argentinian ambassador and Vyshinsky, and confirmed by an antisemitic article running in *Pravda* the next morning.

So the two large interpretive claims in the second half are not equally supported, and the runs disagree about them. The June 1941 claim is argued from what a man had proved over sixty years. The February 1953 claim is argued from a register, a newspaper date, a rocket ring, a bomb schedule and a suppressed letter. Read whole, both look like one author's habit of inferring from character. Read chapter by chapter, one is a habit and the other is an argument.

The frame also shifts between the first run and the last. Part 1 recorded the stated purpose — to understand rather than to condemn, from a man who admits he stood in the funeral queue hating the subject. The Afterword condemns at length and ends on Revelation. The change is legible and the book does not hide it, but a merged reading averages the two into a tone that exists nowhere in the text.

Willingness to reach a conclusion rises as the witnesses become interviewable, and that is a finding about the book rather than about the deaths. Nadezhda Alliluyeva's death, in Part 3, is left open with the accounts set side by side. Krupskaya's, in Part 4, is described from the medical file and stopped there. Stalin's own, in Part 5, gets two readings and a stated preference between them. `[n≥3 PATTERN]` The difference is that an old man in a kitchen with thick-lensed glasses was still alive to be interviewed, read the typescript back, and sign it — so the confidence tracks the availability of a living witness rather than the strength of the documents.

---

## Which of the seven the book never reached

Six of the seven questions the method hunts for get worked hard, and one is barely present.

What is real, what makes things happen, what shape time has, what a person is, how people should relate to each other, and how anybody knows anything — all six are thoroughly evidenced across the twenty-eight runs. The last is the book's own obsession. How a fact gets manufactured, who is allowed to know it, what a commission produces, and what a register records because nobody thought it worth destroying.

The thin one is what is worth having. The book is very good on the value of power and nearly silent on the value of anything else. What did an ordinary person in that country think a good life was? It surfaces twice, both times by accident, and both times it is the best material on the page. Peter Shirshov's diary in chapter 26 has the balcony, the plan for another child, the talk of the South — and the same man three months later coming home quietly at night in case the miracle had happened. Lina Prokofieva in a camp stops beside the slop buckets to tell the other women about Paris.

Neither is developed, because the book's subject is a man for whom the question did not arise. That is a limit of the source rather than a gap to be filled from elsewhere, and it is stated bounded: no material answering it was found in the range read, lines 302–7878. A history of the same period written from below would be the instrument for it, and there is none in this vault yet.

One more absence is worth naming, because the book keeps walking past it. Nadezhda, Svetlana, Polina Zhemchuzina, Valechka Istomina, Zhenya Alliluyeva and Zhenya Garkusha are all present, and every one of them appears as the object of somebody else's decision. Polina's interrogation is the closest the book comes to giving a woman a position of her own, and even there the reconstruction of what she was not permitted to say belongs to the author rather than to the file.

---

## What the by-chapter reading recovered

The merged report this file supersedes made five or six findings, because only what recurs survives a merge. The twenty-eight runs made those and kept the ones that appear once. Consistently, the single-appearance findings are the sharpest material in the whole build.

Ruslan G. on the hut with hoarfrost on the floor and the soldier who did not want to bend down. Molotov unable to answer a question about a ballet tour without a telegram from Moscow. Three circuits of a table, and the question asked three times before the answer came. A pocket watch stopped at half past six on a dining-room floor. A neighbour taking cuttings from her indoor plants so there would be something to put on Prokofiev's coffin. Nine men named Pepelyaev in one letter.

None of those recurs anywhere else in the book. **Every one would have been deleted by a whole-book synthesis, and together they are most of what this book actually knows.**

---

## Evidence

This file cites nothing the runs did not cite. Line ranges by part: Part 1, 302–1575. Part 2, 1576–3310. Part 3, 3311–5356. Part 4, 5357–6684. Part 5, 6685–7878. Each part's own Evidence section carries the documentation notes, the inference flags and the bounded-absence statement for its range.

A note on the chapter map. Parts 1–4 worked from a boundary list placing chapter 27 at line 7311, and Part 5 corrected it to 7219 — the heading at 7311 is a section inside chapter 27, not its opening. No run's coverage was affected, because Part 4 ends at 6684 and Part 5 reads from 6685 to the end. The corrected list is in Part 5's banner.

A note on register across the build. This is a hostile biography, and the risk it carries is the mirror of the usual one. A hero-narrative reads paradigm-obvious acts as genius; this book leans toward reading them as design. The two-piles section in each part exists to separate those, and the paradigm-obvious pile is where the correction lands — bargaining over spheres of influence, building a bomb once an enemy had one, screening the archives after a leader dies. None of those needs a theory of the man.
