# What Their World Took For Granted — Radzinsky, Introduction and Chapters 1–4

> **The Introduction and chapters 1–4 of Edvard Radzinsky, *The Rasputin File*** — a corpse pulled from the Malaya Nevka and the people who came with buckets, a police file that vanished and turned up at a Sotheby's auction, a birth date nobody could establish, a beating with a stake that changed a man, and a court waiting for an emissary from a country that no longer existed. Read from `RAW/books/The Rasputin File.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
>
> **This report covers two books**. Parts 1–4 run Radzinsky by chapter; parts 5–7 run Moynahan, *Rasputin: The Saint Who Sinned*; the synthesis reads across both.
>
> **Siblings:** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-part-2|Part 2 — Radzinsky, Chapters 5–6]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-part-3|Part 3 — Radzinsky, Chapters 7–11]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-part-4|Part 4 — Radzinsky, Chapters 12–15, Epilogue and Afterword]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-part-5|Part 5 — Moynahan, Preface and Chapters 1–7]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-part-6|Part 6 — Moynahan, Chapters 8–15]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-part-7|Part 7 — Moynahan, Chapters 16–22]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-synthesis|What Runs Through All of It]].
>
> ⚠ **Supersedes** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology|the original whole-book report]], which was written from vault concept pages rather than from the chapters, and merged both books into one account.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/radzinsky-rasputin-file|Edvard Radzinsky, The Rasputin File]]*

---

## Introduction — A body in the river, and the people who came with buckets

On 19 December 1916 a corpse came up through the ice of the Malaya Nevka in Petrograd, its face mutilated. The startling thing was the hands.[^1] They were bound, and they were raised — because down there under the ice the man had still been alive, beaten and shot, and still trying to get free.

Then the part that describes a country rather than a murder. **Great numbers of people hurried down to the river with flasks, jugs and buckets**, and the police wrote it in their report. They came to ladle up the water the body had been floating in. They wanted to scoop up, with the water, his diabolical strength, which the whole of Russia had heard about. The witnesses agree about his face in the photographs — weather-beaten, a large irregular nose, thick lips, a long beard, hair combed forward to hide a small bump his daughter said was like a budding horn.[^2] They agree about the eyes: the instantly blazing magnetic gaze, the deep-set unendurable eyes, the hypnotic power.

**Away from the photographs they stop agreeing about anything at all**. Tall. Short. Neat in a peasant way. Filthy and sloppy. Slender. Stocky with broad shoulders. A singer who saw him many times reports rotten teeth and foul breath; a writer who knew him extremely well reports that his teeth were perfect down to the last one and his breath absolutely fresh; his own secretary reports blackened stumps; an admirer who visited often reports strong white teeth.[^3]

The tsar's sister said he was as changeable as a chameleon, and one witness described the changes happening in a single sitting — a crude illiterate peasant scratching himself, then an inspired prophet, then something shamelessly predatory behind the wrinkles, then a grizzled Siberian who had spent thirty years searching the world for God.[^4]

The question the whole book is built on is not about him. **It is about the blindness of one family**, and it is put as a list of people the tsarina chose not to believe.[^5] The courtiers — understandable. The police reports — perhaps explicable. The large Romanov family, the tsar's mother, his brothers — harder. And then the one that is not explicable at all: her own beloved sister, to whom she was so close.

Maybe she simply did not *want* to believe.

*Read: lines 795–831.*

---

## Ch. 1 — Everyone who knew him was interrogated, and the transcripts went missing

On 4 March 1917 the Provisional Government set up an Extraordinary Commission of Inquiry into the illegal acts of the tsar's ministers, and for seven months it worked out of the Winter Palace.[^6] Twenty-seven boards of inquiry. Russia's leading poet, Alexander Blok, deciphered the transcripts and put them into shape, and recorded the throne room with the fabric torn off the walls and the throne removed because the soldiers wanted to break it up. One board was called the Thirteenth Section and its remit was the *dark forces* — which in the political slang of that spring meant Rasputin, the tsarina, and the people around them.

What the cells looked like is the best single image of the year. Delivered to the Peter and Paul Fortress, where political prisoners had been kept under the tsar, were the men who had put them there: two prime ministers, the interior minister, the head of the Department of Police and his replacement, the aged court minister, the chairman of the Council of State, the palace castellan, the tsarina's closest friend.[^7] **The damp cells resembled nothing so much as a brilliant Winter Palace ball**. Then in October the Bolsheviks took power and sent the Provisional Government's ministers to the same cells — where they were greeted, *not without humour*, by the tsarist ministers they had recently imprisoned there.

What survived of all that work is where the chapter's real subject starts. In 1927 the Bolsheviks decided to publish part of it for the tenth anniversary, and the purpose was stated: to demonstrate the senescence of a regime controlled by an ignorant, debauched peasant.[^8] The editor was Schyogolev, a former revolutionary who had done time in the same fortress and then joined the new regime — evil tongues said his flat contained furniture from the Winter Palace. He published seven small volumes out of an immense quantity of material. **Those seven volumes were for many years the chief documentary basis for every book written about Rasputin**.

What was left out was not random. It was the testimony of the people who had liked him — his publisher, the friend in whose flat he had lived, his devotees, the women. That point of view was unacceptable, so it did not appear.

The forgeries are the next layer, and they were manufactured by the same man. In 1927 the magazine *The Past* began publishing Vyrubova's diary, and all Russia was besotted with its intimate revelations.[^9] It was written by Schyogolev with the novelist Alexei Tolstoy, the *Red Count*, a Bolshevik collaborator with whom he had already co-authored a hit play about a palace revolution. A Rasputin diary was drafted as the sequel — and the archive copy has somebody's pencil correction on the subheading, so that *written at his dictation* reads *as if written at his dictation*. It was abandoned only because the story got out, thanks to a Red Count who was highly gregarious and frequently drunk.

Meanwhile the state had been watching him with an obsessiveness that produced its own kind of record. External surveillance agents wrote a daily account of his movements, his visitors, his absences, where he went and whom he met. **No public figure received a more detailed description of his life over several years than this semi-literate peasant**.[^10]

Most of it is gone. Part burned when the secret police headquarters went up in February 1917. Part was destroyed by the police officials themselves — because they had been among his visitors and he among their guests. The former interior minister Khvostov testified to how it was done: when he left the service, the prime minister took the documents to his office, especially the ones concerning Rasputin, and *everything was burned at once*.

The autopsy report follows the same pattern and adds a worse detail. It was in the Academy of Military Medicine in the 1930s and then vanished — and soon afterwards a number of research assistants who had seen it also disappeared.[^11] It was the time of the Stalinist terror. The Commission's own investigators did not agree either. One of the Thirteenth Section's principal investigators, Vladimir Rudnev, resigned in August 1917 and wrote afterwards that he had asked to be released *in view of the attempts of the President of the Commission to incite me to patently biased actions*.[^12]

**What replaced the old legend, seventy years later, was the same legend inverted**. After perestroika the holy devil became the holy elder, and a nationalist historian proclaimed the murder a ritual killing by Jews manipulating Masons under their control.[^13] The joke the chapter draws out of that is worth having: before the revolution the nationalists of the day had accused Rasputin *himself* of being a Masonic agent, and called him a Jewish stooge surrounded by Jewish secretaries. Russian myths about devils and saints — bloody Nicholas and then Nicholas the saint, the father and teacher Stalin and then the bloody monster Stalin, the saintly Lenin and then the bloody Lenin. And they could go on making whatever claims they liked, dismissing the police reports as lies, declaring that he never got drunk and never engaged in lechery — because there was no testimony by his friends.

Then the File came back, and the manner of its return says something about what happened to Russian archives in the twentieth century. In a Bolshoi dressing room after a première, Rostropovich told the author he had a present for him, bought at a Sotheby's auction.[^14] It was handed over in a Paris living room draped with Winter Palace curtains, under a portrait of Nicholas by Serov. Nearly five hundred pages on Commission forms, with the Commission stamp, each transcript signed by the person interrogated — Vyrubova, the gendarme chief, a colonel, a doctor of Tibetan medicine, the interior minister, the head of the Moscow secret police. Many transcripts in the investigators' own hand, whose specimens are held in Moscow, **so establishing authenticity was not very difficult**.

There is a famous photograph, compulsory in every biography, captioned only *Rasputin surrounded by his devotees*. The File makes it possible for the first time to identify everyone in it — and contains direct testimony from several of them, so that the people who saw him almost every day begin to speak.[^15]

*Read: lines 832–1140.*

---

## Ch. 2 — A country with a second, hidden church inside it

The greater half of his life is obscure, and the chapter is honest about what that means for everything in it.[^16] The Commission's interviews with his fellow villagers produced an ideological version — the peasant given to drunkenness and thievery from youth. His daughter's memoirs, written after she emigrated, are the fruit of her own imagination and a journalist's. His own account, *The Life of an Experienced Wanderer*, was told to the royal family in 1907 and is a kind of Life of Saint Grigory — a legend, written for people who wanted to hear it. Even his birth date was a riddle, and the reason for the confusion is his own. The parish registers show no Grigory before 1869 and the registers from 1869 on have disappeared; a Tyumen census supplies 10 January 1869, the day of Saint Grigory.[^17]

He added four years to his age in 1907, five in 1914, and eight in the notebook the tsarina kept of his sayings. **The reason is a word**. *Elder* in Russian church usage means a monk marked by a special sign, given the power to prophesy and to heal. In ordinary Russian it also means a very old man. He was younger than the tsar, and his prematurely aged peasant face made the arithmetic easy.

The surname is not a coincidence either, and the attempts to launder it are dismissed briskly. *Rasputin* comes from *rasputa* — an immoral, good-for-nothing person. Deriving it from *rasputitsa*, the mud season, or from a crossroads, merely attests to a poor knowledge of Russian name derivation.[^18]

Then the incident the whole transformation is hung on, and it is a beating. A fellow villager caught him stealing haystack fence, chopped and loaded on his cart.[^19] Rasputin came near to hitting him with an axe. The man hit him with a stake so hard that blood ran from his nose and mouth, and thought at first he had killed him. **After that beating, he said, he turned kind of strange and stupid**.

Soon afterwards horses were stolen from the common pasture, and the same witness saw Rasputin ride up to them with his comrades — but Rasputin let the horses go and went home. When the matter came to court, his comrades were banished to eastern Siberia and he was released.

What is offered as the explanation is a category that will run through the rest of the book. During the beating, with the blood on his face, he felt something he would later call **the joy of abasement — the joy of suffering and abuse**. *Abuse is a joy to the soul*. That is why he went unresistingly to be punished, and why he did not go to town to sell the horses. Then a conversation with a seminarian on the Tyumen road, about a merciful God who waits for the prodigal son until the last human breath, so that in the eleventh hour it is still not too late. And the essential words: *go and be saved*.[^20]

Wandering, in Russia, was not eccentric. **Every peasant made a pilgrimage to holy places, and the gentry made them too** — in carriages, while the peasants went on foot with knapsacks, and even the empresses Elizabeth and Catherine the Great went.[^21] By the end of the nineteenth century only isolated individuals did it. Holy Rus was becoming a legend. For him the wandering produced a God who lives in the trees and resounds in the voices of birds, and a Satan who was not an abstraction but somebody nearby — appearing as a beggar to whisper to a thirsty man that it is many versts to the next village.[^22] A witness told the Commission that after one pilgrimage he seemed abnormal, singing something and waving and threatening with his hands.

He also had a saint. Simeon of Verkhoturye, a wanderer on the same river three centuries earlier, dead of extraordinary abstinence in 1642, whose coffin was noticed half a century later to be rising out of the earth with the uncorrupted remains visible through splintered boards.[^23] The first man healed at that grave was named Grigory and took earth from the coffin and rubbed his limbs with it. Rasputin said Simeon healed him of insomnia, and his first gift to the royal family would be an icon of Simeon. When the royal family perished in 1918, Simeon's relics perished too, thrown out of the monastery by the Bolsheviks.

**The largest finding in the chapter is that there were two churches in Russia, and only one of them was official**. Christianity had been adopted a thousand years earlier and paganism had not gone anywhere.[^24] Churches were built on pagan holy places. The god Volos became Saint Vlasy the Miracle Worker; the thunder god Perun was supplanted by the prophet Elijah who made the storms rumble. Of the Trans-Volga it was said: *they lived in the forest, they prayed to stumps, they married standing around a spruce, and devils sang to them*.

Into those forests went the losers of the Time of Troubles, and then the Old Believers after the seventeenth-century schism over whether to cross oneself with two fingers or three. A unique *Russian America*. For the whole three-hundred-year history of the dynasty there existed alongside the official church an unofficial, powerful, secret church of the people.

Meanwhile the official one had been made a department of state. Peter the Great destroyed the patriarchate and set up a Synod under a chief procurator appointed by the tsar.[^25] Under Nicholas's father the post was held by Pobedonostsev — one of the cleverest men in the country, whose whole mind was directed towards oppression, and who worked to contain church life within ruthless bureaucratisation and to make the hierarchs recognise one law only, the command of the tsar. The result is stated in one line: **the official church found itself in a condition of profound lethargy**. People with troubles went either towards revolution or to holy fools, elders and sectarians.

The sect that mattered was the Khlysty, and its theology is the key the book uses on everything that follows. It taught that any man may become Christ and any woman the Mother of God — one had only to rid oneself of the sin of the flesh and nurture Christ in oneself.[^26] To illiterate peasants that literalism was joyously clear.

And then the turn that makes it dangerous. **The suppression of lust took place through boundless debauchery**. In some communities abstention became, during the rite of *rejoicing*, promiscuous sexual relations among the membership — because they sin in order to suppress the flesh, and drive out sin with sin.

The reasoning behind it is set out plainly, and it is not stupid. In a religious person sin is always followed by great suffering; suffering leads to profound repentance; repentance produces a great purification that brings the person closer to God. **Sin, repentance, purification — the essential gymnastics of the soul**. Without grasping that, the chapter says, we shall not understand Rasputin.

The author saw a rejoicing himself, in 1964, on an island in the Caspian, having sworn to remain silent for thirty-three years — and the thirty-three years had passed.[^27] White flaxen shirts over naked bodies. A cellar, candles, a verse from the Easter canon. An old man with joyful light-coloured eyes, the local Christ, whirling in place and whipping himself while the choir prayed more and more savagely. Then the cry: *Brothers! I feel it, the Holy Spirit! God is within me!* Sweat running in rivulets, candles going out, everything in darkness. They called the whirling *spiritual beer*, because it acts on the brain like alcohol.

The other branch went the opposite way and was worse. The Skoptsy split off in the mid-eighteenth century preaching absolute asceticism through the fiery baptism of castration, on the strength of one verse in Matthew about eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven.[^28] **He who is able to receive this, let him receive it** — taken by semi-literate peasants as a guide to immediate action. Castration by red-hot iron, sometimes by axe; on women, the removal of external organs, nipples, whole breasts; and a *supreme degree* was invented. Landowners, officers and clergymen did it voluntarily.

Both sects reached the aristocracy. A Khlyst circle operated in the Mikhailov Castle in Petersburg in the early nineteenth century under a colonel's wife who had felt the Holy Spirit enter her on converting to Orthodoxy, and generals, dukes and a government minister whirled there nightly.[^29]

And in 1803 the Skoptsy put a proposal to Alexander I. Their living Christ would take his place beside the emperor, and **each minister would have his own Christ**. The plan's author was sent to a monastery. The chapter's comment on it is one line: *no matter — the time would still come for one of God's people to rule the country*.

The last piece is vocabulary, and it will matter later. Driven underground, the Khlysty worked out rules for the world: they called each other *ours* and *our own*, and used conspiratorial aliases in place of real names.[^30] **All of this would soon be heard in the royal palace**. His own writings carry the doctrine's fingerprints — contempt for the book learning of the hierarchs, whose learning remains insignificant but who listen to your simple words. And one sentence that describes his entire strategy: *at the present time, those who are able to give counsel have all been driven into little corners*.

He was first denounced to the Tobolsk Consistory in 1903, for odd behaviour towards women visiting him from Petersburg and for an acquaintance with Khlyst teaching picked up in the Perm factories. Nothing incriminating was found. **The tag never left him**.

*Read: lines 1141–1524.*

---

## Ch. 3 — The wretched stranger who arrived with a letter of introduction

His own account of reaching Petersburg is a set-piece and the File takes it apart in a paragraph.

In the *Life* he arrives unknown, in worn-out boots and a pauper's coat, walks to the Alexander Nevsky Abbey and asks the doorman to announce him to a bishop.[^31] **The doorman did me the courtesy of a blow on the neck. I fell on my knees before him**. And the doorman, understanding there was something special in him, announced him. Feofan, interrogated in 1917, gives the real version in one sentence: Rasputin came to Petrograd from Kazan with a letter of introduction from the archimandrite of the Kazan eparchy, and stayed at the abbey with Bishop Sergius.[^32]

So there was no unfortunate wanderer, no doorman and no blow. His fame had already travelled beyond Siberia, he had admirers in Kazan, and a church hierarch had written him a letter to one of the best-connected clergymen in the capital.

**And the letter was well aimed**, which is the part that says most about the moment. Sergius was chairing the religious and philosophical colloquia at the Geographical Society — a hall packed to overflowing with clergy and the flower of Russian culture, trying to close the gap between the church and the intelligentsia and to pull the church out of its lethargy.[^33] The complaint made there was that the official church was becoming associated with obscurantism, that its preachers never spoke of the prophetic and mystical side of Christianity, and that it had left earthly life out of the account. The colloquia ran twenty-two sessions and were then banned by Pobedonostsev. A Siberian prophet of the people arriving in the middle of that argument was, as the chapter dryly puts it, interesting. And the man who found him interesting was made Stalin's first Patriarch of All Russia in 1942.

What he did next is the pattern for the following decade. At tea in Sergius's lodgings, in front of monks and seminarians, he amazed them with psychological perspicacity — telling students he was meeting for the first time that one would be a writer, that another was ill, and that a third was a simple soul whose simplicity his friends took advantage of.[^34]

Then the prophecy. Asked whether Admiral Rozhdestvensky's squadron would beat the Japanese, he said: **I feel in my heart that it will be sunk**. Tsushima followed.

The chapter offers three readings and refuses to choose. An intelligent peasant who knew from the inside the whole unhappy weakness of his country. Or a man who had read what every Russian newspaper was saying — that a squadron of antediluvian ships sailing without concealment against a modern fleet was doomed. Or it was given him to comprehend the mysterious.

The route upward ran through two sisters. Militsa and Anastasia, daughters of the Montenegrin king, one married to the tsar's cousin, the other spending her days and nights at her sister's palace.[^35] The court called them the *black women* for their hair and their country. Militsa passed for a great expert on mystical literature, took a lively interest in everything supernatural, had learned Persian to read the Persian mystics in the original, and was almost considered a prophetess. They were closer to the tsarina than anyone, and the reason is in one line: from the day she arrived in Russia she had met the coldness and hostility of the court, and the Montenegrins had known how to surround her with warmth and an almost servile deference.

And then the riddle, which the chapter leaves standing. **Every biography of Rasputin says that Militsa and Feofan took him to the royal palace**. Feofan, under interrogation, says he has absolutely no idea how Rasputin came to know the family, definitely states that he took no part in it, and adds that Rasputin got there by indirect means, against Militsa's will — and hid the acquaintance from her.[^36]

*Read: lines 1525–1652.*

---

## Ch. 4 — A family waiting for an emissary from a country that no longer existed

The chapter's argument is that he was not discovered. **He was expected**, and the expectation had been assembled over several years by people who kept auditioning candidates.

The family's own sense of what was coming rests on three hundred years of arithmetic. Peter sentenced his son to death. Two lawful tsars were murdered in family coups during the reign of Nicholas's enlightened great-great-grandmother.[^37] Paul I was murdered in a plot involving his own son. Petersburg itself, built on a marsh with the blood of thousands of workers, had been cursed by Peter's first wife from the convent he exiled her to: **may you be barren**.

Nicholas grew up at Gatchina, where the servants claimed to see the unshriven spirit of the strangled Paul, and he and his sister were afraid and dreamed of seeing the murdered emperor. He became heir on the assassination of his grandfather.

He also thought the date settled it. He was born on the day of the long-suffering Job, and told his prime minister: **I have more than a presentiment. I have a deep certainty that I am doomed to terrible ordeals**.[^38] His sister recorded him saying it too, and his wife wrote it back to him in a letter in 1915. Alix wept the whole time when replying to his proposal, and said only *I cannot*.

Then the coronation, which was supposed to be a mystical betrothal with Russia, and which ended with a night spent carting hundreds of trampled bodies off Khodynka Field.[^39] Then the bombs: in the first years of the new century a minister of education, a governor-general and two ministers of the interior. His diary answers each with the same formula. *One must endure with humility and steadfastness the trials sent to us by the Lord*. His wife was a different character. She would struggle against her fate, and she looked for protection.

What she was offered came from Montenegro, where the aristocracy was much closer to the common people. **Truth, miracle and strength are hidden in the simple folk. An alliance must be forged with the people, bypassing the venal officials and the arrogant court** — the people and the tsar with no one between them.[^40]

The joke the chapter makes of this is the most useful thing in the run. That idea united everybody in Russia who hated each other. Tolstoy, Dostoevsky and Turgenev quarrelled endlessly and agreed that only the common people, destitute and illiterate and downtrodden, possessed a hidden truth — that only in the gloom of their huts had the true spirit of Christ survived. And the tsar confessed to the same idea. A shy man of short stature and un-tsarlike appearance who felt awkward at balls and among ministers, where it seemed to him they were always comparing him to his giant of a father, and who was far happier among the common people in an atmosphere of adoration.

So emissaries of the people began arriving, one after another, and the first was a fiasco. A minor official named Klopov had written endless letters about embezzlement in the flour-milling business; the letters were read with delight; he was summoned and sent off with the broadest secret plenary powers to scour Russia and bring back the people's truth about official abuses.[^41] **Unfortunately he had no understanding of anything except his flour-milling business**.

Then Mitya of Kozelsk, called the Nasal-voiced for his difficulty pronouncing words — long unbound hair, barefoot the year round, a staff, a monk's cassock. Journalists later called him an idiot and Vyrubova lied to the Commission to protect the family, saying she did not think he had ever been at the palace.[^42] The tsar's diary for 14 January 1906 records a visit and an image drawn from a vision, and that they talked for about an hour and a half. He was not an idiot. The Department of Police files record that his influence on the popular masses was immense, that he gave away the money his admirers gave him, and that he was rumoured to have foreknowledge — and Feofan testified that he outlined the circumstances of his life precisely at a first meeting and predicted the fall of Port Arthur.

His prayers did not produce a boy. Nor did Matryona the Barefoot, who arrived in rags shouting barely comprehensible prophecies, brought an icon, and vanished as suddenly as she came. **The chapter notes the route she used: bring a miracle-working icon that will assist in the birth of a son**.

The full dress rehearsal was a Frenchman. Nizier-Vachod of Lyons, a soothsayer and healer who said it was given him to speak with the dead and that he lived on the borderline between two worlds.[^43] He was more agreeable to a tsarina who had not forgotten Europe, and whose ears were tired by Mitya's mumbling. He used cheap circus theatricality and the tired baggage of the eighteenth-century adventurers — and what the Paris press had mocked produced an indelible impression in Petersburg. The state checked him. The Department of Police used its Paris agents; the report came back frightful; the French called him a crooked adventurer, and a Russian agent sent an ironical newspaper article about one of his public hypnosis shows.[^44]

**The tsar gave the order to sack the agent responsible in twenty-four hours**.

Then the phantom pregnancy. He determined the child would be a boy, the doctors expressed doubt after tests, and she forbade them to examine her — with her Montenegrin friends and Philippe, now officially certified a Russian doctor of medicine, as her doctors instead.[^45] Nine months passed. In August 1902 an obstetrician was finally summoned, about her sudden loss of weight, and told her she was not pregnant. The announcement in the *Government Herald* was muddled enough that rumours spread through all classes that the empress had given birth to a monster with horns which had to be strangled.

**None of it shook their confidence in him**. He explained the failure as her own weakness of faith: a miracle can occur only in the presence of absolute faith, and no sooner had she doubted and called the obstetrician than the miracle ended.

They called him *Our Friend*. They met him in secret at the Montenegrins' palace to avoid the dowager empress and the family, and the tsar's diary records the evenings — *we listened to Our Friend all evening, we came back at night in the marvellous moonlight*. She wrote to her husband: **how rich life is since we know him and everything seems easier to bear**.[^46] He also left a promise. He would die soon, and would return to the circle of his friends **in the form of another**.[^47]

What she was eventually persuaded to ask for instead was Russian, and her sister Ella supplied the argument. The Russian tsars had no need of foreign wizards, because they had patrons in heaven who were far more powerful — the saints, who become the defenders of tsars and people and act in concert as a Guardian Assembly or Golden Chain.[^48]

So Serafim of Sarov was canonised, over the Synod's resistance, because she forced it. In July 1903 the whole family walked to the monastery and the tsar and the grand dukes carried the coffin of relics around the church. At night she and Nicholas bathed in the saint's spring, praying for an heir. There was another Serafim prophecy they did not know about then, concerning terrible future insurrections exceeding all imagination, and rivers of Russian blood. Alexei was born on 30 July 1904. Then haemophilia, and the chapter's own line about it: his fragile blood vessels could not withstand the pressure of his blood, and **the empire's vessels were worn and fragile too**.[^49]

The last thing to say about this run is what they were actually waiting for, because it had already gone. The religious writer Nilus recorded a nun of his acquaintance who could no longer travel by train for the abuse and mockery poured on her, and who had to put on a dark blue skirt to pass for a peaceable old woman.[^50] An ascetic he cites: *a Godless, faithless time has come for Orthodox Russia. He is an Orthodox Christian in name but no longer in spirit*. **They were waiting for an emissary from Holy Rus. The chapter's judgement is that Holy Rus no longer existed**, and that its place had been taken by a resentful, impoverished people with an ever-diminishing faith in its clergy — the same people who, after the Bolsheviks came, took an eager part in destroying their own churches and burning their own icons.

Militsa produced the candidate at last, and took one precaution. Before introducing him she made him swear not to meet the tsars on his own, so that he would remain under her auspices — a new Philippe, met at her house.[^51] He promised.

*Read: lines 1653–1950.*

---

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, Introduction and chapters 1–4 `[SPECULATIVE]`

A note on whose decisions these are. **The subject of this book has almost no power in these four chapters**, so the sorting below is mostly about the court, and that is the correct outcome for a first part rather than a shortfall. Paradigm-obvious, and reading any of it as distinctive is the biographer's error. Going on pilgrimage. Every peasant did it and so did the gentry and two empresses; what was unusual by 1900 was only that so few still did.

A court consulting mystics. Alexander I received the founder of the Skoptsy; a Khlyst circle ran in the Mikhailov Castle with a minister of the crown attending; the Montenegrins had a working pipeline of candidates before Rasputin was heard of. Suppressing a police report that embarrassed a favourite. Sacking the Paris agent was ordinary court behaviour, and the same thing would be done again. Publishing a selective archive for a political anniversary. Schyogolev's seven volumes were commissioned to prove a thesis, which is what state anniversaries were for in 1927.

Adding years to his age. Every wandering holy man in that tradition had an incentive to look older, and his face made it cost-free. Paradigm-breaking, and the cost is what marks it.

Refusing to sell the stolen horses. This is the strangest decision in the four chapters and the chapter builds everything on it. A man who has just been beaten half to death for stealing goes willingly to be punished, and then declines the proceeds of a second theft that was already complete. Whatever happened during that beating cost him the money and the company of his accomplices, who were banished while he was let go.

Refusing to let doctors examine a pregnancy. A woman with four children, an obstetrician available and a dynasty depending on the outcome, who forbade the examination for nine months on a magus's assurance. The cost was public humiliation severe enough to produce rumours of a horned monster, and it did not change her mind.

Canonising a saint against the Synod. Alix forced the church to make Serafim of Sarov a saint on the strength of a prophecy that had named her and her husband. Nothing in that court's practice required the empress to overrule the ecclesiastical authorities on a canonisation, and she did.

Swearing an oath and immediately breaking it. Militsa's one precaution was a promise not to approach the tsars alone. He gave it and, on Feofan's testimony, reached them by indirect means against her will and then concealed it from her. **That is the only decision in this part that is unambiguously his, and it is the one that made the rest possible**.

## Ch. 1 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the File. Five hundred pages of signed testimony about the most watched man in Russia, deliberately excluded from publication because it came from people who liked him, then lost, then sold at auction in London, then bought by a cellist as a present.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/archive-as-resistance|the archive as resistance]]** would say the interesting question is not what was destroyed but what pattern the destruction follows, and would point out that it follows the same pattern three times. The surveillance files were burned by policemen who had been in his kitchen. The autopsy report vanished, and so did the people who had read it. And the testimony of his friends was omitted from a publication designed to prove he had no friends worth quoting. In every case the material removed was the material that complicated a usable story — and in every case somebody with a position to protect did the removing. The counsel is that a gap in an archive is itself evidence, and that the shape of the gap tells you who was frightened.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/chimalpahin-annals-indigenous-historiography|the annalist's practice of keeping the incompatible versions side by side]]** would go at the recovery rather than the loss and be less comforted by it. The File does not settle anything. It adds the testimony of devotees to the testimony of enemies, and the two do not resolve — the same man has perfect teeth and blackened stumps, is tall and is short, is a saint and is a fraud, in signed statements taken by the same investigators in the same building. The counsel is that the honest form of the record is the contradiction preserved, not the contradiction settled, and that a historian who has just recovered the missing half of a file is under the greatest pressure of his career to make the two halves agree.

They do not converge, and the spread is the useful part. The first reading treats the File as recovered truth. The second treats it as a second set of interested statements. What both agree on is the finding that survives either way: **for seventy years, every book about this man rested on a selection made by one editor to serve one anniversary**, and nobody writing those books knew what had been left out.

A third voice, from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/scapegoating-as-stress-displacement|scapegoating as stress displacement]], is about the inversion and has predictive value. The 1990s legend is the 1917 legend with the sign flipped — the holy devil becomes the holy elder, and the same man who was once denounced as a Masonic agent and a Jewish stooge is now said to have been murdered by Jews manipulating Masons. **Neither version required new evidence, because neither version was ever about him**. The transferable part is that a figure who serves as an explanation is available to be re-signed whenever the thing needing explanation changes, and that the tell is an interpretation reversing entirely while its cast of villains stays put.

## Ch. 2 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: making transgression a stage in a purification cycle.

The Khlyst doctrine is worth extracting from its horrors, because as a mechanism it is coherent and it explains more than one career. Sin is followed in a religious person by great suffering; suffering produces profound repentance; repentance produces purification; purification brings one closer to God. Therefore sin, performed deliberately and at scale, is not the opposite of holiness but an instrument of it. **They drive out sin with sin**.

What makes it powerful rather than merely convenient is that it is falsifiable from the inside. The cycle only works if the suffering and the repentance are real, and a person going through it can tell whether they are. That is why it held serious people, and why it was not simply a licence.

What makes it dangerous is the same feature. **Every observable behaviour is compatible with both the doctrine and its abuse**, and no outside observer can distinguish a man performing spiritual gymnastics from a man enjoying himself with a theory. The distinction lives entirely in an interior state the doctrine says only the practitioner can inspect.

Scope conditions. This holds where the tradition has no external test — no rule, no elder with authority over the practitioner, no visible marker that the cycle has completed. Where such tests exist, the doctrine either dies or becomes ordinary asceticism, which is why it flourished in communities driven underground and hidden in forests, and why the official church could only ever suppress it rather than argue with it. Remove the secrecy and it cannot survive scrutiny; remove the scrutiny and nothing bounds it.

The general form, stated about the material. **A doctrine that relocates the evidence of virtue inside the practitioner has made itself unfalsifiable from outside and unaccountable by design**. Modern equivalent: any practice whose failures are explained as necessary stages, where the only person qualified to judge progress is the person making it, and where a fall is evidence that the ascent has begun. The tell is not that the claim is strange. It is that no observation could count against it.

## Ch. 4 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

A live alternative, and it was tried by name. The Romanov family did not merely complain about Philippe; the dowager empress commissioned a police investigation through the Paris agents, obtained a professional report calling him a crooked adventurer, and had it put in front of her son. Grand Duke Nikolai Mikhailovich went further and travelled to see Tolstoy, hoping the most famous man in Russia could reach the tsar. The report was accurate, timely, and produced by exactly the machinery a state maintains for the purpose. **It cost the agent who wrote it his job within twenty-four hours**.

A constructed alternative. Suppose it had been acted on — Philippe sent home in 1901 rather than 1903, the phantom pregnancy never occurring, the Serafim canonisation not forced. The forecast is not that Rasputin never reaches the palace, because the Montenegrins would still have been searching and the court would still have wanted an emissary from the people. It is narrower and more interesting: **the template would not have existed**. Philippe established the whole procedure — the secret meetings at Znamenka, the name *Our Friend*, the explanation that a failed miracle proves insufficient faith, the rule that family criticism strengthens rather than weakens the favourite, and the promise to return in the form of another. Rasputin did not have to invent any of it. He inherited a working position.

The scope condition, and it is what makes this transferable. **A discredited predecessor in the same role is more useful to a successor than no predecessor at all**, provided the discrediting was done by people the principal has already learned to discount. Every objection to Philippe had been made and survived; when the same objections arrived about Rasputin they were not new information but a familiar noise, and had been pre-emptively answered. The general form: an institution that defeats a first instance of a pattern without changing the conditions that produced it has trained the next instance for free.

## What Transfers — the vacancy in a court `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: recruiting for authenticity.

The court was not deceived into wanting a peasant prophet. It advertised. Between roughly 1900 and 1905 it auditioned a flour-milling official, a barefoot mumbling clairvoyant from Kozelsk, a woman in rags with an icon, a French hypnotist, an ascetic bishop, and the most famous priest in Russia — and the specification never changed. The candidate had to come from outside the official structures, carry no institutional office, and be unmistakably of the people.

The reason the specification was written that way is the most transferable finding in the part, and it is not about mysticism. **Every institution around that couple had failed them or was suspected of it** — the ministers were venal, the court was hostile, the church was in lethargy and answerable to a procurator, the doctors had been wrong about an heir. What they wanted from a candidate was precisely the absence of any of those affiliations, and the only available proof of that absence was the candidate's obvious unfitness for them.

Scope conditions. This works where the principal has lost confidence in every credentialed channel, where a private need exists that no channel will address, and where the search is conducted by intermediaries with their own stake in whoever is found. Remove the third and it becomes eccentricity rather than a system. The Montenegrins were not neutral talent-scouts: their standing in the family depended on the candidate's success, which is why Militsa took an oath from him before making the introduction.

The general form, stated about the material. **When credentials have been discredited, the absence of credentials becomes a credential** — and the selection then runs on markers that are cheap to fake and impossible to check, because any check would have to be performed by the institutions already ruled out. Modern equivalent: any organisation that has stopped trusting its own experts and begun recruiting on authenticity, where the qualifying evidence is that the candidate is not one of them.

---

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/The Rasputin File.md`, lines 795–1950: Introduction (795–831), ch. 1 (832–1140), ch. 2 (1141–1524), ch. 3 (1525–1652), ch. 4 (1653–1950).

The strongest documentation in this part, and it is unusually good because the book's organising subject is its own sourcing. The File itself — nearly five hundred pages of signed interrogation transcripts on Extraordinary Commission forms, whose authenticity was checked against handwriting specimens held in Moscow. Bishop Feofan's testimony, which is the load-bearing document of chapters 3 and 4 and contradicts the standard account on two separate points. Vyrubova's testimony, including a demonstrable lie about Mitya. The Tobolsk parish registers and the Tyumen census that fix the birth date at 10 January 1869. The 1903 Tobolsk Consistory denunciation. Nicholas's diary, quoted with dates. Alexandra's letters. Polovtsev's diary and Grand Duke Konstantin Konstantinovich's, both written by insiders with no motive to flatter. And the Department of Police report on Philippe from the Paris agents.

Where the evidence is legend and is labelled as such. Rasputin's own *Life of an Experienced Wanderer* is treated throughout as a Life of Saint Grigory — told to royal admirers who wanted to hear it — and is used only for traces rather than for facts. His daughter's memoirs are set aside as the fruit of her imagination and a journalist's. The Commission's interviews with his fellow villagers are described as having produced an ideological version. **The chapter is explicit that the greater half of his life is obscure**, which is a stronger statement than most biographies make about their subjects.

Where the reasoning is the author's rather than the record's. That the beating with the stake was the moment of transformation, and that what he felt was the joy of abasement. The evidence for the beating is a witness statement; the evidence for the interior state is a phrase he used to a writer years later, applied backwards. That the Khlyst *sin, repentance, purification* cycle is the key to his whole character. And that Holy Rus no longer existed by 1905 — supported by Nilus and by an unnamed ascetic, and offered as a general claim about a country.

A note on the source's own position. This is a book with a detective plot, and the plot is the recovery of a document. That shape carries a specific risk and it is worth naming: **a narrative built on finding the missing file has an interest in the file settling something**. Against that, the author repeatedly declines to resolve what the File does not resolve — the three readings of the Tsushima prophecy are left standing side by side, Feofan's contradiction of every previous biography is reported without being explained away, and the physical descriptions are left irreconcilable. Bounded absence. No claim is made about material outside lines 795–1950.

# What Their World Took For Granted — Radzinsky, Chapters 5–6

> **Chapters 5 and 6 of Edvard Radzinsky, *The Rasputin File*** — a shadow bending over a sick boy's crib, a salon hostess who ended up begging barefoot, an interrogation in which the most influential woman in Russia persuaded her investigator she had no influence, a prime minister brought down by one report, and a letter that meant one thing to the woman who wrote it and another to everyone who read it. Read from `RAW/books/The Rasputin File.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
>

## Ch. 5 — How a peasant got into a palace, and what it did to the women who helped

He had made an impression on the tsarina at once, and Feofan says so plainly: the sovereign, however, fell under his influence only after Rasputin had given him something to ponder.[^1] What moved her at the first meeting was a sentence about her own subjects — that the people would not let their tsar down — delivered to a woman who had just watched a revolution. His own version of what he told them, reported later to a friend, was blunter: when revolution raised its head they were very scared and it was *let us get our things together*, and he talked to them a long time and persuaded them to spit on all their fears and rule. The route he then took to the tsar is the most instructive thing in the chapter, and it did not go through the court. It went through a woman's illness.

Olga Lokhtina was a little over forty, still very good-looking, a Petersburg salon hostess laid up with an intestinal complaint that meant she could only move by holding the wall.[^2] A priest brought Rasputin to heal her, two days after his first meeting with the royal family. Her own account: from the moment of Father Grigory's appearance in my home I felt completely restored.

He moved into her flat, and the chapter is unsentimental about why. Her husband was an engineer with the civil rank equivalent to general, and he was in charge of the paved roads at Tsarskoe Selo — where the royal family now lived as virtual recluses to keep the heir's illness secret. **Through the Lokhtin family, Rasputin was privy to all the court rumours**. Then he wrote to the tsar himself, offering an icon of Simeon of Verkhoturye, and the telegram survives.[^3] It is fluent and correctly phrased, and it differs so much from the incoherent telegrams he later sent that the chapter attributes it to Lokhtina.

What it produced is a letter from Nicholas to his prime minister on 16 October 1906, and it is the pivot of the whole book. A few days ago I received a peasant from the Tobol province, who brought me an icon of Saint Simeon of Verkhoturye. He made a remarkably strong impression on Her Majesty and on me. And instead of five minutes, our conversation lasted well over an hour. He has a strong desire to meet you and bless your injured daughter with the icon.

Stolypin's dacha had been blown up by terrorists and he had carried his injured daughter out of the wreckage. He received the peasant, who prayed over her. And somewhere in that first audience, he asked to see their son — speaking of the boy's illness as if he had known about it for a long time, and asking permission to relieve his suffering with prayer.[^4] What the family saw is described once and never improved on: a room lit only by the lamps in front of the icons, a huge crooked shadow bending over the crib in prayer, the boy growing calmer and falling asleep, and waking healthy.

The chapter offers three explanations and takes none of them. Pagan Siberian healing secrets. Hypnotic suggestion. Or a real and inexplicable power he had genuinely found in himself. *For us, this is a matter of reflection and doubt. But for her, there could have been no doubt after that meeting*.

Two months later the tsar was personally arranging to change the peasant's surname, because the tsarina was upset by how it sounded.[^5] The head of the royal chancery told the interior ministry that His Majesty had deigned to express his special desire that the request be respected, and on 22 December 1906 the petition was granted: he might henceforth call himself **Rasputin-Novy** — Rasputin the New.

The official story was that the heir had clapped his hands and babbled *the New one, the New one*. The likelier reading is in the word itself. Philippe had been Our Friend. This was Our New Friend, and the promise to return in the form of another had been kept in the paperwork of the royal chancery.

Then the arrangements for concealment, which tell you what the court had already learned. After Philippe they were cautious, so the peasant was summoned along with Feofan, a man of official standing, and appeared in the very modest role of a lay brother.[^6] Later he was brought to Vyrubova's little house in Tsarskoe Selo instead, and the tsar's diary records the evenings — *we dropped in on Anya and saw Grigory and talked with him for a long time*. And when he had to enter the palace itself to treat the boy, there was a procedure. He would come as if visiting Maria Vishnyakova, the children's nurse — which allowed him to avoid having his name written down in the lobby register, where every visit to the tsars was recorded.[^7]

A governess who caught him in a darkened corridor asked what he was doing there, was told he needed to see the nurse, pointed out that she was busy and that he was not supposed to be there, and he left without speaking. The nurse's reaction was: *oh, I'll catch it from Anna Alexandrovna*. Which brings the chapter to the woman it treats as its real subject.

**Anna Vyrubova is described by every witness as dim**. Had difficulty passing the examination for home-study teacher. Not interested in anything. Hard to understand how she could have had such a relationship with the highly educated tsarina. She will enter history so described.[^8]

The chapter's flat contradiction of that is the sharpest reading in the run, and the evidence for it is her own interrogation. She chose a part — the naive, simple-hearted, childishly dim-witted Anya she had played in the royal family — and played it in a fortress. Blok, who was present, wrote: *a person who is degraded and in trouble becomes a child. Remember Vyrubova. She lied childishly*.

Asked whether Rasputin held exceptional interest for her: Exceptional? No! — very sincerely — followed by a womanly complaint about how hard it was to live at court where there was so much envy and slander. Asked why she burned a stack of documents: *I burned almost nothing* — from a woman who had filled a fireplace with ashes. Confronted with her own political correspondence: *everybody came by with all sorts of questions*. Pressed that they came by for years on end: It was terrible, that's what it was! They never left me alone!

She was being questioned by two men and she treated them as two different problems. Against Girchich there was only naivety. **Rudnev, a sentimental provincial who yearned for human nobility, could be turned into an ally** — so he was shown unswerving devotion to a fallen family, and a willingness to lie only for their sake, and Christian forbearance about being spat at and beaten by guards, a story her mother told him rather than she.[^9] She asked him not to punish those responsible, in case it made things worse for her. He transferred her out of the fortress without checking whether the taunting had happened.

Then the trump card. All Russia was saying she had been the concubine of the tsar and of Rasputin, so she insisted on a medical examination. She was a virgin, at thirty-two, ten years after a divorce. After that he believed everything, and wrote in his summary that she enjoyed no influence whatever at court and could not have, given the empress's superiority of intellect and will over the limited, weak-willed, selflessly devoted Vyrubova. That is the assessment of the most influential woman in Russia, written by the man appointed to find out what she had done.

Her marriage in 1907 was arranged to stop a rumour, and the rumour was about the tsarina. Courtiers were describing the friendship as an intimacy grounded in sexual psychopathology; a monarchist salon hostess recorded the phrase *unnatural friendship* more than once, and a naval aide's story of a night when the yacht struck a rock and the tsar slept alone in a cabin while the tsarina took Vyrubova to her stateroom.[^10]

She married a naval lieutenant and divorced him after eighteen months, testifying that he had turned out to be mentally ill and had gone to Switzerland for treatment. **He had not**. He remarried, lived quietly on his estate from 1913 to 1917, and was elected district marshal of the nobility in Polotsk.

What the chapter proposes instead is a game, and it is proposed as a reading rather than a finding. Underneath the friendship lay a feeling that was profoundly secret and repressed, which both drew the tsarina to her and frightened her — and to hide it from a religious woman, Anya invented a public, harmless, unrequited love for the tsar.[^11] Her maid testified that Vyrubova was in love with the tsar, received letters from him, and told the servants that if she died suddenly the letters in her safe were to be returned to him.

The tsarina's own letters carry the traces. *Lovy, you burn her letters so that they should never fall into anybody's hands?* And: *if now not firm, we shall be having stories and love-scenes and rows like in the Crimea*. And: *be nice and firm — she always needs cooling down*. Now the cost side, and it falls entirely on women. Lokhtina is the clearest case in the book of what proximity to him did to a person.

Her husband eventually issued an ultimatum and stopped giving her money, and got the answer: he is holy — you are banishing grace.[^12] She was driven from her home in 1910, her share of the property taken, and left with a knapsack on her back to walk to Tsaritsyn, begging for alms on the way. A Petersburg salon hostess in a black dress and a white peasant kerchief. And the paradox the chapter draws from it: her rank as a state councillor's wife could never have opened the least accessible palace in Europe, and **her rank as a semi-literate peasant's faithful follower did**.

She also did real work. She transcribed his spoken homilies into a publishable pamphlet, correcting his grammar and, she insisted, improving none of his thoughts — which was difficult, because his speech was incoherent by every account, most of the effect coming from his eyes and his hands. She understood what he failed to express in words, and it was apparently from her that the tsarina learned the art of writing his sayings down. What that devotion turned into is in the testimony of his own publisher, who walked in on it one morning in 1911. Behind the screen that separated the bed from the room, Rasputin was desperately beating her — in a white dress hung with little ribbons, holding onto his member, shouting You are God! The publisher rushed over: *what are you doing, you are beating a woman!* And Rasputin: **She won't let me alone, the skunk, and demands sin!** And Lokhtina, from behind the screen: *I am your ewe, and you are Christ!*[^13] The witness adds, in the same statement, that she regaled him with so many witty remarks attesting to her great intelligence — and every other witness who met her says the same about her quick brain and malicious wit.

1910 is when the front opened, and it opened everywhere at once. Hermogen turned against him. Feofan turned against him. Lokhtina was expelled from her home. The governess Tyutcheva spoke out. The nurse Vishnyakova told her story. And the newspaper campaign began, with the largest papers running articles about the semi-literate depraved peasant-Khlyst popular in certain court circles.[^14]

Feofan's attempt is the one that shows what the tsarina had become. He asked for the tsar and got the tsarina, with Vyrubova sitting in the room — which told him at the door that he was finished, because Rasputin had brought Vyrubova into play and she would have to support him out of gratitude.[^15]

He spoke for an hour and demonstrated that Rasputin was in a state of spiritual temptation, citing theology. **She objected, citing theological works. He destroyed all her arguments. She reiterated them: *it is all falsehood and slander.*** He thought afterwards that Rasputin must have told the family he was speaking out of envy. The chapter corrects him: *poor Feofan did not understand that it was not Rasputin, but Alix herself who had reached that conclusion*. Rasputin then came to see him as though nothing had happened, was told *go away, you are a fraud*, and fell on his knees asking forgiveness — because, the chapter notes, he did not like conflict and was ready to humiliate himself to be reconciled with a kind and naive man.

Feofan wrote again, using a repentant devotee's written confession, and got no answer. He became quite ill: it turned out he had a palsy of the facial nerve. And Rasputin could celebrate, because Mama could now be certain that the face of the man who had moved against him had been stamped by heaven itself. He was transferred out of Petersburg to the Crimea. The nurse's story is the hardest thing in the chapter and the chapter handles it carefully, because everyone had a motive. The rumours said Rasputin had raped Vishnyakova at Pokrovskoe; the present-day defenders of *holy Grigory* declare it a fabrication; **and her own testimony is in the File**.[^16]

She gives her autobiography first — given as a child to a peasant family, trained as a nurse at somebody's expense, taken straight into a ducal household and then into the royal one at twenty-four. She defends her former employers throughout, describing a mother who would not let her children be fed or bathed without her. Then: Rasputin behaved decently in relation to me for several days, and then one night he appeared in my room, started kissing me, and after reducing me to hysterics, deprived me of my virginity. Waking accidentally in the night on the way back, she saw him lying in a berth with another of the women. She reported it to the empress on returning. The empress did not give any heed to her words, and forbade her to talk about it.

Her statement ends by breaking: *I cannot testify any more. I implore you to end the interrogation, since I do not have the strength to speak any more about my unhappiness — and consider it my right not to go into the details*.

What was done instead is recorded by the tsar's sister. When the rumours reached him he ordered an investigation, and they caught the young woman in bed with a Cossack of the Imperial Guard. That, evidently, is what he was told.

The same sister then had her own experience of him, in Vyrubova's house, with the tsar and tsarina out of the room for a few moments.[^17] He came over, put an arm around her shoulders and started stroking her hand. She moved away without saying a word. Her husband told her to avoid him in future, and she wrote that it was the first and only time she knew her husband was right. The governess got her audience with the tsar, and it produced the one unguarded sentence he is recorded saying about any of it.[^18] Usually he cut off attacks by observing drily that his relations with Rasputin were a personal matter. This time he blurted out: **but what will you say if I tell you that I have lived all these years only thanks to his prayers?**

She told him it filled her with fear that such a person could be near his daughters. He answered: *am I then the enemy of my own children?*

And the last dimension in the run is the strangest, because it is about who else in Russia wanted a Khlyst. The intelligentsia had been visiting the sect for years. Rozanov went to live in a community and wrote a book about them. Merezhkovsky and Gippius lived in one in 1902 and wrote to Blok that everything they saw was *ineffably beautiful*. Blok and Remizov went to a meeting together.[^19] An old poet told the author, grinning under his moustache, the sentence that explains it: **Rasputin was attractive and in fashion because he was a *Khlyst***.

What drove them was the same sense of looming apocalypse that had driven the 1903 colloquia, and the same hope — that the true religious aspirations of the people were gathering in the sects, and that an alliance between the intelligentsia's spiritual wing and the people's could stand athwart the coming storm. The intelligentsia would later mock the royal couple for their faith in a benighted peasant. And at the same time, however paradoxically, they dreamed of the same thing. One of his devoted followers in these years was an expert on Russian sectarianism named Bonch-Bruevich, who was also one of Lenin's closest associates, and who would become a founder of the Cheka.[^20]

## Ch. 6 — A prime minister, a letter, and a file that recorded every step

The chapter opens on a book, and the question of who wrote it is not a literary aside. It is the chapter's title.

His impressions of Jerusalem were published in 1911, and his publisher testified that he had not corrected or smoothed the aphorisms but conveyed them verbatim.[^21] The prose is genuinely beautiful. **The sea comforts without any effort. Conscience is a wave, but whatever waves there may be at sea, they will die away, while conscience will be calmed only by a good cause**. And of the tomb: *Lord, resurrect me Thyself from the depths of sin*.

He could not have written it. He wrote his later notes to ministers — a few words each — at great effort in a monstrous scrawl. So *verbatim* means his words, taken down by somebody else. The publisher supplies the identification without meaning to: the proofs were corrected by the empress. The reading offered is that the person who corrected the proofs was the person who had written the words down. Only the tsarina, with the literary gift her own letters show, could have conveyed what he said in that register. And she did not work alone, but worked with the Friend who also adored writing.[^22]

For her that work was contact with the hidden. For the Friend it was one more thing binding her to Alix. And the effect on the family is stated in one line that reaches forward six years. They, who had never been to the Holy Land, would see it through his eyes . A few years later, as they were preparing for their own Golgotha, they would remember what he had told them. Then the chapter's largest event, and it is a demonstration of what the peasant now weighed against.

Stolypin ignored a note from the tsar demanding an end to the press campaign and kept collecting information. In autumn 1911 he went to the tsar with the file — the Department of Police material, everything compromising, including the bathhouses with women.[^23] The answer he got, on the account Rasputin gave his friend Sazonov: **I know, and he preaches Holy Scripture there**. Then the tsar ordered him to clear out and threw the report into the fireplace. The friend's conclusion is dated: *that is why a month before Stolypin's murder I knew his fate was sealed*. And the chapter's own reading is flatter still. Stolypin was deposed not by the Duma, not by the rightists or the leftists. That mightiest of prime ministers was brought down by his attack on the peasant.

The peasant then gave voice to what the tsarina thought, which is how his political interventions usually worked: *Rasputin said of Stolypin that he had seized too much power*. And the chapter notes the mechanism precisely — the weak tsar did not forgive accusations of weakness.

What happened next is the strangest documented episode in the two chapters, and it is corroborated from two sides. Rasputin told Sazonov he had received an assignment from the tsars: to find a replacement minister of internal affairs.[^24] They travelled to Nizhny Novgorod so that a semi-literate peasant could offer the post to its governor. Khvostov's own account: ten days before Stolypin's murder, Sazonov arrived with a man he had never seen. Sazonov stayed in the parlour. Rasputin came into the study, spoke of his closeness to the tsar, said he had been sent to *look into my soul*, and offered him the Ministry of the Interior. Khvostov said the position was already occupied. **Rasputin answered that Stolypin would nonetheless be leaving**.

It seemed so strange that Khvostov spoke to him in a half-facetious tone, refused to introduce him to his family, and did not invite him to dinner. He left angry. The reason the offer was not believed is the interesting part: a serious man in 1911 could not credit that the tsar would entrust that post to a publisher and an uncouth peasant. Stolypin was shot in the Kiev Opera on 1 September and died two days later. He turned towards the empty royal box and blessed it with a sign of the cross.[^25]

The killer was a revolutionary who had been recruited by the security service and had had no contact with it for years. He turned up on the eve of the festivities claiming to know of a plot. A monarchist told the Duma directly that in recent times a whole series of Russian dignitaries had been killed with the collusion of the political police. A Senate investigation was about to begin, somebody got nervous, pressure was applied, and at the tsar's command the case was closed.

Rasputin was in Kiev that day, and the rumour that he had foretold the death was in the Petersburg parlours within weeks. The Commission investigated the link in 1917 and found no evidence. The chapter's own view is deflationary: if he predicted the departure, he did not need to be a prophet, because he knew the intentions of Tsarskoe Selo. From 23 January 1912 he was under systematic police surveillance, and this is where the chapter's picture of him becomes total.[^26] He was given the code name **Russian** — underlining the image of a simple Russian peasant, which was the image dear to the tsars' hearts.

The tsar had been forced to agree to it, and had been sold it as protection: his enemies might lie in wait and beat, maim or kill him. *Thrash, maim and kill were things the peasant understood very well*.

What it produced is a chronicle. He had only to come out of his building and agents followed the unprepossessing bearded man in the peasant coat. The Russian went to the store at 10:15. After four or five minutes he emerged carrying what appeared to be a bottle of wine. Almost daily visits to one flat; the same three or four women gathering there. The entire afternoon in their company. Drives in a borrowed brougham or a motor taxi.

And then, in the same reports, the other life. He rarely appeared outside alone. Whenever that happened, he would go off to a street where there were prostitutes, select one of them, and go to a hotel or a bathhouse.[^27] Passing time with highly placed ladies has not ended his visits to prostitutes.

The women in the reports are named, with ages and husbands' ranks. One of them gives the clearest account of what he did to people who were afraid of him. Lili Dehn's son was ill. Rasputin arrived, prayed over the sleeping child, then started shaking him to wake him up. She was frightened that a stranger would startle the boy.[^28] **To her amazement he woke saying *uncle* and reached out to Rasputin**, who held him a long time, petted him, and talked to him the way one talks to children. The boy started to get better the next day. Her first feeling on seeing him had been fear, and it passed as soon as he started talking in a very simple way. Now the letter, which is the chapter's other great set-piece and the one where every reader is wrong in a different way.

A monk who had been his friend stole it from him at Pokrovskoe in 1910, along with letters from the grand duchesses. It eventually reached the Speaker of the Duma.[^29] It begins *my beloved and unforgettable teacher, saviour and mentor*. It contains the sentence that did the damage: **I wish only one thing then: to fall asleep, to fall asleep forever on your shoulders, in your embrace**.

Historians did not believe in it. Then the police tracked down a follower with whom the monk had left the originals, searched her premises, and confiscated them. The prime minister read them and confirmed the long one from the empress matched the copies circulating.

The one man who read it correctly was the one with the least reason to be kind. Badmaev, a doctor of Tibetan medicine and an operator with no loyalty to anybody, testified: *after reading the copies of the letters, I was convinced that they contained no evidence whatever that the tsarina was sleeping with Rasputin*.[^30] As an experienced doctor he saw a woman tormented by her son's illness and by foreboding, pleading for release from her suffering. She was writing in the only idiom that would mean anything to the man she wrote to — his own lofty, love-filled one. The prime minister saw the same thing and put the problem exactly: the parts of the letter that were a manifestation of her mystical tendencies provided a pretext for the most disgraceful gossip.

And having understood it, Badmaev handed it to her enemies. Once the tsar had the originals there was no gratitude to be had from her, so he decided to earn some from the Duma instead.[^31] He showed the manuscript to the Duma's Deputy Speaker, who asked permission to show it to two more men, pledged not to use it, and violated the pledge. Hectographic copies of four or five letters were soon circulating around the city.

What the interior minister did with the originals is the part that shows how the court read intentions. He was advised to give them to the empress directly, because handing them to the tsar would put him in an awkward position and earn her implacable enmity.[^32] He handed them to the tsar. The tsar turned pale, took the letter out, glanced at the handwriting and said **yes, the letter is genuine**. Then he opened a desk drawer and flung it in, with an abruptness the witness found uncustomary. The prime minister's verdict on hearing the story was one sentence: *your dismissal is assured*.

What the minister should have done, the chapter says, is destroy the letters and announce that they did not exist — and he did none of it. What the tsarina took from the episode was that he had shown outsiders her letter to Our Friend, which she wrote down as a grievance four years later.
