## Ch. 13 — Everyone knew about the treason, and there was none

By late 1916 one belief had settled over the whole country, and the chapter's job is to say what it was made of.

Rasputin and treason were not even discussed. They were referred to as self-evident.[^6] A grand duke's diary carries the texture: *Alix is remarkably unpopular*. *O God, save Russia! Anything but that shameful peace*. And, from a nurse at the Winter Palace: they have a secret telephone line for conversations with Berlin.

A main task of the Extraordinary Commission in 1917 was to establish the empress's secret dealings with her German relatives. **It established nothing of the sort, and what it found pointed the other way**. When the German government approached the Entente with a peace offer at the end of 1916, Nicholas replied that the time had not arrived, since Russia had not yet taken Constantinople and the Straits or created a free Poland.

What Rasputin actually said is on record too, from the man who saw him most. *If I had been there at the beginning of the war, there would have been no war. But since they have already started it, it has to be carried through to the end*. And about her: she is terribly in favour of continuing the war — though there had been moments when she wept, thinking her brother wounded or killed. The master of the royal yacht says the same about both of them, and no document has been found saying otherwise.

One thing does not fit, and the chapter neither hides it nor resolves it. Ashes were found in her fireplace after the February Revolution, and a great many documents had been burned.[^7] The argument against the obvious reading is that the intimate letters — the jealous ones, the ones about Vyrubova — all survived. So what she burned was something dangerous rather than something private, and the likeliest candidates are her brother's letters, which the correspondence itself refers to from September 1915.

Meanwhile the machinery of government had become a chain of delegations, and the chapter names it in one paragraph. **The tsar, at Headquarters, had ceded the disposition of power to the tsarina. She had entrusted it to the peasant. The peasant had entrusted it to crafty rascals. And the country's financiers bought the power from the rascals**.[^8] All of them schemed against each other, drew each other into traps and slung mud, practising the art of mutual extermination to perfection — without noticing that it was rocking the boat they were all sitting in.

The code they used for it came out of the sect. Nicknames concealed real names among the Khlysty, and the tsarina, who liked secrets and was used to hiding her inner life from the court, made his nicknames part of the cipher in her letters.[^9] The railway minister was *Steely*. The prime minister was *the Old Chap*. The last interior minister was *the Tail* and *Fat Belly*. A friendly bishop was *the Gopher*. The tsar and tsarina were *Papa and Mama*. And the new interior minister was *Kalinin*, which was not his name at all — when this was pointed out, Rasputin said it did not matter, because everybody at the sovereign's laughed when he called him that.

How he treated the men he had installed is on record from his own secretary. During meetings he would shout at the empire's highest official: **don't you dare go against Mama's wishes! Make sure I don't turn my back on you! Then you'll be done for!** Then the speech that ended it. On 1 November the leader of the largest opposition party told the Duma that dark rumours of betrayal and treason had spread from border to border, had reached the highest circles, and had spared no one — the empress's name repeated ever more frequently along with those of the adventurers around her. Then the question the country repeated for four months: *is it stupidity, or is it treason?*[^10]

The word *treason* fitted the mood of a badly wounded army. It was taken on faith at once and rooted in the consciousness of millions.

What the government did about it is a scene worth a chapter. The tsarina demanded action and the prime minister, too frightened to refuse, summoned the Speaker of the Duma. He had sprained his ankle. So a helpless old man lay in bed with his leg elevated, trying to reprimand an enormous, powerful man towering over him. The Speaker refused to send him a copy of the speech and told him Rasputin was a first-class scoundrel and that hanging would not be enough for him. And from the bed came the prime minister's answer, in six words that carry the whole of the last year: **it is what is desired on high**.

The man at the centre of it was living in fear. All anybody had to do was shout that an attempt was being readied, and he would put on his jacket and fur coat, pull his cap down and rush for the exit.[^11] His guard was now only the security branch detail, and he understood that they could hand him over at any moment. His publisher describes what the visits had become. He would try to get drunk as quickly as possible, demand Gypsies and entertainment, and the one thing he was keen on was dancing.

In October a friend found him melancholy with wine on the table, drinking as if to quiet a foreboding, repeating *the times are changing, everything will be changed*. On parting he was very affectionate, said he appreciated the man's warmth, remembered his late father kindly, and said he would perhaps be killed himself and they would not see each other again. Then, as if suddenly coming to, he said: *no, no, we shall see each other*.

The conspiracy meanwhile was being assembled in the family, and the chapter's reading of who started it goes against the surviving account.[^12] The prince who wrote the memoirs presents it as his own idea, with the grand duke agreeing to join. **The likelier version is the reverse** — that it began with the soldier rather than the civilian, and that the two decided together after the last failed warning to the tsar in November. Others knew. The prince himself wrote of a *conspiracy*, and the tsar later wrote to the grand dukes that the consciences of many were not clear, since Dmitry was not the only one involved.

The strangest corroboration is a departure. Ten days before the murder the tsarina's sister abruptly left Petrograd, and not for anywhere — she went to pray at the monastery holding the relics of the royal family's patron saint, for ten days. Both of the killers were her own protégés. One had lived with her family; the other she called *my Felix* and had helped to bring up.

The prince's letter to his wife in the Crimea says the rest. Instead of the usual words of love, he told her about the murder he was planning. *I'm terribly busy working on a plan to eliminate Rasputin. That is simply essential now, since otherwise everything will be finished*. And then: you too must take part in it. He closed by telling her to have his mother read the letter.

Access was bought with a body. He arrived at the flat complaining of chest pains, brought by the devotee who trusted him, and was treated.[^13] His own brief account to the investigator: *Rasputin made some hypnotic passes over me and it did seem to me that there was a certain relief*. His fuller Paris account has him lying on the leather sofa while Rasputin moved his hands over his chest, neck and head, then knelt with his hands on his head, mumbling a prayer, his face so close that the prince could see only his eyes. **And the grand duke who knew him well could not make it fit**. *I cannot understand Rasputin's psyche. How is one to explain his boundless trust in the young Yusupov — the trust of someone who trusted no one at all, afraid he would be poisoned or killed?*

His answer was that there had been a carnal element, and the chapter neither endorses it nor discards it. What it does note is what the word *healing* meant in this vocabulary: exorcising the demon of lechery — which, in this case, would mean the prince's desire for men.

However it worked, it worked. He came up the back stairs each time, avoiding the agents, and the explanation for that was ready-made — his family were enemies of the elder and he did not want a row at home. So the peasant was trained to expect him at the back door and to keep the visits from witnesses.

The rest was logistics. Cyanide obtained from an opposition politician who had made the great speech about Rasputinism, in crystals and in a small vial.[^14] A plan agreed in a railway carriage: gather at midnight, poison the pastries and the wine by half past twelve, then collect him by car — not to the front entrance but to a door off the yard, **so the silhouettes would not show through the iron grating of the gate**.

And a basement remodelled for the occasion into an old-Russian dining room. Chinese porcelain in wall niches. Carved chairs in leather from the storerooms. Ivory chalices. An inlaid ebony cabinet with concealed drawers. A sixteenth-century Italian crucifix of rock crystal chased with silver, standing on top of it. One conspirator who came to inspect the room approved of it on other grounds: the walls were thick and the two little windows were at pavement level, so it would even be possible to shoot.

*Read: lines 8206–9150.*

## Ch. 14 — He told everyone where he was going

The day before he died went as usual. The devotee arrived before noon and stayed until ten. She testified that he was excited and said today I'm going, without saying where.[^15]

Vyrubova came at eight and he told her he was going with the young prince to treat his wife. She did not know the wife was not in Petrograd. She advised him to refuse, on the grounds that **it was degrading that they were ashamed to receive him openly in the daytime and chose night instead**. He promised her he would not go.

The chapter's reading of this is the sharpest thing in it. Having promised to keep the trip secret, the peasant took no chances and told every close friend where he was going. He also believed the agents would follow him, and he was wrong, because the interior minister had lied to him about the guard. So he trusted the prince completely and took security measures anyway.

At ten a woman of about twenty-five arrived and stayed an hour — one of the transitory visitors to the little room with the sofa. His niece, who was staying in the flat, said plainly what she was for: she helped him remove the tension that took hold of him against his will. He was refining his nerves before a night that promised him so much.

His daughters came home at eleven. The elder testified that as she was going to bed he told her he was going to visit *the Little One*. And around midnight the interior minister called in.

The evening itself is documented from both directions, which is why it can be checked. The murderers wrote it up. So did a building custodian, a maid behind a kitchen curtain and a porter.

Wet snow was falling and the temperature was two or three degrees above freezing. A military car, rare then, arrived at the palace, waited, drove off, came back — **because the courtyard gate was closed, the prince having forgotten the arrangement**. After circling twice they gave up and went to the main entrance.[^16]

Downstairs, the basement had become what one of them called an elegant confectioner's box in the style of the old Russian palaces. A fire in the fireplace. The ivory crucifix on the mantel. A table under the window with sherry, port, madeira and marsala. A polar bear skin on the floor in front of a settee. Then they sampled the pastries before poisoning them — little pink and brown petits fours, chosen to match the colour of the wall.

They drank tea and waited nervously for half past eleven, when the agents would leave the flat on Gorokhovaya and the outside surveillance would be lifted.

The custodian saw the car arrive after midnight at locked gates. A man got out and went straight to the door, and when asked where he was going said: to Rasputin's. He was beardless, with a black moustache, a long fur coat and a black fur cap. The custodian pointed him to the front door. He went to the back one instead.

He felt his way up an unlit stairway and had difficulty finding the door. The chain jangled, the bolt squeaked, and he stepped into the kitchen. **He sensed someone watching him and instinctively pulled his cap down over his eyes** — correctly, because the maid slept in the kitchen behind a curtain, and she parted it and saw that it was the Little One who had come.

The bedroom was lit only by an icon lamp. Rasputin lit a candle. The bed was rumpled; he had probably been resting. His fur coat and beaver cap were ready beside it. He was wearing a silk shirt embroidered with cornflowers, girded with a thick crimson cord ending in two large tassels, wide black velveteen trousers and high boots.

What the prince wrote about the next moment is either remorse or its performance, and he wrote it in Paris years afterwards. He was overwhelmed with infinite pity. He was ashamed of the dirty, monstrous lie he was using. He despised himself and asked how he could have conceived such a base crime. Rasputin noticed none of it, and the prince asks the question the whole book has been circling. *What of his clairvoyance? What good was his gift of foresight if he did not see the trap that had been set for him?*

Then they went out into the dark stairwell and Rasputin locked the door behind him. **He took the prince's arm roughly and said *better let me guide you*, and led him down the dark stairs**.

*Read: lines 9151–9635.*

## Ch. 15 — Air in the lungs, and a report that vanished in the 1930s

The famous part of the story is the poison that did not work, and the chapter takes it apart with two arguments that both hold.

The first came from a grand duke who did not believe in devils and had used cyanide on insects. **The solution was too weak**. In their haste and anxiety they had made it up badly for the wine glasses. That is a plain explanation and it probably covers the wine.[^17] It does not cover the pastries, which had enough chipped into them to kill an ox. So the second argument is that he never ate them.

He kept a strict diet: no sweets, no meat, no pastries. His daughter says so. So does his secretary. So do the police chief and the interior minister in their testimony. His publisher explains that he tied the diet to his healing ability — fish, and no sweets — and says he did not break it even when drunk. A deputy chief of a judicial chamber who travelled with him described the boxes of candy in the compartment: he shared them and did not touch them.

So the pastries are a fabrication, added later as part of a story about a devil that ordinary men heroically destroyed. He drank a little of the wine and ate nothing. Which leaves the real question, and the chapter is honest that it cannot answer it. **He was in that basement for more than two hours, and by one careful account nearly three** — a nervous, impatient man, waiting for a woman who was not in the city, apparently having forgotten why he came.

Two explanations are offered and neither is asserted. The erotic one takes the grand duke's suspicion seriously: something happened between them, which is why Rasputin was content to wait indefinitely for the promised continuation, and why he did not notice a pistol in the hand of a man he had just been intimate with, and why his intuition was asleep. The realistic one is duller — that it all happened quickly and the long wait is an invention of the account.

What survives from either is one detail neither man would have invented. After being shot, coming to, Rasputin tore the epaulette off the prince's shoulder. **And he kept saying one word: *Felix, Felix***. The chapter reads that as the reason for the disgraceful scene that followed, in which the prince flailed at a dying man with the handle of a dumbbell.

The body came up in a river on the morning of 19 December.[^18] The shirt frozen to it had been pulled up, exposing a bullet wound. There was another bullet mark on the forehead and a bruise on the face from a kick to the temple. A photograph survives of it lifted onto a sledge in the white expanse of the frozen river, **and the raised icy hands could only be lowered after the corpse had thawed**.

The autopsy was done that night in an almshouse that had once been a way palace of Catherine the Great. The heart was removed into a container. The lungs were lifted out and put into alcohol — and the reason they were interesting is that they settled the last question. There was air in them. He had gone into the water alive.

The report was kept by the Academy of Military Medicine. In the 1930s it disappeared. What remains are police photographs of the naked body and its wounds.

The funeral was small and it is the one part of the story where the myths can be checked against witnesses, because four of them testified. A grave already dug in the centre of the unfinished chapel, on the left side of the nave, with the coffin already in it. The confessor and a monk. **No choristers — an assistant deacon sang**. One official watched from behind the bushes and recorded everything, including that he approached the grave beforehand and saw a metal coffin.

There was no opening in the lid. Every eyewitness says so. The story that the tsarina had one cut so she could see his face when she visited the crypt appears in numerous memoirs, and there was no crypt either: the coffin was covered with earth immediately. The tsar's diary for 21 December records it in one sentence, and the word he chose for the killers is the whole of his position. *We were present at a sad scene: the coffin with the body of the unforgettable Grigory, killed on the night of the 17th by monsters in the Yusupov house*.

Then the punishment, which was not one.[^19] The grand duke asked to be tried by court-martial, because he understood that such a trial would make him a hero across Russia — and because it would let the story they had agreed on be told in public, with the blood on somebody else's hands. The tsar understood that too, and there was no trial.

The tsarina's sister wrote asking for a pardon for the prince, and her letter is the clearest statement of how the family had come to see it. She had learned he was killed by a man who would not go into the army because he did not want to shed anyone's blood, and she pictured what he must have gone through before deciding. **The crime, she wrote, may be considered an act of patriotism**. Nicholas did not answer her letter.

*Read: lines 9636–9896.*

## Epilogue — Soldiers with picks, and a body that would not stay buried

The grave was opened because a captain had noticed a daily guard on a building site.[^20]

The chapel was abandoned and boarded up, so he and his soldiers climbed the rafters and got in through an opening on the second floor. They lit torches and set to work with picks. They were there for the jewels the tsarina was said to have put in the coffin.

The zinc-lined coffin lay deep. They pulled the lid off in a hurry and saw a head and arms folded crosswise. There were no jewels. On top of the folded arms was a small wooden icon, with the names of the tsarina and her daughters written on the back in indelible ink, in their own hands, and a line added by Vyrubova: *11 December 1916. Novgorod. Anna*.

The papers called it sacrilege — an icon in a coffin, and the coffin of a fornicator. **And the File shows the tsarina had nothing to do with it**. The icon had been given to Rasputin while he was alive, and the woman who washed and dressed his body put it in the coffin on her own initiative.

What followed reads like a rehearsal. The corpse was taken out of Tsarskoe Selo by railway freight car, packed in an enormous piano box and disguised as a musical instrument. In Petrograd it lay in the garage of the former court department among the royal carriages. On 11 March at dawn it was driven out along the old highway for a secret burial in an uninhabited place. Near Lesnoe the vehicle broke down — as the vehicle carrying the remains of the royal family would do eighteen months later. And it was decided to burn the corpse at once, right there, which is also what would be attempted at Ekaterinburg.

The pattern the chapter draws out of the rest is one that two policemen reached independently and both called superstitious.[^21] A man who reviewed the fates of everyone who had tied himself to Rasputin — the monk, the bishop, the official who made a brilliant career through him and then died of an incurable disease — arrived at the conviction that **Rasputin's hand was a heavy one**. The head of the Department of Police used almost the same words about the fatal disgrace that inevitably came to people who had sought support from him.

Both were thinking about careers. The chapter's point is that they should have been thinking about lives, because February was only the first step. After October, the men who had made the February Revolution were put into the same fortress cells as the tsarist ministers they had put there. One tsarist minister greeted one of the revolution's financiers happily: *so, it is you! Really, you didn't have to give the February Revolution five million*.

And on Gorokhovaya Street, where Rasputin had lived, the Bolsheviks opened the Cheka — the Extraordinary Commission that shared its name with the idealistic one of 1917 and shared nothing else. From that building many of his friends went to the wall.

The closing section says what the author thinks the man was, and it is the only place in the book where he says it straight.[^22] Deeply religious, and a great sinner. **With the simplicity of a century of uneducated peasantry, he tried to combine the passions of the body with the teachings of Christ**, and ended as a sectarian and a profligate while remaining deeply religious.

The poem quoted for it is Blok's, from 1914, and it is the argument in eight lines. *To sin shamelessly, endlessly, to lose count of the nights and days, and with a head unruly from drunkenness to pass sideways into the temple of God*. Three bows to the ground. Seven signs of the cross. A burning brow on a spat-on floor. A copper coin in the plate, and the hundred-year-old icon frame kissed three times or seven.

Happiness in the suffering of repentance, on a scale that matches the sin. And the claim the book ends on is a national one rather than a biographical one. He was the precursor of millions of peasants who, with religious consciousness in their souls, would nevertheless tear down churches — who dreamed of a reign of love and justice, and murdered and raped and flooded the country with blood, and destroyed themselves in the end.

*Read: lines 9897–10116.*

---

## Afterword — A writer at the funeral of his own characters

The last two pages are dated by an event: the coffins arriving from Ekaterinburg in 1998, to be buried in the city that had been renamed back to Saint Petersburg.[^23]

**And everything was as it had been in the peasant's day**. The Romanov family divided. Discord among the people. And church hierarchs inexplicably opposed to the funeral.

At the airport a guard of honour stood in ranks and the wind tore at the standard. The surviving descendants formed up near the plane. The author was there as a member of the government commission, watching, as he puts it, the funeral of his own characters.

Everybody wanted miracles, and the miracles were meteorological. The people who flew in with the coffins reported that as they were carried out of the cathedral in Ekaterinburg the heavens opened with a sheet of water over the church. The people meeting them replied that in Petersburg, where it had rained the day before, the sun had shone brilliantly all morning.

Then the cortege moved, and the quarrels stopped. **An unbroken line of people ran the whole way from the airport to the fortress, many kilometres of it**. They stood in the open windows of the buildings. Some waited on their knees. And the President, who had refused to attend the day before, flew to Petersburg that morning to repent before the coffins for all the evil deeds of the departing century.

They were buried across the river from their own palace, among their ancestors. The author records what the country felt as a long-forgotten sense of joyful union and a moved, happy ease — as if a stone had fallen away, as if some terrible spirit had finally released the tsars and flown away from Russia for good. And then the book's last two sentences, which withdraw it. *Or was it only for a moment? And an illusion, after all?*

*Read: lines 10117–10139.*

---

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, chapters 12 to the Afterword `[SPECULATIVE]`

Paradigm-obvious, and reading any of it as extraordinary is the modern reader's error. A police force running informants inside a protected man's household. This is what a political police did, and the surveillance had been in place since 1912 with the tsar's own consent. A minister and his deputy plotting against each other. Court and ministry factions had operated this way for generations, and the deputy's calculation — hand my chief to the sovereign and take his job — is a standard move, not a novelty.

Buying stolen letters back from a blackmailer abroad. The government had done this before and would do it again; the negotiation was routine and only the errand boy was a plant.

A grand duke expecting no punishment for a killing. Family members were tried by the sovereign's discretion, not by courts. The interesting thing is not that he escaped, but that he asked for a court-martial because he expected it to make him popular. A body burned by the roadside because the truck broke down. Improvisation of this kind was ordinary in March 1917, and the chapter's point is only that the same thing happened twice. Paradigm-breaking, and the cost is what marks it.

Showing a subordinate the money. The minister produced two packets of fifty thousand roubles and then doubled the offer, to a man he had known for weeks, for a murder. **The cost was immediate: the colonel reported it to the man he actually worked for**, and it became the evidence that destroyed him.

Telling everybody where you are going while promising to tell nobody. Rasputin's handling of his last evening is not the behaviour of a man walking into a trap blind — he told the devotee, told Vyrubova, told his daughter, and believed the guard would follow. The cost is that the one precaution he could not take himself had been removed by a minister he had installed.

Buying access with your own body. The prince submitted to being treated, alone, on the sofa, by the man he intended to kill, to earn the trust that would get him into a car at midnight. Whatever happened in that room, the cost was that he could never afterwards give a straight account of the murder, which is why the story he told has a devil in it.

Putting an icon signed by the empress and her daughters into the coffin. The woman who did it acted alone, and every newspaper attributed it to the tsarina. The cost fell entirely on someone who had not done it, at the moment she could least afford another charge. The tsar's word *monsters*. Writing it in his own diary about a grand duke and a prince of the empire, on the day of the funeral, is a break with everything a sovereign's diary was for.

## Ch. 13 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

The road not taken is the investigation that was run and came back empty, and then made no difference at all.

The Extraordinary Commission of 1917 set out to prove the empress had been in secret contact with her German relatives about a separate peace. It had the letters, the ministers, the household staff and the police files. **It found nothing**. And the evidence it did find ran the other way — the tsar's own answer to the German peace approach of late 1916, which was that the time had not come because Russia had not yet taken the Straits. Suppose that finding had been published in February 1917 rather than gathered afterwards. The counterfactual is tempting and it does not survive contact with the material.

The belief was not built out of evidence, so evidence could not take it down. It was built out of a German name, a chain of defeats that needed a cause, a man in the palace who had opposed the war, and a Duma speech that supplied the word. A nurse in the Winter Palace was already telling people there was a telephone line to Berlin. Nobody had seen it, and nobody would have gone to look.

The one document that would have mattered is the one that was burned. Ashes in a fireplace are the only piece of the case that cannot be cleared, and the chapter's own best reading is that what she destroyed was her brother's letters — which would show her receiving peace approaches from the German side and declining them. Innocent, and unpublishable in 1917, because the fact of the correspondence was the accusation.

So the road not taken is narrower than it looks. It is not *could the treason charge have been disproved*. It could, and was. It is **whether a disproof arriving in the middle of a losing war would have changed one mind**, and the answer the chapter's material gives is no — because the same population had been told the truth about the peasant for eight years by prime ministers, bishops and newspapers, and had believed whichever version fitted their existing view.

## Ch. 14 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take Rasputin at eight o'clock on the evening of 16 December, with Vyrubova in front of him telling him not to go.

An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/indirect-agency-deniable-power|deniable power]] would go straight at the arrangement rather than at the risk. Every protection he had was held by somebody else. The guard belonged to a minister he had installed. The surveillance belonged to a department he had helped staff. The route into his own flat had a back door that a young man had been trained to use so that nobody would see him arrive. A man whose whole position rests on being indispensable to other people has no independent security at all, and the counsel is that the moment to notice this is not the night it is withdrawn. He had spent a year making men powerful on condition that they were useful to Mama, and had never once made one useful to himself.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/scapegoating-as-stress-displacement|scapegoating under stress]]** would tell him the country had already selected him and that this was the fact governing the evening. A Duma speech six weeks earlier had put the empress's name beside the adventurers around her and asked whether it was stupidity or treason, and the word had rooted in millions. A losing army needed a cause. He was the only available one who was not a general, not a minister and not the crown — and a designated cause does not get to negotiate the timing of its own removal. The counsel is not caution about one invitation. It is that in the winter of 1916 there was no version of this evening he could have declined enough times.

They disagree about what he should have done. The first says he should have built his own protection. The second says by December there was nothing left to build.

What both agree on is the finding, and it is in his own behaviour rather than in either reading. He told four people where he was going while promising to tell nobody. That is not carelessness and it is not clairvoyance failing. **It is a man who knew he was in danger, taking the only precaution available to a person with no independent means — leaving a trail of witnesses**. It worked exactly as designed: the maid, the porter, the custodian, the devotee, the daughter and Vyrubova between them reconstructed the night within days. He could not save himself. He could make sure the story could not be hidden, and he did.

A third voice, from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|the dichotomy of control]], is about Vyrubova rather than about him, and it is the shortest. She gave him the right advice for the wrong reason — that going at night was degrading, since they were ashamed to receive him by day. She was reading a question of status where the question was survival. And she was satisfied by a promise, which is the cheapest thing a frightened man can give. What was in her power was to send somebody with him, and she did not think of it, because she was arguing about honour.

## Ch. 15 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: relying on a document that only one institution holds.

The autopsy on Rasputin's body settled the last factual question about his death. The lungs went into alcohol, they contained air, and he had been thrown into the water alive. The report was retained by the Academy of Military Medicine, and in the 1930s it disappeared. What survives is police photographs of the naked body, and a policeman's second-hand recollection of what a minister told him the autopsy showed. So the strongest single conclusion in the whole story now rests on hearsay and a set of pictures.

The pattern is not confined to that one file, and this part of the book is where it becomes visible. The prosecution documents on Rasputin were destroyed by officials who had themselves been among his visitors. The testimony of the prostitutes was lost, leaving exactly one deposition. **The last photograph of him alive is described in detail by two witnesses and cannot be found**. Each loss is separately explicable, and each removes the item that would have decided a question.

Scope conditions. This bites where a finding is embodied in a single physical document; where that document is held by one institution rather than distributed; and where a later regime has an interest in the subject. All three held — the third decisively, since a report proving the elder was murdered by aristocrats was of no use to anybody after 1930.

The general form. A conclusion is only as durable as the number of independent places its evidence sits. Not the quality of the evidence, not who signed it, not whether it was believed at the time — the count of copies in unrelated hands. Modern equivalent: any finding that exists as one file in one archive, where the custodian outlives the interest that produced it.

The second-order finding is what fills the gap, and it is the reason this book had to be written. Where the document went, the legend grew — the devil who survived cyanide, the crypt with a window in the coffin, the enormous body. Each of those is an answer to a question a missing document used to close. The chapter can refute the pastries because a diet is attested by six witnesses, and it cannot refute anything the autopsy would have covered.

## Epilogue — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

Decision type: reading a pattern off a list of people's fates.

Two men reached the same conclusion independently and both hedged it as superstition. One reviewed the people who had linked their destinies to Rasputin — a monk ruined, a bishop broken, an official who rose brilliantly and then died of an incurable disease — and concluded that **the hand was a heavy one**. The head of the Department of Police used almost identical words about the fatal disgrace that came to everyone who sought support from him.

The chapter accepts the observation and rejects the frame, and the correction is the transferable part. They were counting careers inside a system that was about to kill everyone in it. After October the men who made the February Revolution went into the same fortress cells as the ministers they had put there. The Cheka opened in his old street and sent his friends to the wall from it. The base rate for a well-connected Russian in 1917 to 1921 was catastrophe, whether or not he had ever met a peasant from Tobolsk.

Scope conditions. The error appears wherever a striking outcome is observed in a selected group; where no comparison group is looked at; and where a causal story is available that feels explanatory. All three held. The group was self-selected by proximity to power, nobody counted the fates of equally placed men who had avoided him, and *a heavy hand* is a satisfying story.

The general form. **A list of bad outcomes among people connected to one person is evidence of nothing until you know what happened to the people who were not connected to him**. The observation may still be true; it is simply not yet a finding. Modern equivalent: any claim that association with a person, product or place is unlucky, made from a roster of the associated and no roster of anyone else.

What makes this one worth keeping rather than dismissing is that the men making the error were professionals at assessing evidence, and one of them ran the Department of Police. They were not credulous. They were inside the selected group, which is the condition under which the error is invisible, because every case you can think of is a case that reached you through the same filter.

---

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/The Rasputin File.md`, lines 7572–10139: ch. 12 (7572–8205), ch. 13 (8206–9150), ch. 14 (9151–9635), ch. 15 (9636–9896), Epilogue (9897–10116), Afterword (10117–10139).

The strongest documentation in this part. Komissarov's testimony on the double reporting line, the safe flat and the gifts — a witness with no reason to invent the humiliating parts. Beletsky's testimony, which is self-serving on the murder plot and precise on everything else, and which is corroborated by Komissarov on the money and the poison bottles. The surveillance reports quoted with dates, including the petitioner's statement to the porter on 3 November 1915. Yusupov's letter to his wife, which puts the plan in writing before the event. The tsar's diary entry of 21 December. The four eyewitness statements on the burial, which agree with each other and against every memoir. The tsarina's letters, which date the dropping of the case against Rasputin's secretary to the week before the murder. And the physical evidence: the police photographs of the body, and the recorded fact that there was air in the lungs.

Where the evidence is a witness with a motive, and the text says so. Yusupov's memoirs are treated throughout as an account constructed to make the killing heroic — the chapter says outright that the pastries were added later as part of a fable about destroying a devil, and demonstrates it from six independent statements about his diet. Purishkevich's account is the same document in a different voice. Grand Duke Nikolai Mikhailovich's diary is used as the sharpest reading available and is also the source of the erotic hypothesis, which the chapter carries without endorsing. `[CONTESTED]` And Vyrubova's testimony is again performance, though here it is corroborated on the burial by three other witnesses.

Where the reasoning is the author's rather than the record's, and it is heavy in these chapters. That the conspiracy began with the grand duke rather than the prince. That the tsarina burned her brother's letters. That the long wait in the basement is explained by an encounter between the two men. `[PLAUSIBLE — needs corroboration]` That the healing sessions were an exorcism of the demon of lechery in the sect's own sense. And the closing claim of the Epilogue — that Rasputin was the precursor of the peasants who would tear down churches — which is a thesis about a nation drawn from one biography, offered without qualification. `[n=1 OBSERVED]`

A note on the source's own position. These chapters are where the book's method is at its most powerful and its most exposed, and the two are separated by about forty lines. The demolition of the pastries story is exemplary: a claim from a hostile memoir, checked against six independent statements, and dropped. The reconstruction of the three hours is the same instinct with no documents under it, and the reader is given no marker that the operation has changed. The Afterword is a different register again — the author placing himself in the story as a member of a government commission, watching the funeral of his own characters — and it closes by withdrawing its own consolation in two sentences. Bounded absence. No claim is made about material outside lines 7572–10139.

# What Their World Took For Granted — Moynahan, Preface and Chapters 1–7

> **The Preface and first seven chapters of Brian Moynahan, *Rasputin: The Saint Who Sinned*** — a city where the censors' ink blots were called caviar, a boy who saw a white flash under a larch tree, a woman dragged naked behind a horse for adultery, four out of five guardsmen drowned in a bog, and a French butcher's boy who told an empress she was carrying a son. Read from `RAW/books/Rasputin the Saint Who Sinned.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
>
> ⚠ **Second book**. Parts 1–4 cover Radzinsky's *The Rasputin File*, which is built out of the 1917 interrogation records. This one is a narrative biography written in English for a general reader, and its strengths are the opposite ones — the texture of the village, the city and the court, which the File does not carry. **The two books are read separately and joined only in the synthesis**.
>
> **Siblings:** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-part-1|Part 1 — Radzinsky, Introduction and Chapters 1–4]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-part-2|Part 2 — Radzinsky, Chapters 5–6]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-part-3|Part 3 — Radzinsky, Chapters 7–11]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-part-4|Part 4 — Radzinsky, Chapters 12–15, Epilogue and Afterword]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-part-6|Part 6 — Moynahan, Chapters 8–15]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-part-7|Part 7 — Moynahan, Chapters 16–22]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology-synthesis|What Runs Through All of It]].

## Preface — What kind of thing the book thinks he was

The Preface states its position in one sentence and then spends the rest of the book on it. He was not mad, or monk, or saint — and the three words are the three legends, taken in the order they are usually met.[^1]

What replaces them is a list rather than a verdict, and the list refuses to resolve. Intelligent. Ambitious. Idle. Generous to a fault. Spiritual. And utterly amoral.

The economics of his fame are worth having, because they explain the source problem for everything that follows. While the censors forbade any public mention of him, **newspaper editors were happy to trade heavy fines for the guaranteed increase in circulation he brought**. After his death the memoirs of people who had known him became a small industry — politicians, a defrocked priest, secret police officers, women admirers. His murderer rebuilt part of a fortune the Bolsheviks had seized, with bestselling accounts of the killing and a slander suit against a Hollywood studio. So almost every account of him was written by somebody with a financial or reputational stake in the version they told.

The Preface also does something the other book never does: it says why he is still readable, and one of the reasons is not historical at all. For all the medieval trappings, he was curiously modern. His skills as a spiritual leader and a manipulator of souls match the latter-day guru's. Keep the sex, change the drugs to drink and the rock 'n' roll to Gypsy music, **and the blend of charisma and outrage is the precursor of the modern superstar**.

And it notes the calendar, which matters for every date in this part. Russia used the Julian calendar, twelve days behind the Western one in the nineteenth century and thirteen in the twentieth. The murder on 16 December 1916 is 29 December in the West — and the book applies Russian dating even to events outside Russia.

*Read: lines 73–94.*

---

## Ch. 1 — A city where the censors' ink was called caviar

The book opens in the last winter, and its method is to describe the place rather than the man.

Two streetlamps in three were unlit. The sidewalks were no longer swept and filled with rubbish and slush, and with queues of ill-clad men and women from four each morning. Families from territories lost to the Germans huddled in sheds by the railway stations, dying of typhus and simple exhaustion, blown away like gossamer.[^2]

The buildings themselves were an act of will. Pink granite and yellow- and green-washed stucco in faultless lines, **raised out of bogs on piles driven by gangs of forced labourers two centuries before**. When onshore winds lifted the Neva, alarm bells told people to go upstairs before the floods came into the basements.

And through all of it, one word. *Rasputin, Rasputin, Rasputin* — in the food lines, the salons, the rooming houses. It was like a refrain, one woman wrote. *It became a dusk enveloping all our world, eclipsing the sun. How could so pitiful a wretch throw so vast a shadow?*

The book puts the incredulity where it belongs, in the physical detail. He was a dark peasant from a distant Siberian bog. He had shat in the open like an animal as a boy. He still sucked soup from the bowl and ate fish with his fingers, his body gave off a powerful acrid smell, and he could barely scrawl his name. And he was rumoured to have the ear of the empress, to appoint the mightiest officials of state with her, to be plotting a separate peace, and to see the future. He was also visible — a shaggy figure with a sable coat thrown over peasant boots, catching cabs and dining in restaurants.

**The censorship produced the opposite of what it intended, and the book's word for it is the best thing in the chapter**. They daubed ink over the newspaper columns that mentioned him, and the black blotches were called *caviar*.[^3] Readers knew whom the caviar was protecting. So they invented stories of their own.

What they invented is on record because it was printed and sold. Crude cartoons of him emerging from the naked empress's nipples to tower over Russia. Playing cards in gambling dens with his head in place of the tsar's on the king of spades. A caricature icon showing him with a vodka bottle in one hand and the naked tsar cradled like the Christ child in the other, hellfire licking his boots, naked women with angels' wings and black stockings flying round his head. A society hostess, sick of hearing about him, put a printed sign in her dining room: *we do not discuss Rasputin here*. They discussed him.

**A poet's diagnosis of the country is the chapter's frame**. It had become a large lunatic asylum — one that looked normal, like an asylum on open day, but where the inmates were all mad. She had renamed the capital too. The name had been changed from the German-sounding St. Petersburg to Petrograd at the start of the war, and she called it Devil-town.

The statistics under the mood are the ones that carry. The suicide rate tripled, in a country at war, while it was falling everywhere else — and two victims in three were under twenty-eight. The grand mistress of the court calculated that half her circle were divorced, and made the sharpest observation of the year about it: **have you noticed that nobody understands the story of *Anna Karenina* nowadays? Today Anna would have divorced her husband and married Vronsky, and there the story would have ended**.

Flour had doubled since the war began. Sugar had risen fourfold. **Aspirin had risen fifty times**. In one factory district the living had less space than the dead in the municipal cemetery.

Then the front, and the chapter's central atrocity, which is not committed by any villain in the story. At Kovel in the autumn of 1916 the Guards attacked seventeen times in three months across open marsh. They were sent into a swamp. German aircraft strafed them as they struggled in the mud, then refuelled, rearmed and came back.[^4]

The British attaché called these regiments physically the finest human animals in Europe. In under a fortnight four out of five of the empire's best troops were gone. Half-trained replacements were ordered to continue, advancing in long thin lines, dressing to the left, officers at the head and sergeant majors behind to shoot deserters — because their officers did not think them capable of manoeuvre. So many corpses lay in no-man's-land that the Germans refused a truce to bury them, and **the heaps became a physical obstacle to further Russian attacks**.

What the tsar wrote when he had to dismiss the general responsible is the whole of the chapter's case about him. *What an honest and well-bred man he is! I have given him leave for two months. I have promised that if some vacancies occur in the Guards Corps to appoint him there*.

And what the soldiers believed is where the last year came from. They no longer thought of themselves as Russian soldiers; they were just men who were going to die. They told each other the government had been paid a billion roubles by Berlin to make sure as few of them survived as possible. Their special hatred was for the German-born empress — that she had a radio hidden under the eaves of her palace, that she passed secrets to her sister in Prussia, and that to accept a decoration from her meant certain death.

*Read: lines 142–313.*

---

## Ch. 2 — A boy under a larch tree, and a woman dragged behind a horse

The village is described before the man, and the description is the argument.

Pokrovskoye was rough wooden cabins on a Siberian riverbank. The farming year was two brief bursts of labour — men with scythes, **women following with sickles to reap what was left** — then threshing with iron chains on wooden handles, then a string of autumn cyclones that left the village mud-bound. Then the same again.[^5]

Elsewhere Russia was producing great writers, musicians and industrialists, and revolutionaries famous across Europe for their love of violence. In Pokrovskoye eternal silence was master. Politics were irrelevant — no politician came, they had no vote, newspapers meant nothing to men who could not read. There was no university in Siberia's four and a half million square miles.

What filled that space was religion, and the book is precise about the mechanism. Monotony and freezing distance conspired to make Siberians religious. **The beauty of the Orthodox service, the hypnotic chants, the ecstatic Easter cry, fell on arid minds like mystic liquid**. Ragged pilgrims passed through on the high road, tapping on doors for a night's lodging on their way to one monastery or another.

At a service when he was fourteen the priest read a passage he never forgot. *The Kingdom of God cometh not with observation. Neither say they, Lo here! or Lo there! for behold the Kingdom of God is within you*.

His parents walked home for Sunday dinner. He went into the woods, lay on the ground and had the experience the whole life rests on. A spark grew in his mind, coming nearer and brightening — a soft golden glow that erupted in a blinding white flash. He prayed with tears on his face and ran home to tell his mother: *I can only say I almost saw God*. She was frightened, and told him only great saints see God, and whatever he did he must not tell his father, who would certainly punish him.

Years later he took his own children back to that larch tree and told them what he had understood there. *God is here, inside, this moment — forever*.

Then the other half of the same childhood, and the book refuses to arrange them into a sequence. He did little work on the farm. He mooned about without friends and got into fights with boys who called him *coward*. He started drinking vodka at fifteen and more after his marriage at twenty. **Neighbours gave evidence to a church investigator that he was a thief**, and one of them described catching him with a cartload of stolen fence poles.[^6]

That neighbour's testimony is the most useful thing in the chapter, because of how it ends. He demanded that the thief take the poles to the constable. When he refused and moved to strike with an axe, the neighbour hit him with a pole so hard that blood ran from his nose and mouth in a stream and he fell unconscious — and at first the man thought he had killed him. A pair of the same man's horses were stolen from his meadow soon after.

The village met to discuss exiling him and his two companions to eastern Siberia. The companions were expelled for horse stealing. He survived — and faced a local court on the fence poles. And then the scene that shows what the village actually was, which no amount of description of the farming year would supply.

A young widow took a wanderer into her cabin and her bed. The village gossip spotted it and raised the alarm. **Rasputin's own father was one of the men who caught her and hauled her to the priest**. The priest pronounced the punishment for a woman taken in sin: she was to be stripped naked and whipped out of the village.[^7]

Her dress was ripped off. Her hair was shorn with shears. She was tied to a horse's saddle and dragged between a double line of villagers who beat her with sticks and leather straps — eyes popping, lips drawn back. Bleeding and unconscious, she was pulled out of the village. He found her in a field afterwards and comforted her, and as he touched each wound in turn the bleeding stopped. That is his daughter's account, told long after, and it is where the healing begins in this version.

The next day, at a wedding, two boys gave him vodka and talked about finding a woman. Drunk, he said he knew where one was and led them to her refuge. **Their noisy arrival terrified her**. He insisted they leave her alone and then ran off in tears.

His own account of the years that followed went to a newspaper two decades later, and it is worth having in his words. *When I was fifteen, in my village, in the summertime, when the sun shone warmly and the birds sang heavenly songs, I walked along the path and did not dare go along the middle of it. I was dreaming about God. My soul was longing to fly afar. I often wept and did not know where the tears came from and what they were for*.

At eighteen the light came back while he was ploughing. It exploded out of the furrows and became a vision of the Virgin, surrounded by throbbing light, her hand above his head in blessing. He led the plough horse back to the barn shaking. He called it his awakening. The chapter's own comment on the two accounts is the honest one. The introverted, sensitive boy of the newspaper interview was a stranger to the investigator's witnesses, who remembered a lout with a swagger.

## Ch. 3 — The one career a peasant could have

Three months at a monastery in the foothills of the Urals changed him, and the church's own investigator says so in the language of a case file. **It ended the first, early, wild and loose period of his life**, after which he became a different person for a long time.[^8] What he was there to learn is the chapter's real subject, and it needs explaining because English has no word for it. Hermits lived in huts in the surrounding forest in self-denial, eating black bread and water and sleeping on bare mud in celebration of poverty. **The huts were called *skites*, and the men in them were *staretsy* — elders**, holy men held to have a special grace from God.

What an elder did was described best by Dostoyevsky, and the book quotes him because the description is closer to an Indian guru than to anything Western. The elder takes your soul and your will into his soul and will. Having chosen him, you surrender your will in complete obedience and self-abnegation — and in return you attain a total freedom, meaning freedom from yourself, and escape the fate of people who live without ever finding the self inside them. The binder and the bound were linked in perpetual confession. The particular elder he walked to daily was fifty, and had **squandered an inheritance on drink, cards and whores before a sudden aversion to pleasure struck him**. He wore penitential chains and kept a flock of raucous chickens, starving himself until he had beaten the temptation and then giving the eggs away.

What the young man took from him is stated plainly and it is a technique rather than a doctrine. That strange force of will, that almost magnetic glance — which he acquired so strongly himself. Then the chapter says the thing that makes the whole life legible, and it is an argument about labour markets rather than about souls.[^9]

To be an elder was thought a noble calling. To a sly man it was a career — the most brilliant open to a peasant. A handful of his contemporaries climbed out of the ranks of the army to become generals. A few became writers and scholars. Rather more succeeded in commerce. He was undisciplined, unbookish and no tradesman, and the church itself offered little to an ambitious peasant with a wife.

**No barriers applied to elders**. Dostoyevsky's was a former officer from a landowning family. Others were peasants. Some — the holy fools — were half-wits. The requirements were self-confidence, insight into unhappy minds, and the ability to calm them, and he had all three. A good elder dressed himself in philosophy, homespun or complex, but the fundamental skill was to seek out nervous and troubled people and lead them by the nose.

What he was like when he came home is on record from three separate villagers, and none of them says *holy*. He seemed to have become a madman — coming home without his hat, hair loose and flowing, singing and gesticulating. Standing in the church he stared wildly and looked about him. He would arrive before the priest, take a place in the choir, **and strike his head on the floor until blood flowed**. Asked a question he would be silent a long while as though thinking hard, then, half awake, utter a few mysterious disconnected phrases.

The church investigator's own summary is the coldest and the most useful. The visit left anguish in his soul in the form of extreme nervousness, constant restless jerky movements, incoherent speech, and the permanent alternation of extreme agitation with depression. The book's gloss on that is four words: the lout had found God and turned manic depressive.

What is not disputed is the change in habit. He gave up drinking, smoking and meat, started to shun people, prayed a great deal, and learned to read church Slavonic. The smoking and the meat stopped for good. He committed phrases and half-chapters of the Bible to memory and mumbled them as he walked. Then he went on the road, because hardship was the qualification. **He was never a monk and he was never solitary** — he was a *strannik*, a wanderer, and the pilgrim trail was where he won his spurs.

The kit is listed and it is worth the space: a sheepskin coat, boots, a peasant cap, and a pack holding a spare blouse and bark sandals, a cross and a Bible, a water bottle, a knife, an icon and an emergency loaf. His feet were bound to the calf with strips of cloth, and he muttered *Lord have mercy, Lord have mercy* to their rhythm. A ragged army of the same men crossed the empire. Some went barefoot in winter with chains on their legs, rejoicing in the trail of blood they left on the snow.

**And the police could do nothing about them**, which is the chapter's sharpest institutional observation.[^10] The Okhrana chief called them the out-and-out anarchist element among Russian peasants: a wanderer had no papers or false ones, concealed his real name with the utmost persistence, and so escaped every obligation the state could impose. It was his duty to suppress them and he admitted that in practice this was uncommonly difficult.

The reason it was difficult was popular rather than legal. Russians had a special feeling for *blessed are the meek*, and pitied those in need. **They remembered the robbers beside the crucified Christ and called them *unfortunates***. It was an honour to feed and shelter a wanderer. He walked up to thirty miles a day and got as far as Mount Athos, two thousand miles from home — a peninsula where no smooth-faced man and no female of any kind was admitted, so that even the cattle grazing the steep fields were all bulls.

One detail marks him out from the crowd he walked in. **Wandering was normally what men did between the end of their working lives and death**. They sold their tools and livestock, gave the money to their children, and set off for the holy places, working for their tickets to heaven. He was in his prime. He was preparing for life.

Back home his wife ran the farm well enough to afford two servants. He returned often enough to father three children. And while he was there he practised. The men laughed at the idea of him becoming an elder. The women were less sure — and started bringing him hysterical girls, lame widows and sick children.

## Ch. 4 — The city as a machine for swallowing peasants

He arrived in the capital **like a projectile from the medieval past**, tattered, black and muttering.[^11]

The inventory is exact because a hostile monk wrote it down. A cheap grey coat with beggars' pockets bulging as if full of food. Threadbare trousers whose seat *flapped like a torn old hammock*. Peasant boots blackened with tar — and the tar became part of the technique, because he left traces of it on the skirts of fashionable women he embraced, as a keepsake.

What the city normally did to men like him is the chapter's context and it is brutal. Peasants found it awesome, foreign, almost astral. It sucked them in as unskilled labourers and gave them the witless faces of zombies. One observer's description of the work: apart from muscle power nothing significant is required, neither literacy nor skill nor even quick-wittedness — carrying iron, loading wagons, digging pits. **His chief task is to survive on seventy kopecks a day**. They kept country habits, and walked past the glittering shops on their hours off with doltish wonderment.

The city itself was an argument in stone. It was not Russian, and not truly European. It was moored at a swampy edge of the empire it ruled, on a level with Greenland and southern Alaska, damp with sea fog in winter and hazed with the smoke of burning forests when summer lightning struck. Gogol thought everything in it breathed falsehood. Its great architects were Italian. Its streets were wide and perfectly straight, and the main avenue ran two and a half miles between palaces and arcades.

It was unmistakably a city built to a prescription by autocrats, and it was dynastic: statues of Romanovs glared blindly at its flat horizons.

Two buildings a few hundred yards apart carry the whole political system. On the northern shore, the cathedral where generations of Romanovs were buried. **Close by, the fortress, its thick walls surrounded by water, in whose cells with iron-sheeted windows generations of their enemies had languished**.

The economy was the fastest growing of any major country and it ran on foreign money.[^12] British and French investors held millions of roubles in high-yielding government bonds. Foreign businessmen had their own Anglican, Lutheran and Catholic churches, an English bookshop and a nine-hole golf course. Four transactions in five went through one exchange.

The prices are given because they show who the city was for. A room with a bath at the best hotel from seven and a half roubles — about three dollars. Dinner at the grand restaurants, two and a half roubles, a dollar.

Against that, the students: a *university proletariat* with thin pinched faces in blue caps and shabby greatcoats, **aged prematurely from hunger and exhaustion**. Livelier souls formed circles to plot revolution. Lenin's elder brother had been hanged for planning to kill a tsar with a bomb hidden in a medical dictionary. Three government ministers had been murdered by students since the turn of the century.

And over the whole thing the same nervousness that runs through chapter 1, arriving here fifteen years early in a poem. The Pale Horse charging into a storm of cars, buses, whirling signs, cracking whips and screaming newsboys. *Time quivers and the Look is Terror. In letters of fire the Horseman's scroll spells Death*. Then the vision passes, and only a woman from a brothel and an escaped madman still stretch their hands towards it.

**The chapter's conclusion is one sentence and it explains everything the next twelve years contain**. He took to the city without fuss, because the city — restless, satiated, craving sensation — was ready for him. The law courts were crowded with hysterical women listening eagerly to details of bloody and prurient crimes.

## Ch. 5 — A blood disease, a French butcher's boy, and an empress who was never liked

This chapter is about the woman rather than the man, and it starts from a fact of biology that decided the reign. Her grandmother was Queen Victoria, whose nine children and thirty-five grandchildren included kings of England, the German kaiser, the queen of Spain and this empress. She was also the origin of the disease.[^13]

The mechanism is given plainly. Haemophiliacs cannot synthesise the protein that lets blood clot. The slightest wound produces prolonged bleeding, and internal bleeding can start for no reason, **with such violence and pain that joints become deformed**. It passes through the female line to male children only.

Her own mother had watched it happen. A brother lamed by constant haemorrhages. Then her own son, who cut his ear at two and bled continuously, and who at three ran across the room while she was practising Chopin's Funeral March, tried to steady himself on an unlatched bow window, fell two storeys into the garden and died of a brain haemorrhage that evening. She was six when her mother died. Her mother had caught diphtheria from embracing the surviving son to break the news of his sister's death — what the British prime minister called the kiss of death.

What the grandmother taught her instead of a childhood is the other half of it. **She was drilled to hold her head high and still for ten minutes at a time**, and practised social graces by touring a room and talking to pieces of furniture as though they were people. She was painfully shy outside the family and covered it.

The marriage began at a funeral and never recovered from it.[^14] The old tsar's coffin took a week to reach the capital, stopping in cities for services. She arrived behind it, half-masked by driving sleet, and onlookers said: she has come to us behind a coffin.

The wedding was brought forward to the week after the funeral because it fell on the dowager's birthday, when protocol allowed court mourning to be lifted for twenty-four hours. The bride had no trousseau. She wore a diamond tiara and a necklace of 475 carats, and the court went back into mourning the same afternoon. Her own line about it: *one day in deepest mourning lamenting a beloved one, the next day in smartest clothes being married*.

**Society did not like her and she did not like it**. She was shy and her smile was thin-lipped. She preferred children and old people to her own contemporaries. The director of the imperial theatres said her face blotched red with the effort of holding a conversation, and that people ignored her, so that she was only a name, a walking picture.

The coronation carried the omen the whole reign was read through. The tsar's chain of an order fell from his shoulders during the five-hour ceremony, and the incident was kept secret. The next morning half a million people came to an open-air feast for free beer and coronation mugs, so densely packed that a patrolling Cossack found his horse lifted off the ground. A rumour went round that the beer was running out.

The official death toll was 1,389 and the real figure was probably higher. **The couple were advised by the tsar's uncles to attend a gala ball that evening as planned, and did**, with her eyes red from crying. They visited the injured and gave each family a thousand roubles. The folk memory stayed, and with it the superstition that these two would lead Russia to tragedy.

The politics of the marriage are summarised in a single exchange. When the tsar rebuked a provincial council for its *senseless dreams of participation* in government, his old tutor in absolutism exploded and was asked who could have advised him to do such a thing. Have you not guessed? Of course, it is the young empress.

How could she, when she knew nothing of Russia? **She thought she knew everything**, the old man replied, and was obsessed with the idea that her husband did not assert himself enough. *She is more autocratic than Peter the Great, and perhaps as cruel as Ivan the Terrible. Hers is a small mind that believes it harbours great intelligence*.

Then the succession, which is where the holy men come in.[^15] By 1901 she had four children, healthy and lively, and all girls. A half-mad tsar a century earlier had expressed his hatred of women in general and his mother in particular by abolishing primogeniture and replacing it with Salic law, under which no woman could inherit. So four daughters counted for nothing, and the tsar then fell ill with typhoid. The man they found was a French faith healer whose real name was not the one he used, who had started work at thirteen in a Lyons butcher's shop and set up as a healer in his early twenties. He was a peasant's son and proud of it, a dabbler in right-wing politics, and — like the man who replaced him — he **drew close to people and told them in a few words what was troubling them, and what they did not dare confess**.

He claimed he could tell the sex of an unborn child.

What followed is the part the book uses as a template. The imperial couple visited the palace where he was staying almost every other evening and practised spiritualism. The French ambassador was told he had raised the ghost of the dead tsar to advise his son on how to govern Russia. Others said he controlled the weather to keep the seas smooth for the imperial yacht.

And one exchange catches the whole atmosphere. The richest man in Russia bowed to a grand duchess whose carriage passed him in the Crimea, and was cut. He asked her later why. You couldn't have seen me, she explained, for I was with the doctor, and when he wears a hat he is invisible, and so are those with him.

The state's own machinery had already reported on him and been punished for it. The empress wanted his medical status officially recognised, so the Okhrana's man in Paris was asked to persuade the French government to grant him a diploma. **He protested that this was impossible and prepared a report on the man's actual activities**, describing a clever confidence trickster who exercised power over people with weak personalities. He was promptly sacked by the interior minister. The consequences reached the money. A Rothschild in France told a Russian minister he feared for his enormous Russian investments, because a country whose court had been penetrated by a charlatan was no place to put money.

Then the healer overreached and the mechanism broke on its own. In 1902 he convinced her she was carrying a son. She stopped wearing a corset.

## Ch. 6 — A fleet sailing round Africa, and a crowd singing hymns

The chapter runs two stories in parallel — a naval expedition and a peasant's arrival — and the parallel is the argument.

The fleet sailed to relieve a besieged port, and the book's judgement on it is a question mark. **Rarely, never, has a naval expedition been so botched**.[^16] The commander called his second-in-command *the sack of shit*. Three ships collided almost at once, and the funeral party for a dead petty officer could not fire a salute because the men did not know how to load their rifles.

Suez was closed to them so they went round Africa. The commander was terrified of running out of fuel and piled coal on the decks and around the gun turrets, sealing the ventilators and portholes against coal dust so that men dropped with heat exhaustion in the tropics. **No gun drills could be practised without dislodging the coal**.

While they were off Nigeria, the Japanese took the high ground above the port and sank what was left of the fleet they were sailing to relieve. They reached Madagascar to learn that the garrison had surrendered the week before. Supply ships from home brought thousands of winter uniforms instead of ammunition and wireless sets.

When the number two died as they neared the strait, the commander did not bother to tell the man who was supposed to succeed him, and the dead man's flag went on flying from his battleship. Four battleships were sunk before nightfall on the first day. **The sealed coffin was found floating among the debris**.

Meanwhile, in a village in Siberia, a man read the reports of the strikes and riots that were following the defeats and began to feel that God required some mission of him. His wife believed he had seen another vision of the Virgin, commanding him to go to the capital. He said nothing of it himself.

What he arrived into was the massacre.[^17] A procession of workers in padded jackets, students with scarves over their ears, and women and children in their Sunday best, marching with church banners, icons and Russian flags. No red was to be seen, not a red handkerchief. They carried no weapons, not so much as a penknife, and they sang hymns as they walked to the Winter Palace. **Their Little Father was not in the capital**.

*Save us, O Lord, your people! How glorious is our Lord in Zion!*

The troops blocking the avenues had been issued live ammunition and an extra vodka ration the night before, and told that the workers were plotting to destroy the palace. At least 150 were killed and three times as many wounded. The light failed and the sun went out in a foggy red circle. In mid-afternoon a rainbow glistened, and then the wind came up and it snowed in early darkness.

The priest who organised it reached a writer's flat that evening, disguised, his beard cut in tufts, blue with cold and hysteria. **Give me something to drink. Wine. Everyone's dead**.

Ten days later the tsar received a hand-picked delegation of workers and told them: *I believe in the honest feelings of the working people and in their unshakable loyalty to me. Therefore, I forgive them*. The workers spat at the delegates and called the fifty thousand roubles he gave the victims' families blood money. And the priest left a letter to be read out: *there is no tsar!*

Three weeks later a bomb of nitroglycerin blasted a grand duke into slicks of flesh that stuck to the Kremlin gate as he drove through it. The assassin made no attempt to escape. The widow visited him in prison and offered to plead for his life if he expressed sorrow. He refused, saying his death would speed the fall of the autocracy. **She withdrew from society into prayer and built an abbey**. And this is where the peasant becomes useful, and the book's explanation of why is the sharpest sentence in the part.

Violence spread in the cities and there was cattle maiming and barn burning in the provinces. The rich needed reassurance. He provided it — a man of the people, a symbol that the real Russia had not turned on them, a tsar-loving and God-fearing peasant who was also a phenomenon, unique and exciting. He took minds off dark events. What he actually did in a drawing room was watched and written down by a scholar of the sects who was invited to observe him, and the account is a procedure.[^18] He arrived late, walked straight in though he had never been in the house, and **attacked his hostess about her collection of paintings and antiques**. *Why is it, Mother, that you hang up so much?*

The eyes are described the same way as everywhere else — pupils sparkling with a phosphorescent light, groping listeners with his eyes. Sometimes his speech slowed to a drawl and he told a confused story as if his mind were far away, then snapped to with *what's the matter with me?* and changed the subject.

Then the technique proper. He picked out one woman and stared at her. Then turned abruptly and talked to somebody else. **Fifteen or twenty minutes later he broke off mid-conversation and went back to her** — *it's no good, Mother, no good, well* — and she was flustered.

The room did the rest. They whispered that he had guessed something, that he had said the truth, that he saw a lot. The atmosphere became nervously heightened, and the observer named it precisely: it was the feeling you get in monasteries, around elders and prophets.

The salons then competed for him, and what they did to him is the chapter's last comment on the whole arrangement. The unbalanced society ladies could talk and think of nothing else. They taught him how to dress, to groom himself, to wash — and much more besides. They embroidered silk blouses for him and bought him fine trousers and red leather boots. **He learned to pomade his beard, and ruined its scent by washing his body with cheap pungent soap**.

## Ch. 7 — The middleman arrives

By the summer of 1908 he was back in the capital in a different condition — full of self-confidence, well dressed in peasant style and shod in high varnished boots.[^19]

The self-promotion was calibrated by sobriety, and the calibration is worth having. Sober, he bragged of his intimacy with the grand-ducal families. Drunk, he bragged about the tsar and empress. The head of the tsar's own police recorded what he had started to think: that he was destined to play a special role with the tsar, and that he would save Russia. The chapter's real subject is the man who arrives in it, and where he came from.

He was a Jewish fixer they had first met in Kiev, and **he had nearly been killed in the great pogrom there**. His shops were looted; his business manager and several relatives were murdered. His own life was spared because he was useful — an *our man* for the local police chief, who smuggled him out of the city. As he left he saw the corpses of murdered Jews by the synagogue. His first high-level contacts had been made through two gambling brothers who served in the tsar's personal retinue. So the arrangement that dominates the last five years of the story begins here, and its parts are ordinary: a peasant with access and no money sense, a man with connections whose community had no legal protection at all, and a court that could be reached through neither.

*Read: lines 1338–1453.*
