# What a Mauryan Statecraft Manual Took For Granted — Chapters 4–6

> **Chapters 4–6 of Thomas R. Trautmann, *Arthashastra: The Science of Wealth*** — workplaces, markets, and the long view. Read from `RAW/books/Arthashastra-The Science of Wealth.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
>
> **Siblings:** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/trautmann-arthashastra-worldview-archaeology-part-1|Part 1 — Introduction and Chapters 1–3]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/trautmann-arthashastra-worldview-archaeology-synthesis|What Runs Through All of It]] · thread map: [[LAB/Threads/the-ledgers-blind-spot-arthashastra-and-jyotish-compared-threads|The Ledger's Blind Spot]].
>
> ⚠ **Supersedes** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/trautmann-arthashastra-worldview-archaeology|the original whole-book report]], which merged six chapters into one account.
>
> **Whose worldview this is**. The subject is the world of the *Arthashastra* itself — a hypothetical Indian kingdom of roughly the first or second century CE — reported through Trautmann. Where a claim is his rather than the text's, it is marked.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/trautmann-arthashastra-science-of-wealth|Thomas R. Trautmann, Arthashastra: The Science of Wealth]]*

---

## Ch. 4 — Workplaces

**What is real, and the landscape is a made thing**. The country is not taken as nature gave it. The king is to provide for farms, pastures and trade routes — matching the three branches of livelihood — and also for mines and forests, and the ideal territory is one with a variegated landscape because each zone produces something the kingdom needs.[^1] Everything else is defined against the first zone. The chapter that follows the settlement of farmland is called *Disposal of Non-agricultural Land*, and that title says the whole thing: pasture, wilderness for Veda study, animal forests, materials forests and elephant forests are all what is left once farmland has been taken.[^2]

**How people should relate — the state deals with the farmer directly, and by preference with a shudra**. The instruction is explicit about who should be settled:

> He should cause settlement of the country, which had been settled before or which had not been settled before, by bringing in people from foreign lands or by moving people from overpopulated regions in his own country. He should cause villages to be settled consisting mostly of Shudra farmers with a minimum of one hundred families and a maximum of five hundred families, with boundaries extending over one krosha or two kroshas and affording mutual protection. (2.1.1–2)[^3]

**Not a landed warrior aristocracy**. Farming and warfare are pulled apart, and the relation runs from king to farmer with no landlord in between. That is the ideal from the king's seat, and Trautmann notes it was often not achieved. Tax-free grants do go to brahmins, and to overseers, accountants, cowherds, elephant-trainers, physicians, horse-trainers and couriers — but most of the land goes to farmers.

**What is worth having is possession, and the price of it is use**. *He should allot to tax-payers arable fields for life. Unarable fields should not be taken away from those who are trying to make them arable. He should take away fields from those who do not till them and give them to others*.[^4] The tenure runs for a life and appears to become hereditary in practice, since elsewhere in the text farmers sell, mortgage and bequeath. But the condition is production. A field that stops yielding tax stops being yours.

**What makes things happen, and the tone is a father's**. The king lends the means as well as granting the ground:

> He should favour them with grains, cattle and money which they should repay later at their convenience. And he should grant them favours and exemptions which would cause an increase to the treasury, but avoid such as would cause loss to the treasury. For a king with a small treasury swallows up the people of the city and the people of the countryside. He should grant exemptions at the time of settlement or as people come. He should, like a father, show favours to those whose exemptions have ceased. (2.1.13–18)[^5]

The middle sentence is the hard one and it is an argument from self-interest again. A poor king eats his own people. Generosity to farmers is not charity; it is the alternative to the ruin that follows an empty treasury.

**What a person is, when that person is a king, part two**. A farmer with a very large operation. The overseer of royal farmland must know farming, water-divining and the science of rearing plants, collect the seeds of all kinds of grain, flower, fruit, vegetable, bulb, root, creeper-fruit, flax and cotton in season, and get them sown *through serfs, labourers and persons remitting their fines through personal labour*.[^6] He must also make sure the work is not delayed by ploughing machines, implements and bullocks, or by the smiths, carpenters, basket makers, rope makers and snake catchers whose work it depends on. If they lose the crop through negligence, the fine equals the value of the crop.

**How you know how to farm, and it did not come from a book**. One passage carries the smell of the field:

> The treatment of seeds of grain is soaking in dew by night and drying in the heat by day for seven days and nights; for three or five days and nights for seeds of pulses; smearing at the cut with honey, ghee and pig fat mixed with cowdung for cuttings that serve as seeds; smearing with honey and ghee for bulbs; smearing with cowdung for stone-like seeds; and in the case of trees, burning in the pit and fulfilment of the trees' longing with cow bones and dung in season. And when they have sprouted, he should feed them with dried fish along with the milk of the snuhi plant. (2.24.24–25)[^7]

The trees' longing is not a figure of speech. Trees were held to have cravings, like the cravings of an expectant mother, and the cravings had to be satisfied when they were about to bud. Practical knowledge passed down orally in the vernacular, collected and written up in the learned language by an interested non-farmer.

**Who lives where, and it sorts the whole population**. Farmers live in villages. So do cowherds, who work in the pastures and do not live there. So do elephant-keepers and the physicians who treat elephants, who work in the forests and do not live there. Pastures are inhabited by robbers and wild animals, and the overseer of pastures must clear the lowlands and forests of both.[^8] Forests contain forest people, outside the caste system, organised in tribes, difficult for the king to control and essential to him because they know things village-dwellers do not.

Troops recruited from forest people are less certainly loyal than other soldiers, and they are especially useful as guides and scouts, on certain terrain, against certain modes of fighting, and against the enemy's own forest troops.[^9] The thing that makes them valuable is the same thing that makes them hard to hold.

**What is worth having, at the root of everything**. *The treasury has its source in the mines; from the treasury the army comes into being; with the treasury and the army, the earth is obtained, with the treasury as its ornament*. (2.12.37)[^10] Four steps from a hole in the ground to a kingdom. The king holds a monopoly on subsoil metal and on salt, mints the coin, and licenses others for a fee or partners with private operators on shares.

**And the tax that reaches everyone without exception**. Salt. Nobody can live without it, which is exactly what makes the levy valuable and what makes it fall hardest on the poor, since a rich man eats no more of it than a poor one.[^11] Indian kings monopolised, licensed and taxed it. So did the British, who tried to plant a continuous impenetrable hedge around their territory to stop the smuggling that always accompanies a salt tax, and who jailed Gandhi for walking to the sea to make some.

**How people should relate, at the elephant forest, and it runs on a census**. Guards mask their scent with elephant urine and dung, cover their bodies with branches, and move with five or seven female decoys, working out herd size from sleeping places, footprints, dung and damage to river banks.

> They should maintain a record in writing of every elephant, whether moving in a herd, moving alone, lost from a herd, leader of a herd, and whether wild, maddened, a cub, or released from captivity. (2.2.10–11)[^12]

Anyone who kills an elephant is to be killed. Anyone who brings in the tusks of one that died naturally gets four and a quarter panas. The animals are protected, individually recorded, and the record is kept by men who live in the forest for a king who does not.

**What a person is, at the bottom of the scale**. Enslaving an Arya by his own kin is a crime punishable by a severe fine, across all four castes — and Trautmann's observation is the useful one: the whole discussion would be unnecessary if it did not happen.[^13] Among non-Aryans slavery is permitted as customary among them. Debt-servitude runs through the text in several forms, and so do people remitting a fine or paying tax through labour on the king's farms, mines and workshops. That temporary labour is cheap and it is the least desirable kind, because the worker is unskilled and will not be there long.

**And what actually divides the countryside is not slavery**. It is landlessness. Wage labour and share-cropping on the king's farms imply people with no field of their own, who must work for hire or on somebody else's terms.[^14]

**The one place the king is told to employ people because they need it**. The textile house:

> He should get thread spun out of wool, bark-fibre, cotton, silk-cotton, hemp and flax, through widows, crippled women, maidens, women who have left their homes and women paying off their fine through personal labour, through mothers of courtesans, through old female slaves of the king and through female slaves of temples whose service to the gods have ceased. (2.23.1–2)[^15]

Every category on that list is a woman with no household protecting her. Protecting people who have nobody is a recognised royal virtue, and here it takes the form of piecework. The rule that follows is the sharpest small thing in the chapter. Women who stay at home are visited by a female slave of the overseer; those who come in are inspected under a lamp; and if the overseer's man looks a woman in the face, or talks to her about anything other than business, he is fined.[^16]

**What makes things happen in a workshop, and it is suspicion**. Artisans working gold are searched thoroughly on the way in and on the way out, and their tools and unfinished work stay in the building.[^17] The text lists the ways artisans cheat customers at length, and — because some loss is unavoidable in working metal — it also states the allowable loss, so that an honest man is not blamed for physics.

**The shape of time, and it is deeper than the kingdom**. Pottery, woven cloth, metal-tipped ploughs and farming villages are the pattern that made Indian civilization, and it was in place long before the *Arthashastra* and before the Indus cities five thousand years ago.[^18] It is the surplus from that pattern that allowed cities, kings, monumental architecture and court luxury to exist at all. The economic zoning of the chapter sits on top of something much older than the king who arranges it.

*Read: lines 990–1258.*

---

## Ch. 5 — Markets

**What is real — most of the economy never touches a market**. The bulk of the population were farmers provisioning themselves directly, with land passing to sons as co-sharers, so the core activity involved no buying or selling.[^19] The king did the same at scale, supplying the royal family, the state employees and the army out of his own farms, mines, forests and workshops. And the main way a surplus was pulled out of agriculture was tax, not trade. Markets sit at the edges of that, and they matter because even a subsistence farmer needs things he cannot make.

**How people should relate, and the king is on both sides of the table**. He trades through his officials for profit to the royal household, and he regulates and taxes everybody else's trade with an eye on the treasury and on public order. **He is a player and a referee in the same market**, exactly as he is in farming.[^20]

**What makes things happen, and it is the thing the whole chapter is organised against**. Scarcity of capital, and violent uncertainty of price. That is the single most important difference between this economy and a modern one, and it is what the price policy exists to dampen.[^21]

**What is worth having — land, and it is genuinely owned**. The sale procedure proves it, and every clause of the procedure also limits it:

> Kinsmen, neighbours and creditors, in that order, shall have the right to buy land that is for sale. After that, others who are outsiders may buy. Owners shall proclaim a dwelling for sale in front of the house, in the presence of members of forty neighbouring families, and a field, a park, an embankment, a tank or a reservoir at the boundaries, in the presence of village elders who are neighbours... saying, 'At this price who is willing to buy?' When it has been proclaimed three times without objection, the buyer is entitled to buy. But, if the price increases because of competition among the buyers, the excess together with the tax shall go to the treasury. (3.9.1–6)[^22]

Three things are happening at once. Buyers are ranked, with the stranger last, which recognises how tightly farmland is bound to family. The sale must be public, in front of as many as forty neighbours, and the price called three times *without objection* — and the objection a neighbour would raise is that the price is wrong. And any excess produced by competitive bidding is confiscated.

**So there is private property, and there is no price-making market**. The village knows what land is worth, because the customary price tracks the annual yield. Competition cannot move it. With multiple buyers at the announced price, the sale falls to whoever is socially nearest the seller.[^23]

**How you know a fair price when nobody at the gate knows the land**. Outside the city gate the same procedure runs on merchandise — declare quantity and price, proclaim three times, excess to the treasury, heavy penalties for understating to dodge duty or for bidding up to shut out a rival.[^24] But there are no expert neighbours there. So the expertise sits in one official, the overseer of trade, whose job description is a knowledge specification:

> The Overseer of Trade should be conversant with the differences in the prices of goods of high value and of low value, and the desirability or undesirability of goods of various kinds, whether produced on land or in water and whether they have arrived by land routes or water routes, and he should know about times when it is appropriate to disperse or concentrate markets, and for buying or selling. (2.16.1)[^25]

Dispersing and concentrating markets is a price instrument. Too much of a commodity and the price falls, so he gathers it into one place and forbids others to sell until it clears, to keep the traders from being ruined. And on royal goods he is told to sell so as to favour the subjects, and *to avoid even a big profit that would be injurious to the subjects*.[^26]

**What a fair profit is, and it is a transport charge**. Five per cent above the permitted purchase price for local goods, ten per cent for foreign.[^27] Profit is made proportional to distance, which conceptualises the trader's return as a fee for carrying things to where the buyers are rather than as a reward for judgement or risk. The aim, stated plainly, is to keep traders in business by guaranteeing a fair return and protecting them against a glut, while keeping prices and profits from rising enough to hurt the public.

**Foreign trade is wanted, and wanted asymmetrically**. Imports are encouraged with concessions and tax exemptions that let the carrier make a profit, and *no lawsuit in money matters should be allowed against foreign traders*, except members of local guilds.[^28] Exports are permitted only for goods in abundant supply at home. That is the reverse of a modern trade balance and it follows from the orientation: the point is the goods, not the money.

**And the two trade routes get compared on their contents**. The teachers said the Himalaya route beats the southern one for elephants, horses, perfumes, ivory, skins, silver and gold. *No, says Kautilya*. All of those except blankets, skins and horses are more plentiful on the southern route, which also has conch shells, diamonds, rubies, pearls and gold.[^29] Every item in the comparison is treasure or one of the two war animals.

**How people should relate when a deal goes wrong — two courts, two kinds of law**. The first is the Law of Transactions, heard by panels of three judges with the rank of ministers, stationed at the frontier post, the headquarters of ten villages, the headquarters of four hundred villages, and the capital.[^30] These are civil suits: somebody has to bring them. The list of transaction types is the list of ways people get entangled — marriage, inheritance, immovable property, non-observance of conventions, debt, deposits, slaves and workers, partnership, sale and purchase, gifts, sale without ownership, robbery, slander, battery, gambling and betting.

**The second court has a name and the name is a metaphor**. *Removal of thorns*.[^31] Here the king starts the process himself, because the wrong is against the kingdom rather than against a person. A separate panel of three magistrates handles it, and **the first two topics under it are Keeping a Watch over Artisans and Keeping a Watch over Traders**. Weavers, washermen, tailors, goldsmiths, metalworkers, physicians and actors are all thorns to be watched.

**What makes things happen when the watching fails, and it is a ruinous number**. *For artisans who by conspiring together bring about deterioration in the quality of work or increase in profit or cause a hindrance to buying or selling, the fine is one thousand panas. For traders, too, who by conspiring together to hoard goods or sell them at a high price, the fine is one thousand panas*. (4.2.18–19)[^32] A thousand panas would put most men into debt-servitude working it off for the king. The severity is evidence of weakness: harsh penalties are what you use when surveillance is incomplete and enforcement is patchy.

**What a person is, if he trades**. Useful and suspect. Trade is to be enhanced, routes made safe, imports encouraged, traders protected from price crashes — and traders are also to be watched for false weights, counterfeit goods, collusion over prices and excessive profit.[^33] There is no comparable suspicion of farmers anywhere in the book. From the king's seat, farming makes wealth and commerce moves it.

*Read: lines 1259–1476.*

---

## Ch. 6 — The Arthashastra in the long view

**What a kingdom is, summed up in one word, and the word is not despotism**. *At every step we meet, not the idea of despotism and the royal ownership of everything, but the idea of the king's share*.[^34] Not Aristotle's Persia where the king owned all and everyone was his slave, but a king who is a co-sharer with his people in wealth-making enterprises — in language drawn from fathers and sons working land together, or from partnerships of traders.

**What makes things happen inside that arrangement**. Mutual interest, and it is unsentimental. The co-sharers are by no means equal. But a share means both parties gain by the crop being larger, and that is what motivates the instruction to take land off a farmer who will not till it and give it to somebody who will.[^35] **The king's enormous powers to extract are also powers to enlarge**, and the text's argument is that enlightened self-interest, not restraint, is what stops the extraction becoming unlimited.

**What is worth having, for a king, and there is no formula**. A full treasury, a strong army, a prosperous people, and effective dispute resolution to keep the peace — four ends that overlap and sometimes compete. *The Arthashastra cannot guarantee success but it shows kings and their ministers the way to a rational approach in making choices*.[^36]

**How you know whether any of it worked, and the evidence is duration**. Not accounts, which do not survive, but the length of reigns. In the late classical period the average reign was twenty years, against an average generation of twenty-five — which means succession disputes were not frequent enough to destabilise rule.[^37] The Eastern Chalukyas lasted four hundred years, the Palas of Bengal and the Cholas over three hundred each. Constant warfare over farming populations and constant shifting of boundaries, inside a structure that held.

**What the book cannot show you, and it is the potter**. He is practically invisible, because pottery is valued at nothing in a king-centred inventory — and his product is the one that survives everywhere in the ground and lets archaeologists date everything.[^38] The absence is a fact about the author, not about the economy.

**And the other invisible man is the one getting rich**. The *Arthashastra* does not show the widening circulation of trade and money producing a new figure: the merchant whose wealth begins to rival the king's.[^39] The Buddhists celebrated one, Anathapindaka, and the story about him is a contest of wealth. He wanted to buy a wooded tract from prince Jeta as a gift for the order of monks, and the prince, who did not want to sell, named a price he thought impossible — as many coins as would cover the ground. Anathapindaka covered it.

**How people should relate across two thousand miles, and it is visible in a poem**. The Tamil Sangam poets praise a Pandya king with a picture of Greek ships:

> ... while every day you take your pleasure as women wearing their shining bangles bring you the cool and fragrant wine carried here in their excellent ships by the Greeks and the women pour it for you out of pitchers made of gold that have been fashioned with high artistry...[^40]

The Greeks appear here *as a matter of fact, as a part of royal material culture*, remarkable for being normal. And the whole poem's theme is the king giving precious ornaments away to those who come to him in need — probably including the poet. Luxury is converted into the royal virtue of liberality by being handed on. Roman wine jars turn up in the ground at Arikamedu to confirm it, along with eighty separate hoards of Roman coins from India and Sri Lanka.

**What is real, at the largest scale**. A trade so unbalanced that it drained precious metal out of an empire. Warmington's conclusion is that Rome could not offer enough of its own products to balance what it imported, so coined money went east and stayed there.[^41] When later Roman emperors debased their gold, Indian kings such as the Guptas began minting their own.

**The shape of time, and the book ends by watching its subject disappear**. Kingship was the dominant political form in India and in the world for thousands of years, and that dominance is only now ending — replaced by the republic, which is the modern form of the very thing Book Eleven treated as the kingdom's rival.[^42] Nepal's monarchy ended in 2009 and Bhutan is the last in the subcontinent. The republic lost to the kingdom on economics and came back two thousand years later.

*Read: lines 1477–1705.*

---

# Below the Line

*Everything above is sourced to the chapters named. Everything below is built rather than found, and is not measured by `assessgate.sh`*.

## Ch. 4 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Tie tenure to production and you never have to value the asset**. A field is yours for life while you till it, and goes to somebody else when you stop. *Applies when* the asset's worth is entirely in its output, the output is observable from outside, and the holder cannot easily fake working it. *Fails* where the asset appreciates by being held — the rule would force the sale of anything slow-maturing, which is why it works for fields and would be ruinous applied to an elephant forest, and why elephant forests are handled by census instead.
*Decision type:* power consolidation.

**Argue for generosity from the giver's balance sheet, not from virtue**. *For a king with a small treasury swallows up the people of the city and the people of the countryside*. Seed, cattle and money are advanced to new farmers on repayment at their convenience, and the case for it is that the alternative bankrupts everybody. *Applies when* the beneficiary's prosperity is measurably your own revenue, so the argument can be checked. *Fails* the moment the link is indirect enough to be denied — which is the position of the trader in chapter five, whose prosperity is not obviously the king's, and who is watched rather than lent to.
*Decision type:* when to compromise a core value.

## Ch. 5 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and it is the one the text will not take**. Let the price move. Every mechanism in the chapter exists to stop it: ranked buyers, public proclamation three times, confiscation of any excess from competitive bidding, a fixed percentage profit tied to distance, an overseer concentrating or dispersing a market to hold a level, and thousand-pana fines for hoarding.

The alternative was available in practice, because it is what the mechanisms are fighting. Traders bid each other up at the city gate, hoarded to create scarcity, and understated quantities to dodge duty — and the penalties tell you they went on doing it. **The road not taken is one where the excess above the customary price stays with the seller instead of going to the treasury**.

What Trautmann says in the text's defence is worth keeping, because it is a live alternative and not a rationalisation: capital was scarce and price swings were violent, so uncertainty was a bigger danger to the king and his people than the dead weight of a fair-price regime. His own comparison is a modern government under pressure to intervene when prices move sharply.

## Ch. 5 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A Buddhist monastic advisor on the price of land**. The Buddhist orders in India held property, took endowments, and ran their houses on rules for strangers rather than on kinship — a stranger monk's place in a house he has never entered is settled by his years of ordination, not by who he is related to. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/faxian-worldview-archaeology-part-2|What the Buddhist Kingdoms Took For Granted, Chapters XIV–XXVI]].

Put that beside the land-sale rule and the divergence is exact. The *Arthashastra* ranks buyers kinsman, neighbour, creditor, stranger — and the point of the ranking is that the stranger comes last even if his money is the same. A monastic reading would say the rule is not really about price at all. **It is a mechanism for keeping land inside a set of people who already know each other**, with the fair-price machinery doing the work of making that look like a market.

And the story of Anathapindaka in chapter six is the counter-case sitting inside the same book. A merchant covers the ground of the Jetavana in coins to buy it for the order — a stranger, outbidding the whole ranking, for a purpose that is not farming. That transaction is exactly what the land rule was built to prevent, and it is the one the Buddhists chose to commemorate in stone.

## Ch. 6 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Measure an institution's success by the length of its reigns, not by its accounts**. Twenty-year average reigns against twenty-five-year generations; dynasties of three and four hundred years; constant boundary warfare inside a structure that did not change. *Applies when* the internal records are gone or were never kept, and when the institution's chief failure mode is succession — duration then measures the thing you actually care about. *Fails* where longevity is enforced from outside, or where the institution survives by shedding the function it existed for, in which case a long life is evidence of nothing.
*Decision type:* succession.

**An inventory's silences are its author's, and can be read as such**. No potters in a book about wealth, in a country carpeted with broken pots. *Applies when* you have one source and need to know its angle: what a document counts, and how finely, is much harder to fake than what it claims. *Fails* as evidence about the world — the missing potter tells you what the king thought was worth writing down, and nothing whatever about how many pots there were.
*Decision type:* when to compromise a core value.

## What Runs Through All of It

Almost every rule in this book is argued from the ruler's own interest rather than from his virtue, and the arguments are made to a man who is expected to check them. The opening line says the king's happiness lies in the happiness of his subjects. Chapter four says a king with a small treasury swallows up his own people. Chapter six says the co-sharers are unequal but both gain when the crop is larger. Even the ideal of the sage-king is put practically: a life of constant labour and self-control, because a man who gambles and drinks cannot run the thing. **Nothing in the book asks the king to be good and everything in it explains what goodness pays for.**

The word doing the work everywhere is *share*. The king's tax is his *bhaga*, one-sixth, and it applies across the produce of land and other transactions alike. A share means the ground is not his — four kinds of land exist and only one is the king's — and it means he and the farmer have the same interest in a bigger harvest. It also runs downwards into the smallest arrangements: herdsmen are paid either a wage with the whole yield going to the king, or a share of ghee and a fixed sum per animal and the hides of the dead. Partnership is the grammar of the whole system, between parties who are nowhere near equal.

Everything of value in this kingdom is graded, and the grades are named by where a thing came from. Horses run from Kamboja and Sindhu at the top down through Bahika and Sauvira, and *the rest are inferior*. Elephants run from Kalinga and Anga down to the Punjab. Pearl necklaces run from 1,008 strings down to one. Milled rice runs from war elephants down through soldiers, chiefs, queens and the king, on a scale of milling ratios. Ration units are proportionate to status and to body size, read off the same table, and a young elephant and a slave sit at opposite ends of one continuous list.

Concentration is the kingdom's whole advantage and its whole exposure, and the book knows it. A republic is closely knit and unassailable because power is spread across a warrior class that debates in assembly. A kingdom is less cohesive, and can be taken by killing one man. So the palace has hidden passages. The queen is cleared by old women before he visits her, the birds are watched for poison, and the fort's garrison is given several commanders instead of one. **The concentration of royal power is protected by deliberately dividing military power.**

Trust is scarce, and the book treats it as a resource with a cost. Officials are tested by religion, gain, lust and fear, and the tests are known to be risky. Spies work as students, monks, nuns, farmers, traders and hermits, both to gather information and to shape opinion. Officers are assumed to be skimming — *we cannot know when a fish swimming in water is drinking water* — and forty kinds of embezzlement are listed. Written records are demanded everywhere and are never claimed to solve it. The sharpest thing said about any of this is the refusal to test the prince: a fresh object absorbs whatever it is smeared with, so a loyalty test proposes the disloyalty it is looking for.

Prices are treated as a danger to be contained rather than as information. Buyers are ranked with the stranger last. The price is called three times in front of forty neighbours. Any excess produced by competitive bidding is confiscated. The trader's profit is fixed at five per cent local and ten per cent foreign, which makes it a transport charge proportional to distance rather than a return on judgement. The overseer of trade gathers a glutted commodity into one place to hold the price up. He is also told to avoid even a big profit that would injure the public. **There is true private property here and there is no price-making market.** The two facts sit together without strain.

Farming is trusted and commerce is watched, and the asymmetry never softens. Farmers get seed, cattle and money advanced on repayment at their convenience, and get treated *like a father*. Traders and artisans appear in Book Four under the heading of removing thorns, alongside the first two topics of the whole department — keeping a watch over artisans, and keeping a watch over traders. **There is no comparable suspicion of farmers anywhere in the six chapters.** From the king's seat, the land makes wealth and the market only moves it.

The severity of the punishments is the best evidence of how badly the rules held. A thousand panas for artisans or traders conspiring to hoard or raise prices would put most men into debt-servitude working it off. Anyone killing an elephant is killed. The men who bury the emergency treasure on the border are executed so the location dies with them. **Harsh penalties are what a state uses when its surveillance is incomplete**, and there is a whole department for detecting the theft that Book Two says cannot be detected.

## Which dimensions the book never reached

The *Arthashastra* has no account of what is ultimately real, and the silence is a positive feature rather than a gap. It has no cosmology, no creation, no doctrine of the soul, and no ritual theory. The gods appear once, in the king's evening worship at the twilight and in the blessings he takes from his chaplain and gurus in the last part of the night. The Vedic tradition sits behind it and supported kingship with rituals of consecration. This book supports the same kingship with practical secular advice instead. **It was written by men who had a religion and left it in another book.**

Its treatment of the moral world is equally flat, and deliberately so. Liquor shops, butchers, courtesans and gambling are handled as normal features of a kingdom, taxed, regulated and in some cases participated in, without a line of moralising. The southern trade route is preferred to the northern on the grounds that it carries better goods, with none of the stigma other texts attach to the south. Dharma is ranked above artha in the doctrine the book opens with, and inside the book itself dharma is mostly a court — three judges called upholders of dharma, hearing suits about debts and partnerships.

Nothing in any chapter reports what a farmer, a herdsman or a forest person thought about anything. They are counted, settled, taxed, watched and rationed. The women in the textile house are named only as categories of unprotected person — widows, crippled women, maidens, women who have left home, mothers of courtesans, retired temple slaves. We know what they were paid to do, and nothing about what they made of it.

The potter is the emblematic absence. Pottery gets one clause in the whole inventory, because a king-centred list values it at nothing, and it is the single most abundant surviving product of that economy. The merchant rich enough to rival a king is the other absence — Anathapindaka, who covered the ground of the Jetavana in coins, exists in Buddhist stories and not in this book. Both gaps are facts about the author's angle rather than about the country.

## Where two chapters pull against each other

Chapter two's republic and chapter six's conclusion are the same comparison drawn twice, and they end up in different places. Chapter two treats the republic as an obstacle — closely knit, unassailable, to be broken by sowing dissension among its warrior class. Chapter six treats it as the ancestor of the political form that eventually won: kingdoms beat republics on economics and flourished for two thousand years, and now the republic is back and the last Hindu kingdom ended in 2009. **The instrument Book Eleven describes for destroying republics is the reason the writing about them survives at all.**

Chapter one's account of a book that killed its ancestors and chapter six's account of the potter are the same mechanism seen from two directions. The *Arthashastra* was so good that nobody recopied the works it drew on, and they are gone. Manu was so successful that the *Arthashastra* itself nearly vanished — seven manuscripts against thousands upon thousands. Meanwhile pottery survives everywhere precisely because nobody valued it enough to be selective about it. **What gets preserved is what nobody had a reason to replace.**

Chapter four's landscape and chapter five's market describe the same kingdom and barely acknowledge each other. In chapter four the country is a set of production zones, farming first and everything else defined as non-agricultural land, with the king as the largest farmer in it. In chapter five most of that economy never touches a market at all, and the market chapter is about the thin edge where it does. Trautmann says both things and does not reconcile them, which is honest: the manual he is reading does not reconcile them either.

## What the by-chapter reading recovered

Seven separate runs surface material that a merged reading flattens into policy. The birds that report poison — the shrieking parrot, the frantic heron, the faint pheasant, the intoxicated cuckoo that dies, the chakora whose eyes discolour. The list of dead kings killed by a brother in the queen's chamber, by a son in his mother's bed, by a queen with a poisoned anklet, a poisoned girdle-jewel, a poisoned mirror, and a weapon in a braid of hair. The overseer's man fined for looking a spinning-woman in the face. Trees with cravings that must be fed with cow bones and dung. Guards masked in elephant dung, moving with seven female decoys, keeping a written record of every individual elephant in a forest.

None of those recur, and every one of them belongs to a chapter rather than to the book. **The condemned men who bury the permanent treasure on the border, and the sentence that does not say what happens to them, only exist in chapter two.**

## Introduction — The missing conqueror

A man's soul lives in horsehair. A warrior herder tied strands from his best stallions to the shaft of a spear just below the blade, and that was his Spirit Banner, his *sulde*. He planted it outside his camp to say who he was and to guard the place. It stayed out in the open air under the Eternal Blue Sky, and the wind kept the hair moving.[^1]

What that motion does is the point, and it is a theory of how a life gets directed. The blowing hair captured the power of the wind, the sky and the sun and channelled it into the man. It inspired his dreams, and it lured him away from where he stood — toward better pasture, new opportunity, a fate he made himself. **Then the union grew so tight that when he died his spirit stayed in the tufts**. The body was abandoned to nature quickly. The soul lived on in the horsehair.

What is real, in this account, is a soul that has an address outside the body and travels on the weather. Genghis Khan had two banners, one of white horses for peacetime and one of black for war. The white one vanished early. The black one survived as the place his soul lived, and monks of the Yellow Hat sect guarded it in a monastery for centuries. Then in 1937 Stalin's men killed thirty thousand Mongols, shot the monks, burned the scriptures, and the banner disappeared.[^2]

What is worth having, in the Mongol account of a good death, is nothing built. He died in a nomad's *ger* essentially like the one he was born in, and his soldiers carried the body home for secret burial with no mausoleum, no temple, no pyramid, and not so much as a tombstone.[^3] The reason is doctrinal rather than practical: **the body of the dead should be left in peace and needs no monument, because the soul is not there**. It is in the Spirit Banner. Then soldiers sealed several hundred square miles and killed intruders for eight hundred years.

How you know anything about this at all is a question with a strange answer, and it is the frame of the whole book. There is no portrait made in his lifetime. He never allowed anyone to paint him, sculpt him, or put his name or face on a coin, and the contemporary descriptions are more intriguing than informative.[^4] A modern Mongolian song about him says: *we imagined your appearance but our minds were blank*. So every culture drew what it wanted. The Chinese made him an elderly sage with a wispy beard and empty eyes. A Persian miniaturist made him a Turkish sultan on a throne. The Europeans made him a barbarian with fixed cruel eyes, ugly in every detail.

The record that would settle it was written and then locked up. Rashid al-Din, a century after the death, described an authentic chronicle *in the Mongolian idiom and letters* — and warned that it was kept in the treasury, hidden and concealed from outsiders.[^5] A copy turned up in Beijing in the nineteenth century, written in Chinese characters used as a code for thirteenth-century Mongolian sounds, which is why it is called *The Secret History of the Mongols*. Under Communism the deciphering of it was mortally dangerous in Mongolia itself, and an underground scholarly movement grew around it, whispered from camp to camp.

**And the researchers' own test of the text is the sharpest methodological line in the book**. Weatherford's team could not sift the competing readings without standing where the events happened. *Books can lie, but places never do*.[^6] They went back to the same places in different seasons, because being there in the wrong weather told them nothing. Herders navigated the open steppe the way sailors cross the sea, identified where their ancestors would have camped, said which spots had too many mosquitoes for summer or were too exposed for winter, and raced horses between two points to see how long it took.

What a person is, in this world, gets settled early and by other people. He grew up in a world of tribal violence — murder, kidnapping, enslavement — in an outcast family left to die, and probably met no more than a few hundred people in his whole childhood. He feared dogs and cried easily. His younger brother was stronger, a better archer and a better wrestler. His half brother bossed him around.[^7]

Two relationships formed before puberty and both held for life. He swore eternal friendship to a slightly older boy who became his closest childhood companion and the most dedicated enemy of his adulthood. And he found the girl he would love forever. **The dual capacity for friendship and enmity forged in those years is Weatherford's candidate for the defining trait of the man**.

What the Mongols left the world is a list of things they did not make. They made no technological breakthroughs, founded no religions, wrote few books, and gave the world no new crops. Their own craftsmen could not weave cloth, cast metal, make pottery or bake bread.[^8] What they did instead was carry. German miners to China and Chinese doctors to Persia. Carpets everywhere, lemons and carrots from Persia to China, noodles and playing cards and tea westward. A metalworker from Paris to build a fountain on the dry steppe, and Chinese fingerprinting to Persia.

The only permanent structures he erected were bridges. He spurned castles, forts, cities and walls, and probably built more bridges than any ruler in history, spanning hundreds of streams to move armies and goods faster.[^9] The combinations were the invention. Chinese gunpowder plus Muslim flamethrowers plus European bell-casting produced the cannon.

How people should relate, under the new order, is a set of policies that read oddly against the reputation. He smashed the feudal system of aristocratic privilege and birth and built one on merit, loyalty and achievement. He organised the trading towns of the Silk Route into the largest free-trade zone in history. **He lowered taxes for everyone and abolished them altogether for doctors, teachers, priests, and educational institutions**.[^10] He ran a census and the first international postal system, granted religious freedom while demanding total loyalty, and insisted that the law held rulers as accountable as the lowest herder.

The shape of a reputation over eight centuries is the introduction's last subject, and it moves entirely one way. Chaucer gave Genghis Khan the longest story in the *Canterbury Tales* and wrote in undisguised awe. Voltaire made him a wild Scythian bred to arms and practised in the trade of blood.[^11] Nineteenth-century scientists classified Asians as Mongoloid to show inferiority, and doctors explained a white mother's disabled child by an ancestor raped by a Mongol warrior. Then the name became an excuse. Russia's backwardness was the Tatar Yoke and Persia's decline was the destroyed irrigation. An Arab politician could tell his followers that Muslims would have built the atomic bomb first if the Mongols had not burned the libraries.

*Read: lines 112–277.*

---

## Ch. 1 — The Blood Clot

A conqueror walks into a mosque and asks whether it is the sultan's house. Of the thousands of cities the Mongols took, history mentions one that Genghis Khan entered. Usually he withdrew to a pleasant camp while his warriors finished the work — but in March 1220 he rode into Bukhara, the centre of Muslim piety, called the ornament and delight to all Islam.[^12] Told the largest building was the house of God rather than the sultan, he said nothing.

What is real, for a Mongol, cannot be housed. The one God is the Eternal Blue Sky that stretches horizon to horizon in all four directions. He presides over the whole earth and cannot be shut in a house of stone like a prisoner or a caged animal — nor, as the city people claimed, can his words be captured inside the covers of a book.[^13] Genghis Khan had heard that God speaking directly to him in the open air of his own mountains, and by following the words had taken great cities.

Then he dismounted and walked in, the only such building he is known to have entered in his life. He ordered the scholars and clerics to feed his horses, which freed them from further danger and put them under his protection, as he did with almost all religious personnel who came under his control.[^14]

How people should relate, on the steppe, is a system of raiding rather than warfare, and it runs on a calendar. Hunting, trading, herding and fighting were one seamless web, and every male learned all four from the time he could ride. When the hunting was poor and there was nothing to trade, the Mongols still organised hunting parties — only they went out across the steppe to hunt for humans, approaching people with the tactics they used on animals.[^15]

**What is worth having is the goods, and only the goods**. Revenge was the usual pretext and rarely the motive. Prestige came from what a man brought back and shared with family and friends, not from honour won on a field. Victorious warriors remembered their kills and there was no collecting of heads or scalps, no notches, no emblems for the number of men killed. *Only the goods mattered, not the kill*.[^16]

That system also explains how poor the north was. Metal and textiles trickled up from the trading cities south of the Gobi family by family, *ger* by *ger*, and so little reached the far north that among the Mongols the man with a pair of iron stirrups ranked as the highest of aristocrats.[^17]

What a person is begins with a name and a verb. Hoelun's first son was called Temujin after a Tatar his father had killed, and Mongols got only one name in life, so the choice carried weight — it conferred character, fate and destiny. Her three youngest children were Temujin, Temuge and Temulun, all from a root meaning to rush headlong, to be inspired, to have a creative thought, even to take a flight of fancy.[^18] A Mongolian student gave Weatherford the working translation: *the look in the eye of a horse that is racing where it wants to go, no matter what the rider wants*.

**And a person's soul is in their smell**. Where other peoples hug or kiss on meeting, steppe nomads sniff, and the gesture runs from parent and child up to lovers. Each person's breath and body aroma is part of their soul.[^19] So when Hoelun was kidnapped and sent her first husband away to save his life, she pulled off her blouse and pushed it into his face: *Take this with you so that you may have the smell of me as you go*. He rode over the pass clutching it, turning back so often that his braids beat like whips across his chest.

How people should relate, when a man dies, is by rules that have nothing to do with sentiment. A widow should be taken by one of her husband's brothers, or by a son of his by another wife, because that gives a younger man an experienced wife without gifts or bride-service.[^20] Hoelun had too many children and no family wealth or useful ties, so nobody took her. **The message that she was outside the family came, as Mongols always send such messages, through food:** the old widows organising the ancestral meal did not tell her, cutting her off from the food and from membership at once.

Then the band moved down the river and left two women and seven children behind. One old man objected loudly and a Tayichiud rode back and speared him to death in front of Temujin, who was about ten.[^21] Hoelun's response was to grab her dead husband's Spirit Banner, mount, and chase the fleeing clan waving it over her head — which was not waving an emblem but parading his soul in front of them. They felt enough shame, and enough fear of what the soul might do, to come back to camp. Then they slipped away one at a time in the night and took the animals.

What makes things happen, in the killing that defines his childhood, is a rule about sexual succession. Begter was the eldest son and could command his siblings, take from them, and — as a widow's stepson — had rights of sexual access to Hoelun. When Temujin and his brother complained about a stolen fish, their mother sided with Begter and reminded them of the founding ancestress who bore more sons after her husband died.[^22] The implication was that she would accept Begter as her husband when he was old enough.

So the brothers stalked him through the grass the way they would stalk a resting deer, one circling to the front and one climbing the back of the knoll. Begter would not run or defend himself. He told them their real enemy was the Tayichiud. Then he said *I am not the lash in your eye, the impediment in your mouth — without me you have no companion but your own shadow*, sat cross-legged, and asked only that they spare his full brother.[^23] They shot him from front and back and left without approaching, to avoid contamination from his blood running onto the earth.

Hoelun read it in their faces and screamed the longest monologue in the *Secret History*: *Destroyer! Destroyer! You came from my hot womb clutching a clot of blood in your hand*. She compared them to a wild dog gnawing its own afterbirth, an attacking panther, a lion without control, a monster swallowing its prey alive. Then she repeated Begter's line back as a curse: *now you have no companion other than your shadow*.[^24]

How you know whom to trust is the lesson the chapter says he took from captivity. The Tayichiud, his close kin, had put his family out to die and now wanted to kill him. A poor servant family with no kinship tie to him fed him, took the cangue off his neck at night to let him sleep, and hid him when he escaped — risking their lives.[^25] **In later life he judged people primarily by their actions toward him and not by their kinship bonds, which was a revolutionary idea in steppe society**.

The shape of time here is a chronology with a hole in it. Mongol sources acknowledge one brief captivity. A contemporary Chinese chronicler wrote that he endured more than ten years in slavery, and some scholars suspect that a long enslavement accounts for the glaring absence of detail about his childhood.[^26] Everyone associated with it had reason to keep silent — it was shameful for him, and lethally dangerous for the descendants of the families that had held him.

What is worth having, at sixteen, turns out to be a coat. His bride Borte brought black sable, the most prized fur on the steppe, as the customary gift to a husband's parents. With no father to give it to, he took it to Torghil — Ong Khan of the Kereyid — who had been his father's sworn brother.[^27] **On the steppe, politics runs entirely through the idiom of male kinship**, so every alliance between unrelated men has to be converted into ceremonial kinship. By giving the coat he was calling the old man father. By accepting it, Ong Khan was calling him son, and owing him protection.

*Read: lines 293–522.*

---

## Ch. 2 — Tale of Three Rivers

A woman hears horses through the ground. The old woman the family had taken in slept with her head on the earth and felt the vibration of a Merkid raiding party before dawn. She shouted, the seven boys got their boots on and reached their hobbled horses, and Temujin fled with his mother and sister — leaving behind his new bride, his stepmother, and the old woman herself.[^28]

What a person is, in that moment, is a calculation. Facing annihilation, nobody had the luxury of chivalry: leaving three women as booty would slow the raiders enough for the others to reach the mountains.

What is real is a landscape with a spirit in it that can be prayed to and that tests you. The Mongols stayed animists while the other steppe tribes took up Buddhism, Islam or Christianity, praying to the Eternal Blue Sky, the Golden Light of the Sun, and the forces of nature.[^29] They split the world into earth and sky. **A human soul sits not in the body's stationary parts but in its moving essences of blood, breath and aroma — and the soul of the earth sits, likewise, in its moving water**. Rivers run through the earth like blood through a body. Three of them start on Burkhan Khaldun, which is why it is the khan of the mountains.

How you pray, if you are him, is by taking your own strength off. He sprinkled milk into the air and onto the ground for the spirits. Then he unwound his sash — worn only by men, and the centre of a man's identity — and hung it around his neck, removed his hat, and put his hand on his breast.[^30] **Removing the sash removes his strength and makes him powerless in front of the gods**.

What makes things happen is that worldly power and supernatural power come out of the same source and cannot be separated. To triumph over anyone you must first be granted power from the spirit world, and a Spirit Banner has to be filled with it before it can lead to victory. Three days on the mountain began an intimate lifelong relationship with it.

**The mountain answers by presenting a choice, and the choice is three rivers**. Go back southeast down the Kherlen and herd, and lose it all in the next raid. Take the Onon northeast into wooded, sheltered country with poor pasture. Or fight for a place in the hierarchy he had spent his life avoiding.[^31]

How people should relate, once he chooses, works through the coat he gave away years before. Ong Khan agreed to raid the Merkid immediately — he had his own feud with them, and the request gave him a pretext — and sent Temujin to recruit Jamuka. The two sworn brothers took the two wings of the army, and the Merkid were routed rather than fought.[^32] Riding through the burning camps shouting Borte's name, he did not recognise her when she ran at him and grabbed his reins, and nearly attacked her before they threw themselves on each other.

What is worth having, in the *Secret History*'s account of the aftermath, is silence. Borte was pregnant, and the text goes quiet about her for the whole pregnancy.[^33] The son was named Jochi, and the question of who fathered him reverberated through Mongol politics for a century.

**How a friendship is made is by exchanging the things that carry a soul**. For the third time Temujin and Jamuka swore brotherhood, now as grown men in public, standing before a tree at the edge of a cliff. They exchanged golden sashes and strong horses. Exchanging clothing shares body smell, and therefore the essence of a soul; the sash in particular is the symbol of manhood. Then they feasted, drank, and slept apart from everyone under a single blanket.[^34]

How people should relate, under the older system, is by bone. The closest lineages, those forbidden to intermarry, were white bones. More distant kin, who could intermarry, were black bones.[^35] Temujin and Jamuka were distant cousins descended from one woman by two husbands: Jamuka from her first, a steppe herder; Temujin from the forest hunter who had killed that husband and kidnapped her.

That descent is what breaks them, and it breaks them over livestock. On the move in May 1181, Jamuka told Temujin to take the horses and camp near the mountains while he took the sheep and goats and camped by the river — the white-boned horse herder giving orders to the black-boned shepherd boy.[^36] Temujin dropped back to consult his mother and was unsure what to do. **Borte interrupted and told him to break with Jamuka**, and that night they slipped away and rode until morning.

What makes things happen after that is the pattern the whole steppe runs on and nobody can stop. The Jurched rulers south of the Gobi kept the tribes at war with one another so none could threaten them, allying with the Tatars one year and against them the next. Today's allies are tomorrow's enemies, and a tribe conquered today has to be conquered again in a ceaseless cycle.[^37] **No victory was ever decisive and no peace permanent** — and Weatherford makes that the lesson that eventually produces everything Temujin builds.

How you get elected is by who turns up. A *khuriltai* was a council where families, lineages and clans voted merely by showing up, and not appearing counted as a vote against.[^38] In 1189 Temujin summoned one at the Blue Lake by the Heart-Shaped Mountain and was made khan of a small following. No tally survives, which may mean the turnout was modest.

Then the second reform, and it is the one that separates him from every other steppe khan. A chief's court, his *ordu*, normally consisted of his relatives and functioned as an aristocracy over the tribe. Temujin assigned about a dozen jobs by ability and loyalty without regard to kinship — the highest going to his first two followers, Boorchu and Jelme.[^39] The first appointments were cooks, because his father had been poisoned. His brother guarded the camp and his half brother the reserve geldings.

What is worth having, and what it costs to take it wrongly, is shown by his rival's atrocity. In 1190 Jamuka routed him, then beheaded a captured leader and dragged the head from a horse's tail, and reportedly boiled seventy young male captives alive in cauldrons — a death that destroys the soul and annihilates a man completely.[^40] Seven is an unlucky number for Mongols, so the seventy may be embellishment. But it horrified people and damaged Jamuka, and it drew the line hard between aristocratic lineages based on inherited power and the lower-ranking ones based on ability.

*Read: lines 523–720.*

---

## Ch. 3 — War of the Khans

Nineteen men eat a wild horse out of its own skin. After the wedding invitation turned out to be a trap and Ong Khan's army chased him across the steppe, Temujin reached muddy Lake Baljuna with nineteen survivors and no provisions. A wild horse appeared from the north, his brother brought it down, and they made a bag out of the hide, put the meat and water in it, heated stones in a dung fire, and dropped the stones in.[^41]

What makes things happen, in their reading of that horse, is not luck. As the most important and honoured animal in the Mongol world, the horse solemnised the occasion and served as a sign of divine intervention. Its sacrifice fed the men and further empowered the Spirit Banner.[^42] They drank the muddy water of Baljuna, and he raised one hand to the sky and swore with them.

How people should relate, in the oath sworn there, is the whole book in one paragraph. The nineteen men came from nine different tribes, and probably only Temujin and his brother were Mongols; the rest included Merkid, Khitan and Kereyid. Temujin worshipped the Eternal Blue Sky and Burkhan Khaldun, and the nineteen included several Christians, three Muslims and several Buddhists.[^43] **They were united only by devotion to him and by the oath to him and each other**.

Aside from his brother, the men at Baljuna were his friends and not his relatives. His uncle — one of the two men who had helped kidnap his mother — had gone over to Ong Khan against his own nephew.

How you win a war before the fighting is the chapter's technical centre, and it is entirely psychological. The primary objective of a campaign was never to fight a battle at all, but to frighten the other side into fleeing. Spirit Banners of the opposing leaders and their ancestors were displayed and given animal sacrifices. A lineage on one side could hardly fight when kinsmen on the other had paraded the banner of their common ancestor. That would be attacking one's own grandfather.[^44] Shamans read the future in the cracks of burned sheep shoulder bones, climbed promontories to pound drums, and claimed to control the weather.

**Then propaganda becomes his weapon of choice, and the book says so directly**. After Ong Khan escaped and died at a border post, the Mongols circulated a story that the Naiman queen kept his head on a white felt cloth in the place of honour in her *ger*, with a fiddler playing while her daughters-in-law sang and danced for it.[^45] Nothing could be more offensive to Mongol sensibilities than a bloody head inside a home, and nothing more dangerous than the head, which is the seat of the soul. The story assured everyone the old khan was dead and shamed the court he had fled to.

They ran the same machinery on themselves. Jamuka was said to terrify the Naiman with descriptions of Mongols who *have chisels for noses and sharp awls for tongues* and *can live by eating the dew and riding the wind*. Their bodies, he said, were made of copper and iron fastened so tightly no awl could get through.[^46] The Naiman meanwhile sent a captured Mongol's skinny horse and primitive saddle from camp to camp in mockery. Temujin had each man light five campfires a night, so his small army seemed to have *more fires than the stars in the sky*.

What a person is, in his new army, is a unit rather than an individual. He tested the formations before committing. First the Moving Bush, in which dispersed squads of ten advanced silently from different directions before dawn. Then the Lake, a long line that fired and was replaced by the next line, like waves. Then the Chisel, narrow at the front and extremely deep, to channel maximum force at one point.[^47] **They were no longer an attacking swarm of individuals; they were a united formation** in which every man knew the manoeuvres and responded without hesitation.

How people should relate, at the end of a twenty-year enmity, is the emotional peak of the *Secret History*. Rather than take revenge, Temujin offered to unite with Jamuka again: *Let us be companions. Now, we are joined together once again, we should remind each other of things we have forgotten. Wake each other from our sleep*.[^48] Jamuka answered in the same register — *we ate the food that is not to be digested, and we spoke to each other the words that are not to be forgotten* — and then refused.

What Jamuka asks for instead is a death with a specification. He asked to be killed in the aristocratic way, without shedding his blood on the earth or exposing it to the sun and sky. And he offered to be a better friend dead than alive: *Kill me and lay down my dead bones in the high ground. Then eternally and forever, I will protect the seed of your seed, and become a blessing for them*.[^49] Legend says he was buried in the golden belt Temujin gave him when they swore the oath.

How a ruler becomes legitimate is not by winning. Victory on the battlefield conferred nothing until it was publicly acclaimed at a *khuriltai* with representatives from every part of the territory. A group that sent nobody rejected his rule, could not be claimed by him, and could not claim his protection.[^50] He waited a year, then summoned the largest such council in steppe history at the headwaters of the Onon in 1206.

The ceremony is a physical demonstration of consent. His followers put him on a black felt carpet spread on the ground, a designated speaker pronounced the people's pleasure, and he was told that whatever authority he had was derived from Heaven.[^51] Then they raised him on the carpet above their heads and carried him to the throne, and bowed their knees nine times. Shamans beat drums and sprinkled fermented mare's milk into the air, and the crowd prayed standing in ranks with palms turned up to the sky.

**What he then abolished is the thing that had been done to him**. He named the people *Yeke Mongol Ulus*, the Great Mongol Nation, and abolished inherited aristocratic titles in the lineages, clans and tribes. All offices belonged to the state rather than to an individual or a family.[^52]

What is worth having, in the new law, is an end to the specific grievances of his own life. **His first new law forbade the kidnapping of women** — his wife had been taken — and he forbade the abduction and enslavement of any Mongol, having been enslaved himself.[^53] He declared all children legitimate whether born to a wife or a concubine, because the question of whose son Jochi was had cost him so much. He forbade the selling of women into marriage. He made animal rustling a capital offence and built a lost-and-found system across the empire, remembering the eight geldings stolen from his family.

He also closed a season. Hunting was forbidden between March and October during breeding time, hunters had to limit the kill to what they needed, and the law specified the manner of butchering so nothing was wasted.[^54]

**And the law he wrote against himself is the sharpest one**. He made it a capital offence for any member of his family to claim the office of khan without election, and ruled that the death penalty could be applied to a member of his family only through a *khuriltai* of the whole family and never by an individual. That outlaws the exact act he used to begin his rise — killing his half brother.[^55]

What is real, in this law, is a group rather than a person. The solitary individual had no legal existence outside the family and the larger units above it, so a family carried responsibility for its members and a crime by one could bring punishment on all. A squad of ten bore the same liability. **To be a just Mongol, one had to live in a just community**.[^56]

Where it goes furthest is at the top. By subjecting the ruler to the law he achieved something no other civilisation had. In western Europe monarchs ruled by the will of God and stood above the law; here the Great Law applied as strictly to the ruler as to anybody. His descendants managed to keep that for about fifty years after his death.[^57]

How you know what the law is is a writing system taken as loot. No Mongol is known to have been literate. In defeating the Naiman in 1204 he found Tayang Khan's scribe, who wrote down pronouncements and sealed them, and took him into service.[^58] He made his adopted Tatar brother supreme judge, charged to *punish the thieves and put right the lies* and to record decisions on white paper bound in blue books, the sacred colour of the Eternal Sky. **The Mongolian word for book, *nom*, comes from the Greek *nomos*, meaning law** — in the thirteenth century the law and the written word were the same thing.

How you hold an empire together is by taking hostages and then not treating them as hostages. Every commander of a thousand and of ten thousand sent his own sons and his sons' best friends to form Genghis Khan's personal unit. Instead of threatening to kill them for a relative's misbehaviour, he trained them as administrators and kept them as a ready reserve to replace any disloyal official.[^59] The threat of being replaced by a man you sent yourself did more for loyalty than the threat of a dead son.

And messages move on a relay. Fast riders called arrow messengers ran a postal service that ranked alongside the army, with stations about twenty miles apart, each maintained by twenty-five families, and men allowed to serve in it instead of the military.[^60]

What a person is, when that person is his mother, is settled in one gesture at sunrise. When the shaman Teb Tengeri turned Genghis Khan against his brother Khasar, Hoelun hitched her white camel to her black cart, rode through the night, charged into his *ger*, untied Khasar and put his hat back on his head. Then she sat down cross-legged, ripped open her *deel*, and pulled out her breasts — so worn from feeding five children that even held up in her hands they rested on her knees.

> *Have you seen these? These are the breasts that you sucked*![^61]

She used the same words she had used over Begter, about an animal that gnaws its own umbilical cord and chews its own afterbirth. He restored Khasar's freedom and some of his followers.

*Read: lines 721–919.*

# Below the Line

*Everything above is sourced to the chapters named. Everything below is built rather than found, and is not measured by `assessgate.sh`*.

## Ch. 2 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and the source states it as the expected course**. After Borte was taken, abandoning her would surely have been what anyone expected — his small group could not possibly take on the Merkid. He could find another wife in time, though he would have to kidnap her, because no family would voluntarily give a daughter to a man who had already lost one to more powerful men.[^31]

That is the fork, and both roads are on the page. The one he did not take is the one his own father took, and it is what produced him: Yesugei could not afford the gifts or the bride-service, so he took a woman off a cart. **Choosing to fight for Borte is choosing not to become his father**, and the *Secret History* records that he made the choice on a mountain over three days rather than in a moment.

## Ch. 2 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Take the men nobody else values and the value is loyalty**. He appointed cooks, herders and guards by ability and loyalty rather than kinship, in a world where a chief's court was his relatives. *Applies when* the existing hierarchy is closed, so the talent it excludes is available cheaply and has nowhere else to go. *Fails* the moment your outsiders acquire alternatives — the arrangement is held together by the fact that a promoted shepherd cannot go anywhere better, and Jamuka's aristocrats defected the moment Temujin's reforms cost them their distribution rights.
*Decision type:* alliance formation.

**Postpone the payout to the end of the campaign and you convert looters into soldiers**. Warriors had always stopped to loot the camps they took, which let the defeated fighters escape and regroup. Ordering that no one loot until the campaign ended, with the goods distributed centrally afterwards, produced both complete victories and larger hauls.[^62] *Applies when* the participants trust that the distribution will actually happen — he backed it by stripping men who broke the rule of everything, including their share. *Fails* against people who can defect mid-campaign, which is why the reform had to arrive after the squads-of-ten reform and not before.
*Decision type:* timing a bold move.

## Ch. 3 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Turn the hostage into a promotion queue**. Every commander sent a son; the sons were trained as administrators and held as replacements for their own fathers. *Applies when* the thing your subordinates fear losing is their office rather than their child, and when the replacements are genuinely competent — the threat only works if the reserve is real. *Fails* where the sons build their own faction, which is exactly what Teb Tengeri and his six brothers did with a different power base in the same decade.
*Decision type:* power consolidation.

**A rule that binds you retroactively is the only kind anyone believes**. He outlawed killing a family member without a full family council, having begun his own rise by shooting his half brother in the back. *Applies when* your legitimacy problem is that everyone knows exactly how you got here, so the useful move is to name the act and close the door behind you. *Fails* on the next generation, which did not do the act and therefore does not feel the rule — his descendants kept it about fifty years.
*Decision type:* succession.

## Ch. 3 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A Kautilyan advisor on the *khuriltai***. The *Arthashastra* reads a bonded confederacy as the hardest thing to beat and prescribes finding the resentments and cultivating people quietly on each side. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/trautmann-arthashastra-worldview-archaeology-part-1|What a Mauryan Statecraft Manual Took For Granted, Introduction and Chapters 1–3]]. That manual also insists that election is a danger and that the concentration of power in one man is what a kingdom is for.

From that seat, Genghis Khan's law that the khan must always be elected by a *khuriltai*, on pain of death for claiming the office without one, looks like a deliberate acceptance of the republic's weakness in exchange for the republic's strength. A Kautilyan reader would predict exactly what happened: it holds while the man who made it is alive and collapses into succession war among his grandsons. **What that reader would miss is the thing the rule bought**. A tribe that voted by turning up cannot be split by an outsider naming a rival heir, because there is no heir to name — which is why the Jurched policy of playing steppe tribes against one another stopped working the moment the tribes stopped having separate aristocracies to buy.

**And a Nahua advisor on the same institution**. The Mexica ran power alternately between two royal houses on a three-generation schedule, precisely to keep the losing family from wrecking the winner. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/camilla-townsend-fifth-sun-worldview-archaeology-part-1|What the Nahuas Took For Granted, Chapters 1–4]]. Both systems refuse primogeniture, and both give the reason as competence in a fluid world.

Where they diverge is on what to do with the losers. The Mexica kept the rival line alive and scheduled, and it held for a century. Genghis Khan killed the aristocratic lineages, married their women to his sons, and abolished the titles — which removed the rivals and also removed the schedule. **The Nahua counsel would be that a rotation needs somebody to rotate to**, and that a nation with only one family left in it has solved this generation's problem by guaranteeing the next one's.
